That pruning even improved classic baselines in about 91.5 percent of cases. The paper maps which model and setting choices make the sampler work best.
arxiv-2512-16170:
Weihua Liu classifies symmetry theorems in probability in a 2025 mathematics paper on arXiv. De Finetti-type theorems say that when a sequence of random variables has enough symmetry, it must arise from a simple random mixture. Versions exist in both classical probability and free probability, a noncommutative cousin used in random matrix theory.

Liu shows every nontrivial finite sequence carries a maximal symmetry of a special kind, described by a Woronowicz C star-algebra, the structure behind compact quantum groups. That yields a probability-based way to classify those quantum groups. He then classifies all de Finetti-type theorems for star-random variables under such symmetries. Only finitely many types exist, and they match the so-called easy quantum groups of Banica and Speicher. The result ties probability, algebra, and quantum symmetry into one tidy list.
arxiv-2512-16570:
Dimitris Fotakis, Charalampos Platanos, and Thanos Tolias tackle online resource allocation, where buyers arrive one by one and ask for sets of items. Each buyer has a value drawn from a known chance model, and the seller must decide at once, with no knowledge of who comes next.

The focus is on fixed, nameless bundle prices when buyers value items as packages, so plain per-item prices fail. The authors give one pricing method that works across auctions and network routing, with scores that improve fast as item copies grow. Matching lower bounds show that no online method can do much better.
arxiv-2512-16670:
Ole Beisswenger, Jan-Niklas Dihlmann, and Hendrik Lensch present FrameDiffuser, a neural method that turns geometry and material data, called a G-buffer, into photo-like frames for games and interactive scenes. Past tools either made each frame alone, losing steadiness over time, or needed whole clips at once.

FrameDiffuser works step by step, guided by the G-buffer and its own last frame, so output stays steady over hundreds to thousands of frames. It pairs a ControlNet for structure with a ControlLoRA for time coherence, trained in three stages. The team tunes one model per scene, trading broad reach for speed and strong light, shadow, and reflection quality in that scene.
arxiv-2512-16770:
William English and coauthors present GinSign, a tool that turns plain English system rules into temporal logic, the formal language used to check that machines behave as required. Past tools often guessed the link between words and system atoms, or got it wrong.

GinSign learns that grounding step on its own. It first predicts the predicate label for each lifted phrase, then picks the typed constants that fit, turning free writing into a sorting task that small masked language models can run. Across domains, tools without grounding made logic that looked right but meant the wrong thing. GinSign reached 95.5 percent grounded match scores, 1.4 times the best past score.
arxiv-2512-17070:
Zahra Ahmadi and Mahdiyar Noorbala examine the noise that drives stochastic inflation, the frame treating early-universe field wiggles in classical chance terms. Textbook work, from Starobinsky on, assumes white noise, a memory-free driver, thanks to several background beliefs.

Loosening the exact de Sitter background keeps noise white, with a time-varying strength. Loosening the sharp window function or the Bunch-Davies start state can color the noise, giving it memory. For a piecewise linear window they compute the spectrum and memory in full. A colored case from the start state must be built from two-particle pieces, and that route also breaks Gaussianity, unlike the other two.
arxiv-2512-17170:
Dmitry Pasechnyuk-Vilensky and Martin Takáč build one algebra frame for a pattern that shows up across math: a primal problem and its dual mirror. Their tool comes from homological algebra, a field that measures how structures fail to fit together exactly. They call a map ethic when going to the dual twice returns it unchanged.

Breaks in that round trip are counted by groups called Ext groups, arranged in layers. The first layer matches the familiar gap between a problem and its dual in optimization. Higher layers list deeper blocks. The same frame then covers graph duality, coding, dynamical systems, and choice problems. One test for exactness, with a ranked list of what blocks it, is the payoff.
arxiv-2512-17470:
Dennis Gross, Jørn Eirik Betten, and Helge Spieker carry a curious effect from labeling tasks into step-by-step decision making. The Rashomon effect names a set of models that give the same answers for different inner reasons, each leaning on different clues. For a decision agent, the echo is stranger: many policies act exactly alike, step for step, yet reason from different features inside.

Proving two policies truly match is hard when the world itself rolls dice. The team uses formal verification to compare each policy's full pattern of likely behavior. Their experiments confirm the effect is real for sequential tasks. Mixing policies from the lookalike set survived shifts in the data better than any single one. Looser policies drawn from the set also cut the cost of safety checks.
arxiv-2512-17770:
Axel Brandenburg and three co-authors rethink how a star's or galaxy's magnetism leaks into the space around it. Textbooks cap a dynamo with a tidy current-free field, in which the dipole pattern fades slowest with distance. Real exteriors are turbulent and conduct poorly, so the field does not settle tidily; it diffuses outward instead.

Under diffusion, the ordering flips: a quadrupole pattern can grow a toroidal part that fades even more slowly than the dipole. The field still dies off fast beyond a magnetosphere boundary. That kills one hopeful idea, that galaxies collectively seeded the magnetism found in cosmic voids; those void fields must be primordial leftovers. Radio telescopes may test the picture, since quadrupole glow should ring evenly around its galaxy.
arxiv-2512-17870:
Alexander Keimer, Lukas Pflug, and Jakob Rodestock study control problems where flow at each point depends on the whole crowd, not just nearby points. Traffic and flocking often behave this way: speed here answers to density far ahead. They ask whether a best control exists for such systems, and what happens as the far view shrinks to a local one.

For a broad class of set ups, with freedom to tune the start state, the speed law, and the reach of the influence, they prove a best control does exist. As the reach fades to a point, those best controls settle onto the best controls of the matching local problem. Number tests close the paper.
arxiv-2512-18970:
Tuo Wu and six co-authors make the theory of vehicle-to-everything wireless honest about small hardware. Fluid antennas shift position to dodge fading, and smart surfaces bounce signals around obstacles. But existing performance analyses assume huge surfaces, via the Central Limit Theorem. Real deployments cannot afford that assumption, constrained by cost and city infrastructure. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and accepted by IEEE Transactions on Vehicular Technology, fixes the finite case.

Using a Gamma distribution approximation, they derive a closed-form expression for the outage probability, the chance a vehicle loses its link. Simulations confirm the new formula tracks reality far better than the old asymptotic one, especially for small surfaces. Network engineers designing roadside units on real budgets now have numbers they can trust before pouring concrete.
arxiv-2512-19270:
Zhaoyang Liu, Weitao Zhou, Junze Wen, and Cheng Jing prune self-driving training data by keeping the most informative trips. Fleets record far more routine driving than rare, useful moments. Storing and training on all of it costs much and teaches little.

Their method scores data by the entropy of its trajectory spread, then keeps samples that best preserve the full set's statistics, with no model in the loop. Theory ties high entropy to a small gap between the kept set and the original distribution. On the NuPlan benchmark, the dataset shrank by up to forty percent while closed-loop driving scores held steady.
arxiv-2512-19570:
Angjelin Hila examines what happens to shared knowledge when people lean on language models. His theory of collective epistemology treats warrant as spread across a community, not locked in one head. Two kinds of justification matter: understanding why a claim holds, and reliably passing true claims along.

Reflective knowledge needs the first kind, plus honest checks on sources when the basis is out of reach. Models, Hila argues, deliver the second kind only: dependable transmission without reflective grasp. If reflective work is widely outsourced to fluent outputs, the community's standards for knowing can quietly erode. The paper rethinks collective intelligence under that pressure.
arxiv-2512-19770:
Michał Marczenko, writing in the proceedings of the 2025 International Nuclear Physics Conference, revisits a speed limit inside dense matter. Relativistic kinetic theory implies a constraint on the speed of sound squared, a quantity that encodes how stiff the equation of state of dense matter is at each density. Such stiffness governs the behavior of matter in settings like neutron star interiors.

Marczenko shows the kinetic-theory constraint can be rewritten in terms of the average sound speed, an integrated quantity accumulated over density. That reformulation exposes the interplay between momentary stiffness and its running average, and lets the bound be drawn as an excluded region in the plane of the two quantities. The note offers a compact visualization tool for testing proposed equations of state.
arxiv-2512-19870:
Hao-En Li and Lin Lin design quantum methods for the harder half of chemistry. That half is excited states. Ground states get most of the focus in the field. Yet light uptake, photochemistry, and spectra all run through excited states. Making them on quantum devices is still a thin field. Their trick is to redesign dissipation itself. They reshape the Lindblad dynamics so the wanted state is the one the system settles into.

In effect, the task becomes a ground-state task for a designed channel. Three plans cover unlike kinds of prior knowledge. One uses symmetry labels. One uses a rough energy for the target state. Tests on atoms and molecules show the plans at work. They span flat conjugated molecules and transition-metal complexes. The authors offer the route for work on strongly correlated systems.
arxiv-2512-19970:
Surya Jayakumar and four co-authors forecast the sustainability of Irish dairy farming. Their tool is a graph neural network that knows geography. The framework is the first county-scale use of such networks for this task. It builds composite sustainability indices from herd-level records. The records come from the Irish Cattle Breeding Federation. A variational autoencoder first fattens the sparse data. It keeps the joint patterns of the records intact.

A factor method then distills four pillars. They are reproductive efficiency, genetic management, herd health, and herd management. Weighted sums turn the pillars into the indices. The network then models spread across counties and change over years. It projects the indices for 2026 to 2030. The tool is also framed for what-if policy checks.
arxiv-2512-20070:
Jungwoo Kim, Jun-Hyuk Kim, and Jong-Seok Lee compress images for machine eyes in a way that lets receivers stop early. Progressive compression with fine granular scalability sends one bitstream decodable at many quality levels, ideal when a downstream vision model needs only enough detail to decide. That capability existed for human-oriented codecs but not for machine-oriented ones, until PICM-Net.

Built on trit-plane coding, the codec adapts a human-oriented design through a spatial-frequency modulation adapter, a low-rank hyper-synthesis adapter, and training that anticipates progressive decoding. An adaptive controller then judges at inference time whether the current quality suffices for the desired confidence, requesting more bits only when it does not. Experiments show efficient, adaptive transmission while downstream classification performance stays strong.
arxiv-2512-20170:
Vili Heinonen and Jani Lukkarinen examine a two-dimensional quantum gas whose particles do not interact with each other. The gas sits in a weak random potential whose irregularities stretch over long distances. They ask what happens over long times to the spread of particle momenta, which starts out sharply peaked in one direction.

Scattering off the random potential gradually makes the momentum distribution round and broad. The authors derive a formula for its long-time average and check that formula against computer simulations. They also discuss how the momenta lose their preferred direction and how the particles spread through space. The results clarify how disorder alone reshapes motion in a clean quantum system.
arxiv-2512-20370:
Wei Zhang and a large team build the first white matter atlas spanning newborns and adults in one space. Atlases for each group exist separately, which blocks direct comparison of brain wiring across development. Their neonatal and adult brain atlas, NABA, is built from diffusion MRI tractography of both populations.

A data-driven fibre clustering pipeline constructs the atlas despite large anatomical differences between baby and adult brains. With NABA, the team maps tracts jointly, tracks development across neonatal ages, compares the sexes, and studies preterm birth. Long-range association tracts gain fractional anisotropy quickly, while cerebellar tracts lag. Girls develop faster overall; preterm babies develop slower overall yet faster in a few specific pathways.
arxiv-2512-20870:
Junyang Huang and seven co-authors examine a quantum dot that could link quantum computers over telecom fiber. Quantum networks need stationary qubits that trade entanglement with flying photons at telecom wavelengths. Semiconductor dots emitting there are promising, but the trapped spin's behavior must be measured precisely first.

Using only the timing and polarization of emitted photons, the team benchmarked both the electron and the hole inside their dot. The hole came out ahead as the better qubit for spin-photon entanglement. Full tomography of the hole's state then exposed small directional quirks in its precession. Knowing those quirks helps engineers cut phase errors when generating multi-photon entanglement.
arxiv-2512-21170:
Yogesh Kumar, Vrushank Ahire, and M. A. Ganaie teach an old classifier family a new trick for reading brain waves. Electroencephalogram signals are non-stationary, noisy, and scarce, a hostile mix for seizure detection. Their classifiers extend a proximal support-vector design built on generalized eigenvalue problems, and add Universum learning: extra data from neither class, used to shape the decision boundary. One variant folds the Universum in through a ratio objective; the improved variant uses a weighted difference, so class separation and Universum alignment tune on their own.

On the Bonn University recordings, separating healthy from seizure traces, the improved model peaks at eighty-five percent accuracy for eyes-closed recordings. For eyes-open it reaches eighty percent. Averaged, it stays ahead of the baselines at about eighty-one and seventy-eight percent. Lightweight eigenvalue methods remain competitive for clinical screening where deep models are impractical.
arxiv-2512-21270:
Andre Sonnet and Epifanio Virga ask what a thin shell loses when its deformations are handcuffed. In the direct approach to shell theory, the shell is a mathematical surface. Its stored energy splits into three independent contents tied to three deformation modes: stretching, drilling (twisting about the surface normal), and bending. Their study is deliberately coordinate-free, following the surface's intrinsic geometry as it moves.

They impose metric restrictions on which deformations are admissible, the sort of limits real physical constraints might enforce, and trace the consequences for each of the three energy contents separately. The lesson is cautionary: restricting one aspect of a shell's motion can hamper its elastic response in ways intuition does not predict, because the three modes interact through the metric. Continuum mechanicians and shell-model builders gain a clean map of which constraints are innocent and which secretly amputate a shell's repertoire.
arxiv-2512-21370:
Future space observatories will hear gravitational waves that massive objects have lensed, bending and splitting the signal on its way. Tianlong Wang, Tianyu Zhao, and four colleagues want a faster way to spot those events than matched filtering, whose cost is heavy. Their answer is a dual-channel extended LSTM network built to read lensing features across the whole millihertz band.

A matrix-valued memory and a memory-mixing mechanism let the network track amplitude patterns spanning the crossover from wave optics to geometric optics. Trained on point-mass and isothermal-sphere lens models, it scores above 0.99 in area under the curve, catching over ninety-eight percent of events at under one percent false alarms. Performance holds across noise levels, lens types, and masses.
arxiv-2512-21470:
B. Guo, F. Yan, and a large team of co-authors report on HAT-P-70b, an ultra-hot Jupiter exoplanet. Using the CARMENES and PEPSI spectrographs, they recorded the planet's dayside heat glow from its permanently lit face. Such spectra reveal which chemicals fill the atmosphere and how temperature changes with height.

Cross-correlation detects emission from aluminum, aluminum hydride, calcium, chromium, iron, magnesium, manganese, and titanium. Aluminum and its hydride appear in such an atmosphere for the first time. The temperature profile shows a strong thermal inversion, with the upper atmosphere hotter than the layers below. Retrieved amounts broadly match the Sun's makeup, with hints of extra nickel and loss of some easily condensed elements. Very high amounts of ionized iron and calcium defy equilibrium chemistry, suggesting the atmosphere is escaping into space.
arxiv-2512-21670:
Subramanyam Sahoo and Jared Junkin open up the black box of a deepfake detector. Models flag synthetic media with high accuracy, but nobody could say which internal features drive their verdicts. The authors apply interpretability tools to a vision-language model trained to spot deepfakes.

They combine sparse autoencoder analysis of the model's internal features with a forensic manifold analysis. The second probes how feature geometry responds when forensic artifacts are manipulated in a controlled way. They find that only a small fraction of latent units is active in each layer. The feature manifold's dimensionality, curvature, and selectivity vary with the type of deepfake artifact. Mapping units to artifacts is a first step toward detectors that are not just accurate but explainable, and toward spotting weaknesses before attackers exploit them.
arxiv-2512-21870:
Garima Rani, Anupam Sengupta, Hartmut Löwen, and their co-authors study how bacteria colonize soft surfaces and organize into young biofilms. Biofilms grow on everything from medical implants to natural tissues, yet how the softness of the surface shapes the earliest stages was poorly understood.

Combining experiments with agent-based simulations, the team varied the substrate stiffness over a hundredfold range. On soft surfaces, colonies expanded slowly, grew in an elongated, anisotropic pattern, and piled into multilayers early. On hard surfaces, bacteria spread quickly and evenly as a single layer before stacking. A cell-level mechanical model explains the difference through drag: soft surfaces deform under the cells, creating direction-dependent drag that resists spreading and pushes growth upward. On hard surfaces the drag is lower, delaying the move to multilayers. The authors suggest surface compliance could be engineered to steer biofilm formation.
arxiv-2512-22070:
Fully charm tetraquarks, exotic states of two charm quarks and two antiquarks, can be produced and probed electromagnetically, but leading-order predictions miss gluon radiation. Xinran Liu, Yefan Wang, and Ruilin Zhu compute the next-to-leading-order QCD corrections to their decay amplitudes into two photons.

The corrections prove significant for the scalar and tensor states' two-photon decays, shifting predictions. The authors then fold the corrected amplitudes into photon-photon fusion in ultra-peripheral proton and nuclear collisions and in electron-positron collisions, predicting production cross sections for the states. The results give current and future experiments concrete electromagnetic benchmarks for identifying these exotic hadrons.
arxiv-2512-22170:
Jiesong Lian and eight co-authors tackle reward models, the scorers that teach video generation systems to match human taste. Current scorers learn from pairwise labels collected inside a single prompt, which introduces noise. Their designs are also under-explored, and generators can learn to game them, a failure called reward hacking. The team's system, SoliReward, attacks all three problems at once.

SoliReward collects cheaper, cleaner data through single-item yes-or-no annotations, then builds preference pairs across different prompts. A hierarchical progressive query attention mechanism strengthens feature gathering inside the model. A modified loss handles wins and ties explicitly and spreads scores more evenly among good samples. Benchmarks covering physical plausibility, subject deformity, and semantic alignment show gains in scorer quality and in downstream video training.
arxiv-2512-22470:
Sadia Asif and four co-authors introduce DarkPatterns-LLM, a benchmark for detecting when language models manipulate their users. Current safety tests mostly use coarse yes-or-no labels and miss the psychological and social methods that make manipulation work. Their dataset sorts harmful behavior into seven categories, from legal and economic harm to psychological, emotional, physical, autonomy, and societal harm.

A four-layer pipeline analyzes outputs at multiple granularities, examines intent at several scales, harmonizes threats, and aligns risk with deep context. The dataset holds 401 curated instruction-response examples with expert annotations. Evaluating GPT-4, Claude 3.5, and LLaMA-3-70B showed wide performance spread and a consistent blind spot: patterns that undermine user autonomy were hardest for every model to catch.
arxiv-2512-22570:
Md. Abdur Rahman and six co-authors present ReFRM3D, a neural network for characterizing gliomas, among the most aggressive brain cancers, in 3D scans. Segmentation models struggle with the wide variability of tumor imaging, and radiomic texture analysis is usually bolted on after segmentation, too late to guide it. ReFRM3D, built on a 3D U-Net, weaves the two together with multi-scale feature fusion, hybrid upsampling, and extended residual skip connections.

Its radiomic conditioning mechanism extracts texture and intensity descriptors from an intermediate coarse segmentation and feeds them back into the decoder to refine the result. On the BraTS 2019, 2020, and 2021 benchmarks, mean overlap scores exceeded ninety-two percent. The model also generalized to the BraTS-Africa dataset despite different scanners and patient populations.
arxiv-2512-22770:
Naoki Kitamura, Yuichi Sudo, and Koichi Wada map out exactly how much computing power two tiny autonomous robots have. The robots work in Look-Compute-Move cycles and differ by whether they carry memory, can communicate, and move in lockstep or independently. For larger robot teams this landscape of models was mostly known, but the two-robot case had resisted a complete answer.

The full chart turns out to differ from the general case in surprising ways. Under full synchrony, a model with only private memory matches one with lights for communication plus memory, because perfect timing can substitute for both when only two robots exist. Memory-only and communication-only models are also shown incomparable in both directions. All separations and equivalences come from a new simulation-free method, giving the first exact picture of coordination at the smallest possible scale.
arxiv-2512-23070:
Boyang Zhang and co-authors design FLEX-MoE, a way to run mixture-of-experts models across federated edge devices. Mixture-of-experts networks scale by activating only some specialist subnetworks per input. But edge clients in a federation cannot store the full expert set. Their skewed local data leave some experts overloaded and others idle. Both problems degrade the shared model.

FLEX-MoE scores how well each expert fits each client's data, using training feedback. It then runs an optimization that assigns experts to maximize specialization while enforcing balanced use across the system. That balance constraint is the difference from greedy personalization schemes, which ignore system-wide load. Experiments across resource-constrained scenarios show better accuracy together with consistently balanced expert utilization. The authors aim the framework at next-generation wireless and Internet of Things deployments, where models must live on small devices with uneven data.
arxiv-2512-23670:
Francesco Piatti, Thomas Cass, and William Turner build time-series models from randomly wired continuous-time reservoirs. Their base tool is the controlled differential equation, which lets a hidden state evolve in response to an incoming signal path. Instead of training the whole system, they randomize a large reservoir's parameters and train only a linear readout layer on top, making learning fast and scalable.

Two variants follow. Random Fourier CDEs first lift the input with random Fourier features; Random Rough DEs work directly on rough paths through a log-ODE scheme using log-signatures. In the infinite-width limit the two recover, respectively, an RBF-lifted signature kernel and the rough signature kernel, tying random features to path-signature theory. Across time-series benchmarks both models matched or beat the state of the art.
arxiv-2512-23870:
Yuyang Zhang, Yang Hu, Bo Dai, and Na Li upgrade the soft actor-critic, a leading algorithm in maximum-entropy reinforcement learning, where policies are rewarded for staying random as well as for performing. In practice the ideal energy-based policy is squeezed into a simple parametric family for efficiency, sacrificing expressiveness and robustness. The authors instead let a flow-based model represent the policy, with its much richer shapes.

Evaluating such a policy uses the instantaneous change-of-variables technique, and updating it uses an online flow matching variant developed for this work, importance sampling flow matching. This learns from samples of a distribution the user chooses rather than the unknown target. Their theory characterizes how the sampling distribution's choice affects learning efficiency. A case study on maximum-entropy linear quadratic regulator problems shows the algorithm learning the optimal action distribution.
arxiv-2512-24270:
Sandro Claudio Lera and Andreas Haupt explain why socio-economic networks collapse suddenly. Cities, firms, and collaborative projects can look resilient for years. Then participation erodes and decline cascades. Their framework is a network game of strategic abandonment. Each agent picks an activity level. Agents stay only while participation beats an improving outside option.

As outside options rise, agents exit on their own. Exits force the remaining network to readjust. Strategic complementarities govern what happens next. Weak complementarities give slow, local decay like bootstrap percolation. Vulnerable clusters can be spotted in advance there. Strong complementarities give rupture instead. Metastable plateaus end in abrupt system-wide collapse. Standard indicators predict little in that regime. Interventions differ too. Supporting central agents works best under strong complementarities. Helping marginal agents matters most when they are weak.
arxiv-2512-25070:
Nikhil Chandak, Shashwat Goel, Ameya Prabhu, and colleagues train language models to forecast open-ended questions about the future. High-stakes decisions need reasoning under uncertainty, but training data for forecasting is scarce. They synthesize questions from global events in daily news with a fully automated, careful curation recipe, building the OpenForesight dataset.

An offline news corpus prevents leakage of future information during training and evaluation, and retrieval uses the same corpus. Qwen thinking models trained on the data are guided by a small validation set. AI readers get a scalable route to forecasting skill, with leakage control as a central design discipline.
arxiv-2601-00170:
Jintao Huang works with Lu Leng, Yi Zhang, and Ziyuan Yang on telling people apart by their heartbeat. ECG signals serve as identity proof in wearables. Each person has a distinct pattern, and the signal proves a live body. Older methods treat each beat as one uniform blob. That view wastes the structure inside a cardiac cycle.

Their framework reads each heart phase on its own first. Related phases then merge in a staged, grouped way. A final step blends those groups with adaptive weights. The design keeps phase cues from tangling with each other. Enrollment also changes under their scheme. Many beats form a gallery of several prototype templates. That spread cuts the harm from one noisy beat. Tests on three public datasets lead the field. Gains hold in both closed and open set trials.
arxiv-2601-00470:
Andrea Dupree, Paul Cristofari, Morgan MacLeod, and Kateryna Kravchenko report evidence for the wake left by a companion star moving through Betelgeuse, the famous red supergiant. Recent work suggests a small companion, named Siwarha, orbits in about two thousand days at only a few stellar radii, deep inside the giant's outer atmosphere. Speckle imaging has likely caught the companion itself.

Dupree and colleagues examined optical and ultraviolet spectra and found changing absorption and outflows that follow the same roughly two thousand day cycle. Absorption in manganese lines and outflow signatures in iron, silicon, and magnesium lines grow after the companion crosses the star's face, then fade before the next crossing. The pattern fits a trailing, expanding wake stirred up by the companion.
arxiv-2601-00670:
Argha Kamal Samanta, Deepak Mewada, Monalisa Sarma, and Debasis Samanta bring clinical language into brain-wave modeling for intensive care. Continuous EEG monitoring watches for seizures and other harmful patterns in critically ill patients, and deep learning detects seizures well. Most systems, though, are trained on discrete labels and judged by accuracy alone, which poorly matches how clinicians actually read and summarize EEG.

Harmful patterns overlap, experts often only partly agree, and findings persist over time. The authors' Wave2Word framework aligns EEG signals with text, learning representations tied to clinical descriptions rather than labels alone, and handles several tasks together. The aim is models whose internal picture of brain activity corresponds to the language of neurocritical care reports.
arxiv-2601-00770:
Simon Paquette-Greenbaum and Jiangbo Yu apply language model agents to a core banking task: building investment portfolios that balance return against risk under a limit on how many assets may be held. That cardinality-constrained problem is a mixed-integer quadratic program, and exact solvers cannot crack realistic instances, so practitioners develop many heuristic algorithms and pool their solutions to trace better efficient frontiers.

Building and tuning those heuristics takes extensive labor. The authors explore agentic frameworks, in which language model agents carry out parts of the workflow, as a way to generate and combine heuristic solutions with less human effort. Their study treats portfolio optimization as a test case for agents across combinatorial optimization, where pooled approximate solutions often beat any single method.
arxiv-2601-00870:
Samet Ünsal is the sole author of a 2026 paper on a new security question for quantum systems. Standard checks ask whether a user is who they claim to be. Ünsal asks a different question: is this run a true heir of one past run? He names that the Quantum State Continuity Problem. A fork attack splits a run into two heirs, and old checks cannot catch it.

To close the gap, he proposes a witness tool built from quantum states. The tool links each run to its past by a chain of quantum steps, with audits that pile up. In simulations, fork attacks fail at a rate that drops off sharply as the chain grows. The tool also held up under noise and changed settings. The paper marks run continuity as a security goal in its own right. It gives system builders a fresh threat to design against.
arxiv-2601-00970:
Boris N Oreshkin and twelve co-authors present, in 2026, a forecaster trained on data that no real sensor ever recorded. Zero-shot forecasting means calling new series with no training on them. Real past data are scarce, skewed, and tangled in privacy and licence limits. The team built a fast simulator based on a classic seasonal model. Naive runs of that model often blow up into useless paths.

Their fix has three steps. First, they sample only from the model's stable zone. Next, they stack paths to build rich, multi-season patterns. Last, they add heavy-tailed noise, for bursts and gaps. Models trained on about a billion such series followed. On two big test sets, they beat strong statistical tools and fresh foundation models. In one twist, the students beat their own teacher model. The work suggests fake data, made with care, can ground real forecasts.
arxiv-2601-01070:
Mikołaj Sienicki and Krzysztof Sienicki write in the numbered, step-by-step style of an old philosophical tract to sketch a testable theory of consciousness. They push against two habits: treating awareness as a strange extra substance, and treating it as nothing but outward behavior. Their sketch keeps three things apart on purpose.

The three are what shows up for a person, what that person can report or act on, and the patterns that stay fixed when descriptions change. A conscious moment, they argue, lasts a short span in which many inner signals are bound into one view that can guide action. The self is not a hidden thing but a role that links moments over time. They also stress a limit: any test touches the system and changes it, so some cases must honestly stay undecided.
arxiv-2601-01470:
Four authors led by Konstantinos Delimaris analyze open waveguides whose cores twist electromagnetic waves, a property called gyrotropy found in ferrites and some plasmas. The cores are not circular, and the cladding stretches to infinity, so the usual textbook methods falter. The team develops two independent full-wave methods to find how signals propagate along such guides.

One method extends an integral equation technique; the other expands the fields in a Chebyshev series. Both describe the core fields with a recently developed set of cylindrical wave functions built for gyrotropic materials. Neither method leans on approximations in the general case. Results from both agree with a commercial finite-element solver, and the authors benchmark their speed and accuracy. A microwave example computes propagation along ferrite rods under an applied magnetic bias. The tools extend waveguide theory to structures that modern devices increasingly use.
arxiv-2601-01670:
Some differential equations include delays that depend on the current state of the system, and sudden jumps called impulses. Ferenc Hartung studies a class of such nonlinear equations where the delayed time can adapt and must stay monotone, or at least rise steadily piece by piece.

Hartung proves that the starting-value problem has exactly one solution, using approximations built from equations whose arguments stay constant on short steps. Those step-based approximations are then shown to approach the true solution evenly over any fixed time span. The result gives both a firm theoretical footing and a practical route for computing solutions to this family of delayed, impulsive systems.
arxiv-2601-01770: Kenan Zhang recalls Calderón-Zygmund theory on the unit ball. He uses it to derive a weak-type estimate for the projection onto the H-harmonic Bergman space. The estimate is the weak (1,1) bound. Notes of this kind record the endpoint boundedness of a projection operator. Harmonic analysis relies on such bounds when stronger estimates fail.
arxiv-2601-02070:
Rydberg atom receivers sense radio fields with quantum sharpness but only over a narrow bandwidth. Mickael Branco and seven co-authors optimize a modulation transfer protocol. Their group demonstrated it recently. Phase modulation of the coupling laser widens the bandwidth. The atoms convert that modulation into an amplitude signal on the probe beam.

A theoretical model tunes the modulation frequency and depth to maximize the atomic response. Once optimized, the protocol beat the conventional one. It won whenever the radio signal was detuned by more than a few megahertz. In experiment it bridged two Rydberg transitions. They sit one hundred sixty-six megahertz apart. Simulations and measurements agreed throughout, giving quantum receivers a practical bandwidth upgrade.
arxiv-2601-02470:
Mustafa Gündoğan, Roy Barzel, and Dennis Rätzel design a quantum clock experiment that could feel the slowing of time caused by gravity. Clocks at different heights run at slightly different rates, an effect called gravitational time dilation. Their setup stores a photonic clock, a light based timer, in two quantum memories placed one above the other, so the joint state evolves as a superposition of two different proper times.

After storage, the light is retrieved and sent into a Hong Ou Mandel interferometer, and the authors derive formulas for the detection patterns that result. Using frequency entangled states with many photons instead of pairs amplifies the time dependent phase by the photon group factor, so the interference signal collapses and revives faster. They also map where finite memory efficiency and lifetime still leave the effect observable.
arxiv-2601-02870:
Yuqi Huang, Vincent Y. F. Tan, and Sharu Theresa Jose propose a quantum version of a classic decision problem, the contextual bandit, where an agent picks actions and learns from rewards. Neural network methods for this problem struggle to scale, and quantum neural networks add troubles of their own, such as unstable training and flat error landscapes. The authors sidestep training altogether by freezing the quantum network at its random start.

Their method, QNTK-UCB, uses the frozen network's tangent kernel to guide choices with an upper confidence bound rule. Theory shows it needs far fewer parameters than the classical neural method for the same error guarantees. Tests on synthetic tasks and a quantum chemistry problem show strong learning from little data, pointing to a practical route for quantum decision algorithms.
arxiv-2601-02970:
Junseok Kim and three co-authors make a popular reasoning trick for language models cheaper. Self-consistency samples many answers to the same question and votes, which improves reliability but costs a lot of computation. Adaptive versions stop sampling early, yet their count-based stopping rules treat every response as equal evidence, so they still sample more than needed.

Their method, ReASC, reframes the question as evidence sufficiency: it weighs each response by its confidence, not just its frequency. A first stage settles questions that one confident sample can answer, and a second stage gathers weighted evidence for the rest. Across five models and four datasets, ReASC gave the best accuracy for the cost, cutting inference spending by up to seventy percent on one math benchmark.
arxiv-2601-03270:
Lokendra Kumar, Neelesh S. Upadhye, and Kannan Piedy survey semantic textual similarity, the task of scoring how close two texts are in meaning. The field has grown fast since 2021. Transformer models, contrastive learning, and domain-specific methods all drove the growth. The survey sorts progress into six areas. They range from transformer-based models and contrastive learning to multi-modal, graph-based, and knowledge-enhanced methods.

Recent transformer models and contrastive methods have set new accuracy marks. Domain-adapted systems show how scoring can be tailored to fields such as medicine and finance. Multi-modal and knowledge-integrated models push semantic understanding further. By analyzing these strands together, the survey maps current methods and practical uses. It also names the challenges that still face researchers and practitioners.
arxiv-2601-03570:
Barry Menglong Yao and six co-authors track how language models learn and forget individual concepts during continual pretraining, the long training that keeps feeding new text. People organize the world through concepts, but a model's grip on each concept can rise and fall as training proceeds. The team links those shifts to concept circuits, small internal subnetworks tied to specific concepts.

Their analysis found that circuit signals track learning and forgetting in a consistent way. Circuits grew early, then shrank and stabilized as training continued. Concepts with the biggest learning gains tended to be forgotten more later, and similar concepts interfered with or boosted each other. Graph measures of circuit shape helped describe these patterns. Understanding concept turnover could lead to training schedules that protect hard-won knowledge.
arxiv-2601-03670:
Zhitong Chen and nine co-authors introduce DisastQA, a benchmark for question answering during disasters, where facts are uncertain and sources conflict. General benchmarks built on clean evidence cannot capture that mess. DisastQA contains three thousand carefully verified questions, split between multiple-choice and open-ended forms, spanning eight disaster types, and built through a pipeline pairing humans with language models.

Models are tested from closed-book answering up to noisy evidence integration, separating stored knowledge from reasoning under imperfect information. For open answers, a human-verified keypoint protocol scores factual completeness over wordiness. Testing twenty models showed rankings diverging sharply from general leaderboards, and performance fell hard under realistic noise. Emergency agencies eyeing AI help now have a harder, more honest test to demand.
arxiv-2601-04270:
Anherutowa Calvo, writing alone, formalises a pattern seen in deep learning training: gradients can often be predicted from their own past and move inside a low-dimensional space. Worst-case bounds miss that structure. Calvo introduces two measurable quantities to capture it directly from training runs.

One quantity is a prediction-based path length, scoring how well past gradients forecast the next ones. The other is a predictable rank, the effective temporal dimension of gradient changes. Classical online and nonconvex guarantees are then restated so convergence and regret depend on these quantities instead of worst-case variation. Across convolutional networks, vision transformers, language models, and synthetic tasks, gradient paths stay locally predictable with strong low-rank structure. Light random projections suffice to diagnose both traits from logged gradients.
arxiv-2601-04570:
Jidu Yu and Jidong Zhao solve a boundary problem that follows from how their simulation method sees the world, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Material Point Method tracks matter with moving particles over a fixed grid. is splendid for large deformation but miserable for imposing heat-flux boundary conditions, because the true boundary rarely sits on grid lines and refuses to stay still.

Their Virtual Heat Flux Method sidesteps the geometry entirely. A virtual flux field is constructed on an auxiliary domain around the boundary so it satisfies the prescribed condition exactly. Turning the awkward surface integral of the weak form into an easy volume integral. No boundary tracking, no special particles, no surface reconstruction. A unified formulation covers scalar, vector, and tensor flux conditions. Benchmarks from one-dimensional transients to rotating three-dimensional shapes show accuracy matching conforming node-based methods and clearly beating conventional particle-based ones.
arxiv-2601-04670:
Akiyoshi Tomihari examines why reinforcement learning makes language models more certain and less varied, in a 2026 arXiv paper. RL post-training is where modern models gain alignment and reasoning polish, but its side effect — outputs collapsing toward a few safe patterns — is poorly understood. He studies the training dynamics through the empirical neural tangent kernel, a tool borrowed from supervised learning theory. Splitting it into two components to trace how an update on one example propagates to others.

The analysis shows that when feature representations vary little across samples, RL updates systematically push confidence up everywhere at once, which mechanically explains the diversity loss. Effective learning then hinges on shaping the classifier head of the network quickly. His remedy, classifier-first RL, prioritizes those updates before plain RL begins; experiments confirm faster optimization and the predicted confidence pattern, through a mechanism distinct from the analogous guided trick.
arxiv-2601-04770:
Encheng Su and eleven co-authors argue that a science model can reach the right answer the wrong way and still fail, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Benchmarks today check formatting tricks or final answers, both blind to whether a model honoured the conditions that make a solution valid as science. Their benchmark, SciIF, tests scientific instruction following directly: university-level problems across disciplines, each paired with set constraints from a fixed catalogue.

The constraints span three pillars — science conditions like boundary checks and stated assumptions, semantic stability in units and symbols, and required answer processes such as a specified numerical method. Unusually, SciIF demands auditable evidence that each constraint was satisfied, not silent compliance. Scoring correctness and adherence separately exposes compositional failures invisible to plain benchmarks, a diagnostic the authors offer toward language models that can be trusted inside science's strict systems.
arxiv-2601-05270:
Tarun Prajapati's 2026 paper designs a knowledge base that updates in real time without losing its history. Retrieval-augmented systems face a tension: vector indexes are optimized for fast queries but handle continuous updates poorly, while data lakes version data well but add query latency. LiveVectorLake, the proposed architecture, aims for real-time semantic search over current knowledge plus complete version history for compliance, auditing, and point-in-time retrieval.

The design uses a dual-tier structure with content-addressable chunk-level synchronization among its core contributions. Systems that remember every version can answer what was known at a past moment, not only what is known now. That capability matters for regulated industries where an AI answer may later need legal reconstruction.
arxiv-2601-05370:
Rose Lopez's 2026 mathematics paper studies gerbes on moduli spaces of curves and the Brauer group of a classifying space. A gerbe is a higher geometric object layered over a space, and the specific one here collects curves of a given genus carrying an automorphism of fixed order. Lopez asks which cohomology classes the components of that stack can realize, focusing on curves whose quotient by the automorphism is a genus-zero curve.

For those components she completely determines the Brauer classes. The key technical input is computing the Brauer group of the classifying space for a smooth, connected, semisimple algebraic group. Brauer groups classify certain twisted geometric structures, so the calculation resolves which twists can actually occur on these moduli spaces.
arxiv-2601-05470:
Tingwei Xie and 2 co-authors present ROAP, a 2026 pipeline that helps layout transformers read documents in the right order. These models extract key information from forms and receipts, but they often ignore logical reading order. Visual tokens can also dilute attention away from the text that matters.

ROAP first builds reading sequences from complex layouts with an adaptive gap-based tree method. Those sequences enter attention as a position bias, so order guides the model directly. A second prior boosts text-to-text attention and suppresses visual noise. Tests on the FUNSD and CORD benchmarks improved both LayoutLMv3 and GeoLayoutLM backbones, without retraining them, supporting the design as a general add-on.
arxiv-2601-05570:
Cooper Lin and 8 co-authors introduce Crisis-Bench, a 2026 benchmark that tests whether language models can manage corporate crises with strategic discretion. Standard safety training rewards universal honesty, which can clash with professional duties like negotiation or PR work, where withholding information is a normal, accepted part of the job. The authors call that cost a transparency tax.

Inside the benchmark, a public relations agent handles a model run with eighty storylines across eight industries over seven modeled days. Private and public narratives stay strictly separate. A market loop converts adjudicated public sentiment into a modeled stock price, creating real incentives. Some models capitulated to ethical pressure, while others withheld information strategically and stabilized prices, exposing a gap in current alignment.
arxiv-2601-05670:
Luigi Caputi and 2 co-authors study, in a 2026 mathematics paper, the homotopy type of multipath complexes built from bidirectional path and polygon graphs. A multipath complex encodes collections of vertex-disjoint directed paths. The work was motivated by chessboard complexes, a related family with known topological behavior.

The authors show bidirectional path graphs yield objects homotopic to spheres, meaning they can be deformed continuously into spheres. Polygon versions turn out to be highly connected. A Mayer-Vietoris spectral sequence computes their homology groups. They also study operations on graphs that correspond to suspensions of these objects, discuss shellability, and close with new open questions for this corner of combinatorics. In plain terms, the team asks what shape these sets of paths make when they are glued together.
arxiv-2601-05770:
Yifan Zhang and 5 co-authors ask in 2026 whether a transformer's weights can be turned back into a readable program. Method extraction aims to recover executable mechanisms from a trained model without using human-written target code. For transformers, overlapping internal aspects, known as superposition, tangle representations and block that recovery.

Their Discrete Transformer builds discreteness in through temperature-annealed sampling, pushing internal states toward symbolic form. Hypothesis testing and symbolic regression then extract human-readable programs from the trained weights. Performance matched a recurrent baseline on shared discrete tasks, while extending extraction to tasks with continuous intermediate steps. Architectural biases also gave fine-grained control over the synthesized programs, making the system a testbed for interpretability research. In short, the design trades some freedom in the model for a clear view of what it has learned.
arxiv-2601-05970:
Dan-Na Liu and 2 co-authors analyze in 2026 how electrons tunnel through electrostatic barriers in bilayer graphene, where two carbon sheets stack in the AB pattern. A full four-band description reveals multiple channels, some propagating and some fading, that couple at each interface. Channel selectivity turns out to govern transmission, especially for head-on incidence.

Perfect transmission can occur at discrete energies when a single internal mode phase-matches inside one barrier, forming an effective cavity without true bound states or extra channels. The authors derive compact transmission formulas and resonance conditions for single and double barriers. In multibarrier structures, these phase-matching resonances coexist with familiar Fabry-Perot resonances from interbarrier interference, giving a unified channel-resolved picture.
arxiv-2601-06270:
Space dust that spins gives off microwaves, yet the glow does not match the old models well. Zheng Zhang and 3 co-authors ask what sets the shape of that glow in a 2026 study. They mix model work with real sky data. The glow peaks at one pitch, and the width of the peak holds clues to the dust.

Three things rule the peak: how big the grains are, what shape they take, and a trait of the gas phase near them. Wide mixes of grains blur the peak. Dense star clouds matched the data in full. Dark clouds were close, with small gaps. Zones of hot gas were off by a lot in peak pitch. That gap fits a known lack of tiny grains in such zones. To match the spread seen in the sky, mixes must vary in both grain size and the phase trait.
arxiv-2601-06370:
Thomas Hogancamp and 2 co-authors split a key math tool into unitary parts in a 2026 paper. The tool is the Laplace operator, the core of the Poisson task in heat, flow, and charge work. Quantum machines can run sums of unitary parts with ease, so such a split is the way in.

Their splits cover five kinds of edge rules: wrap-around, fixed, flux-free, mixed flux, and blends of these. They work on a line and on box grids in more ways. The count of parts does not grow with grid size. It grows in a straight line with the count of ways. Each part comes with its own circuit, and the depth and gate cost grow at most with the log of the grid size. Costs in a quantum solver look kind. The trick extends to tasks with first-order terms whose weights change by place.
arxiv-2601-06470:
The old frame for how systems settle rests on rules named for three men: Dobrushin, Lanford, and Ruelle. F. H. Haydarov and 2 co-authors stretch that frame past its straight-line roots in a 2026 math paper. Their new parts grow from a clan of bent maps that act on spreads of chance.

A q-rest state is a spread that those maps leave just as it was. The team sets terms for when such a state must be there, and when it must be the sole one. A trait called near-scope plays the key role in the build. They also show q-rules with no rest state at all. For a line of spins at low heat, more than one q-rest state can stand, though the old rest state stays sole. The work opens a fresh path in this field.
arxiv-2601-06770:
Sofiia Huraka and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers structure-preserving learning and prediction in optimal control of collective motion. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Wide-spread adoption of unmanned vehicle technologies requires the ability to predict the motion of the combined vehicle operation from observations.

While the general prediction of such motion for an arbitrary control mechanism is difficult. For a particular choice of control, the dynamics reduces to the Lie-Poisson equations [ 33 , 34 ]. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-06970:
José de Brito and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers splitting proximal point algorithms for the sum of Prox-Convex functions. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. -34.14322pt Abstract The work addresses the minimization of a finite sum of prox-convex functions under Lipschitz continuity of each component. The authors propose two variants of the splitting proximal point algorithms proposed in [ 2.

5 ] : one deterministic with a fixed update order. And one stochastic with random sampling, and we extend them from convex to prox-convex functions. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07570:
Mitali Mondal reports predictions from the EPOS4 model for lead-lead collisions at a new energy. The 2026 preprint concerns the quark-gluon plasma, a hot state where nuclear matter comes apart into its basic parts. Heavy-ion experiments at the Large Hadron Collider study this plasma. Run 3 of the collider reached a center-of-mass energy of 5.36 TeV per nucleon pair.

Models like EPOS4 predict what detectors should see before data are analyzed. Global observables summarize each collision as a whole rather than tracking single particles. Comparing predictions with measurements tests how well the model captures plasma behavior. Mondal's paper supplies those reference predictions for the new energy. Heavy-ion physicists use such benchmarks to spot where models and reality part ways.
arxiv-2601-07670:
Javier Rubio proposes a new way to create dark matter just after the universe's inflationary burst. His 2026 preprint describes gravitational production driven by curvature-induced tachyonic instabilities. Tachyonic growth means small ripples grow explosively rather than oscillate. The framework uses a real spectator scalar field, one that watches inflation without driving it. That field couples quadratically to invariants of spacetime curvature.

Most earlier work used non-minimal couplings between fields and gravity. Rubio departs from that route deliberately. A purely gravitational production channel is attractive because it needs few new assumptions. If it works, dark matter could arise from gravity and curvature alone. The paper speaks to cosmologists building dark matter origin stories. It adds a fresh mechanism to compare with freeze-out and other standard ideas.
arxiv-2601-08070:
Shailesh Rana studies a simple sounding test that large language models keep failing. His 2026 arXiv paper looks at negative constraints, such as telling a model not to use a given word. Models break such rules with striking regularity, and the reasons have stayed poorly understood.

Rana presents a broad mechanistic study of why negative instructions fail. The title names the effect a semantic gravity well, where the banned word pulls the model toward itself. For readers who build or test language models, the paper gives a clearer picture of a basic instruction-following flaw. It treats the failure as a mechanism to explain, not just an error rate to report.
arxiv-2601-08770:
Sean Siddens and a team from four sites study a hidden leak in chips that run many tasks at once. Chips may swap the order of read and write steps to gain speed. That swap can be seen by a foe who times the chip with care. Past tests made this leak show up by stressing the chip hard.

The team shows the leak can work with no timer and less stress than once thought. The order swaps leave a trace that a smart test can pick up. That trace can cross from one task to a next task on the same chip. A reader who guards chip work gets a clear risk note. Calm use, not just hard stress, can let order leaks show.
arxiv-2601-09070:
Ayumu Shoshi and six co-authors report rings and gaps in a disk round a young star named CrA IRS 2. The star is of Class I, still young and wrapped in fall in stuff. The ALMA scope saw the disk at fine scale. Such rings in old disks hint at new planets. In a young disk, they may show a more early start to world birth.

The team ties the rings to a flux driven bubble in the disk. Field flux can blow a bubble that sweeps gas to a ring. That path needs no planet to start the ring. A reader in star birth gets an early disk with form. It hints that disk shape work starts young, by more than one road.
arxiv-2601-09170:
Dung Ta Nguyen Duc and five co-authors build a lean tool to spot rice leaf ills on a phone. Rice feeds half the world, so leaf ills can cut food for a vast set of folk. Early spots save a crop. But farm zones oft have weak phones and no net. A tool must be small, fast, and true on a plain phone shot.

Their tool is N-EIoU-YOLOv9. Its core is a new box fit loss that weighs hard cases with care. The loss splits shape facts so a box can fit a long or round spot well. A reader in farm tech gets a phone fit spot tool, built for fields, not labs.
arxiv-2601-09670:
Nasser M. Ahmed reports a new star cluster found beside a known one. His 2026 arXiv paper uses Gaia DR3 data to study the region around the Czernik 38 cluster. An earlier study by the same author examined Czernik 38 in detail.

The new cluster sits 32 arcminutes from Czernik 38's center. Its position is given with tight error bars in both sky coordinates. A companion cluster so close may share an origin with its neighbor. The paper also discusses a complex tide linked to the pair, hinting at how the two clusters pull on each other.
arxiv-2601-09770:
Chen Chen and six co-authors give interface agents eyes that choose where to look. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents GUI-Eyes, a reinforcement learning framework for active visual perception in graphical interfaces. Vision-language models have advanced GUI automation, but most still take one static screenshot.

A passive agent cannot zoom, re-check, or look at the right moment. GUI-Eyes learns when, whether, and how to observe the screen. Active looking should ground clicks and typing in what is actually shown. That promises fewer blind errors in agents that book, buy, and fill forms.
arxiv-2601-10370:
Jian-Wen Peng, Jun-Jie Luo, and Abubakar Adamu solve balance tasks in a Hilbert space. Such tasks ask for a point where no move can gain. They span games, flows, and best fit tasks. The cost rule here is quasi monotone, a weak form of a known rule.

The team give a two step method with a drift term. Step sizes set them in two ways. One is self tuned. One is of Armijo type, checked by a line search. They prove the path still lands on a solve point. They do so with no bound on how fast the cost can shift.
arxiv-2601-10670:
Archita Gupta, Tejbir Lohan, and Pooja Singla study characters of two matrix groups over local rings. The groups are GL2 and GU2, built from two-by-two matrices. The base ring comes from a non-archimedean local field, cut down modulo powers of its maximal ideal. The residue field has odd characteristic, a standing assumption in the work.

The authors sort out which characters are real-valued and which conjugacy classes are real. Such questions sound narrow, but they shape how representations of the groups behave. Real characters link to symmetry inside the group's own structure. The results serve representation theorists who work with groups over local rings, a key case in number theory.
arxiv-2601-10770:
Runyuan Cai, Yu Lin, Yiming Wang, Chunlin Fu, and Xiaodong Zeng present GPA, a single speech model for many tasks. Speech systems have long used separate models for text-to-speech, speech recognition, and voice conversion. Split pipelines limit scale, efficiency, and transfer between tasks. GPA instead uses autoregressive transformers for all three jobs at once.

The name plays on the school grade average: the goal is solid results across all audio subjects. One shared model can pool what each task teaches the others. Recognition may sharpen synthesis, and conversion may sharpen both. The work speaks to teams that want one speech engine for products instead of three narrow ones.
arxiv-2601-10870:
Guo-Niu Han and Lihong Yang add a doubly refined count of alternating sign matrices. These matrices, filled with zeros, ones, and minus ones under strict rules, have a famous counting story. The alternating sign matrix conjecture of Mills, Robbins, and Rumsey, from 1982, was proved by Zeilberger and by Kuperberg. Since then, refined counts that track extra parameters have been a steady pursuit.

Behrend and co-authors reached a quadruply refined enumeration by adding parameters. Han and Yang give yet another doubly refined version. Each refinement tests how deep the pattern runs. These counts tie into statistical physics and combinatorics, where the same numbers count ice-type models and plane partitions.
arxiv-2601-10970:
Canwen Wang and co-authors model couples therapy with a multi-agent simulation. Couples therapy helps partners resolve conflict and grow closer. Training new therapists leans on textbooks and roleplay. Those tools often miss the complexity and emotional nuance of real couple dynamics. A simulator could let trainees practice against lifelike partners and a therapist agent.

The system is multimodal and multi-agent, modeling multi-party interaction in the therapy room. Each party is played by an agent with its own stance. Trainees can face hard moments safely and repeat them. The work speaks to clinical training and to the wider study of how AI can model delicate human interaction without putting real couples at risk.
arxiv-2601-11170:
Web crawling for South Slavic tongues is the topic of this 2026 preprint. The authors are not named in the record held here. Their team built the CLASSLA-web text sets by crawling whole country domains. That method works well for tongues with few digital texts.

An early round of crawling gave the largest sets yet for this group. Those sets were called CLASSLA-web 1.0 in the first release. The new work looks at a fresh round of crawling, named 2.0. It weighs what repeat crawls add in new text. It also weighs the costs and flaws that come with each new round.
arxiv-2601-12270:
Reshabh K Sharma, Dan Grossman, and David Kohlbrenner build a compiler defence against a new class of side channels. Classic side channels leak secrets via unsafe instructions, memory access, or branch choices. Constant-time code rules block those patterns and are in wide use.

Data memory-dependent prefetchers open a fresh leak path that those rules miss. Their tool, named in the work, splits secrets at compile time to block that path. A compiler fix can guard much code at once. The work is in systems security.  The defence is built in at compile time for all runs.
arxiv-2601-12670:
Yuxuan Du and five co authors hunt for exotic dibaryon states in nuclear physics. A dibaryon is a system of two baryons bound or resonant together. The famous deuteron is the simplest case, made of a proton and a neutron. The team look for deuteron like states with one bottom quark and set values of strangeness.

They work inside the chiral quark model, a standard frame for such searches. They study strangeness values of minus one, minus three, and minus five. Their scattering calculations yield two resonance states at strangeness minus one. Predicted states give experiments a target to confirm or rule out. The work adds to the map of exotic hadronic matter.
arxiv-2601-12870:
Lazlo Bleker and five co authors present Text2Structure3D, a model that generates structures from text prompts. The model is graph based and aims at equilibrium structures, designs that balance their loads. It supports intuitive design exploration in the conceptual phase of structural design. Engineers could sketch ideas in words and see candidate forms at once.

The approach combines latent diffusion with a variational graph auto encoder and graph transformers. It generates structural graphs close to an equilibrium state. Close matters, since a pretty form that cannot stand is useless. Their work was published in an engineering results journal. Generative tools like this may reshape early stage design work.
arxiv-2601-13170:
David Lipshutz and Robert J. Lipshutz prove calm for a self sorting neural net. Real brain nets reshape their own links by local rules. One rule grows links that fire in sync, a Hebbian step. Its twin shrinks such links, an anti Hebbian step. How local steps yield sound whole net acts is still open.

An past model used both steps to do principal subspace work, a way to find the main axes of data spread. But no one had shown that the bent link flows stay calm from all starts. The pair now prove that whole calm. For brain and learning staff, the proof firms up a model of how nets can sort data on their own.
arxiv-2601-13270:
Matteo Acclavio and Roberto Maieli join two tools that rarely meet, Bayes nets and logic code. A Bayes net maps how chance facts lean on each other. It is a stock tool for chance sense. To fold it in a logic code frame is hard, since the net's web is rich.

Their tongue is called probLO. It grows the LO tongue of Andreoli and Pareschi, built on linear objects. In it a Bayes net can be both stated and run as code. That join lets chance sums be run by proof steps. For AI and logic staff, the work opens a path where chance nets gain the clear rules of logic code.
arxiv-2601-13470:
Gabriel Avanzi Ubiali, Jose Carlos Marinello Filho, and Taufik Abrao share the load of a huge antenna array for 6G nets. Extra large MIMO uses vast antenna grids to give fast links with even grade. Its resource work is huge if it leans on fresh channel reads for each pick.

The team picks three things at once. They pick which subarrays to use, which users to serve, and which pilots to assign. They give closed form marks for signal to noise plus clash in both central and spread uplink forms. Closed forms let picks be made with no fresh full reads. For 6G teams, that cut is what makes huge grids real.
arxiv-2601-13570:
Tingting Dan, Jiaqi Ding, and Guorong Wu model brain acts with a geometric state space net on curved manifolds. State space models track how hid neural states shift over time and yield the signals we read. Deep nets add flex to that frame. Pairs of the two have fit brain scan data well.

Brain state spaces are not flat, though. Their true shape bends, as on a Riemannian manifold. The team's net, GeoDynamics, holds states on such a curved space by build. That build may fit brain paths that a flat model warps. For brain teams, a model whose space matches the data's shape can read acts with less twist.
arxiv-2601-13870:
Yanbing Zhang, Ruifeng Yuan, Liyan Luo, and Lei Wu speed up simulations of rarefied gas flows in 2026. Rarefied gas is thin gas where wall effects rule the flow. Heat-flux boundary conditions are hard to apply in a fast way. The wall-reflected gas temperature and density must be found as the computation runs.

Their work sits in the general synthetic iterative scheme, or GSIS. That scheme solves the Boltzmann kinetic equation in an outer loop. Macroscopic synthetic equations run in an inner loop. An efficient heat-flux treatment could cut cost for aerospace and vacuum work.
arxiv-2601-14270:
Liangming Pan and a team at Peking University survey a young field in this 2026 paper. Large language models can solve problems that take many reasoning steps. Yet the inner workings behind that skill stay unclear. Past surveys mostly cover engineering tricks that raise scores. This one takes a distinct path.

The survey maps the mechanisms inside multi-step reasoning. It asks what parts of the model do the work, and how. The title calls this opening the black box. For readers, the paper offers one full view of what is known so far. It sorts a fast-growing set of studies into a clear frame.
arxiv-2601-14370:
Alessandro Trinca and six co-authors study the first giant black holes in this 2026 paper. Supermassive black holes appear very early in the universe. Their rapid emergence challenges current models of black hole growth. One proposed path is the direct collapse black hole scenario. In it, gas in pristine, low-metallicity halos forms supermassive stars first.

Those stars then collapse into massive black hole seeds, under specific environmental conditions. The team hunts such objects around high-redshift quasars. Their focus is both formation and detectability: how these seeds arise, and whether telescopes could spot them. Readers get a guide to one leading answer to the early giants problem.
arxiv-2601-14470:
Mohamad Salim, Jasmine Latendresse, SayedHassan Khatoonabadi, and Emad Shihab count token use in AI coding teams in this 2026 paper. LLM-based multi-agent systems now automate complex software engineering tasks. The work spans requirements engineering, code generation, and testing. Yet their operational efficiency and resource use stay poorly understood.

That gap hinders practical adoption, since costs and environmental impact are unpredictable. Tokenomics, the authors' term, quantifies where tokens are used in agentic software engineering. Tokens are the text units models read and write, and each one costs money and compute. Readers get a breakdown of where the spend goes when agent teams build software.
arxiv-2601-14570:
Xiaojie Yang and six co-authors forecast crowds at a world expo in this 2026 paper. Accurate forecasting of daily attendance is vital for managing transportation, crowd flows, and services at large-scale international events. Their case is Expo 2025 Osaka, Kansai, Japan. Existing approaches often rely on multi-source external data, such as weather, traffic, and social media, to improve accuracy.

That reliance often leads to unreliable results, because the available historical data are insufficient. The team's study is an empirical attendance predictive study, as its title says. Its subtitle is Place with Intention. The team kept the plan lean. It works with the kind of data a host can get in real life. Readers get a forecast method tested on a real mega-event, built to work when rich side data cannot be trusted.
arxiv-2601-14770:
Tobias Raichle, Erfan Amini, and Bin Yang adapt speech enhancement at test time in this 2026 paper. Adapting speech enhancement models to unseen environments is crucial for practical deployments. Speech enhancement removes noise from recordings. Test-time adaptation for it remains largely under-explored, though. A lack of understanding of how these models degrade under domain shifts is one cause.

The team observes that mask-based enhancement models lose confidence under domain shifts. Their predicted masks become flattened, losing decisive speech preservation and noise suppression. Their method works via mask polarization, pushing masks back toward firm decisions. Readers get an adaptation scheme that fixes a named failure mode, not just a score.
arxiv-2601-15270:
Hirotaka Onuki studies smooth surfaces over a ring that mixes two worlds of arithmetic. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with regular del Pezzo surfaces in mixed characteristic. The base ring is the Witt vectors over a closed field of prime characteristic above two.

The surface sits inside a flat, projective three-fold over that ring. Its anticanonical sheaf, a key bundle for this class of surfaces, is ample. Onuki proves a global regularity result for these surfaces. The plus sign in the title marks the strong form of that global regularity claim.
arxiv-2601-15370:
Maciej Kilian, Oleg Mkrtchyan, and co-authors stack two kinds of sparsity to make expert models cheaper. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with mixture-of-experts layers. Weight sparsity is their usual trick: each token wakes only a few experts.

Data sparsity is the mirror trick: each expert handles only a few tokens. Expert-choice routing does this, but it breaks causality in autoregressive models. Training and inference then mismatch. The authors compose both sparsities in one design. The aim is much better compute efficiency without the causal flaw sneaking back in at inference time.
arxiv-2601-15670:
Fan Gao and Runze Wang study representations of covering groups in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their objects are genuine Iwahori-spherical representations of central covers. Each carries positive real Satake parameters. For these, they prove an upper bound for geometric wavefront sets. The bound was formulated for general genuine representations in earlier work by Gao and co-authors. Wavefront sets measure the size and shape of a representation in geometric terms.

The pair also show the bound is sharp in key cases. Equality holds for covers of type A groups. It also holds for some representations of covers of exceptional groups. An upper bound plus cases of equality gives a firm picture. Representation theorists use such results to classify and compare representations.
arxiv-2601-15770:
Jue Xu and four co-authors mimic quantum motion on normal computers in a 2026 arXiv paper. Clean quantum dynamics are hard to mimic. Tensor-network methods slow down as entanglement grows and fills the system. Pauli-truncation methods cope, but they lean on noise or chance. Neither fits clean, quiet dynamics well. The team proposes the Low-weight Pauli Dynamics algorithm, or LPD. It tracks local observables for short-time dynamics with no noise.

Local observables are what most tests in the lab measure. A fast classical method for them helps check quantum hardware. It also lets theorists test ideas with no quantum device at hand. The title stresses that the method uses no randomness. Fixed, repeatable methods are easier to check and reproduce. In benchmarking disputes, that is a real virtue.
arxiv-2601-16470:
Yonatan Ashenafi lifts state space to a high size to track wild chance paths. His 2026 preprint deals with Bayes grain tracks of chance moves. Wild curves in the move maths make tracks hard to keep true. Grains spread, clump or miss the true path in such cases. Ashenafi maps the wild model to a high size straight model.

The map can be turned back, so no facts are lost. Straight Gauss form in high size is far more easy to track. Tracks then hold true through wild bends in the path. Firm tracks serve drive, flight and fund path tools. The work gives a fresh frame for hard tracks.
arxiv-2601-16570:
Leonardo Zambrano and three coauthors certify quantum traits with flawed reads. Their 2026 preprint deals with checks that a state is as claimed. Such checks back all claims made for quantum gear. Reads in real labs are never free of flaws. Past proofs oft take reads as if they were exact.

The team gives a proof path that takes read flaws in count. It works for bent sums of state traits, a wide class. Flaw aware proofs keep claims true on real lab data. They stop teams from claims that rest on false exact reads. The work firms up quantum gear checks.
arxiv-2601-16670:
André Brandão, Diogo Matos, Miguel Guimarães, Simão Cunha, and João Saraiva look at the energy cost of code. Their 2026 preprint centers on Lua, a small and loved script tongue. World plans urge cuts in the carbon cost of tech. The tongue a program uses shapes its power draw. Tongues that run line by line tend to use more power.

Fast tongues like C sip power by contrast. Lua trades speed for ease and small size. The authors weigh that trade with care. They ask what the green cost of Lua truly is. Their work can guide teams that want light code. It also feeds the wider push for clean tech.
arxiv-2601-17270:
Max McKinnon, Samir Khaki, Chandan KA Reddy, and William Huang test voice activity detectors. These tools tell speech from silence in audio. They feed speech recognition and many voice apps. The team asks a plain design question. How much does window size change detector accuracy? Window size is the span of sound judged at once.

They test three known detectors: Silero, WebRTC, and a root mean square method. Tests run on varied real-world audio streams. They also try hysteresis, a trick that stops fast on-off flicker.
