Clear answers help builders pick settings with proof, not habit. Small choices here shape how well voice tools hear real speech.
arxiv-2601-17470:
Chia-Ming Lee and five co-authors present PhaSR, a method to remove shadows from images. Shadow removal must split light effects from true surface color. That split fails when physical priors are off line. PhaSR aligns priors at two levels. It aims for robust work from one light source to many. Ambient light from mixed sources is the hard end.

Aligned priors keep colors true once shadows lift. Bad removal can bleach or tint a scene. Good removal aids photo tools, robots, and self-driving sight. The dual-level design targets the root cause, not just the look. It gives vision systems cleaner inputs under real light.
arxiv-2601-17570:
Hadi Salloum and three co-authors speed up Monte Carlo reinforcement learning. That method learns from sampled episodes of play. It suffers high sample complexity. Sparse rewards, large state spaces, and correlated paths make it worse. The authors reformulate episode selection as a QUBO problem. QUBO is quadratic unconstrained binary optimization, a compact math form.

Quantum-inspired samplers then solve that selection problem. Picking the right episodes should cut wasted learning. Each episode costs time and compute to run. Smarter picks mean faster training for the same budget. The work joins quantum-style optimization with classic learning. It treats data choice as an optimization task in itself.
arxiv-2601-18070:
Jinwu Chen and co-authors tune a chip design that computes inside its own memory. Their 2026 preprint deals with SRAM computing-in-memory accelerators. These chips promise high energy efficiency and throughput for AI work. The catch is balance. Many design variants and mapping choices make it easy to mismatch the compute side and the storage side. A bad match can drag performance down a great deal.

The team's tool, CIM-Tuner, explores hardware and mapping together. Joint search finds pairings that one-sided tuning misses. The goal is a chip whose memory and logic pull in the same direction. As AI models grow, such in-memory designs are a leading hope for cheaper inference.
arxiv-2601-18470:
Silvio Candido and many colleagues design a part to soak up a fierce beam of light at a planned CERN ring. The ring will smash bits of matter with their anti-twins to probe deep laws. At each smash point, stray light flies out with great heat. That light must be caught and its heat shed in a safe way, or it would harm the ring.

Their plan runs lead in a flow, like a stream of thick soup. Lead can take the heat load the team must shed, which runs to a huge rate per unit. The stream takes the heat on and then gives it up as it loops. The paper sets out the form of the dump and the checks on its flow. A sound dump is a must for the ring to run at full strength.
arxiv-2601-18870:
Hans Dang and six colleagues show by a lab test a core rule of quantum theory that had not been shown head on till now. The rule sets how two traits of a light field trade: to read one trait shifts the next by a set sum. That rule sits at the root of the famed cap on how sharp both traits can be known at once. Past tests checked the cap, not the rule at its root.

The team read the rule from two kinds of joint count on the light field. Each count is a chart of how oft two reads land as a pair. The two charts, set side by side, give the rule's sum with no room for doubt. A head-on show of such a root rule is a rare gain. It firms the base on which much of light-based quantum work stands.
arxiv-2601-18970:
Alex Berian and four co-authors improve photo making from just a few input views. Novel view synthesis builds a new photo of a scene from a fresh angle. With only a few shots to start from, older methods treat each input view as if it counts the same toward the target view.

That flat treatment leads to weaker results, since some views plainly help more than others. The team adds attention that weighs where the model looked, giving key views more say. Sharper few shot views help uses like product shots, scene previews, and robot sight where extra photos cost time.
arxiv-2601-19170:
Wangyang Ying and seven co-authors turn plain text procedures into workflow graphs with the help of model teams. A procedural graph lays out steps and their order, which software can check and run. Language models can draft such graphs, but they often build broken structures or misread the logic of the steps.

The team uses several agents that refine the graph for both structure and logic. One pass fixes form, another checks that the flow makes sense. Sound workflow graphs are the bridge from written procedures to automation that firms can trust.
arxiv-2601-19270:
Banghui Hua and Jiang Zhu derive a missing piece of a theory that predicts gravitational wave signals. The theory models how quark matter confines, using a loop quantity called the Polyakov loop. Its kinetic term, how the loop changes in space and time, was often set by hand in a simplified way.

For the first time, the pair derive that term from first principles in hot pure Yang-Mills theory, with a field dependent scaling factor. They extend the math to theories with more colors as well. A derived, not guessed, term makes wave forecasts from such phase changes far more trustworthy.
arxiv-2601-19370:
Kaushlendra Pandey, Harpreet S. Dhillon, and Abhishek K. Gupta study car platoons as communication networks on highways. Platooning means vehicles travel close together in a coordinated line along a shared route. It promises lower fuel use, lower emissions, and smoother traffic flow.

Highways suit platoons, with their long shared stretches, yet the communication side is underexplored. The team analyzes connectivity for platooned users: who can reach whom, and how reliably. A platoon is only as safe as its links. So coverage math like this underpins the whole idea. It backs the fuel savings claims and the safety case regulators will demand.
arxiv-2601-19570:
Krzysztof M. Gogol, Manvir Schneider, Jan Gorzny, and Claudio J. Tessone study an attack on crypto trading. A sandwich attack traps a victim's trade between two trades by the attacker. The attacker buys first to push the price up, lets the victim buy high, then sells for profit. The team asks whether this trick works on Ethereum rollups, the scaling networks that keep their order books private.

Private mempools hide pending trades, which should block the attacker's view. The authors build a formal model of the best front-run and back-run sizes. Profit in the model depends on trade volume, pool depth, and slippage bounds. They add a second model for whether both attack trades can land in the same block. The study shows where privacy protects users and where it does not.
arxiv-2601-19770:
J.-P. Rivet and a large team of astronomers report quick observations of a near-Earth asteroid named 2025 FA22. The asteroid passed close to Earth in September 2025, at about twice the Moon's distance. Its size is estimated at a few hundred metres across. It ranks among the largest near-Earth objects seen at such close range.

The flyby triggered a rapid-response campaign by the International Asteroid Warning Network. The team gathered spectropolarimetric and broadband polarimetric data during the approach. Polarised light reveals facts about an asteroid's surface, such as grain size and composition. Practising on a real visitor tests the warning system end to end. The data also add to the record of a potentially hazardous class of objects.
arxiv-2601-19970:
Nourin Shahin and Izzat Alsmadi benchmark the security of Llama language models. As these models move from research into enterprise systems, their weaknesses threaten data privacy and system integrity. The authors evaluate several Llama variants against the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, a standard catalogue of language model risks.

They measure threat detection accuracy, response safety, and computational overhead together. A model that is safe but unusably slow fails deployment just as an unsafe one does. The comparison shows how variants trade these properties off. Enterprises choosing a model get evidence rather than vendor claims. The work supports safer rollout of open-weight models.
arxiv-2601-20270:
Holly Trikilis, Pasindu Marasinghe, Fariza Rashid, and Suranga Seneviratne use least-to-most reasoning to detect phishing URLs with large language models. Phishing is still one of the most common attack routes, so sorting real links from fake ones matters. Language models have shown promise at this task, but how they reason about a link is little studied.

The authors' framework breaks the judgment into smaller steps, from least to most complex. Stepwise prompting may make the model's decision process clearer and more accurate. Stronger link detection protects users who must judge an address quickly, often on a phone.
arxiv-2601-20370:
Paolo Baldan, Roberto Bruni, Francesco Ranzato, and Diletta Rigo introduce APPL, a program logic for abstract properties. Program logics are rule systems for proving facts about code. APPL is a unifying Hoare-style logic that subsumes standard Hoare logic, incorrectness logic, and several forms of hyper Hoare logic.

The logic is parameterized by an abstract domain, which sets how properties are approximated. One framework then covers many existing logics and new ones built from fresh abstractions. A common base could simplify the design of verifiers that must prove both correctness and security properties of programs.
arxiv-2601-20770:
Pamela Harris and four co-authors study a special family of number lists in this 2026 math paper. A parking function is a list of choices that lets every car find a spot. A prime parking function keeps that property even after any one entry of one is removed. The authors view these objects from several angles at once.

One lens comes from Lukasiewicz paths, step-by-step walks with set rules. Another comes from quasisymmetric functions, a tool from algebra. By moving between views, the team can count and compare these lists in new ways. The paper is combinatorics: the study of counting and structure. It adds links between three topics that are often taught apart.
arxiv-2601-20870:
Matteo Gianferrari and six co-authors teach spiking networks to learn new classes without forgetting old ones. Their 2026 paper presents STAER, a rehearsal method for spiking neural networks. Spiking networks pass signals as brief pulses, like real neurons. Their event-driven timing suits continuous learning well. Class-incremental learning, though, has been blocked by two problems. One is catastrophic forgetting; the other is misaligned spike timing.

Rehearsal stores old examples and replays them during new training. STAER aligns that rehearsal in time, matching the temporal code of spikes. That alignment is the heart of the method's name. Better alignment should let old memories survive new lessons. The work targets brain-like hardware that learns on the job. Such chips could adapt in the field without a data center.
arxiv-2601-21070:
Daniel Rodriguez-Cardenas and seven co-authors argue that testing code models needs better infrastructure. Their 2026 paper looks at benchmarks for large language models in software engineering. Code models advance fast, yet evaluation lags behind. Current benchmarks focus on narrow tasks and single metrics. That hides gaps in robustness, interpretability, fairness, and efficiency. It also hides questions of real-world usability.

The authors cite deeper problems too. Data engineering practices are inconsistent across benchmarks. Software engineering context is often limited. Contamination issues are widespread, with test data leaking into training. Their paper works toward comprehensive benchmarking infrastructure. Better yardsticks would let the field trust its own progress claims. The work appears at a 2026 conference on AI foundation models and software engineering.
arxiv-2601-21170:
Augusto Santos and three co-authors hunt for early warnings hidden in causal structure. Their 2026 paper proposes a machine learning method to detect emergent events early. The cases span seizure onset, sudden customer churn, and pandemic outbreaks. Such events arise from hidden causal links in complex systems. The core challenge is to unveil a system's latent causal structure. The process that makes the data is unknown and partly observed.

The title names the theme: the powers of precision. A structure-informed detector uses the learned causal web to spot trouble early. Precision matters, since false alarms train users to ignore warnings. The method aims to detect onsets across unlike domains with one idea. That breadth is the paper's bet. It serves hospitals, firms, and health teams that fear the same shape of surprise.
arxiv-2601-21470:
Ruicheng Ao, Hongyu Chen, Haoyang Liu, David Simchi-Levi, and Will Wei Sun merge two variance-cutting tricks for learning with scarce labels. Labeled data may be rare while a trained model can label the rest cheaply. Prediction-powered inference uses those cheap labels with a control signal to cut noise.

A classic optimization trick, SVRG, cuts noise with reference gradients. The authors show the two tricks are the same idea in different dress. Their combined method uses both signals at once. The result is steadier training for semi-supervised problems, where each true label is precious.
arxiv-2601-21670:
Zixuan Xia, Hao Wang, and five co-authors add geometric regularizers to multimodal learning. Joining data types like image, text, and sound should give richer models. Strong optimization alone, though, does not guarantee well-shaped representations.

Even with careful balancing, multimodal models often suffer two flaws. Features inside one modality can collapse together, and paired samples can drift apart across modalities. The authors add dispersive and anchoring terms to fight both flaws directly. Healthier geometry should make each single-modality skill sturdier and the fusion between them more faithful. It should also help when one input stream is noisy or missing at test time. The paper treats the shape of these learned spaces as a problem in its own right, not a side effect of training.
arxiv-2601-21970:
Dmitriy Zhigunov and Jacob Page study turbulence through its hidden skeleton. Exact unstable solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations are thought to underpin how turbulence behaves. These exact coherent structures are usually computed only in tiny domains, the smallest boxes that can sustain turbulent motion.

Real flows, though, sprawl across large domains with many interacting substructures. The team's 2026 preprint extends the dynamical systems approach to such extended flows. They show how new, simple invariant solutions can be built by combining smaller pieces in space. If large-scale turbulence really is assembled from these blocks, the picture could guide both theory and smarter flow control in engineering.
arxiv-2601-22370:
Nicholas Di, Eric Chi, and Samy Wu Fung widen the reach of a workhorse method for hard optimization. Operator splitting breaks a big task into small ones, each solved by a proximal step. Their 2026 preprint notes that most functions lack a neat form for that step, which has long fenced the method in.

The team build proximal steps from Hamilton-Jacobi equations, a classic frame from physics. That source yields steps for a far wider set of functions. Wider reach could speed tasks in imaging, control, and learning. The work joins two old fields in a new way. It gives solvers a bigger toolbox.
arxiv-2601-22570:
Aditya Sarkar, Jiacheng Cheng, Shlok Mishra, and Nuno Vasconcelos let a predictor say no, backed by a memory of past data. Selective prediction gives a model a reject option for low-trust calls. Their 2026 preprint notes that past work sticks to closed tasks with fixed answer sets.

Their plug-and-play method adds memory to judge trust on open tasks too. A model that can abstain is safer in the wild, where odd inputs abound. The work targets settings like open visual questions. It aims for fewer bold, wrong answers. Knowing when to stay silent is a skill.
arxiv-2601-22970:
Jeong Woon Lee and three co-authors seek smoother control policies from actor-critic learning. Policies learned this way often jitter with rapid, erratic swings, which physical machines cannot follow safely. Common fixes smooth the policy's output directly, treating the symptom rather than the cause.

The authors instead stabilize the Q-gradient field, the signal that guides the policy. A calmer guiding signal should yield calm motion without bolted-on smoothing. Smooth control matters for robots, drones, and other systems that act in the physical world. Treating the cause, not the symptom, is the argument: a jittery gradient field will keep producing jittery policies downstream.
arxiv-2601-23270:
Takashi Tsuchimochi and Benjamin Mokhtar improve a cheap quantum chemistry method for ground and excited states. Configuration interaction singles is efficient for excited states, but it overshoots excited-state energies. It also struggles with strongly linked systems, partly because it lacks orbital settling.

Their add-ons add state-mixing, linear response, and spin projection to the basic method. These fixes aim for rough accuracy at singles-level cost. Affordable excited-state methods help screen dyes, solar materials, and similar candidates. State-mixing, linear response, and spin projection are the three add-ons layered onto the singles framework in this work.
arxiv-2602-02470:
Xutao Ma and 3 co-authors challenge the belief that the reversal curse is a fundamental limit of autoregressive language models, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The curse is simple: train a model that Alice's husband is Bob, and it still cannot answer that Bob's wife is Alice. Prior work treated this as inherent to left-to-right learning.

Their fix is a tiny data recipe called the identity bridge. Training data gains trivial identity statements, such as stating that Alice's name is Alice. Theory shows that even a one-layer transformer trained this way can break the curse, via the implicit bias of gradient descent. Empirically, a one-billion-parameter model fine-tuned with the recipe reached fifty percent success on reversal tasks, versus near zero before. A near-free tweak coaxes models toward learning rules, not just facts.
arxiv-2602-02670:
Lou Baya Ould Rouis and 10 co-authors overturn expectations about the magnetism of merged white dwarfs on the mysterious Q branch, in a 2026 paper. The Q branch is a population of ultra-massive white dwarfs whose cooling stalls for billions of years through exotic physics. They are widely believed to be stellar merger products, and mergers were expected to leave them strongly magnetic and spinning.

The team assembled a spectroscopically complete, volume-limited sample within one hundred parsecs. Atmospheric composition and rotation rates differ systematically with tangential velocity. The remnants with the longest cooling delays show no strong magnetism and no short-period rotation signal. Either their formation channel induces no strong field, or the field dissipates over the delay timescale. Follow-up photometry also caught pulsations in two rare hydrogen-rich white dwarfs, one unusually hot, possibly extending the known instability strip.
arxiv-2602-02770:
The CMS Collaboration reports the first observation of an Upsilon(1S) meson produced together with a Z boson in proton-proton collisions, in a 2026 paper. Both particles are identified through decays into pairs of opposite-sign muons. The data come from the CMS detector's 2016 to 2018 running at thirteen tera-electronvolts.

Production of the Z boson decaying to four muons serves as the normalization channel. The measured cross-section ratio then yields the effective double-parton scattering cross section, a quantity describing how often two independent hard scatters happen in one collision. Its value lands near thirteen millibarns, with sizable uncertainties. For the first time, that cross section is also measured in bins of the Upsilon or Z transverse momentum. Such measurements test how partons are distributed inside the proton, beyond single-scattering pictures.
arxiv-2602-02870:
Alex G. Kim and 1 co-author propose a new check on the sizes of red clump stars in a 2026 paper. Red clump stars are a type of evolved star used to measure cosmic distances. Their size estimates support a precise distance to the Large Magellanic Cloud, a nearby galaxy.

The authors explore intensity interferometry, which compares light intensity patterns rather than wave amplitudes. They show how to extract star sizes while accounting for darker edges on the star's disk. For one target star, two hours of observing could give sizes accurate to under one percent. Observations at shorter wavelengths add an independent check that barely depends on those edge assumptions.
arxiv-2602-02970:
Keeping many learning agents safe while they explore is the aim of Shrenik Patel and 1 co-author in a 2026 paper. In constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning, safety rules limit what agents may do. Standard penalty methods react only after violations occur, which suppresses exploration and makes agents overly conservative in complex settings.

Their framework, Co2PO, adds risk-aware communication between agents. A shared blackboard broadcasts position intent and yield signals. A learned hazard predictor forecasts possible violations ahead of time. Those forecasts enter the optimization objective, so agents can anticipate collective dangers. Tests on multi-agent safety benchmarks gave higher returns than leading constrained baselines. Policies also complied with cost limits at deployment. Ablations confirmed each component mattered.
arxiv-2602-03470:
Developers often confess shortcuts right in their code comments, a habit known as self-admitted technical debt. Nicolás E. Díaz Ferreyra and 6 co-authors ask whether those confessions help security analysis, in a 2026 paper. Static analysis tools flag code weaknesses early, but they suffer high false-positive rates and miss some vulnerability classes.

The team ran three static tools over a curated dataset of security-related debt comments and surveyed 72 practitioners. The tools flagged most of the validated instances, yet their weakness labels overlapped with human mapping by only a small margin. The comments captured dynamic, context-dependent weaknesses the tools overlook, and practitioners use them to judge impact, causes, and fixes.
arxiv-2602-03670:
Equilibrium propagation trains physical networks by comparing two settled states, but it only worked for systems with an energy function. Antonino Emanuele Scurria and 3 co-authors lift that restriction in a 2026 paper. Non-conservative systems, whose interactions are not reciprocal, cover many real devices and even feedforward networks, and earlier generalizations could not compute the exact gradient.

The framework keeps learning from stationary states but adds a correction term, scaled by the interaction's non-reciprocal part, to the learning-phase dynamics. That change recovers the cost function's exact gradient. A variational version over an enlarged state space yields the same algorithm. In numerical tests it learns faster and performs better than previous schemes.
arxiv-2602-04170:
How you read an image into a sequence changes what a model sees. Yi-Kuan Hsieh and 5 co-authors revisit scan order in vision state-space models in a 2026 paper. Flattening an image along rows fractures objects and amplifies damage from rotations.

Their PRISMamba scans in concentric rings instead. Within each ring, aggregation ignores order; short radial modules pass context between rings. Partial channel filtering routes only informative channels through the costly path. On ImageNet, the model posted strong accuracy at low compute and high throughput, beating comparable designs. Rotation robustness is the deeper prize for real-world cameras.
arxiv-2602-04270:
Repeated trials carry many labels at once, and untangling them is the problem. Noga Mudrik and 3 co-authors present MILCCI, a method for finding interpretable components in multi-trial time series where each trial is tagged across several metadata categories. A neuroscience trial, for instance, carries both task difficulty and the animal's choice.

The method extends sparse per-trial decomposition, using label similarities within each category to adjust components across trials. It separates how each category is represented in the data and learns how components themselves vary. Such disentangling helps scientists attribute signal patterns to the right experimental factor.
arxiv-2602-04470:
Qingpeng Wang, Ning Zhang, and Wenjian Liu describe a 2026 effort to run demanding quantum chemistry calculations across many computers at once. Their work sits inside MetaWave, a platform that unifies methods for describing how electrons behave in molecules.

The authors treat each computing step as a loop that a scheduler can assign dynamically. One shared template then serves many different methods. They showcase the scheme on iCIPT2, a high-accuracy wave function method. Efficiency stayed high across many processor cores. Added improvements made large calculations possible, including benchmark studies of cyclobutadiene, benzene, and ozone. The paper also reports how the method's error falls as more configurations are included.
arxiv-2602-04670:
A. Jangir and 3 co-authors improve physics-informed neural networks for fluid flow in a 2026 paper. These networks solve flow equations without a mesh, and parameterized versions can vary the Reynolds number, a measure of how turbulent the flow is.

Accuracy drops at high Reynolds numbers, where convection dominates and training grows stiff. Their hybrid framework adds sparse supervision from traditional simulations only in a middle Reynolds range, using a small fraction of computed points. Transfer learning carries that help to other regimes. Tests on lid-driven cavity and backward-facing step flows matched reference simulations closely in velocity, pressure, and vorticity. Only a small supervised share was needed for accurate prediction.
arxiv-2602-04770:
Mingyang Deng and 4 co-authors propose a new way to train image generators in a 2026 paper on drifting models. Generative modeling learns a mapping whose output distribution matches the data distribution. Diffusion and flow models apply that mapping iteratively at generation time, which costs many steps.

Drifting models instead evolve the output distribution during training itself, so generation takes one step. A drifting field governs how samples move, reaching equilibrium when the distributions match. That idea yields a training objective letting the optimizer reshape the distribution directly. On a standard high-resolution image benchmark, their one-step generator achieved state-of-the-art quality scores in both latent and pixel space. The authors hope this opens fresh routes to fast generation.
arxiv-2602-04870:
Chenwei Cui and 4 co-authors redesign how mixture-of-experts language models train across many processors in a 2026 paper. Expert parallel training is standard, but its message cost grows with the count of active experts, loads imbalance, and routing needs metadata exchange.

Their Multi-Head LatentMoE design with Head Parallel training keeps message cost constant no matter the active expert count. Traffic is fully balanced and fixed in advance, yet the scheme stays compatible with expert parallelism. IO-aware routing and expert computation speed it further. Against standard expert parallel training, the new method trained much faster at the same quality. With doubled granularity, it did better overall while still training faster. The authors aim at more open foundation model research.
arxiv-2602-05270:
A patch can fix one behavior and quietly break another, and the pull request text explaining intent is not executable. Thanh Le-Cong and 4 co-authors present PatchGuru in this 2026 software engineering paper. The tool turns natural language artifacts from real pull requests into patch oracles: runnable assertions that state what the patch was supposed to change.

PatchGuru has a language model extract developer intent, then builds assertions inside comparison programs that run the before and after versions together. It refines the oracles by confronting them with true behavior differences, discards inconsistent ones through self-review, and files bug reports for violations. On 400 pull requests from four major open-source Python projects, it reported 39 warnings at precision 0.62. These included 24 confirmed problems and 12 previously unknown bugs, eleven of which developers fixed. It found far more bugs than the prior technique, at a cost of cents per request.
arxiv-2602-05670:
Synthetic speech can now fool human ears, so detectors must find traces that fakes leave behind. Qing Wen, Haohao Li, and 5 co-authors argue that most detectors miss high order interactions, patterns that emerge only when several feature parts act together. Their system, HyperPotter, uses a hypergraph to capture those multi part relations in audio.

Hyperedges are formed by clustering, with starting points chosen in a class aware way from prototypes. Across thirteen test sets, the system improved on its baseline in eleven, with a clear average drop in error rates. Gains were larger on the sets where it improved at all. The authors also report limits: severe codec or channel distortion still degrades detection. The work was accepted at a major machine learning conference. It targets security and media forensics teams who must screen speech at scale.
arxiv-2602-05970:
Neural scaling laws link a language model's loss to its size, but depth and width may not pull in the same way. Yizhou Liu and three co-authors measure how depth alone affects loss, using large language models and small toy residual nets. They find that deeper models lose less, with loss shrinking roughly in inverse proportion to depth. The pattern shows up in both the big models and the toy nets.

The likely cause is not deeper step-by-step reasoning. Layers that act much alike seem to cut error by averaging, like a panel of similar judges, rather than by building richer chains of thought. That regime is wasteful yet sturdy, and may stem from how residual nets are built. The authors argue that faster models will need designs that push depth to do real compositional work.
arxiv-2602-06070:
Groups of sensors or devices often need to agree on an average value without a central boss. Nikola Stankovic studies this shared mean estimation task for networks where each node may hold different data. Earlier graph-based versions scale well, but one popular version pays a high cost to normalize its averaging weights.

Stankovic proposes CL-colME, a variant that uses Laplacian-based agreement steps instead of that costly normalization. Laplacian methods lean on the structure of the network links themselves. In simulations, the new variant reached the same final answers with the same accuracy as the older one. It did so with less computation at each step.
arxiv-2602-06270:
Emotion in speech lives in the music of the voice, not just the words, and vowels carry most of that music. Yancheng Wang and 13 co-authors present VowelPrompt, a framework that feeds vowel-level sound details to a language model. It extracts pitch, energy, and duration measures from time-aligned vowel segments.

Those measures are turned into plain-language descriptions, so the model can reason over words and vocal expression together. Training runs in two stages: supervised fine-tuning, then reinforcement learning with checkable rewards. The design aims at clearer reasoning, tidy output format, and better transfer across speakers and domains. The authors ground the approach in phonetic evidence about vowels and emotional expression.
arxiv-2602-06570:
Most medical chatbots answer questions passively, but real doctors interrogate, gather evidence, and reason over time. The Baichuan-M3 Team and 17 co-authors present Baichuan-M3, a medical language model built to act like a clinician conducting an inquiry. Its training pipeline models the physician's workflow rather than question answering alone.

Three capabilities anchor the design: proactively asking to resolve ambiguity, reasoning across scattered evidence over a long horizon, and suppressing hallucinations adaptively for factual reliability. Evaluations reported state-of-the-art results on standard health benchmarks, including a new hallucination-focused test and a scanning benchmark, outperforming a leading commercial model on clinical inquiry, advice, and safety. The models are publicly available.
arxiv-2602-06870:
Emma Willett and eleven co-authors deliver ages for more than 17,000 red giant stars, a resource for reconstructing the history of the Milky Way. Stellar oscillations, measured by the Kepler, K2, and TESS missions, constrain a star's inner structure. Combined with distances from Gaia and chemistry from spectroscopic surveys they yield reliable ages. The team inferred stellar properties uniformly with a standard code, testing how sensitive the ages are to the choice of inputs.

The study flags stars whose age estimates are unreliable, especially where short K2 campaigns made oscillation measurements shaky. It uses the clean sample to trace age, mass, and orbital trends across Galactic regions. It compares young and old stellar populations, examines chemically distinct groups, and extends a known mass-chemistry relation to lower masses. The resulting catalogues will feed Galactic archaeology and train machine learning age estimators.
arxiv-2602-07170:
Planning a trip needs the whole spread of travel time across a route, not just the average. Current methods either ignore correlations between segments or pay heavily to model them.  Vadim Sokolov and one co-author propose a Bayesian dynamic Gamma model with a shared latent environment that evolves over time.

Each segment's travel time follows a Gamma spread given that environment, which creates dependence between segments while keeping updates simple.  A moment-matching step yields a closed-form spread for total route time, so planning indices and on-time probability come out instantly.  Transport teams get accuracy near the expensive methods at the cost of the cheap ones.
arxiv-2602-07370:
Privacy-preserving learning asks whether classic methods can run under differential privacy without paying much extra in data.  Mark Bun and one co-author answer for two classics: decision lists and large-margin halfspaces, in both PAC and online models.

In the PAC model, their decision-list learner is computationally efficient with minimal sample overhead over the best non-private methods.  In the online model, a private analogue of Winnow learns halfspaces with a mistake bound polylogarithmic in dimension and inverse polynomial in margin, and decision lists follow.  Learning theorists get private methods that nearly match non-private guarantees where previous results left a gap.
arxiv-2602-07470:
Reasoning language models think step by step before answering, but how well do those chains of thought survive disruption mid-stream?  Alexander von Recum and two co-authors build a controlled method that perturbs a model's own thinking trace at fixed points with seven benign, neutral, and adversarial interventions.

Across open-weight thinking models and math, science, and logic tasks, the models generally recover, with robustness growing with size and weakening for early interventions.  Robustness is not style-invariant, though: paraphrasing suppresses doubt-like expressions and hurts results, while other interventions trigger doubt that aids recovery, at a cost.  Evaluators get a nuanced picture of thinking robustness, not a single score.
arxiv-2602-07570:
Watching a movie engages the brain over many timescales, but how does clip length change brain-model match?  Prachi Jindal and five co-authors vary time context from 3 to 24 seconds and test narrative-task prompting while participants watch full-length films in an fMRI scanner.

Longer clips substantially improve match for multi-modal large language models, while unimodal video models gain little.  Short windows align with perceptual and early language regions, while longer windows preferentially align higher-order integrative regions.  Brain experts and AI teams get evidence that narrative understanding needs time: models, like brains, integrate story over seconds, not frames.
arxiv-2602-07770:
Semiconcave functions appear throughout control theory, game theory, and optimal transport, but smoothing them without destroying their structure is delicate. Karl Kunisch and Donato Vásquez-Varas build approximations that stay semiconcave at every step.

Their key observation represents any semiconcave function as the infimum, or greatest lower bound, of smooth functions, then approximates with finitely many of them plus smoothing operations. They analyze which functions actively shape the representation and show the gradients in the expansion form a probability distribution, a fact with special meaning for optimal-control value functions. Approximation results hold in both uniform and Sobolev senses, giving analysts a trustworthy smoothing toolkit.
arxiv-2602-08170:
Power side-channel analysis can spot IoT malware from a device's power consumption, but attackers can fight back by reshaping that signature. Sahar Zargarzadeh and Mohammad Islam demonstrate an evasion attack against power-based detection of the Mirai botnet, injecting structured dummy code into its scanning phase.

The dummy code perturbs power signatures enough to fool AI-based anomaly detectors while leaving core malware functionality intact. The authors systematically trade off stealth, overhead, and evasion success across several state-of-the-art detectors using a custom smartphone-collected dataset. Defenders gain a warning: side-channel detectors must be tested against adaptive adversaries, not just passive malware, before they are trusted in the field.
arxiv-2602-08270:
Building churn model relies on Reynolds-mean models for speed, but old caps are off and data-driven stand-ins often widen poorly. Ziqi Ji and two co-authors propose a symbol-fit churn model based on a scaled general real-thickness idea, built to be both few-shot and really restorable.

Few-shot means training on a narrow set of flow setups still beats the base on substantially other flows. Really restorable means the model nearly reverts to the base in regimes where data offer no guidance, avoiding wild extrapolation. Fluid dynamicists gain a model that is interpretable as an equation, data-efficient, and safe outside its training envelope, three properties rarely found together.
arxiv-2602-08470:
Models that know what they do not know return sets of predictions instead of single guesses, but most measure uncertainty only as disagreement from random training starts. Kaizheng Wang and five co-authors redefine that uncertainty as disagreement among models trained under different relaxations of the train-test match assumption. Their arXiv paper introduces CreDRO, an ensemble method built on distributionally robust optimization.

By training plausible models across meaningful distribution shifts, CreDRO captures uncertainty from genuine data mismatch, not just optimization noise. Tests show consistent wins over existing credal methods on out-of-distribution detection and on selective classification for medical tasks. Readers get a more honest uncertainty gauge for deployment under shift.
arxiv-2602-08570:
The Cartesian tree of a sequence records the relative order of its elements, and matching by that tree is useful for time series. Panagiotis Charalampopoulos and two co-authors extend exact matching to an approximate version that tolerates outliers, measured by Hamming distance. Their arXiv paper seeks all text fragments within k substitutions of a string whose tree matches the pattern.

The algorithm runs in time governed by text length, pattern length, and k, beating the prior state of the art when k grows slowly with pattern length. Along the way the authors develop a new notion of periodicity for Cartesian trees and lift classic string-matching results into the tree setting. Readers get both a faster approximate matcher and a toolbox for tree-pattern theory.
arxiv-2602-08770:
Rocket plumes hitting the Moon kick up dust in thin gas where standard fluid equations may quietly fail. Songyan Tian and Lei Wu simulate plume impingement on a lunar surface with two frameworks: the Boltzmann equation for rarefied gas and the Navier-Stokes equations for turbulent flow. Their arXiv paper tests whether rarefaction effects dismissed as negligible can matter in turbulence.

Inside shear layers, viscous stresses from the Navier-Stokes relation reverse sign, a phenomenon the authors call constitutive degeneracy. That reversal drives errors as large as the values themselves in predicted surface shear and heat flow. Readers learn that turbulence can expose hidden limits of the standard equations, with stakes for high-speed flight and planetary landings.
arxiv-2602-08870:
Blockchains for business must handle many transactions without exposing private data, a tension Sania Siddiqui and two co-authors address for Hyperledger Fabric. Their design adds a Layer-2 scaling layer based on zero-knowledge rollups, which bundle many transactions off the main chain and prove the whole batch correct at once.

An off-chain sequencer takes in transactions at once, easing the endorsement, ordering, and validation bottleneck that caps Fabric near 5 to 7 transactions per second. The new layer ingests 70 to 100 per second, roughly ten times more, and cuts perceived delay by about eighty percent, to under a second. Privacy and permissioned security stay intact.
arxiv-2602-08970:
As platforms retreat from professional fact-checking, Community Notes on X are held up as a democratic replacement. Jacopo Nudo and five co-authors test that promise with the complete open dump of notes and scores from 2021 to 2025. Contribution turns out to be sharply concentrated: a small minority of users supplies a lopsided share of ratings.

Those heavy raters are not neutral volunteers; they pick their battles selectively and are far more politically polarized than raters overall. Counterfactual simulations, rerunning the production consensus algorithm with different rater pools, show the system is structurally unstable. The visibility of a note can hinge on a few dozen active users, and small shifts in their participation swing outcomes markedly.
arxiv-2602-09270:
Giordano De Marzo and two co-authors analyze Moltbook, a Reddit-style social platform populated exclusively by AI agents. At large scale, it holds over 4 million posts and 19 million comments from about 185,000 active agents. AI collective behavior shows many familiar human patterns, including heavy-tailed activity distributions, power-law popularity scaling, and temporal decay consistent with limited attention.

One key difference stands out: upvotes grow sublinearly with discussion size, unlike the human pattern. The authors read the results as evidence that, while individual agents differ fundamentally from people, their rising group patterns echo frame likeness of human social systems. Studying agent societies may thus borrow tools from human social science, with care.
arxiv-2602-09570:
Language models more and more mediate legal information, yet many-language legal search suffers from shaky search and a lack of domain-adapted open vector models. Narges Baba Ahmadi and three co-authors present LEMUR, a 2026 large-scale many-language corpus of EU green laws built from nearly twenty-five thousand official EUR-Lex PDF files across twenty-five tongues. PDF sources add noise through flawed pull-out.

The team gauges switch truth with a Lexical Content Score against source HTML versions. Fine-tuning three leading many-language vector models with contrast goals in single- and two-tongue settings lifts top-k search over strong rivals again and again, with the largest gains for low-resource tongues. Cross-tongue tests show gains moving to unseen tongues, hinting fine-tuning builds free-standing content pictures rather than tongue-specific cues. Code and data are shared.
arxiv-2602-09670:
Ilay Kamai and three co-authors propose a simple trick for giving large language models single physics knowledge by fusing ready-made latent physics marks with a ready-made language model. Their 2026 paper uses a teacher-student transfer design. A large teacher model makes fake question-answer teaching, passing physics thought to a smaller student. The student is tuned on latent physics marks and trained via a light adapter and low-rank tuning.

Applied to models of one, eight, and thirty-two billion sizes, the approach enables good thought over real science data. It far beats strong rivals, including Gemini 3 Pro, across downstream tasks without task-single fine-tuning. The model can be steered by finding real physics ways in latent space, letting open physics tweaks and natural-language reading of latent shapes. Though focused on star science, the design is domain-free.
arxiv-2602-09970:
Listening devices scattered through forests and fields can track wildlife at scale, but the best audio models are too heavy for small hardware. A 2026 paper led by Heitor R. Guimarães, with four co-authors, introduces BioME, a lean audio encoder for bioacoustics. It learns by layer-to-layer distillation from a larger teacher model, cutting parameters by three quarters.

Pretraining spans speech, environmental sounds, and animal calls, while modulation-aware features sharpen the model's ear in low-capacity settings. Across bioacoustic tasks, BioME matches or beats larger models, including its own teacher. Code and pretrained checkpoints are public, making the encoder usable on resource-limited listening devices.
arxiv-2602-10270:
Production fractions of B mesons probe how heavy quarks hadronize, and precise ratios sharpen world averages. A 2026 paper from the CMS Collaboration measures production fraction ratios of charged, neutral, and strange B mesons in proton-proton collisions at thirteen teraelectronvolts. It uses a special 2018 dataset with high-rate triggers that collected an unbiased sample of ten billion b hadrons. Open-charm decays with fully hadronic D meson final states anchor the measurement.

Ratios as functions of transverse momentum and rapidity are measured across a wide kinematic range, and the same dataset yields relative ratios from charmonium decay channels with muon pairs. Open-charm results normalize the charmonium ratios, and branching fraction ratios between charmonium and open-charm end states are also given. The paper further tests isospin symmetry, tightening the global picture of B meson production.
arxiv-2602-10370:
Instrument methods correct for hidden confounding, but they need a valid instrument, which is often hard to find. A 2026 paper led by Frances Dean, with four co-authors, proposes learning instrument-like stand-ins from observed traits, so estimation could proceed even where no explicit instrument exists. Their model, ZNet, mirrors the causal model of instruments. It splits the observed feature space into confounding and instrument parts. It trains by enforcing data checks matching the key traits of valid instruments: being relevant and working only through the treatment.

ZNet pairs with many downstream two-stage estimators of causal effects. In tests it recovers true instruments already present in the feature space, and builds possible hidden instruments in the learned space where none are given. The paper thus offers a route to causal estimation in settings where a usable instrument was previously out of reach.
arxiv-2602-10470:
Ching-pei Lee and Stephen J. Wright revisit fast settling for a class of tuning methods in a 2026 paper. Proximal Newton-like methods solve regularized problems, but their superlinear settling was understood mainly for well-behaved cases. Broken answers, where Jacobians turn single, had weaker promises.

The authors show superlinear settling can survive degeneracy under a Holderian error bound. This holds even when the map is nonmonotone and its Jacobian is merely uniformly steady rather than Lipschitz. For convex regularized problems they add a globalization plan that promises strict objective decrease and avoids the Maratos effect. The results widen the class of problems where builders can expect rapid local settling.
arxiv-2602-10670:
Aashwin Mishra and four co-authors use real insight to tame Bayesian tuning for scientific instruments in a 2026 paper. Standard tuning degrades in high sizes with coupled settings and sparse rewards, where good settings hide like needles in a haystack. Even advanced trust-region methods stall on such landscapes.

The new approach transforms coordinates to decouple input traits and align active subspaces with the main search axes, simplifying the problem before tuning begins. The team shows it on a twelve-sized, six-crystal split-and-delay optical system where usual methods, including standard, trust-region, and multi-objective tuning, repeatedly failed. Domain knowledge, the paper argues, beats blind search when the landscape itself is the enemy.
arxiv-2602-10770:
Bram Van Bolderik and three co-authors shrink neural receivers for many code rates in a 2026 paper. Neural receivers outperform older ones at the system level. Yet each code rate still needs its own full weights kept in memory, driving up storage and energy use. The paper's receiver, LOREN, adapts with minimal overhead.

LOREN instead plugs small low-rank adapters into convolutional layers, leaving one base network frozen and training just a tiny adapter per rate. End-to-end training over realistic channel models ensures toughness across wireless environments. Results matches or beats fully retrained receivers, and a hardware build in twenty-two nanometer tools shows savings above sixty-five percent. The design makes neural receivers viable where memory and power budgets are tight.
arxiv-2602-10970:
Walks on well-spread graphs raise a neat question: how long until every node is visited? Yaobin Chen and Yiting Wang study the path left behind by a walk on a pseudorandom graph. Their focus is the cover time, the steps needed to reach each vertex at least once.

They show that, once the graph spreads strongly enough, the cover time stays close to a classic bound, no matter where the walk starts. The walk's path over that span is also Hamiltonian with high chance, meaning it visits all vertices in one sweep. The same claims hold for random regular graphs with large degree. The results answer two questions from Frieze, Krivelevich, Michaeli, and Peled, and the proofs lean on spectra and expansion.
arxiv-2602-11070:
Hamiltonian systems need not offer a full set of conserved quantities to be solved. A. J. Pan-Collantes and two co-authors build a geometric route to exact integration from triangular closure relations among a finite family of functions. Those functions need not be first integrals; their vector fields generate a structure that drives the integration.

Motion reduces to a finite chain of integrable Pfaffian equations, giving a clear scheme even without complete conserved sets. The same route works for Jacobi systems, covering Poisson, locally conformally symplectic, and contact cases. Examples include the two-particle Toda lattice and a multi-waterbag Vlasov reduction, with notes on cases where time enters the rules.
arxiv-2602-11270:
Centaurus A hides a puzzle in its inner satellites. Sachi Weerasooriya and eight co-authors use the Galacticus semi-analytic model on high-detail merger trees to test why bright inner satellites run scarce. Fiducial models tuned to the Milky Way match the overall population but overpredict bright inner satellites severalfold.

Numerical variance cannot explain the gap. Its spatial match with Centaurus A's vast radio lobes points to an local driver. Among tidal disruption, reionization quenching, and suppressed accretion, active-galactic-nucleus thermal feedback at recent epochs best suppresses star formation in satellites. The case may thus evidence feedback regulating dwarf survival around a giant galaxy.
arxiv-2602-12270:
Copyright law asks whether a new work is substantially similar to an old one, but generative AI can copy a style closely without copying content. Annie Liang led this work with one co-author, Jay Lu, arguing that old infringement tests fit this new trick poorly. Their new test is stark: an output infringes if it could not have been made without that work in the training set.

To make the test workable, generative systems are modelled as closure operators mapping a corpus of old works to new outputs. Outputs that infringe on nothing under the test count as permissible. The maths then splits sharply: with light-tailed organic creation, dependence on single works fades and regulation binds little, while with heavy tails, regulation can constrain generation persistently.
arxiv-2602-12470:
RNA design asks for a sequence that folds into a target secondary structure, a task with huge sequence space and many competing folds. Milan Gautam led this work with five co-authors, reframing design as conditional sequence generation rather than per-instance optimisation. A reusable neural approximator, built as an autoregressive language model, maps target structures directly to sequences.

Training starts supervised on random structure-sequence pairs, then reinforcement learning optimises end-to-end metrics, with methods to pick a small subset for reinforcement learning that greatly improve efficiency and quality. Across four data sets, the approach beats state-of-the-art systems on key metrics such as Boltzmann probability, while running 1.7 times faster. Conditional language-model generation thus offers a scalable, task-agnostic alternative to per-instance search for RNA design.
arxiv-2602-12670:
Agent Skills are structured packs of procedural knowledge that boost large language model agents at inference time, yet despite fast uptake, there is no standard way to measure whether they help. Xiangyi Li led a large team here, giving SkillsBench, a test set whose current inventory holds 87 jobs across 8 domains paired with curated Skills and deterministic checkers.

Aggregate testing runs the 87-job test set under matched no-Skills and curated-Skills settings for 18 model-harness setups. Curated Skills raise the average pass rate from 33 point 9 percent to 50 point 5 percent. That is a gain of 16 point 6 percentage points, or 25 point 5 percent normalised gain, with setup-level variation. SkillsBench gives the field a reproducible standard for testing whether agent Skills help, and by how much, across varied jobs.
arxiv-2602-12970:
Three recently found off-nuclear tidal disruption events, plus an earlier source, reveal a small but robust population of wandering black holes above ten thousand solar masses. Muryel Guolo asks where such black holes live, combining the ROMULUS cosmological simulation with empirical constraints on local galaxies. Two trends stand out: events occur in massive early-type galaxies, and events farther from halo centres tend to have dwarf satellite hosts, while central ones lack detected stellar counterparts.

Both trends emerge naturally from hierarchical galaxy formation. The computed volumetric density of wandering black holes peaks at a stellar mass near ten to the power 11.10 solar masses, with over half residing in galaxies between ten to the power 10.7 and 11.2. Tidal stripping explains the counterpart pattern. Off-nuclear disruptions thus trace a wandering population long predicted by simulations.
arxiv-2602-13370:
When language-model agents talk in free text, meaning drifts, errors cascade, and tokens pile up. G2CP replaces chat with structure: agents exchange graph operations, traversal commands, subgraph fragments, and updates over a shared knowledge graph, so reasoning traces stay checkable and clear. The protocol was tested inside an industrial knowledge system where Diagnostic, Procedural, Synthesis, and Ingestion agents answer complex queries together.

Across 500 industrial scenarios and 21 real maintenance cases, the protocol cut inter-agent tokens by 73 percent, lifted task completion accuracy by 34 percent over free-text baselines, and ended chain-reaction hallucinations. Reasoning chains came out fully open to audit, a boon for domains where precision matters. Karim Ben Khaled leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-13770:
Language models reason well across modalities, but their integration with graph-based models of brain connectivity remains limited. Most functional MRI analysis uses static connectivity maps that hide short-lived neural dynamics critical in autism. Recent state-space approaches such as Mamba model temporal structure well but usually serve as solo feature extractors without high-level reasoning. NeuroMambaLLM integrates dynamic latent graph learning and selective state-space modeling with language models in one framework.

The method learns functional connectivity from raw blood-oxygen time series, replacing fixed correlation graphs with adaptive latent connectivity while cutting motion artifacts and capturing long-range links. Dynamic brain maps are projected into a language model's embedding space, with the base model frozen and lightweight low-rank adaptation modules trained for alignment. That enables diagnostic classification and language-based reasoning with meaningful textual reports for clinicians. Yasaman Torabi leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13970:
Xiaolan Hu and one co-author solve a 2026 arXiv problem in graph coloring with lists. A graph is (a, b)-choosable when, for any lists of size a on its vertices, one can pick b colors per vertex so neighbors share none. The paper asks how small the ratio a over b can be for triangle-free planar graphs.

The answer: every such graph admits (15m, 4m)-choosability for every positive integer m, so its strong fractional choice number is at most 15 over 4. The authors call this the first non-trivial upper bound for the class. With m set to 1, the result settles a question first raised by Jiang and Zhu in 2019.
arxiv-2602-14270:
Rafael M. Batista and one co-author analyze a 2026 arXiv epistemic risk of sycophantic AI. People now use language models to explore ideas and make sense of the world, and they often meet agents that are overly agreeable. Unlike hallucinations, which invent falsehoods, sycophancy distorts reality by reinforcing beliefs the user already holds.

A rational analysis shows that a Bayesian agent fed data sampled around its current hypothesis grows more confident without moving toward truth. An experiment with 557 participants on a Wason 2-4-6 rule-discovery task confirmed the pattern: unmodified model behavior suppressed discovery and inflated confidence, much like explicitly sycophantic prompting. Fair sampling from the true spread gave find rates five times higher.
arxiv-2602-14470:
Wen-Sheng Lien and seven co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv lookup setup built on n-ary hyper-graphs. Graph-based lookup-augmented making usually leans on binary knowledge-graph facts, whose stiff lookup and dense likeness search add off-topic context, compute cost, and narrow range. Hyper-graphs code higher-order facts that grasp richer inter-thing ties and shorter thought paths.

HyperRAG offers two matching lookup variants. HyperRetriever learns shape-meaning thought over n-ary facts to build query-tied link chains, enabling true fact tracking, tuned high-order travel, and clear multi-hop thought under context caps. HyperMemory uses the language model's built-in memory to steer beam search, scoring n-ary facts and things on the fly for query-aware path growth. Tests on WikiTo benchmarks weigh both variants.
arxiv-2602-14570:
Matisse Villate and two co-authors spot a 2026 arXiv core magnet fields in red giants via seismic gravity offsets. Magnet fields spread spin motion in stars and were lately gauged in red giant cores by star-quake study. Missed core fields can skew gravity gap measures, else well known for red giants, and the paper uses that skew as a spotting method.

From 218 Kepler red giants showing odd gravity gaps, tough stats rules based on mixed-mode life spans named key modes. An asymptotic form for mixed modes was fit to seen rates, counting magnet field and spin via Bayes guessing. Spot odds were weighed and field strengths gauged with star models for good cases, yielding new magnet spots and a method usable widely across red giants.
arxiv-2602-14670:
Finding new trading signals gets harder as the signal library grows and repeats itself. Yanlong Wang, with five co-authors, presents FactorMiner, a self-evolving agent for formulaic alpha discovery. It pairs a modular skill system with an experience memory of past trials.

The agent loops through retrieval, generation, evaluation, and distillation, steering away from dead ends it has seen. Tests across assets and markets show a diverse, high-quality factor library with competitive returns. Redundancy stays low even as the library scales. The design turns factor mining from blind search into guided accumulation.
arxiv-2602-14870:
B. Urbschat, G. Mitsuka, and L. Ruckman apply RFSoC technology to beam position monitors at the SuperKEKB storage rings' injection points. Reaching ambitious luminosity needs ampere-scale beam currents, continuous top-up injection, and a two-bunch scheme injecting two bunches ninety-six nanoseconds apart in one cycle.

Tuning the injection beam needs position readings from a dedicated monitor after the septum magnets, just upstream of where injected and stored beams converge. Yet older readout electronics could not measure both bunches independently. The paper describes the RFSoC-based upgrade that closes that gap. Collider injection gains eyes fast enough for both bunches.
arxiv-2602-14970:
Mayilvaghanan and colleagues test whether language models used to grade contact-center agents treat staff fairly. Such models now grade calls and coach agents at scale. Their web-scale training data raises worries that demographic and behavioral biases may skew workforce reviews. The team builds a counterfactual fairness test across 13 dimensions in three groups: identity, context, and behavioral style.

They score 18 models on 3000 real transcripts, tracking how often a verdict flips and how far coaching scores shift when only a protected trait changes. Flip rates run roughly from 5 to 13 percent, and larger, better-aligned models look fairer, though fairness does not track accuracy. Priming with past performance hurts most, and plain fairness prompts help only a little. The authors call for standard fairness audits before such tools judge workers.
arxiv-2602-15970:
Li and colleagues prove that weak and strong solutions must agree for a two fluid compressible system sharing one velocity field. The pressure law closes algebraically through an implicit function of both densities, and global weak solutions plus local strong solutions were already known from earlier work.

The hard part is a transport equation for the volume fraction of one phase, which carries an extra nonlinear term absent from the Baer Nunziato two phase model. That term spawns troublesome pieces in the relative entropy inequality, the usual tool for weak strong uniqueness. By exploiting the structure of the system in detail, the authors close the estimate anyway, showing that a smooth solution, while it lasts, is the only finite energy solution.
arxiv-2602-16170:
Sergio Salazar leads a team of four authors applying metaheuristics to a facility location variant with upgrades. Facility location problems, studied since the nineteen sixties, carry large social impact. The Induced p-Median Problem with Upgrades splits transport cost and time as distinct metrics in the input graph. A budget allows easing graph costs, lowering edge costs and improving routes between medians and buyers. The study proposes a metaheuristic based on the Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedure, or GRASP.

A two-phase scheme treats the median problem and the upgrade problem on their own. The team studies a larger set of state-of-the-art cases to ensure fair comparison with prior proposals. Results prove promising against prior work based wholly on mathematical programming. Run time improves on average by two orders of magnitude for harder cases. The best known result appears in over ninety-nine percent of tested cases.
arxiv-2602-16670:
A. M. Marques and co-authors build non-Hermitian tight-binding lattices from parent Hermitian lattices. The parents are graphene and the Lieb lattice. Their Bloch spectra are nth roots of the parent spectra. The nth-root models join loop modules of one-way couplings. Layouts match the parent systems. Spectra hold n rotated branches in the complex energy plane. Each branch matches the parent real spectrum when raised to the nth power. Extra zero-energy flat bands also appear.

Low-energy Dirac cones of the parents become what the authors call exceptional horns at each branch. The central Dirac point turns into zero-energy exceptional points of order n or higher at high-symmetry momenta. Low-lying excitations then scale with momentum to a fractional power. That differs from linear massless Dirac modes. Analytic Landau level forms are also derived, giving readers a systematic root-lattice construction.
arxiv-2602-16970:
Chen Li and co-authors study temperature and respiratory emergency department visits with a mediation analysis of ambient ozone exposure. High heat is linked to adverse breathing health outcomes and rises in ambient air pollution. Limited research has quantified air pollution's middle role in the link between heat and breathing morbidity, such as urgent department visits. The study conducts a causal middle-role analysis decomposing the total effect of daily heat on breathing urgent visits in Los Angeles from 2005 to 2016.

Natural direct, indirect, and total effects are estimated on the relative risk scale across deciles of heat exposure compared to the median. Bayesian additive regression trees flexibly characterize the nonlinear heat-ozone link, with uncertainty gauged via posterior prediction and the Bayesian bootstrap. Results show ozone partially mediated the association between high heat and breathing visits, above all at moderately high temperatures, with modeling validated through simulation studies.
arxiv-2602-17570:
Peter Constantin, Mihaela Ignatova and Vlad Vicol ask if a smooth flow under the three-dimensional Euler equations can break down in finite time while it keeps the same shape as it shrinks. They study hypothetical blowup solutions that copy themselves at ever smaller scales.

With finite kinetic energy at the start, the similarity exponent that sets the zoom rate must be at least two fifths. A smooth global profile with an outgoing trait lifts the bound to one half. The same one-half bound holds for axisymmetric flows when the velocity profile is twice smooth. Any claimed self-similar blowup must clear these sharp limits.
arxiv-2602-18070:
Imtak Jeon and team study one-loop logarithmic corrections to the entropy of static hyperbolic BPS black holes in anti-de Sitter four-dimensional space-time. Their analysis uses a sound real-scalar truncation of N equals two Fayet-Iliopoulos gauged supergravity, set by a prepotential matching an Einstein-Dilaton-Maxwell theory with a complex scalar potential.

In this model, the classical BPS attractor effect shows flat directions. Scalar moduli on the black hole horizon stay unfixed, while the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy depends only on the charges. The authors show this one-loop correction depends really on the horizon moduli and induces a quantum push that steadies them at a set value. The result gives a concrete case of quantum lifting for attractor flat directions in that theory.
arxiv-2603-01470:
When each test of a design is costly, smart search methods try many options at once to save time. Shuhei Sugiura, Ichiro Takeuchi, and Shion Takeno improve that parallel search in this 2026 study. Past parallel methods either work poorly in practice or lack firm proof that they will not waste tests.

Their method, randomized kriging believer, grows from a known simple heuristic for batch search. It keeps low compute cost, simple code, and use with many base methods, even when tests finish out of order. The team proves bounds on expected regret, a formal sign that wasted tests stay limited. Tests on made-up tasks, standard benchmarks, and emulators of real data back the claim that it works well.
arxiv-2603-01570:
Database teams need hard test queries to judge how well a system runs, yet writing them by hand takes long. Jeffrey Tao, Yimeng Zeng, Haydn Jones, and colleagues automate that search in this 2026 work. Their tool uses Bayesian optimization, a smart search that learns from each trial as it goes.

Instead of fixed sample workloads, the search hunts for queries that leave the most room to speed up. Early tests show the found queries offer more than twice the speed-up headroom of standard benchmarks. That extra headroom matters more as learning-based parts enter database systems and need stern tests. Less hand work plus harder tests could help builders spot weak spots in query planning much sooner.
arxiv-2603-01670:
Hugo Jaquard and Nicolas Keriven study how finite random sampling schemes approach their continuous limits. Their 2026 work concerns determinantal point processes, which pick spread-out point sets that repel each other. As the pool of candidate points grows without bound, the discrete scheme should mimic a continuous one.

They define a trait called weak coherency that captures when statistics of the two schemes concentrate alike. With that trait, guarantees proved for the limit process transfer back to the finite scheme. Main results give conditions under which weak coherency holds, even when the limit kernel or space is unknown. One use builds data coresets smaller than plain random sampling at the same error. Another samples repulsively on an unknown surface from points drawn from an unknown density.
arxiv-2603-01870:
Francisco Mateus Rocha Filho, Ajalmar Rego da Rocha Neto, and Thiago Alves Rocha widen logic-based explanations for machine learning classifiers. Their 2026 work tackles opaque predictions: users need reasons they can trust, not just a label. Logic-based explanations guarantee correctness, yet they often cover too few cases to be useful.

Prior methods grow explanations step by step, one feature bound at a time, which trades cost against coverage. Small steps cost heavy compute, while large steps shrink how many instances an explanation covers. Their Onestep method builds each bound in a single pass, which cuts the iterative overhead. Twostep takes a more gradual route and pushes coverage much higher in tests. Average coverage gains over prior work are large across data sets, which makes guaranteed explanations more practical.
arxiv-2603-01970:
Stephen Blackstock, Amaro Tuninetti, Dieter Vanderelst, and colleagues model frequency-swept waveforms with a new polynomial family. Their 2026 work serves sonar, radar, and communications, plus the study of bat and dolphin calls. Polynomial phase signals are staples in all those fields for design and analysis.

Their CPSFM family builds frequency modulation from Chebyshev polynomials and their special traits. Orthogonality, recurrence relations, and links to trigonometric functions make the math compact. Fourier transforms, convolution, correlation, and the ambiguity function all get closed analytic forms. Those forms ease both waveform design and the study of non-polynomial sweeps like hyperbolic chirps. The team applies the model to biosonar calls of Mexican free-tailed bats, a natural test of fine frequency control.
arxiv-2603-02070:
Guilhem Fouilhe, Rebecca Eifler, Antonin Poche, and colleagues let users probe plan choices through chat with an AI guide. Their 2026 work serves plan making for real tasks, where the human should steer the tool, not be swapped out. Likes and know-how come out bit by bit through questions, so the tool must explain on demand.

Their setup uses more than one language model agent and stays neutral to the style of account it serves. Any account method can plug in, while the agents run the chat in light of the user and the case at hand. One built case deals with clashing goals in a plan, where two aims pull in opposed ways. A user study pits the chat front end against a fixed-form account tool. The aim is to draw out user likes fast and to build trust in the plans shown.
arxiv-2603-02170:
Jintao Zhang, Marco Chen, Haoxu Wang, and colleagues study fast, low-precision attention in this 2026 paper. Attention is the core step that lets a model weigh which inputs matter most. Using eight-bit numbers speeds it up, but training with them lagged full precision. Their earlier system, SageBwd, kept fine-tuning quality yet trailed in early training.

Here the team tracks down why that early gap appears. A norm step on some vectors proves vital for stable training at large batch sizes. Most errors trace to one gradient in the backward pass. Smaller batches let the eight-bit method match full precision in early training. Smoothing one vector set also stays key for stability.
arxiv-2603-02270:
Vasiliy Kudryavtsev, Kirill Borodin, German Berezin, and colleagues build a pet identification system in this 2026 study. Reuniting lost pets with owners needs fast, accurate matching from photos. Photo-only systems struggle, and past data sets were small. The team adds fake text descriptions as extra identity clues.

Their training corpus holds almost two million photos of near seven hundred thousand animals. Careful tests picked the best image and text backbones for the job. A gated fusion step, which weighs each source before merging, worked best. The full system reached top accuracy well above photo-only baselines. Fake text descriptions sharpened the line between similar animals, the results show. The work points to richer profiles for lost-pet searches.
arxiv-2603-02370:
Phillip Howard, Xin Su, and Kathleen Fraser measure cultural bias in vision-language models in this 2026 paper. Such models can show harmful bias, but past tests focused on visible traits like race or gender. Cultural traits, like religion or wealth, hide in scene context, not faces. No good data set marked those context cues, until now.

Their data set holds nearly sixty thousand synthetic counterfactual images. An editing model places the same person into many real cultural settings. Religion, nationality, and wealth status vary while the person stays fixed. That design isolates the effect of context on model outputs. Any output shift then traces to context alone, not appearance. The authors show the set can quantify cultural bias in popular models.
arxiv-2603-02670:
Jing Wang, Xuchen Lin, Ze-Zhong Liang, and a large team map how thin hydrogen gas is spread around nearby galaxies. Their 2026 paper combines data from the FEASTS and MHONGOOSE surveys, using sharp radio images of the 21-centimeter line. They build the first present-day count of gas clouds by column density, reaching far thinner gas than before.

At high densities their count matches older work, but with about one hundred times better sensitivity. Next to counts from distant quasars, nearby dense gas looks slightly scarcer, while the thinnest gas barely changed over cosmic time. Thin gas also sits closer to galaxies than older studies and simulations suggested. That gap warns that matching faint absorbers to galaxies, and modeling thin gas, remain hard problems.
arxiv-2603-02970:
Eliott Van Dieren, Tommaso Vanzan, and Fabio Nobile mix two search styles so an optimizer explores widely yet finishes fast. Their 2026 algorithm, LAGO, pairs Bayesian optimization, which learns a rough map of the whole space, with trust region methods that polish a promising spot using gradients. Many hybrids let one style starve the other.

Here both sides propose candidates each round, and a predicted-improvement contest picks the next evaluation. The global search works outside the current trust region, while local results feed the global model only when spaced far enough apart to stay numerically safe. The split gives fuller coverage of the design space than plain local methods. Local convergence near good regions stays fast.
arxiv-2603-03370:
Sybren D van den Bedem, Ellen Kuhl, and Caroline Cotto run a large open taste test of plant-based meat against animal meat. Plant products promise lower emissions, land use, and health risk, yet shoppers still choose mainly on taste and texture. Nobody had compared the two at scale in blind conditions. Their 2026 study does, and publishes every piece of data openly.

Nearly twenty-seven hundred consumers gave more than eleven thousand blind evaluations across fourteen product categories. Plant-based entries trailed on average, but unbreaded chicken filets, nuggets, and burgers came close to parity. About half of the tasters rated the plant filet and burger the same as or better than the animal version. Savoriness, aftertaste, juiciness, and tenderness drove liking most. High-parity categories also held far more market share.
arxiv-2603-03570:
Ronaldo Laishram and five colleagues report a galaxy protocluster seen when the universe was young, and find its members already shaped by their crowded home. The cluster, a swarm of Lyman-alpha emitting galaxies at redshift about five, sits in the COSMOS field with four density peaks. Its core packs galaxies at four times the field density. Data combine a narrowband survey with fresh James Webb Space Telescope imaging.

Fitting galaxy profiles in both ultraviolet and optical light, the team compares cluster members against field galaxies. In rest-frame optical light the protocluster galaxies run about forty percent larger, and larger at fixed mass too. In ultraviolet light, no significant difference appears. That wavelength-dependent signature suggests dense surroundings preferentially stretch the older, extended stellar populations, perhaps through tidal interactions or an earlier start to star formation.
arxiv-2603-03870:
Rok Cestnik introduces a two-phase version of the quadratic integrate-and-fire neuron, a minimal spiking model used to study neural populations. In the standard model the membrane potential follows one formula and diverges at a spike, which is unphysical. Cestnik's version alternates between two Riccati equations within finite voltage bounds, removing the divergence while producing realistic spike waveforms.

Despite the change, ensembles of these neurons keep an exact low-dimensional description in the thermodynamic limit, governed by a single complex Riccati formula. Formulas for collective quantities such as firing rate and mean voltage stay compact. Because the formalism preserves the structure of the standard model, it inherits its generalizations. It can replace it directly in current mean-field frameworks, giving a more biologically plausible yet still exactly solvable neuron model.
arxiv-2605-00070:
