Edgar Chaillou, Sebastian Rodriguez, Yves Tourbier, and Francisco Chinesta present CRADIPOR, a tool that predicts numerical dispersion in car crash simulations during post-processing. Finite element crash models are not strictly repeatable, thanks to parallel runs and model detail, so the criteria engineers read off them scatter from run to run. Repeating runs to measure that scatter is usually too expensive.

CRADIPOR instead learns to flag the regions prone to dispersion from a single run's output. A rank reduction autoencoder builds a structured latent summary of the signals, and supervised sorting marks the sensitive zones. On the studied dataset the approach beats a random forest baseline. Wavelet-based and slope-based signal inputs look most promising, with slope changes giving the best sorting.
arxiv-2605-00170:
Michelle L. Hill and 3 co-authors ask how small a rocky planet can be and still hold on to its air. Their model, called STEHM, covers planets from Earth's size down to half Earth's size. Each model planet has a stiff, unmoving outer shell and orbits in the temperate zone of a Sun-like star.

Under Earth-like settings, planets at or above eight-tenths of Earth's size keep their atmospheres for billions of years, while smaller ones lose theirs. Changed settings shift the line only slightly, though the carbon a planet starts with matters most. Planets rich in carbon and heat-making elements, with cool mantles and small cores, hold their air best. The findings help target future searches for habitable worlds.
arxiv-2605-00470:
Muge Mutis, Ufuk Beyaztas, and Han Lin Shang build a robust estimator for a spatial regression model where the predictor is a curve. In scalar-on-function regression, a number, such as a pollution level, depends on a whole function, such as a day's profile, plus the pull of neighboring locations. Standard estimators, likelihood-based or mildly robust, can be wrecked by outliers, odd predictor curves, or strong spatial dependence.

Their framework first compresses the functional predictor with a robust version of principal component analysis. It then estimates the spatial model through bias-corrected equations allowing redescending loss functions, which fully reject extreme outliers rather than merely downweighting them. Theory establishes consistency and the limiting distribution of the estimated slope function. Simulations show the method holds up under clean data and beats classical and Huber-type rivals under contamination. An application to French air-quality data improves prediction as well.
arxiv-2605-00870:
Sara Rimoldi, Arianna De Vecchi, Hazem Hesham Yousef Shalby, and Federica Villa propose a lightweight gate that detects changes in human activity on wearable sensors. With it, a full recognition network need not run constantly. Continuous classification wastes energy during long stretches of unchanged activity. Their non-parametric algorithm uses dynamic template matching, needs no offline training, and does not require target activity classes to be defined in advance.

The gate costs very little computation per step and calls the full network only when a change is detected, cutting load by more than two thirds in realistic monitoring. Tested on smart glasses, watch, and phone data after brief calibration, it misses almost no real transitions while keeping unnecessary calls low.
arxiv-2605-01070:
Amir Moradifam and Gerardo Orozco-Fernandez study how stable certain minimal surfaces are in the Heisenberg group, a space used in geometry and in models of vision. The surfaces minimize a weighted p-area measure while their p-mean curvature is fixed in advance. That such surfaces exist and are unique was already known. But how much they move when the fixed curvature is slightly changed had not been measured, at least when the curvature is not zero.

Using a duality method of Rockafellar and Fenchel, the authors link each surface to a single vector field and prove that this field stays stable when the curvature changes a little. From that link they derive stability bounds for the surfaces themselves, with stronger bounds in two and three dimensions and explicit rates. Computer tests support the theory. The paper gives the first measured stability results for this class of surfaces.
arxiv-2605-01170:
Kaiping Yin and seven co-authors introduce a skin-like conformal sensor that rebuilds its own three-dimensional deformation in real time from distributed strain measurements. Reliable shape sensing is essential for control of deformable systems, but vision methods need line of sight and complex instrumentation, limiting use in occluded or tight settings. Their device embeds a flat array of printed liquid-metal strain gauges in an elastomeric film.

A mechanics-informed observation model and fast optimization routine estimate local curvature, elongation, offset, and orientation under simultaneous stretching, bending, and indentation. The array achieves low mean error with fast response across tested scenarios. Demos include palm gesturing, finger pressing, and contact-induced balloon shape change. They point to motion tracking, haptic interaction, and surgical monitoring uses.
arxiv-2605-01470:
Akshaya Kumar Jena, Aashima Aashima, Pritam Kumar Jana, and Bortolo Matteo Mognetti design a way to grow crystal layers of a set thickness from a soup of tiny colloid beads. Two bead types are used, and the goal is not just the right number of layers but the right order, with each type on its own plane.

The trick is DNA coating. Beads and the base surface carry short DNA strands tuned to react in a chain, so growth starts at the surface and proceeds locally. Settings of the system fix how thick the stack grows. By shaping the reaction speeds so like beads rarely bind each other, the team force the two types onto separate planes. Theory and reaction-diffusion simulations that capture many-body effects back the design. The work shows reaction timing can serve as a dial for the shape of self-built matter.
arxiv-2605-01670:
Carlos Pérez-Arancibia and Catalin Turc compute how radio and light waves scatter off perfect conductors without ever meshing the empty space around them. Boundary integral methods move the problem onto the surface, and their earlier work solved it indirectly, through stand-in unknowns with no physical face.

This companion paper derives the direct form. Maxwell's conductor problem is split into two vector Helmholtz problems, one for each field, and the unknowns become the fields' own surface traces, split into normal and sideways parts. Those traces mean something: the magnetic version hands back the surface electric current directly. A tailored function space handles the mixed smoothness of the parts. Both direct equations are proven uniquely solvable at every frequency, regularized versions behave as second-kind equations, and a charge-aware fix cures the low-frequency breakdown. A high-order solver in Julia validates the lot.
arxiv-2605-01770:
Ohad Vilk and Baruch Meerson ask why life reproduces by splitting in two. They extend a standard invasion model, branching Brownian motion, where walkers wander, branch, and seed a spreading population, to reproduction of higher order, where one parent makes several offspring at once.

Raising the order changes the story qualitatively. Past binary splitting, invasion fronts generally stop existing at all. Even the binary case holds a surprise: its front speed does not depend on how fast the walkers diffuse. Three-way reproduction sits at a critical edge. Push hard and the population collapses into a tightly localized invasion bullet. Ease off and it spreads by plain diffusion. Exactly at criticality, a whole family of fronts appears. The authors suggest nature's near-universal binary division may be less an accident than a constraint set by the mathematics of invasion.
arxiv-2605-01870:
Nikolaos Giarelis, Charalampos Mastrokostas, and Nikos Karacapilidis focus on Modern Greek, a language with little training data for large language models. Big reasoning models can answer hard questions well, but they are huge and slow. The team asks whether their skill can be passed to a smaller Greek model that runs on normal hardware.

They build CulturaQA, a Greek question and answer set made with a large reasoning model and checked by humans. Using it, they train Maistros, an open 8-billion-parameter model, by distillation and fine-tuning. They also give a light method for testing models and compare nine models on nine Greek test sets.
arxiv-2605-01970:
Debeshee Das and colleagues introduce Trojan Hippo Bench, a test for attacks that hide in an agent's long-term memory. Memory lets a stateless agent recall a user across sessions, but a single bad tool output, such as a crafted email, can plant a dormant payload. It wakes only when the user later raises a sensitive topic and then steals private data.

Past work showed such attacks anecdotally, without a shared test across memory designs and defences. The bench pairs an adaptive red-team system that keeps refining attacks with a scoring method that weighs security against usefulness. The aim is a fair, moving target that shows which memory layers hold up.
arxiv-2605-02070:
Jiafeng Chen and Yihong Wu sharpen a classic result in empirical Bayes theory for the normal means model. The problem is to bound the regret of a learned Bayes rule by the Hellinger distance between estimated and true marginal densities. A 2009 result by Jiang and Zhang did this only after regularising the rule and with an extra cubic log factor, via a delicate recursive proof.

Chen and Wu use polynomial approximation and Bernstein-type bounds for weighted norms to bound the unregularised regret directly. The proof is simpler and gives sharper, sometimes optimal, bounds. For priors on a bounded range they prove the sharp form, and the method extends to priors with exponential tails. Heavy tails still need regularisation.
arxiv-2605-02170:
Nawar Turk, Lucas Miquet-Westphal, and Leila Kosseim report a system for SemEval-2026 Task 6, which grades clarity and evasion in answers from United States presidential interviews. The team compares fine-tuned encoder models with prompt-based large language models on two tasks, a three-class clarity task and a finer nine-class task.

Their language model ensemble scored well on both, placing near the top of each field. Across eight encoders, partly unfreezing layers beat full fine-tuning by a wide margin, and mixing English and multilingual encoders helped the ensemble. Prompt-based models, with no task training, beat fine-tuned encoders, notably on rare classes. Adding the full interviewer turn helped language models but not encoders.
arxiv-2605-02670:
Mihály Kovács, Gyula Molnár, and Máté András Száraz make it cheaper to sample Gaussian random fields on metric graphs, networks whose edges have length. Such fields arise as steady solutions of a fractional stochastic equation driven by white noise. Sampling from the standard finite element version needs a costly factorization, whose time and memory blow up on large graphs.

Their fix combines a Neumann-Neumann split of the graph into domains with a lumping step that simplifies the mass matrix. In tests, the combined approach keeps the exact theoretical convergence rates while giving speedups of several orders of magnitude and large memory savings. For engineers and scientists who model flow, transport, or uncertainty on networks, that turns previously infeasible graph sizes into routine work.
arxiv-2605-02770:
Etienne Corman and three co-authors represent maps between surfaces implicitly, to compute clean one-to-one correspondences. Matching two genus-zero surfaces, with or without boundary, is a staple of geometry processing. Mesh surgery and barrier terms make older methods fragile and complex, above all when the starting map is not one-to-one.

A bijection between two surfaces can be seen as a surface inside the four-dimensional product of the two inputs. The authors store that mapping surface as the zero set of a complex function on the product space. Distortion is then cut by minimizing a well-known energy from physics and geometry, using standard tangent-field tools, with no mesh edits. Landmark points and curves can guide the match, and tangled starting maps can be untangled.
arxiv-2605-03070:
Nihan Aliyev and Shahin Mamedov solve a boundary problem for the axial-vector field in the hard-wall model of AdS/QCD, a holographic stand-in for strong-force physics. They impose the bulk-to-boundary propagator conditions on the field's equation of motion.

The equation reduces to a standard differential form with varying coefficients. By solving paired equations and finding the basic solutions, they set out the key relations and the conditions a solution needs. The resulting integral equation mixes Volterra and Fredholm terms and is solved by iteration, with a new scheme that uses those conditions to prove solvability.
arxiv-2605-03270:
Eirik F. Kjønstad, Huanchen Zhai, James Shee, Sandeep Sharma, and Garnet Kin-Lic Chan benchmark a quantum Monte Carlo method on iron-sulfur clusters, a hard test for strongly correlated chemistry. Phaseless auxiliary-field Monte Carlo often works well here, but its accuracy depends on the trial state that guides it.

Across three clusters, better symmetry-broken trials sometimes made the Monte Carlo energy worse, an inverted pattern fixed only at high trial fidelity. Tests show the culprit is the measurement trial, not spin symmetry alone. Measuring with a simple reference while guiding with a rich trial restored accuracy, suggesting past good results leaned on error cancellation.
arxiv-2605-03970:
Sara Sloman, J. Van Butcher, and Chandra Raman test reversibility in a cold atom fluid at low Reynolds number. In that regime, inertia is tiny. For noninteracting rigid particles, reversing the applied force should exactly retrace each particle's path. Their platform is a magneto-optical trap, used as a model overdamped fluid. The open question was whether reversibility survives interactions between particles.

The team applied controlled forces through a linearly ramped magnetic bias field and monitored the cloud's dynamics. Despite complex 3D rearrangement, the system showed exact reversibility when the force was reversed. That matches Purcell's framework for low Reynolds number flow. Reversibility was not universal, though. Under certain trap alignment conditions, clear deviations appeared. Those deviations were tied to hysteresis in the system.
arxiv-2605-04070:
Yuzheng Xu and fifteen co-authors test whether combining human and artificial intelligence judgments beats either alone across diverse realistic tasks. Human-AI complementarity is a promising route to robust oversight of advanced systems, but its achievability was an open question. The team studies two assistance strategies, hybridization and two forms of AI assistance, on a multi-domain dataset of nearly nineteen hundred samples spanning knowledge, factuality, long-context reasoning, and deception detection.

Complementarity gains were only modest. Hybridization beat the AI alone by less than half a percentage point. It was limited by a small region where humans succeed and the AI errs. Confidence-based routing also failed to find that region. Top-two assistance applied at low AI confidence did raise human accuracy above the AI alone, mostly because humans adopted correct suggestions rather than overriding errors.
arxiv-2605-04170:
Mal Landru and seven co-authors demonstrate a magneto-optical trap that simultaneously traps and cools three atomic species: the two rubidium isotopes 85 and 87, plus cesium 133. The demonstration uses an all-fibre, compact, robust laser system based on telecom-wavelength technologies. Multi-species traps are a stepping stone toward cold-atom interferometry with several species at once, but interspecies losses can empty the trap.

The team characterizes two-body interspecies losses in double- and triple-species configurations and calculates trap-loss coefficients for the rubidium-cesium pairs, finding only a small variation in atom number. No losses were observed between the two rubidium isotopes under their conditions. Despite interspecies interactions, the trap holds on the order of a hundred million atoms of each species, which the authors judge suitable for future multi-species interferometry.
arxiv-2605-04370:
Timothy Carlson and Sanjay Govindjee investigate how a magnetic field changes the movement of ions through solid materials, an effect well known for electrons but rarely reported for ionic conductors. Recent battery experiments show field-driven changes far larger than simple estimates would predict.

The authors derive general transport equations for multi-component solids that include magnetic effects, then specialise them to binary and single-ion conductors. They identify which combinations of material properties should make the effect sizable under realistic composition limits. For the binary case, their model fits measured magneto-resistance data well, giving a firmer basis for judging when magnets might help batteries.
arxiv-2605-04970:
Antonin Berthon, Nicolas Astorga, and Mihaela van der Schaar explore teaching language models new skills through special soft tokens they call skill neologisms. Adding skills by fine-tuning risks erasing old ones, while prompt-based methods are limited by context length and expressiveness. A learned token, by contrast, can be added to the vocabulary without changing model weights.

The team first shows pretrained models already carry tokens tied to procedural knowledge. On a controlled synthetic task, learned skill tokens improved the target skill and combined with unfamiliar skills, and separately trained tokens composed without further training. A natural-language benchmark confirmed the zero-shot composition, suggesting a scalable path to continual learning.
arxiv-2605-05270:
Ademir Batista dos Santos Neto and two co-authors forecast weekly oncology appointment demand in the Cariri region of Ceará, Brazil, using a Bayesian model sharpened by boosting. Accurate trend forecasts guide health service planning and resource allocation. Their model treats weekly appointments as a Poisson process with a Gamma prior on the demand rate, keeping updates analytically simple.

A residual-based boosting step, built on a Gamma-Log-Normal structure, helps the model follow persistent directional shifts in both the short and long term. Against baselines including regression, ARIMA, naive forecasts, neural networks, and XGBoost, the proposed model won on trend detection accuracy. In some cases its share of correct trend directions beat the runner-up by a wide margin.
arxiv-2605-05370:
Finding a good drug candidate usually means testing huge numbers of molecules, most of which fail. Rahul Nandakumar, Ben Fauber, and Deepayan Chakrabarti present SPADE, an algorithm that learns from sparse test results. It is built for new proteins where no earlier data exists to guide the search.

SPADE picks which candidates to test next so that strong binders turn up fast. On average it needs only about forty tests to find ten high-quality molecules. Against deep learning and Bayesian methods it won on more proteins, worked faster, and used far fewer tests to reach the same quality.
arxiv-2605-05470:
Planets around binary stars follow orbits shaped by two suns at once. R. Capuzzo-Dolcetta develops a unified Hamiltonian treatment of mean-motion resonances for both kinds of orbit, those circling one star and those circling the pair. Unlike the Solar System case, the perturbing companion here has real mass, and the theory keeps that fact.

Reduced equations reveal a bistability: the effective potential can hold two stable states when the second harmonic is strong enough. That setting supports stochastic resonance. Checks against known binary-planet systems show current ones sit below the threshold, but extreme systems could qualify.
arxiv-2605-05870:
Shapley values fairly divide credit among contributors, but computing them usually means summing over exponentially many coalitions. Majid Mohammadi and four co-authors exploit product games, where a coalition's value factorizes into per-player terms, as in product-kernel and tree models. For such games, each player's Shapley value collapses into a single one-dimensional integral.

The integrand is a polynomial, so Gauss-Legendre quadrature computes the values accurately and stably. What looked like a combinatorial explosion becomes a routine numerical integral. The method, QuadraSHAP, targets explainability workloads where multiplicative structure is already present, as it is in kernel methods and tree-based models alike.
arxiv-2605-06070:
Zhikai Li and six co-authors refine preference training for text to image diffusion models with arena style scores. Direct preference optimization is efficient, since it skips building a reward model, but its binary feedback is coarse. A chosen and rejected pair says nothing about how large the quality gap between them really is.

ArenaPO infers each model's capability as a distribution from annotated pairwise preferences across many models. Each image is then treated as a sample from its maker's capability, and the pair's quality gap is estimated with latent variable inference. That fine grained signal is computed offline, adding no training overhead and no reward model. Trained on two preference data sets, ArenaPO consistently beat existing baselines.
arxiv-2605-06170:
Wang and five colleagues build an evaluation framework that never sits still. Text-to-image benchmarks usually rely on fixed prompt sets, which models can overfit or memorize once the sets circulate. DynT2I-Eval instead builds a structured space of visual meaning from long-form descriptions, splitting prompts into controllable dimensions like subject, logical constraint, environment, and composition. Fresh prompts stream out continuously through task-specific spaces and difficulty-aware sampling, so tuning to one prompt set stops paying.

Models are scored on text alignment, perceptual quality, and aesthetics, with varied outputs unified into prompt-conditioned pairwise comparisons. A dynamic scheduler with micro-batch aggregation and weighted Bayesian updates keeps a stable online leaderboard as prompt distributions shift and new models arrive. Tests with independent prompt streams confirm the ranking stays robust, balancing fast cold starts against late-entry discovery.
arxiv-2605-06270:
Zecheng Tang and seven co-authors speed up feed forward 3D reconstruction from images with asymmetric token reduction. Transformer based models estimate scene geometry and camera poses directly, but video inputs of hundreds or thousands of frames make global attention quadratically expensive. Token merging helps, yet uniform compression ignores that query and key value tokens play different roles in reconstruction.

The authors show query tokens carry view specific geometric requests and resist compression, while key value tokens hold shared scene context and tolerate deep cuts. Spark3R reduces the two kinds separately, merging within query groups and pruning key value tokens, with the rate adjusted per layer. It needs no retraining and plugs into several pretrained models. On thousand frame inputs it reached speedups up to twenty eight times.
arxiv-2605-06470:
Magnus Victor Boock, Abdullah Akgül, Mustafa Mert Çelikok, and Melih Kandemir learn codes for offline reinforcement learning from hitting times, the expected steps needed to first reach a state. Earlier geometry methods often produce symmetric distances or break the triangle inequality. Their framework instead builds a directed temporal geometry inside a Hilbert space.

They prove the code exists under a closure condition and is unique up to a bounded linear change of frame. Error bounds tie global hitting-time accuracy to one-step transition error. Their Isomorphic Embedding Learning algorithm anchors training with direct hitting-time regression, and maze locomotion tests improve on prior base policy results.
arxiv-2605-06770:
Tiger Yu-Yang Hsiao and twenty-four co-authors measure the metal content of the smallest galaxies yet probed in the early universe. The relation between a galaxy's mass and its metallicity reflects how stars forge metals while feedback expels them. Using about thirty hours of deep JWST spectroscopy of a gravitationally lensed field, they catch a faint oxygen line that allows direct metallicity measurements.

Eight such emitters reach down to galaxies a million times the Sun's mass, and combined with literature objects the sample reaches twenty-one galaxies at redshifts six to eight. Their metallicities sit noticeably below local galaxies of the same mass, with a similar slope but larger scatter, suggesting dilution by inflows of fresh, metal-poor gas.
arxiv-2605-07170:
Yufeng Wu sets a reproducible baseline for spotting metaphor in Chinese text, word by word. Metaphor is everywhere in language, but Chinese identification under the MIPVU annotation framework has seen far less work than English. Wu compares three model families on the one widely available annotated Chinese corpus.

The contenders are a fine-tuned Chinese encoder, a metaphor-focused model adapted with a new dictionary-based resource, and a large generative model tuned cheaply. The adapted metaphor model scored best, slightly ahead of the plain encoder and well ahead of the generative setup. Wu releases splits, outputs, and scripts so later Chinese metaphor work can compare fairly.
arxiv-2605-07270:
Johan Mathe and three co-authors release a software library that makes a powerful symmetry tool practical for machine learning. Many tasks are unchanged by transformations like rotation or translation, and the bispectrum captures all information about a signal up to those transformations. Its cost and scattered implementations had blocked wider use.

Their PyTorch library implements selective bispectra for seven group actions as differentiable modules that drop into learning pipelines. Selective computation cuts costs sharply for finite groups and for rotations on disks and spheres. Profiling shows near-exact invariance in under a millisecond on graphics hardware, and pooling tests beat alternatives when data are scarce.
arxiv-2605-07570:
Argyrios Deligkas and three co-authors study coordinated motion planning, where several robots move on a graph from starting points to destinations without colliding. The goal here is to minimize the total travel length of all robots together. The problem is known to be hard in general, though tractable algorithms exist for full grids and bounded-treewidth graphs.

The team gives a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm, parameterized by the number of robots, for graphs that come from discretizing simple polygons. Such graphs model real settings where motion is confined to a polygonal floor plan, and they generalize rectangular grids. The result is a step toward settling the complexity of the problem on subgrids and on planar graphs generally, both prominent open questions.
arxiv-2605-07870:
Clarissa Lauditi and two co-authors track how the weight spectra of deep networks evolve during training. They split the spectrum into a bulk and a few outlier directions tied to learned features. They build a two-level dynamical mean-field theory that follows bulk and outliers together, even when the outlier directions stay statistically entangled with the random bulk.

Applied to wide nonlinear networks and to deep linear ones, the theory predicts how outliers grow with training time, width, output scale, and initialization. One parameterization gives width-consistent outlier dynamics and clean learning-rate transfer; the other drifts with width. For tasks with many outputs, like ImageNet or language modeling, the bulk itself restructures instead. Their toy model reproduces this, while the spectral edge still converges for wide networks.
arxiv-2605-08070:
James Petullo, Sonny George, Dylan Cashman, and Nianwen Xue cut the cost of a popular reasoning trick. Self-consistency samples many answers from a language model and votes. A weighted version scores each answer's confidence with a second model call, which improves accuracy but adds heavy overhead for every candidate trace.

VecCISC instead measures semantic similarity between reasoning traces and filters out traces that repeat others, degenerate, or hallucinate. Fewer traces then need confidence scoring, so the weighted vote stays cheap. The framework is lightweight and adaptive, aiming to keep most of the accuracy gain of confidence-informed voting at a fraction of its cost.
arxiv-2605-08170:
Nicole Hao measures how well neural operators can match maps between function spaces. The error is scored in Sobolev norms. Those norms track both values and slopes. They fit what PDE theory needs for stability and generalization. Yet bounds for operator learning in them were poorly known.

Hao proves a clean bound. A continuous nonlinear operator on a compact input set can be matched by a neural operator. Its size grows at an explicit rate as the target error shrinks. She then checks the framework against Fourier neural operators on the Burgers equation. That ties the abstract size-error link to a concrete, widely used model.
arxiv-2605-08670:
Li and five colleagues automate reusable agent skills, the distilled strategies that help AI agents solve multi step tasks. Agents still struggle with complex, multi step real world work needing domain specific procedural knowledge, and hand curation demands scarce experts. Their framework, MIND-Skill, induces general skills from wins with an induction agent and a deduction agent.

The induction agent abstracts reusable skills from wins, while the deduction agent rebuilds trajectories by following those skills. Quality is guarded by three textual losses: reconstruction loss comparing input and rebuilt trajectories, outcome loss enforcing correctness, and rubric loss judging documentation and abstraction level. Those losses are jointly optimised with TextGrad, and the skills are tested on held out tasks unseen during optimisation. On AppWorld and BFCL-v3, MIND-Skill consistently beats concurrent skill generation methods. The work turns skill curation from manual craft into an automated pipeline with quality checks.
arxiv-2605-08970:
Julien Hiegel and four coauthors rebuild when each tract of the young cosmos lit up with freed charge. That map squeezes the whole tale of that era into one field. Past work read the field from twenty one cm maps with trained nets. Those nets learn from set world models. Their worth is in doubt when real skies stray from the models. The team tests if a net's calls cohere. Calls from maps at unlike ages should match in their stats when the net fits the world.

Nets trained on warm dark mass at the high end cohere like the cold base net. The low end net strays in a clear way. Nets keep a feel for the world they learned.
arxiv-2605-09070:
Carsten Maple, Abhishek Kumar, and Riya Tapwal challenge how jailbreak attacks on language models are usually scored. Most studies report the success rate of one chosen setting, even though these attacks have many settings that can be combined, and results swing widely across them.

The authors propose two added measures: one for how far the best setting sits above the average, and one for the share of prompts that any tested setting can break. In their tests, combining settings pushed coverage far above the best single result, in one case to every prompt in a standard harm test set. They argue such broader reporting should become the minimum standard for this research.
arxiv-2605-09470:
Barré checks how well the thin-element approximation, the beam propagation method, and the wave propagation method work for binary diffractive gratings. The rigorous Fourier modal method serves as the yardstick. Random binary gratings span varying spatial frequency cutoffs and thicknesses, and each scalar method's transmitted field is compared with the yardstick's.

The results become accuracy maps across spatial frequency and thickness, showing where each method holds up. They give practical rules for choosing the forward model in diffractive optics inverse design work. Designing diffractive optical elements increasingly relies on gradient-based inverse design, where a forward model is tuned against structural parameters to minimise a figure of merit. A weak propagation method can then settle on a design that looks good in simulation but poor in practice.
arxiv-2605-09570:
Matykiewicz and six colleagues present the first end to end FPGA keyword spotter that joins a neuromorphic auditory sensor with a graph neural net on a single device. Edge devices in mobile robotics need efficient on device audio processing. Neuromorphic sensors generate sparse, event based data well suited to that task. Their design drops conventional signal preprocessing. It works directly on event based audio streams through a compute near memory net design.

After quantization, the system reaches about 87 percent accuracy on the Google Speech Commands data set processed through the sensor. End to end latency stays below 35 microseconds. Average power stays just over one watt. By unifying sensing and graph neural inference on one FPGA, the work shows a practical route to real time, low power keyword spotting for embedded and robotic platforms.
arxiv-2605-09770:
Pedersen, Lindeberg and Gerstoft rework how spike-based signals are encoded. They treat spiking neurons as a kind of wavelet, a tool that splits a signal into short bursts at different scales. Spikes are the brief pulses brains use. They are sparse and cheap in energy, but past encodings were mostly probabilistic and cut off from standard signal theory. This paper ties them back to that theory.

Its wavelets keep the sparsity and local timing of spikes. They add firm bandwidths and error bounds, so a signal can be rebuilt up to the limits of spike rounding and time steps. Tests on heart recordings and audio reach reconstruction errors close to those of ordinary continuous wavelets. Because the design maps straight onto neuromorphic chips, it suits low-power hardware that works like a brain.
arxiv-2605-09970:
Pham and Ta studied learning an unknown 3-uniform hypergraph with edge-detecting queries, aiming to recover the hyperedge set with as few queries as possible. They focused on random hypergraphs under the Erdős-Rényi model, where each potential hyperedge appears independently with probability q. Prior work used O(m̄ log n) tests but needed Ω(n³) decoding time, where m̄ is the expected hyperedge count.

Extending the binary splitting framework to the 3-uniform setting, the authors kept the optimal O(m̄ log n) test count while sharply cutting decoding time. Decoding takes O(m̄^{5/3} log n) when θ exceeds 2/3, and O(m̄^{5/3} log²m̄ log n) when θ is at most 2/3. Compared with prior work, the result significantly improves decoding complexity while maintaining optimal query complexity.
arxiv-2605-10470:
Jinyi Luo and four colleagues give multi-modal SR its first theoretical footing. SR rebuilds high-resolution images from low-resolution observations. The problem is severely ill-posed: many high-resolution images could match one low-resolution input. Recent meaning-guided and multi-modal methods exploit large models or external priors. Yet fusion of varied modes remains poorly understood. Their 2026 paper models multi-modal SR theoretically.

Analysis shows prior methods are bottlenecked by sub-optimal mode use. The risk bound improves by strengthening alignment between mode weights and their effective contributions, while reducing coding complexity. That insight inspires M3ESR, a Multi-Modal Mixture-of-Experts Super-Resolution framework with dynamic mode fusion for risk control. It uses a spatial weighting module and a time-adaptive temperature scheduling mechanism for flexible spatial-temporal weighting. Tests show M3ESR greatly boosts transfer and meaning consistency.
arxiv-2605-10570:
Tomasz Klimsiak proves a Brézis-Oswald result on positive solutions of semilinear equations. He works with a linear operator whose resolvent is compact and positivity-improving. Assumptions on the sublinear term match classical elliptic theory. But no further smoothing properties of the resolvent are required. His 2026 paper combines sub- and supersolutions with Brézis-Oswald spectral ideas and new abstract arguments.

The paper thus bridges order methods and energy theory of sublinear problems. Whether a positive solution exists turns on asymptotic slopes. These are lower and upper slopes of f over u at zero and at infinity. Call these a0 and a-infinity. Then lambda1 of a0 less than 0 less than lambda1 of a-infinity implies a positive solution exists. The lambdas are key values of the operator shifted by a0 and a-infinity.
arxiv-2605-10870:
Mingxi Zou and eight colleagues reframe agent memory around decisions rather than descriptions. Long-horizon agents run under tight runtime memory, yet most memory schemes rank experience by relevance, salience, or summary quality, none of which measures whether a memory still supports good choices.

Casting memory as a decision-centered rate-distortion problem, the team derives an exact forgetting boundary for what can be dropped safely and a frontier trading memory budget against decision quality. Their DeMem learner refines its memory partition only when data prove that merging states would cause decision conflict, with near-minimax regret guarantees. Tests on synthetic and conversational benchmarks show steady gains at the same budget. Agent builders get a principle worth memorizing: keep distinctions that change decisions.
arxiv-2605-10970:
Moulik Choraria and four colleagues propose context-gated associative retrieval, a two-stage memory model in which a context gate reshapes the retrieval landscape before and during recall. Hopfield networks connect biology, statistical physics, and transformers, yet most models handle retrieval as a fixed query sent to memory, ignoring context.

Theory shows gating widens separation between memories while inducing sparsity, yielding exponential retrieval gains and a unique self-consistent fixed point driven by direct contextual bias plus a second-order feedback loop. A first-order approximation tested on Llama-3 confirms that in-context learning behaves as context-gated retrieval, with context localizing a memory subspace for clean zero-shot discrimination. Memory researchers get a mechanistic bridge from associative theory to language-model behavior.
arxiv-2605-11470: Zijun Zhao and Francesco Evangelista present X2C-DSRG-MRPT2, an efficient one-step relativistic second-order multireference perturbation theory. It uses the exact two-component Hamiltonian within the driven similarity renormalization group framework. The method captures spin-orbit coupling in strongly correlated systems across the periodic table. Through variational treatment of spin-orbit effects, it yields splittings with mean errors below seven percent against experiment, for systems up to sixth-row elements. With fifth-power scaling, it offers a routine route to relativistic effects in strongly correlated molecules.
arxiv-2605-11570: Fernández-Hernández and five colleagues read the Overfitting-Underfitting Indicator, OUI, as a first usable sign of internal structure during training. Activation functions make deep networks expressive, yet training is usually judged through loss, accuracy, return or calibration. Across their tests, OUI appears as an early, label-free sign spotting weak or promising regimes early. In supervised learning it foresees weight decay regimes. In reinforcement learning it tells learning-rate regimes apart early in PPO, and in online control it can drive weight decay adaptation.
arxiv-2605-11670: Yan, Li and Saito propose releasing spin to stabilize vortex states in self-bound droplets of dipolar Bose-Einstein condensates. Once a vortex enters the droplet, spontaneous magnetization arises axially through a Barnett-like transfer of orbital angular momentum to spin. Applying an external magnetic field to the magnetized droplet rotates the whole atomic cloud without changing its shape, readable as mechanical Larmor precession of a large object. A chirally different droplet pair can also form a stable bound state through attraction between spontaneously magnetized droplets.
arxiv-2605-11770: Yuhao Wu, Tung-Ling Li, and Hongliang Liu ask whether AI agent skills actually do only what they claim to do. Their integrity check compares declared against observed skills by pairing code analysis with language-model extraction, then sorts deviations and their causes. Across nearly 50,000 skills, 80 percent strayed from their claims, mostly through developer oversight rather than malice. The detector scored an F1 of 0.946 on a malicious-skill benchmark.
arxiv-2605-11870: Josef Kittler, Sara Atito, and Muhammad Awais supply, in a 2026 paper, a theoretical backbone for self-supervised learning by clustering. By analogy with supervised learning, they formulate clustering-based self-supervision as K-L divergence optimization. A constraint on the teacher distribution prevents mode collapse and leads to normalization with inverse cluster priors, which, via Jensen's inequality, reduces to the familiar batch centering step. Their model thus grounds two common heuristics in theory and points to new research directions.
arxiv-2605-12070: Zhong Guan and seven colleagues repair off-policy fixing in async agentic RL, where delayed updates and partial rollouts lose the old training-side logits needed for PPO-style fixing. The missing-old-logit problem mixes gap repair with age fixing and breaks clipping and masking rules. They propose three exact capture plans, snapshot version tracking, a special old-logit model, and syncing via partial rollout pauses, plus rough routes keeping split fixing. Their revised PPO-EWMA method gains in both training speed and tuning results.
arxiv-2605-12170: In a 2026 paper, Kyriakos Christou and 23 colleagues present ACTING, a platform joining cyber ranges into one training federation. Cyber defence training needs shared range settings for complex, multi-domain drills across spread-out systems. ACTING offers three parts. First, a structured Exercise Description Language for describing range services and drills. Second, automated scoring of trainee actions through shared data collection. Third, multi-domain drills mixing civilian and military settings. Built on H2020 ECHO federation work, it shows how shared drill descriptions and auto scoring support large, lifelike defence training.
arxiv-2605-12370: Mozafari, Piryani and Jatowt ask how passage design affects answers to questions that must be inferred, not just retrieved. They rank hint sentences by convergence, a measure of how well each sentence rules out wrong answers, and build passages from high- or low-convergence hints. Across six language models on TriviaHG subsets, high-convergence passages beat similarity-based selection by a clear margin, and putting the strongest hints first helps a little more. Convergence, they conclude, is a useful guide for building reasoning passages.
arxiv-2605-12470: Oliver and three colleagues simulate how bumps on the core-mantle boundary stir the outer core. That boundary links core to mantle and may shift day length and the magnetic field. Those effects are still poorly understood. The team runs rotating shell convection with finite bumps. They test harmonics and a mantle model drawn from seismic data. They confirm a new instability below convection onset in global geometry. Deformed contours of constant height let buoyancy feed the mean flow. That raises Reynolds and Nusselt numbers by up to about double.
arxiv-2605-12570: Li and nine colleagues classify lung nodules in CT scans by mimicking how radiologists work across scales. Telling benign from malignant nodules matters for early lung cancer screening, yet nodules vary in scale and texture, and most deep models act as black boxes. Their M3Net builds a progressive multi-scale input, from fine nodule detail through local semantics to global spatial relations, with scale-specific encoders. Cross-scale consistency comes from latent space projection and mutual information maximisation, aiming for accuracy clinicians can inspect and trust.
arxiv-2605-12670: Pillay discusses Lie derivatives and linear differential equations on co-tangent spaces of algebraic D-varieties near sharp points. He also gives an account of Ax's theorem, presented as a useful entry point for students. The notes show how they govern tiny change along vector fields and how Ax's theorem constrains answers to those equations on algebra varieties.
arxiv-2605-12770: Young introduces WriteSAE, a sparse autoencoder for matrix updates in recurrent language-model state. Across Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2 and RWKV-7, token writes a matrix update to a recurrent cache, which a residual-stream autoencoder cannot swap. WriteSAE learns rank-1 matrix atoms matching the shape of the model's own write. Where an atom activates, the write is removed and the atom inserted at its activation scale. The atom gives a closer token distribution than deleting the write in 92 percent of positions.
arxiv-2605-12970: Nasvytis and Fan study what sudden insights look like and whether they transfer, using speech from 189 people solving matchstick-arithmetic puzzles aloud. Participants who faced the same kind of non-obvious solution each time improved faster than those facing a new kind each time. Their speech changed too: the faster group grew more likely to name the problem kind spontaneously. The authors suggest transferable insights are marked by being easy to put into words.
arxiv-2605-13370: Goo, Yun and Jung present Phasor Memory Networks, a fix for unstable explicit memory in sequence models. Classic memory designs suffer exploding or vanishing gradients during training through time, blocking practical language modelling. PMNet limits state changes to phase turns around a complex unit circle, preserving gradient norms without special initialization. With an 85 slot memory tree, it nears perfect retrieval on a copy paste task and matches a model three times larger on long context robustness.

arxiv-2606-04070:
P Zentilini and colleagues recast in 2026 a quantum circuit problem as finding a path through a maze. Splitting a circuit into pieces lets several devices optimize in parallel, but no rule existed for when a split is possible without removing the two-qubit gates that link the pieces.

In their picture, those linking gates are maze walls, and a clean cutting path exists only in one regime. They show a percolation transition, a sharp threshold, separates splittable circuits from unsplittable ones, driven by qubit permutations they generate with simulated annealing. Splitting into two clusters proved possible when the number of linking gates is close to the number of qubits. The result gives a practical, scalable test for partitionability.
arxiv-2606-04270:
Cheng-Gang Li uncovers a hidden two-way link in 2026 between two rival versions of diffusion. Diffusion is the spreading process behind heat flow and particle drift. One version caps the spread speed. The other spreads by long jumps.

Both are known to connect to plain diffusion through subordination, a random time-change trick. Li shows the link also runs backward. Plain diffusion can be got back by applying the inverse time change to the capped process. That two-way link sets up a clean duality between the two versions, with plain diffusion at the center. He then extends the duality to a broad family of such process pairs. The result unifies results that had looked separate.
arxiv-2606-04470:
Hu, Lin, and Nechita study how entanglement shared among many parties is computed in random tensor networks, model systems used to probe quantum gravity ideas, in a 2026 arXiv physics paper. The quantity of interest is the Rényi multi-entropy, which generalizes entanglement entropy from two parties to any number q. In the limit of large bond dimension, simple geometric rules are expected to govern the answer.

For Rényi index two and any number of parties, they prove the multi-entropy is determined by minimal multiway cuts, extending the minimal-cut picture of two-party entanglement. When several cuts tie, they characterize all minimizers through compatible families of cuts, with a criterion for when ordinary partitions suffice. For integer index above two, the minimal multiway cut conjecture fails in general: they give counterexamples for a single random tensor and for networks built from isometric tilings.
arxiv-2606-04770:
Qiao, Guo, and Ye build one encoder that answers two different questions about indoor wireless signals, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Indoor propagation depends on scene geometry, and transmitter and receiver placement. Most learning-based prediction methods target a single representation. WiSER, their wireless scene encoder, predicts both jointly.

WiSER maps a sparse voxel representation of the scene plus a transmitter location into a sparse 3D scene memory. Two decoders query it: a ray-corridor decoder for dense path-gain prediction across a receiver plane, and a set decoder for variable numbers of delay and power taps. The team also built a co-registered dataset from ScanNet++ indoor scenes with Sionna ray tracing. WiSER beat scene-specific radiomap baselines and improved delay and power prediction over channel baselines, suggesting reusable scene encoders for wireless prediction.
arxiv-2606-04870:
Southworth presents the first space-based photometric analysis of CV Velorum, a detached eclipsing binary whose two stars also pulsate, in a 2026 arXiv astronomy paper. The system contains two B2.5 V stars in a circular 6.889-day orbit. Both show line-profile variations from gravity-mode oscillations, and their rotation axes are misaligned with the orbital axis.

Combining new space-telescope light curves with published spectroscopy, Southworth determines the masses as 6.065 and 5.950 solar masses, with radius precision limited by the pulsations themselves. He identifies two confirmed pulsation frequencies and two candidates, though the roughly fifty days of light curves are too short for more. CV Vel sits in the first field the PLATO satellite will observe, so it may become the first eclipsing binary with a slowly pulsating B-star to gain a year-long, high-precision light curve.
arxiv-2606-05070:
Clément Elliker and co-authors release RIDE in this 2026 arXiv paper, an open dataset and benchmark for train delay prediction. Delay forecasts matter to passengers and railway operators alike, but the field lacks standardized datasets, prediction targets, and evaluation protocols, so published results are hard to compare. RIDE is built at nationwide scale over the Belgian railway network.

The resource covers 94.5 million train events, 3.6 million journeys, and 35.7 million weather records from 2023 to 2025, organized as a layered pipeline from raw railway and weather sources to model-ready public releases. Its evaluation protocol standardizes the task and supports direct comparison across models. In the first comprehensive comparison of non-learning, statistical learning, and deep learning methods, learning-based models clearly beat non-learning ones. Graph neural networks achieved the best mean performance. The strongest learning models stayed relatively close to one another.
arxiv-2606-05170:
Jason Z Wang argues that hallucination benchmarks hide crucial differences between models by counting errors without weighing their severity, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A wrong date and a fabricated court ruling each count once, yet their consequences differ by orders of magnitude. At matched accuracy, open-weight models can differ sharply in how their errors spread across severity.

Wang introduces Errorquake-10k, a benchmark of 10,000 queries scoring each response on a severity scale from zero to four, across eight domains and five tiers. He fits severity distributions for 21 open-weight models, borrowing the upper-tail slope used for earthquake magnitudes. Among 210 model pairs, 85 had clearly separated severity indices at matched accuracy, and a human validation study confirmed the measurement is reliable. A Non-Reducibility Theorem shows severity profile and error rate carry non-redundant information: mild errors are mostly retrieval slips, while severe ones are fabrications.
arxiv-2606-05270:
Jia-Cheng Song and a large team realize a programmable anisotropic quantum Rabi simulator on a superconducting processor in this 2026 arXiv paper. The quantum Rabi model couples a two-level system to one bosonic mode, and its symmetry shapes its spectrum and dynamics. Experiments had mostly explored the isotropic limit, where the two couplings are locked together.

The device gives independent control of the rotating coupling, the counter-rotating coupling, and a transverse bias. Continuous anisotropy tuning plus a duality mapping opens the full parameter space between the Jaynes-Cummings and anti-Jaynes-Cummings limits. In the deep-strong-coupling regime, anisotropy reconstructs the spectrum and turns complete collapse-and-revival dynamics into incomplete revivals. With adiabatic state preparation and joint tomography, the team resolved an anisotropy-induced ground-state parity switch with no isotropic analogue. They also observed selective tunnelling tied to a hidden symmetry in biased Rabi models.
arxiv-2606-05370:
Nikita Zaigraev constructs novel higher-spin supercurrents for supersymmetric gauge theories in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is N equals 2 supersymmetric theories of integer-spin gauge supermultiplets, formulated in harmonic superspace, and the goal is their cubic interactions, the simplest couplings among three fields. Zaigraev builds the class of abelian cubic vertices that use the minimal number of spacetime derivatives.

Such vertices exist only when the largest spin is at least the sum of the other two, and they take one form: a gauge prepotential coupled to a conserved higher-spin supercurrent. When the two lower spins differ, a new object appears, the complex principal supercurrent, whose real part generates parity-invariant interactions and whose imaginary part generates parity-breaking ones. The supercurrents are built from gauge-invariant higher-spin Weyl supertensors associated with the two multiplets, defined through analytic prepotentials.
arxiv-2606-05570:
Yan and Kjolstad grade coding agents on real repository work in a 2026 arXiv paper. Easy code tests are nearly solved, but harder repo-level tasks are tough to grade fairly. Human review does not scale, and test coverage is often thin. Their benchmark, TensorBench, holds one hundred ninety-nine tasks on a real tensor compiler framework. The framework extends PyTorch with first-class dense and sparse tensors.

Tasks ask for new sparse formats, speed passes, schedule changes, and numeric operators. Grading applies the agent's patch and runs the full test suite. A pass means old behavior survives and the new feature checks pass. Seven agents from three model families, plus one open model, were graded. Scores ran from about sixty-five percent for the best agent to about twenty-two percent for the weakest. Agents passed strikingly different subsets of tasks, so no single ranking tells the whole story.
arxiv-2606-05870:
Vaithianathan, writing for the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, models why brain regions differ in Alzheimer's risk in a 2026 arXiv paper. Gene expression patterns vary across the cortex, and so does thinning in the disease. Earlier work mostly correlated the two maps. This study builds a generative model that learns hidden biological programs linking the two. Gene data came from the Allen Human Brain Atlas, with nine hundred ten landmark genes over sixty-eight regions.

Thinning maps compared nine hundred twenty-six healthy controls with four hundred twenty-six patients. A variational model with spatial smoothing across neighbor regions tied expression to vulnerability. It predicted regional risk with about eighty-six percent of variance explained. The spatial match between predicted and observed maps was very strong, above nine tenths. The learned programs offer candidate mechanisms for the disease's geography. Cross-scale generation, the author argues, beats correlation for imaging-genetics questions.
arxiv-2606-06270:
Patrick Petitjean catalogues ghostly gas clouds silhouetted against quasars in this 2026 arXiv research note. Proximate damped Lyman alpha absorbers are cold gas clouds sitting close to a quasar's own redshift, so the quasar backlight probes its immediate surroundings. Ghostly systems are a strange subset: dense, compact clouds that only partly cover the quasar's emission regions. They are betrayed by absorption from excited atomic levels needing intense radiation nearby.

From the SDSS DR16 survey, Petitjean presents an updated classification and a revised catalogue of one hundred eighty seven ghostly candidates, more than doubling the known count. Stacked spectra reveal a continuous sequence: as excited level absorption strengthens, so do high ionization lines and velocity spread, among the largest known for hydrogen rich absorbers. Most stream outward at up to two thousand kilometers per second. The evidence places these clouds in compact structures near the active nucleus, many tied to its outflow.
arxiv-2606-06470:
Senmiao Wang and co-authors add a training wheel that comes off at test time in this 2026 arXiv paper on language model training. A weight matrix trains badly when its singular values spread too widely: some directions dominate, others vanish, and optimization wobbles. Their PC Layer reparameterizes weights through a low degree polynomial preconditioner that reshapes that spectrum toward a healthy range throughout pretraining, keeping conditioning stable from start to finish.

After training, the preconditioned weights merge back into the plain architecture, so inference pays nothing extra. In Llama 1B pretraining, the layer improved on standard transformers under both the AdamW and Muon optimizers. The team also proves why it works: for certain deep linear networks, bounding each layer's singular values ensures gradient descent reaches a global minimum geometrically. Muon already controls spectra implicitly, so it needs a lower polynomial degree than AdamW.
arxiv-2606-06570:
Akash Amalan, Georgios Smaragdakis, and Tom J Viering draw family trees for malware in this 2026 arXiv paper. Defenders classify samples one by one while malware evolves, and tracing lineage by hand takes months. Their MalTree framework borrows phylogenetic methods from biology, UPGMA and Neighbor Joining, and applies them to embeddings built from structural, behavioral, and image based features of each sample. The output is an evolutionary tree of malware families, computed automatically at scale.

Validation used VirusTotal timestamps: if the trees are real, inferred ancestors should predate descendants. They do, with eighty seven percent temporal consistency across hundreds of families. Evolution speeds vary wildly, some families mutating over ten times faster than others, which argues for family specific detection strategies. Case studies, including the Mirai botnet, matched documented threat intelligence. The authors pitch lineage aware analysis as a shift from reactive classification toward anticipating where threats evolve next.
arxiv-2606-06670:
Forecasting teams often rebuild their models on a fixed schedule, even when little has changed. Katz asks when a rebuild is truly worth its cost in this 2026 arXiv paper. He defines specification debt, the evidence piling up against the form of the model now in use. He turns it into a trigger rule. That rule weighs the evidence against the cost of changing the model.

The rule is tested on five hundred monthly series from the M4 forecasting contest. The best capped version matched full rebuilding on accuracy. It used about twenty eight percent of the computing time. It also produced steadier forecasts from one period to the next. Fixed rebuild schedules, Katz shows, are just a special case of the rule, arising when evidence against the current model grows at a steady rate.
arxiv-2606-06870:
An assistive robot arm shares control with its user, guessing the goal from small joystick nudges. Belsare and co-authors ask how that robot should show its thinking in this 2026 arXiv paper. When the guessed goal stays hidden, users must correct blindly. Mismatches erode coordination and trust.

The team ran a study with twenty five participants. People used a vision based shared autonomy system on two tasks. The design varied feedback channel, visual against auditory. It also varied richness, sparse against full detail. Feedback clearly improved how well user and robot aligned. It cut the need for corrective input. Participants preferred seeing feedback over hearing it. Richness preferences shifted with task complexity. Showing the robot's full belief spread did not reliably help. The authors distill design guidelines: make the goal legible, and match detail to the task.
arxiv-2606-06970:
Live streams change by the second, so recommending them is a moving target. Teng Shi and co-authors build SSRLive for that problem in this 2026 arXiv paper. Standard recommenders label each item with a fixed semantic ID, a learned code for its content. A live room outgrows any fixed code almost immediately.

SSRLive pairs a generative module with a discriminative one. The generative side produces both static and dynamic semantic IDs. Dynamic codes refresh as the room's content shifts. The discriminative side mixes those codes with user features. It also feeds on live interaction signals like likes and orders. Offline tests beat strong baselines consistently. Online A/B tests on a real platform showed gains in watch time and sales value. Interaction measures rose too. Engineering work kept the added delay negligible. The system now reflects both what a streamer is and what a streamer is doing right now.
arxiv-2606-07170:
Self driving planners usually score a fixed menu of candidate paths and pick the best, even if the whole menu is poor. Xu and co-authors instead search against the scorer in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their method, TOAD, treats the learned scorer as a reward function to maximize directly. It runs the cross entropy method at test time, warm started from the planner's own proposals.

No retraining is needed, and the loop plugs into existing planners. Six different base planners all improved under TOAD. Benchmarks included two NAVSIM versions and the closed loop HUGSIM suite. Scores reached ninety four point seven on the first NAVSIM metric scale. The catch is scorer reliability away from its training proposals. Most current scorers degrade off distribution, limiting how far search can roam. The authors argue future planners should build scorers meant for search. A good judge, used only for ranking, is wasted talent.
arxiv-2606-07470:
Mohamed Kiri, Nunes, Francillon, and Rattanavipanon run neural networks on edge devices without trusting those devices, in this 2026 arXiv paper presenting VeCoDI. A model owner deploying to microcontrollers faces 2 risks: a compromised device could steal the model, and results could be fabricated. Existing trusted execution environments protect models but bloat cost and the trusted code base. VeCoDI introduces Shangri-La, a third runtime environment inside ARM TrustZone-M hardware, sitting between the secure and non-secure worlds in privilege.

Untrusted inference code runs in the normal world, while secure support guards model confidentiality and verifies that inference ran on the parameters. The team built the framework on a development board and open-sourced the prototype. Measurements showed a trusted computing base, memory footprint, and runtime overhead. The authors present VeCoDI as a practical middle path for verifiable, confidential inference on the devices where trusted environments cannot fit.
arxiv-2606-07570:
Cheng and a large team test whether language models can recover what a divided research field agrees on, in this 2026 arXiv case study. High-temperature superconductivity has been argued over for decades, with competing mechanisms and evidence scattered across the literature. The team assembled nearly 18,000 highly cited papers spanning 7 decades and used language models to extract a structured knowledge graph linking proposed mechanisms, material families, types of evidence, and citation relations. The question was whether anything coherent survives at scale.

The extracted results did recover clear structure: material families showed clear profiles, evidence types correlated, and citation patterns traced how beliefs evolved over time. Ablating prompts, settings, and the model left it robust. The authors conclude language models can serve as instruments for mapping consensus in fields where claims are implicit, evolving, and contested. Superconductivity serves as the hard test case.
arxiv-2606-07670:
Li, Pal, and Tan ask whether a different kind of neural network can animate three-dimensional scenes more smoothly, in this 2026 arXiv paper from Monash University. The setting is deformable 3D Gaussian splatting, a method that renders a moving scene by shifting a set of soft three-dimensional blobs over time. The usual deformation network treats each moment separately, so smooth motion is never built in.

The authors swap that network for liquid neural network cells, a design whose hidden state follows a continuous-time rule with a learned time gate, while leaving the rest of the pipeline untouched. Across eight D-NeRF scenes and seven NeRF-DS scenes, the liquid version matches or beats the standard baseline overall. Its clearest gains appear on scenes with fast, jointed motion, where built-in smoothness matters most, and the change needs no numerical solver at run time.
arxiv-2606-07870:
Tepper and Willke revisit how to compress vectors for fast similarity search, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Quantisation shrinks database vectors so nearest-neighbour search stays quick; additive quantisers have long set the accuracy standard, while scalar methods recently revived. The authors argue the winning move is the opposite of the usual one: cut dimensions, but spend more bits on each remaining one.

Their framework, ASH, learns an orthonormal projection that reduces database vectors before scalar quantisation, while queries stay in original form. That asymmetry is the point: a learned reduction keeps the information search needs. At equal compression, ASH beats the best additive and scalar quantisers on accuracy. Its similarity computations map efficiently onto SIMD hardware instructions, and learning and encoding are fast. Across many datasets the authors report state-of-the-art recall and speed in every compression regime tested.
arxiv-2606-08070:
Bipin Singh Koranga and Vivek Kumar Nautiyal warn that two ignored effects can corrupt a flagship measurement of neutrino physics, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Long-baseline experiments send neutrinos through Earth to measure CP violation, the matter-antimatter asymmetry of neutrino oscillation. The analysis usually pretends Earth's density is constant along the path, and separately, theorists ask whether Planck-scale quantum gravity perturbs the oscillation.

Using layered density profiles from the reference Earth model, the authors test the shortcut. The bias in the CP parameter stays under a third of a degree up to five thousand kilometres. Then it explodes: about eighteen degrees at seven thousand kilometres, and about one hundred seventy-two at twelve thousand, a complete sign reversal. Worse, quantum gravity corrections can mimic or cancel the density bias, making the two inseparable in fits. For experiments targeting five-to-ten-degree precision, this is a fundamental obstacle.
arxiv-2606-08170:
Yuhong Shi and co-authors keep a human expert in the training loop of self-driving policies, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Data-driven driving models built on large foundation models perceive richly but falter in complex interactions and rare long-tail scenarios, where distribution shift and causal confusion rob them of human-level judgement. Pure imitation inherits those blind spots.

Their HiL-OBC framework runs in three phases: policy initialisation with human intervention, latent behavioural modelling with Bayesian adaptation, and online deployment with updates. A multimodal cloning model refines the base policy through a lightweight network, a takeover trigger summoning the human when needed, and a multi-variant loss. On the LangAuto-Human CARLA benchmark, driving scores of three systems rose by roughly forty-seven, thirty-two, and thirty-two percent after human-in-the-loop optimisation, while traffic violations fell.
arxiv-2606-08370:
Lewandowski and colleagues implement a biologically inspired vision sensor on a processor inside the pixel array itself, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Standard dynamic vision sensors detect changes in brightness over time, offering high speed and dynamic range. The authors ask whether adding further retinal stages, spatial filtering and gain control, helps tasks such as saliency prediction, which estimates where viewers will look. They present the first implementation of a multi-stage silicon retina model on the SCAMP-5 pixel processor array.

Using a lightweight network, the team evaluated the model on intensity reconstruction and saliency prediction. The bio-inspired model reconstructed intensity worse than the standard event representation. But it cut saliency prediction loss by about thirteen percent in the reported experiments, and reduced the event rate by nearly half.
arxiv-2606-08570:
Yunhyung Cho, Myungho Kim, Yoosik Kim, and Euiyong Park build convex bodies encoding the geometry of flag varieties, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Newton-Okounkov bodies attach a convex set to a variety together with a valuation. For well-chosen values the body is a polytope whose volume computes classical invariants. Flag varieties, whose points are nested sequences of subspaces, are central in representation theory. The authors construct such polytopes for Schubert varieties inside partial flag varieties of any type.

Cluster algebras supply coordinates and mutations that the construction exploits to define the valuation. When the main cluster algebra is of infinite type, the authors prove results bounding the resulting bodies for very ample line bundles. The work extends earlier type-specific constructions to all Lie types in a uniform way, giving theorists a new supply of explicit polytopes for Schubert geometry.
arxiv-2606-08670:
Danese and colleagues generate synthetic brain scans efficiently enough for routine augmentation, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Large, balanced datasets are essential for reliable neuroimaging biomarkers. Brain scan synthesis can supply the extra data. Existing approaches either cost too much at volumetric scale or rely on lossy latent compression that may compromise anatomical detail. Their framework, WaveDiT, works in a transformed space instead of raw voxels, the three-dimensional pixels of a scan.

The model performs flow matching in the coefficient space of a wavelet transform, which separates the image into scale and detail bands. Factorized spatio-depth attention keeps the computation tractable. Band-wise uncertainty modeling tracks how variable each band is. The predicted uncertainty feeds into the training loss. The aim is faithful full-volume synthesis on standard hardware, so labs without big compute clusters can still augment their training sets with ease.
arxiv-2606-08970:
Wang and colleagues tackle a paradox of vision-language models: the biggest model loses to a small one on a given query, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-language models answer questions about images, and dozens differ in skill and cost. No single model wins everywhere. The authors built a dataset of 7 mainstream models' outputs on 32,626 image-text queries, then trained a router called ARMS. The router reads a query plus profiles of each model, and picks which should answer.

The paradox is stark. Among queries that GPT-4o answered wrongly, a free open-source model answered 43.18 percent correctly. ARMS exploits such complementarity, and stays small: at 800 million parameters it adapts to models cheaply through incremental or independent training. In tests on familiar and shifted distributions, ARMS beat commercial models hundreds of times its size. The authors release the dataset, code, and models for others studying multimodal routing.
arxiv-2606-09070:
Wu and Wang tackle the tug-of-war between computing and communicating in decentralized optimization, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In decentralized optimization, nodes, robot swarms or compute clusters, jointly minimize a shared objective, with no coordinator. Each round mixes local updates with neighbor communication, whose costs differ sharply: radios drain robot batteries, while big datasets make computation the bottleneck. Classic methods fix local updates in advance, fitting neither world.

Viewing local updates through majorization-minimization, their Robust Inexact Algorithm framework unifies existing multi-update methods and exposes the bottleneck: the worst-case stepsize must shrink in proportion to the number of local updates. AdaDQN escapes this with double-level adaptivity. A safeguarded, consensus-aware rule stops local updates when agreement error outweighs progress, event-triggered communication broadcasts only on significant change, and a memoryless BFGS update supplies curvature cheaply. They prove global convergence and test it against known baselines.
arxiv-2606-09470:
Aditya Parikh and his colleagues build a speech model that grades second-language learners and explains its grades in words in this 2026 arXiv paper. Automated pronunciation assessment usually outputs bare scores, which learners cannot act on. Their rubric-guided SpeechLLM instead predicts several things at once: sentence-level labels for accuracy, fluency, and prosody, plus word and sound level accuracy. All come in a single response with a written rationale.

Training combined supervised fine-tuning with Bounded Direct Preference Optimization, a method that teaches the model to prefer better label sets over perturbed ones. On the SpeechOcean762 benchmark, the joint model matched or beat single-granularity specialists while staying competitive with earlier approaches. The authors then audited the explanations themselves. Sentence-level rationales were plausible and agreed with the model's own scores, but faithfulness weakened at the word and sound level, where references to specific errors were sparse.
arxiv-2606-09670:
Mateo Diaz-Bone and his co-authors harden factory defect spotting for the messy real world in this 2026 arXiv paper. Anomaly detection flags parts that stray from the norm, using only good samples in training. Top methods ace clean lab sets like MVTec. Real lines break their quiet premises: scale, light, view, and backdrop all drift.

The team adds three fixes to a student-teacher design, where a small net learns to mimic a big one's view of good parts. First, visual prompting masks cut the part from its backdrop, so stray marks behind it stop counting. Second, the teacher is partly unfrozen, with guards against collapse, so it can adapt to a new line. Third, fake images from a diffusion model widen the training mix. On the hard AeBAD set, the gains reached three and a half points over the past best score.
arxiv-2606-09870:
Gregory Magarshak designs a storage cloud whose keepers cannot read a byte of what they hold in this 2026 arXiv paper. Safecloud splits each file into fixed chunks and seals each one on the owner's device before it ships. Two node kinds serve the net. Drops are plain browser tabs that stash sealed chunks, while Jets are routing servers that match chunks to homes.

Keys stem from one root secret by a set ladder, so the root alone needs safekeeping. Shared keys let a guest with a scoped grant derive the same chunk keys as the owner. Pure copies of one file yield the same sealed form, so dedup works with no peeking. Three trees share one path: one guards integrity, one hands out keys, one holds grants. A player can derive each next segment key from the last, which makes seeking cheap.
arxiv-2606-09970:
Ji and colleagues use a glowing hydrogen line to look inside one of astronomy's new puzzles, in a 2026 arXiv paper on galaxy evolution. Little Red Dots are compact, red sources found across deep James Webb fields, and their nature is still unclear. The team studies Lyman-alpha emission, light from hydrogen tracing neutral gas around galaxies. Their sample holds one hundred ten confirmed Little Red Dots at high redshift, all with spectroscopy of that line.

They detect emission in thirty-two, with brightness and line strengths resembling normal star-forming galaxies at similar distances. Yet ratios against another hydrogen line fall low, and emission tracks ionized oxygen output closely. For thirteen distant cases, maps show Lyman-alpha light extended, asymmetric, and often offset from the main light. The evidence supports a two-component picture: a compact red source inside a larger host galaxy whose clumpy gas reshapes the escaping light.
arxiv-2606-10470:
Wakabayashi shows in this 2026 arXiv paper that an ordinary transistor measurement can reveal a timing property of a two-dimensional semiconductor that previously needed fast laser equipment. The material is tungsten diselenide, WSe2, in thin multilayer transistors. Its charge carriers sit in distinct energy pockets called valleys, and the intervalley relaxation time, how long carriers take to move between valleys, is normally measured optically. Wakabayashi extends a valley-thermodynamics model with one relaxation equation for each valley's carrier share.

The theory predicts three signatures of that relaxation time. Transconductance should trace a Lorentzian curve in frequency whose peak locates the time. After a sudden gate step, the current should settle in two stages, overshooting in a bilayer device and undershooting in a trilayer. Gate sweeps should leave hysteresis growing with sweep rate, and a sign reversal between two and three layers separates valley effects from charge trapping.
arxiv-2606-10670:
Reddy maps the difficulty of a graph labelling problem in this 2026 arXiv paper in computer science. In signed domination, every vertex gets a label of plus or minus one, and each vertex's closed neighbourhood must sum to at least one; the goal is minimum total weight. The problem was known to be NP-complete on bipartite, chordal, and planar graphs. This paper extends the hardness map: it stays NP-complete on split graphs, a subclass of chordal graphs.

By feedback vertex set number, the problem is W[1]-hard, the sign that no efficient fixed-parameter algorithm is likely. That hardness covers treewidth and clique-width too. But for two stricter parameters, neighbourhood diversity and twin cover number, fixed-parameter tractable algorithms exist, running fast when the parameter is small. Open questions remain on interval graphs, kernels, and more parameters.
