arxiv-2606-10770:
Guancheng Zhou and colleagues fix a distortion in random forest explanations in this 2026 arXiv paper on statistics. Random forests report variable importance, a ranking of which inputs drive predictions, but the calculation ignores correlations among variables. A variable correlated with many others gets diluted or masked entirely, even when it matters, because correlated partners absorb the credit. The authors group variables by conditional correlation, that given the response, so scores can be corrected for this interference.

Two efficient options are explored: one handles each variable alone, separating it from its correlated companions before scoring. The other clusters them by pairwise correlation and scores each group. Experiments on benchmark data sets show both produce sound corrections, restoring those the scores had masked. Although motivated by random forests, the correction applies to scores from predictive methods generally, and such rankings guide model reading, selection, and diagnosis in practice.
arxiv-2606-10870:
Sinclair recasts finite free convolution in this 2026 arXiv paper. The operation, from Marcus, Spielman, and Srivastava, mixes polynomials the way free probability mixes random variables, but at fixed finite size. Sinclair builds it from a reproducing kernel inner product and a multilinear model over the squarefree ring, where additive convolution becomes plain multiplication.

A nilpotent logarithm then straightens the operation and recovers the finite free cumulants of Arizmendi and Perales. The view defines a class of polynomials with nonpositive higher cumulants, closed under it. Every graph Laplacian pencil belongs to it; there the higher terms count Hamiltonian cycles in induced subgraphs.
arxiv-2606-11070:
Winata and a large Capital One team introduce T1-Bench in a 2026 arXiv paper, a benchmark for AI agents doing customer-facing work. Existing agent benchmarks cover few domains, use static tasks, and rarely force an agent to juggle several domains at once. Real service work mixes domains inside one long conversation, demanding sustained reasoning and coordination.

T1-Bench spans twenty-five domains, eleven single-domain and fourteen multi-domain settings, with seventy-six tools and 525 scenario templates, plus extensive human annotations. Twelve proprietary and open-weight models were evaluated, with human judgments complementing automatic scoring. Complexity bites hard: as the number of simultaneously active domains rises toward eight or eleven, turns and token costs climb steeply, and weaker models exhaust their turn budgets without finishing. The hardest tasks consumed up to 1.78 million tokens per conversation in the reported runs.
arxiv-2606-11270:
König, Kazmi, Li, and Chaudhary measure how much bad behavior leaks through model distillation in a 2026 arXiv paper. Distillation trains a small student model on a teacher's outputs. Subliminal learning is the worry: even on entirely benign training data, a student can inherit a teacher's hidden undesirable traits. The team quantifies this with subliminal behavioral transfer ratios.

They steered two teacher models, Llama-2-7B-Chat and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, at varying strengths, then distilled students using only benign data. Judged by GPT-4 on 100 JailbreakBench prompts, transfer was robust but scaled differently per family. Llama-2 showed a sharp threshold: students stayed safe until the teacher was severely compromised, then absorbed 25 to 32 percent of the degradation. Qwen2.5 transferred continuously and higher, with ratios up to 0.61 in the strongest case. The authors argue distillation pipelines need behavioral auditing beyond inspecting training data.
arxiv-2606-11570:
Feiqing Huang, Zongqi Xia, Rong Ma and Tianxi Cai address rare disease research in this 2026 arXiv paper on electronic health records. Their goal is spectral embedding, a technique that compresses many clinical variables into a few summary coordinates for patients and medical concepts. Rare disease groups are small, so the authors borrow strength from a knowledge matrix, a table of concept relationships taken from a much broader patient population.

Their method, called SENT, works in two steps. First it removes parts of the knowledge matrix that do not match the target group. Then a projection step separates structure shared with the broader population from structure unique to the rare group. Unlike older methods, it does not assume the two sources line up one to one. Simulations and a real multiple sclerosis group show SENT beating rival methods, especially when shared signals are weak or only partly aligned.
arxiv-2606-11670:
Zijie Meng leads a Peking University team keeping a person's identity stable in generated video in this 2026 arXiv paper. A generated character must stay recognisable through motion, big viewpoint changes, expressions and blocked views. Standard methods lean on one reference photo, which tangles identity with pose, lighting and background.

Their framework, Argus, instead builds a stacked identity mosaic: a three-by-three grid of informative moments chosen by a multimodal language model from reference images and clips. The mosaic is injected into the video generator as read-only memory, refreshed with the generation process. Extra training with mismatched counterfactual pairs and guidance tricks adds robustness without paired subject videos. On a standard benchmark the system tops the field, scoring above sixty-four in total. On their new HardID-Celeb stress test it beats the strongest rivals by about thirteen points on large head turns and fifteen under first-frame occlusion.
arxiv-2606-11970:
Annika Stiehl and five colleagues detect epileptic seizures from just a few electrodes in this 2026 arXiv paper. Wearable monitors promise patient-friendly seizure diaries, but a behind-the-ear setup sees far less of the brain than a full scalp montage, and the signal is noisier. The team asks whether hybrid neural networks can compensate.

They simulated the behind-the-ear montage from a large public seizure corpus and compared several architectures combining convolutional and recurrent networks. Their best model merges temporal and spectral feature streams. It reached a detection quality score near eighty-six percent and balanced accuracy near seventy-nine percent on held-out patients. Performance held up across different reference montages, nearly closing the gap to full-scalp recordings. The authors caution that false alarms remain too frequent for fully autonomous daily use. They recommend event-based post-processing and validation on real wearable recordings.
arxiv-2606-12170:
Velásquez-Toribio adds controlled randomness to a classic tool for weighing galaxies, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The spherical Jeans equation links how fast stars move inside a round system to the gravity holding it. In scalar-tensor gravity, where gravity's strength is set by an extra field, that strength can wobble by place. The paper models those wobbles as noise added to the gravitational coupling.

The noise makes it a stochastic differential equation, whose solution spreads randomly as radius grows. A Fokker-Planck equation then tracks the probability distribution of the velocity spread. Because the noise is additive, the classic Jeans answer survives exactly as the mean profile, now wrapped in a probability band. Formulas give the variance and covariance too. The framework is worked out for three standard halo shapes and carried through to the line-of-sight speeds observers actually measure.
arxiv-2606-12470:
Touati asks how a black hole dies when space has a grain, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In non-commutative geometry, coordinates fail to commute, imposing a minimal length near the Planck scale. Applied to a Schwarzschild black hole through gauge gravity, the deformation changes its thermodynamics. The Hawking temperature, which classically diverges at the end of evaporation, stays finite. Evaporation halts before completion, and the entropy gains a logarithmic correction.

Touati tracks what particles carry away. The Bekenstein entropy loss per emitted quantum decreases as evaporation proceeds. The total number of emitted particles tracks the entropy's behavior, a consistency sign for radiation that is not thermal. The headline quantity is sparsity: the ratio comparing emission gaps to the quanta's timescale. For this black hole it exceeds one, meaning the radiation dribbles out in quanta, not a continuous flow. Sparsity diverges in the last stage, as the hole falls silent.
arxiv-2606-12570:
Ho and co-authors shake tiny floating sliders on water and read the water's pushback, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Bodies at an air-water interface feel unsteady hydrodynamic resistance: drag plus added mass, the illusion of extra weight from fluid that must move along. At rapid oscillation and small amplitude, theory says the flow beneath a body forms an oscillatory Stokes boundary layer. That thin sheared sheet sets the resistance.

Using magnetic actuation, the team drives planar sliders harmonically and records amplitude response and phase lag in steady state. They vary frequency, mass, size, and shape, from circles of several radii to squares and ellipses. Effective added mass and damping extracted from the responses match boundary-layer theory where surface deformation stays small. Even the startup transient is predicted accurately, by a history integral tracking the boundary layer's growth.
arxiv-2606-12670:
Drillick and Haunschmid-Sibitz introduce a censored stochastic six-vertex model and prove a partial censoring inequality for it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The six-vertex model is a statistical mechanics system readable as particles on a line, whose paths may pass or block each other. In the censored version, vertices are restricted so particles and holes cannot pass there. A censoring inequality says such restrictions only push a system further from steady state.

The theorem shows that, from a step initial condition with all right-hand sites occupied, the censored process stays stochastically dominated by its blocking measure at every time. Configurations therefore remain below the steady-state distribution. That bound controls second-class particles, markers of discrepancies between coupled copies. The proof runs through parabolic Kazhdan-Lusztig R-polynomials, whose appearance is explained by a link with Iwahori-Hecke algebras, and yields an intertwining relation too.
arxiv-2606-12970:
Dasdan presents a unified, formally verified treatment of binary search and its variants, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Binary search is simple in concept yet notoriously difficult to implement correctly. Historically, most published versions worked only for special array lengths, and professional programmers shipped buggy implementations. An integer overflow bug survived for decades in widely used code. The paper systematises the design space behind those pitfalls.

It covers 5 variants, 6 derived query functions, and 4 library implementations, from BSD and glibc to Java and the C++ standard library, each with consistent notation, loop invariants, and analysis. It also introduces a combined search that subsumes all variants in a single call. Every algorithm is provided as synchronised Python code, a Dafny formal proof, and pseudocode. All implementations are checked by over 9,500 tests and 21 Dafny formal verifications, and 6 deliberately faulty versions demonstrate common bug categories and the verifier's ability to detect them.
arxiv-2606-13570:
Kramer, Schubert, and Eisert establish hardness limits for approximating constraint satisfaction problems in this 2026 arXiv paper. The problem family, max-LINSAT, asks for an assignment maximising satisfied linear equations over a finite field. Beating random guessing is hard for efficient algorithms. When each variable appears in only a bounded number of constraints, however, algorithms can beat the random baseline by a margin shrinking with the degree bound. For Boolean variables that margin's scaling was known to be optimal.

Whether the same holds over general finite fields, and for quantum algorithms, was open. The authors extend the hardness to bounded-degree instances over arbitrary finite fields, proving the algorithmic guarantee cannot be improved in general. They then draw out the link to decoded quantum interferometry, a quantum scheme whose performance depends on exactly this approximability. The results draw a sharp line around what either method can achieve.
arxiv-2606-13870:
Ben-Levi and colleagues probe a worrying habit of vision-language models: answering questions about an image that was never shown. Such mirage answers can be right by luck or bias, inflating test scores without real seeing. Their 2026 arXiv paper argues this is not one failure but two. Contrastive probes on internal activations separate answers driven by text habits from answers built on false internal pictures.

Across two open-source models and three benchmarks, mirage behavior could be read off linearly from internal signals at many network sites. A text-only baseline could not recover that signal, ruling out word patterns as the cause. The team also defines a Prior Harnessing Index, measuring how much a model answers from text alone. The split matters for fixes. Cleaning text data may cure text-driven mirages, but false-picture mirages live in the visual parts. Those need fixes at that deeper level.
arxiv-2606-14070:
Umemura, Taniguchi, and Kakogawa upgrade a robot crawling inside three-inch sewer pipes too narrow for ordinary cameras. Japan's network held about thirty-nine thousand two hundred kilometers of pipelines over fifty years old in 2024, and pipes under one hundred millimeters wide resist push-in cameras at bends. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents Xbot-2, linking propulsion units with an articulated differential mechanism of X-shaped linkages. One wire changes the units' posture, adapting to diameter changes.

The first version lacked traction and stuck at pipe joints. The new control detects obstacle contact from current load on the drive wheel motors, then slackens the wire so units flex over the step. In simulated pipe experiments, a three-unit robot passed joint steps smoothly, significantly improving step-over capability. The detection threshold was set experimentally; a more general method is needed before long runs in real piping.
arxiv-2606-14270:
Hou and colleagues teach an armless robot on two wheeled legs to get up after a fall, first lending it an invisible helping hand. Humanoids rise using arms; quadrupeds use spare legs. A bipedal-wheeled robot has neither, only leg actuation. Their 2026 arXiv paper introduces FTSR, a force-guided teacher-student framework with stage-wise rewards. In simulation, an external auxiliary force, tied to the robot's real-time height, supports it; constrained reinforcement learning guides the policy to need that force less and less.

Height-progressive rewards structure recovery: stabilize posture first, then transition to sustained locomotion. The teacher-student setup distills privileged knowledge of force effects into the deployable policy. The policy then ran on a physical robot, recovering robustly from falls under diverse conditions and keeping full post-recovery motion: it stands up and drives on. The framework also transferred to a high-degree-of-freedom humanoid.
arxiv-2606-14670:
Colter Richardson and co-authors review low-frequency gravitational waves from collapsing stars in a 2026 arXiv paper. When a massive star's core collapses into a supernova, waves arise below about fifty hertz. The explosion's global shape drives part of the signal. Anisotropic neutrino emission drives the rest. Part of the signal is linear memory. Memory is a permanent spacetime offset left by passing waves. Here it is sourced by the escaping neutrinos.

The authors explain how neutrino-driven memory is generated. They show results for an example progenitor star of fifteen solar masses. Its composition is solar. For detection they discuss two tools combined. One is a linear predictive filter. The other is matched templating in current detectors. They close with prospects for future instruments. These include Cosmic Explorer, the Einstein Telescope, the space antenna LISA, and a proposed lunar antenna.
arxiv-2606-15070:
Li and coauthors stop reasoning models early by watching their attention patterns in a 2026 study. Large reasoning models often overthink, producing redundant chains that waste tokens and can hurt accuracy. Confidence-based stopping rules misfire because models sound sure on hard problems and unsure on easy ones. The authors look inside the model instead.

Their method, ASAG, reads attention distributions to infer the model's current reasoning state. Attention entropy reflects how focused or diffuse the internal process is. Combined with outside confidence, that signal decides when further reasoning stops helping. The framework needs no training and plugs into existing reasoning models directly. Across nine benchmarks, ASAG improves accuracy on mainstream models of several sizes. On Qwen3-8B it cuts generated tokens by nearly two fifths while raising average accuracy. The authors argue internal information flow is a more principled basis for adaptive generation than output confidence alone.
arxiv-2606-15170:
Askoura presents a new integral for vector-valued functions in a mathematics note from Université Paris II. Classical integration sums real-valued functions against measures, which add up over disjoint sets. A capacity is a set function that need not add up, so integrals against it behave differently. The Choquet integral handles real-valued functions in that setting. The Dunford integral handles vector-valued functions, but only against measures. Askoura merges the two into a Dunford-Choquet integral for Banach-space-valued functions.

The integral is defined through the function's pairings with dual vectors, integrated in Choquet's sense. Askoura establishes basic properties showing the construction behaves like an indefinite integral. Integrating over varying sets yields a new capacity built from the original one. That derived capacity inherits key features such as monotonicity from the starting capacity. The note extends integration theory to vector data under non-additive set functions.
arxiv-2606-15270:
Özer and Filiz derive generalized Schwarzian dynamics from two-dimensional BF gravity in a 2026 theoretical physics paper. The Schwarzian action usually enters as a boundary theory for nearly anti-de Sitter gravity. These authors instead start in the bulk, with BF theory's flat gauge connections. Boundary dynamics then emerge from the theory's boundary phase space after reductions. For the smaller gauge group, the reduction recovers the ordinary Schwarzian action. The larger rank-three case yields a genuine generalization of it.

That dynamics is governed by the second and third Wilczynski invariants. These invariants are projective values attached to curves in projective space. Constant values of them fix the theory's Casimir charges and monodromy data. Those data in turn organize its thermodynamics. The bulk-first route unifies Schwarzian dynamics with projective geometry and gauge theory. It shows the boundary action is emergent, not basic, in this setting.
arxiv-2606-15370:
Odendaal and coauthor reproduce and extend MNet in a 2026 medical imaging paper. MNet outlines organs and tumors in scans whose slices are unevenly spaced, a property called anisotropy. Thick slices break purely three-dimensional networks, while flat two-dimensional ones ignore depth. MNet mixes both views inside each block, and the authors rebuilt it inside the standard nnU-Net framework to check its published claims.

The rebuild matches the original closely, scoring within a point of the published result on prostate MRI. Two additions follow. A learned fusion gate, which blends the flat and volumetric views adaptively, adds a small accuracy gain at negligible cost. A state-space module for long-range depth reasoning gives the best liver score on CT scans and steadier results overall. Both keep the network's robustness when slice spacing grows, which matters because clinical scans rarely arrive with tidy, even spacing.
arxiv-2606-15470:
Başer and coauthors turn a memory quirk into a hardware fingerprint in a 2026 computer engineering paper. A physical unclonable function, or PUF, answers challenges with a device-specific signature born of manufacturing variation, useful for authentication and key generation. The quirk here is simultaneous multiple-row activation: a crafted command sequence opens up to thirty-two DRAM rows at once, and charge sharing between them settles differently on every chip.

Testing 112 commercial DDR4 chips, the team shows the resulting signatures repeat well on the same chip while barely overlapping across chips, and activating more rows improves repeatability. The two-row version also answers faster than the best previous DRAM PUF. Temperature shifts do degrade the match, which deployments must handle. Because DRAM already sits in nearly every computer, a PUF harvested from commodity memory could add hardware identity to systems with no spare silicon budget.
arxiv-2606-15770:
Tan and Dinh describe their SemEval-2026 system for detecting political evasion in 2026, classifying how U.S. presidential interview answers dodge questions. The shared task sorts question-answer pairs into clarity classes and nine finer evasion strategies. The team compares fine-tuning open models cheaply against structured chain-of-thought prompting of large reasoning models.

Prompting wins decisively. Their best system, Grok-4-Fast with extended reasoning and few-shot hierarchical prompting, reaches a Macro F1 of about 0.51 on the nine-class evasion subtask and about 0.80 on the three-class clarity subtask, placing eighth and thirteenth on the leaderboards. Fine-tuned Qwen models trail well behind. Ablations show a hierarchical label taxonomy structures the model's reasoning, and few-shot examples calibrate it. Switching on extended reasoning brings substantial gains, matching the multi-step pragmatic analysis evasion detection demands. Careful prompting of a strong reasoner beat bespoke training outright.
arxiv-2606-15970:
Sheshadri determines in 2026 exactly how far one method for lower-bounding determinantal complexity can reach. Determinantal complexity measures the smallest matrix whose determinant equals a given polynomial. The polar, or conormal, method reads geometric invariants of that matrix representation to prove lower bounds. Sheshadri asks what the method itself can and cannot see.

The answer comes as a matched pair of exact results. On one side, the reading cost of the method is computed in closed form as a polar intersection number with binomial formulas. On the other side, the invariants it can read are bounded exactly. Together they cap every bound from this method at quadratic growth on the diagonal case studied. Small cases match classical projective duality values, which anchors the formulas. The no-go result tells researchers to stop pushing this method past its ceiling and look elsewhere for stronger bounds.
arxiv-2606-16070:
Dong and colleagues present Mind-Studio in 2026, a system that turns gameplay experience into a runnable world model. A world model predicts how a game changes after each action, letting an agent plan without touching the real game. Earlier symbolic methods fit observed transitions or local rules, but yielded no complete program that runs on its own.

Mind-Studio uses large language models to synthesize executable, pygame-style world models from recorded state, action, and next-state traces. Entropy-selected traces and a skill file built from screenshots describe objects, actions, and scenery. A lookahead protocol compares generated rollouts against real emulator rollouts from the same state. On Montezuma's Revenge, chosen-action prediction jumps from 0.3 percent for a prior ensemble to 48.7 percent for Mind-Studio in the reported tests. The program also serves a planner with subgoal rollback, reaching more subgoals than breadth-first search at lower time cost.
arxiv-2606-16470:
Nguyen and co-authors turn demonstration videos into robot commands in 2026 by splitting the job: recognize the action and identify the objects separately. End-to-end systems often fail to tell which objects are functionally involved in an action, yielding ambiguous commands. Their framework pairs Temporal Shift Modules, which classify the action efficiently from video, with an Object Selection algorithm that finds the task-relevant objects.

Object selection classifies objects by their trajectory roles, filters out blurred detections, and minimizes overlap between candidates. Vision-language models then name the chosen objects, which supports zero-shot generalization to categories never seen in training. The output is grammar-free manipulation commands. On a modified Something-Something V2 dataset, the method reaches 86.79 percent action classification accuracy and BLEU-4 scores of 0.337 on standard objects and 0.261 on novel ones, per the report. Selection needs objects spatially well separated.
arxiv-2606-16870:
Ramlal, Chen and Zelek estimate food material properties from fracture behavior in a 2026 simulation paper. Realistic animation of food handling, like peeling an orange, needs material parameters for each region of the item. Those values are hard to measure directly, and the simulator that uses them cannot provide gradients to guide a search.

The team trains a neural surrogate on two thousand forward simulations, then compares an evolutionary optimizer with a reinforcement learning method called PPO. Both search in the original nine-parameter space and in learned four-dimensional latent spaces. Their best system is a goal-conditioned policy: given any target peeling behavior, it outputs parameter estimates in a single quick pass, with no retraining per target. Working in a flow-based latent space, it recovers the target well when checked in the true simulator. Seeding the evolutionary search with the policy's answer improves recovery further, at higher cost.
arxiv-2606-16970:
Ganguly analyzes the risk of stochastic ranking policies in a 2026 information retrieval paper. Search systems increasingly rerank results by sampling from a distribution over orderings, aiming for fairer exposure or more diversity. Such policies are usually judged by their average effectiveness after reranking.

Ganguly asks the prior question: before reranking, how much could effectiveness swing in the worst case from one sampled ordering? The measure is the largest possible change in discounted cumulative gain, a standard top-heavy quality score, over the permutations the policy allows. The theory shows this reranking risk is governed by where the relevant documents sit in the initial list, the recall points, together with how far the policy lets items move. Experiments on runs from a fairness-focused retrieval track confirm the prediction: observed effectiveness changes closely track the theoretical values. The framework gives designers a way to bound surprise before deploying a randomized ranker.
arxiv-2606-17070:
Chen and colleagues forecast ocean evolution in continuous time in a 2026 data mining paper. Ocean forecasting matters for climate monitoring and disaster warning, but the dynamics are nonlinear and step-by-step models are slow. Their network, KFTD, splits the job into interpolation and prediction.

Nonlinear dynamics are lifted into a Koopman space where evolution is linear. Fourier analysis fills in states at arbitrary fine time steps; a light residual network makes the forecast. A special loss attaches partial differential equation constraints end to end, keeping forecasts physically consistent. Unlike diffusion approaches, nothing is sampled, bringing a several-fold speed-up. Across four ocean regions, from the tropical Pacific to the Southern Ocean, squared error drops by a few percent on average and by more for sea surface temperature. Six-month seasonal forecasts also show the slowest error growth among rivals.
arxiv-2606-17270:
Casey and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper measuring dust in the average galaxy across most of cosmic history, from the nearby universe to redshift seven. The study combines JWST imaging from the COSMOS-Web survey with deep far-infrared and submillimetre data from several telescopes. More than half a million galaxies enter the analysis, letting the team constrain how dust dims starlight and how dust itself glows, as two independent checks on each other.

Ultraviolet and optical dimming turned out to underpredict infrared brightness by about a factor of three across much of the range studied. For the most massive galaxies the shortfall grew to roughly tenfold in the worst cases. The team derives practical relations linking dimming, dust temperature, and dust mass share to galaxy mass and era. A sharp drop in small-grain opacity toward early times is also reported.
arxiv-2606-17670:
Markov and colleagues build a classical Hamiltonian theory of radiation from collisions in hot quark-gluon plasma, in a 2026 paper. When a fast color-charged particle plows through this early-universe matter, it sheds energy as plasmon bremsstrahlung, the plasma analogue of braking radiation. Describing that process cleanly calls for a wave theory that handles both the plasma's soft collective modes and the hard particles crossing it.

The authors generalize the Lie-Poisson bracket to a plasma with non-Abelian interactions, splitting the bosonic field variable into two independent components beside two color charges. They write out the Hamilton equations and construct canonical transformations that mix field and particle variables, deriving the matching canonicity conditions as power series. The payoff is a general framework for the effective amplitude of the bremsstrahlung process, worked out in full technical detail.
arxiv-2606-17870:
Könye and colleagues show that a shy class of topological matter still leaves bold fingerprints, in a 2026 condensed matter paper. Fragile topological phases lack the protected surface states of famous topological materials, and adding extra bands can make them look trivial. The authors ask what trace of fragility survives in the bulk band structure of real two-dimensional materials.

For systems with time-reversal and twofold rotation symmetry, they establish a fragile topological index that forces gap closing points, known as Dirac cones, to appear. First-principles calculations on five materials confirmed the prediction in every case, with cones found deep in the valence bands. The result gives experimenters a direct spectroscopic signature to hunt for, and offers a fresh route to finding materials with unusual nonlinear transport behavior.
arxiv-2606-17970:
Zhao and colleagues design wireless signals that communicate and sense at the same time without tripping over their own echoes, in a 2026 paper for future 6G networks. In integrated sensing and communication, the data signal doubles as a radar probe. Random payloads, though, can throw up large spurious sidelobes in their periodic autocorrelation, and those peaks can hide weak targets even when average sidelobe levels look fine.

The team formulates the design as maximizing mutual information under strict peak sidelobe limits and a power budget. For calm, flat channels they show a uniform construction in the autocorrelation domain is asymptotically optimal at high signal-to-noise ratio. Their practical scheme, ACFK, embeds data symbols directly onto the autocorrelation sidelobes of a finite constellation. That gives exact control of the nominal pattern whenever a spectral condition holds, and a measured penalty when it does not.
arxiv-2606-18170:
Sohan and a large industry team present a new network transport built for the data floods of AI training, in a 2026 paper. Training frontier models couples thousands of accelerators in constant collective communication, and the network has become a key bottleneck. The incumbent transport, RoCEv2 over Ethernet, handles multipath routing, congestion, and failure recovery poorly at that scale.

Their Multipath Reliable Connection extends RoCEv2 with composable building blocks: per-packet multipath sending, sender-based congestion control, and a clean split between packet delivery and semantic processing. New mechanisms speed packet-loss recovery and add resilience when ports or paths fail mid-job. The design is open and production-grade, building on existing hardware rather than demanding a clean-slate fabric. A companion paper carries the full empirical evaluation of the transport in real training clusters.
arxiv-2606-18270:
El Hajji and Sjöberg derive a pencil-and-paper model of a toroidal magnetic ring, in a 2026 paper. Such rings are the standard specimen for characterizing soft magnetic materials, and engineers usually simulate them with heavy finite element software. The authors instead solve Maxwell's equations analytically in local polar coordinates for a ring with circular cross-section under sinusoidal excitation, using a complex permeability to fold losses into the math.

The model yields closed expressions for the internal field, flux, complex impedance, and total losses. It also cleanly separates the eddy current, hysteresis, and winding parts. The skin effect inside the conductive core enters through Bessel functions, and an apparent permeability formula maps nonlinear core behavior onto simpler linear models. The authors pitch the result as a fast, accurate foundation for standard ring measurement setups, and a practical alternative to two and three dimensional simulation.
arxiv-2606-18470:
Das constructs exact moving wave-packet solutions of the Dirac equation for an electron in an attractive potential that falls off with distance from an axis, in a 2026 theoretical physics paper. Despite a century of study, nearly all known exact Dirac solutions describe stationary states, and normalizable packets that genuinely propagate in an external potential were missing.

His packets have positive energy and, remarkably, one family uses only elementary functions and reduces in the nonrelativistic limit to familiar Hermite-Gauss packets. Two strange features stand out. The probability density does not depend on the spin orientation at all, even though the Dirac equation inherently couples spin and motion. And as the potential strength approaches a critical value, the packets' time evolution freezes completely. Das also gives a recipe that turns solutions of the two-dimensional Helmholtz equation into further exact Dirac packets, widening a very short catalog.
arxiv-2606-18570:
Hausman and colleagues use machine learning to squeeze far more information out of two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy in a 2026 chemical physics paper. The laser technique maps how electronic excitations in molecules evolve and couple to nuclear motion. Building a full dataset means many pulse-sequence measurements over many delay times, so experiments often run with sparse, noisy data.

Their framework fits a Gaussian mixture model to the underlying spectral density of the system. From even a single measured delay time, the model could extrapolate spectra to earlier and later times and recover quantities such as vibronic couplings and reorganization energies. The team validated it on simulations spanning a photoactive protein, dye molecules in solvents of varying strength, and the green fluorescent protein chromophore in water. An active-learning strategy also recommends which additional measurement would improve accuracy most, cutting experimental cost.
arxiv-2606-19070:
Wang and colleagues study an optimal stopping problem with oblique reflection in a 2026 probability paper. The process moves in the nonnegative quadrant and reflects obliquely at the edges. The payoff is of max type, taking the larger of two scaled coordinates, which creates a kink along a diagonal line. That kink and the boundary reflection each add singular terms that a standard smooth analysis cannot handle directly in the value function.

The authors build a measure-valued form of the obstacle problem that captures all those terms at once. They derive a reflected Itô-Tanaka identity and a killed-resolvent formula for the value in the continuation region. They also show the unrestricted resolvent is generally wrong, since the process is not absorbed on the stopping set. Under a monotonicity assumption, the stopping set takes an epigraph form. A verification theorem confirms when a candidate equals the true value.
arxiv-2606-19170:
Matta and colleagues introduce Dango in 2026, a language model built only from first-language data to study second language learning. The model has about two billion parameters and targets transfer from Japanese to English. Past work on acquisition in language models used smaller or non-decoder models, which cannot generate open text well and make poor simulators of learners. Scaling up raised a new problem for this team.

Monolingual training data turned out to contain hidden English, a contamination that would spoil the simulation. Their filter reduces early exposure to English while keeping a small, realistic amount. The model is then fine-tuned on generated lessons that mimic second language study. Evaluations show Dango develops human-like second language production patterns. It beats both unfiltered and standard multilingual baselines. Model, data, and code are released to support reproducible research on how a first language shapes learning a second.
arxiv-2606-19270:
Anastasio argues in a 2026 perspective that medical imaging AI needs conceptual innovation, not just better algorithms. AI has driven rapid progress and steady benchmark gains in medical imaging. Yet the concepts that define tasks, metrics, and clinical meaning sometimes lag behind the code. The author separates code-level gains, which improve performance inside a fixed framing, from concept-level gains, which reframe the problem and its clinical point.

Current incentives, training paths, and publication norms reward code novelty most, especially for early-career researchers. Concept work is undervalued even though it is essential for clinical translation. Examples from imaging AI show how weak grounding yields misaligned objectives and limited real-world impact. The piece closes with concrete recommendations for researchers, mentors, reviewers, and journals.
arxiv-2606-19370:
Cornelisse and colleagues show in 2026 that human-like driving emerges from self-play plus a small amount of human data. Self-play reinforcement learning trains driving policies without human demonstrations, using cheap large-scale simulation instead. Pure self-play policies can drive effectively yet adopt alien conventions that clash with people. Earlier fixes relied on heavy reward engineering and domain randomization, which are brittle and labor-intensive.

The new method keeps human demonstrations, but only as a regularization objective on top of a minimal safe goal-reaching reward. A little human data goes a long way. The method uses about thirty minutes of demonstrations, thousands of times fewer than comparable imitation learning approaches. Resulting policies coordinate with held-out human trajectories. Training completes in fifteen hours on a single consumer-grade GPU. Scale self-play for skill, then season it with human data for compatibility.
arxiv-2606-19570:
Naaz Sibia and nine colleagues study how computing students use multi-view program visualisations in 2026. Such tools show code beside memory diagrams and metaphor views to help novices follow a running program. Yet students often ignore the extra views, and design research says little about why.

Nineteen undergraduates who had finished two intro courses took part in a within-subjects study. Think-aloud tasks, reflective interviews, and webcam gaze tracking captured their work across scope, loops, and linked lists. Gaze records show students spent nearly half their time on code despite the visual aids. Students with no prior experience anchored even harder in code and barely touched metaphor views. Interviews name three causes: guarding control of their own effort, wide swings in personal fit, and doubts that metaphors look rigorous. Tools framed as checks, with adjustable depth, may earn more student trust.
arxiv-2606-19970:
Xiyuan Wang and six colleagues introduce CrossFlow in 2026, a one-step image generator that jumps straight from latent noise to pixels. Latent diffusion is efficient, yet a separately trained decoder must render the final image, and generated latents can drift from what the decoder expects. CrossFlow removes the split: the training path runs through latent space, but the supervised target is the image itself, with no velocity term to predict.

One model then acts as both generator and decoder replacement for latent pipelines. On class-conditional ImageNet at 256 resolution, the large variant reaches an FID of about one point six in a single function evaluation. Ablations credit the latent encoder and pixel-space perceptual and adversarial losses. Single-step generation with decoder-grade output promises much cheaper image synthesis.
arxiv-2606-20170:
R. Taranko and five colleagues study a fleeting traffic jam for electrons in a nanoscale junction built from two quantum dots in series between a superconductor and a normal metal lead. Their 2026 paper examines the triplet configuration, where both dots hold electrons with the same spin. In that state, on-dot pairing is suppressed, which strongly alters the subgap charge current through the Andreev junction. Because the blockade is transient, it appears only under nonequilibrium conditions, set by the starting state or an applied magnetic field.

Analytical and numerical calculations estimate how long the triplet state lasts and how it evolves, timescales readable in time-resolved tunneling measurements. The effect may matter for superconducting qubits, conventional and topological alike, where unwanted triplet trapping can disturb operations.
arxiv-2606-20570:
Robin Dey and Panyanon Viradecha analyze the infrastructure the agentic web will need, using the Agentverse platform as their case study. Their 2026 paper argues that research has focused on individual agents' behavior and reasoning, while the protocols, services, and platforms mediating agent interactions get little attention.

Agentverse, the agent cloud platform developed by Fetch.ai under the Artificial Superintelligence Alliance, supplies the evidence base. The gap analysis compares what autonomous agents require to operate reliably at scale against what the platform provides. An architecture follows from the gaps. Agents may be the visible actors of the next web, but infrastructure decides whether they can act together at all.
arxiv-2606-20970:
Yifan Shen and ten colleagues introduce CogniRoute in 2026, a framework that routes social evidence inside omni-modal models that take video, audio, and text. Having all modalities does not guarantee using the right one. In social video questions, an answer may hinge on a gesture, tone, timing, or a mismatch between words and expression. CogniRoute uses a training-only cognitive schema to structure that choice.

Each example is factored by cross-modal relation, reasoning demand, and temporal scope. Routing signatures are aligned to that structure during fine-tuning. Route-aware reinforcement learning then rewards correct answers, modality-consistent reasoning, and temporal grounding. A new benchmark, OmniSocialBench, supplies structured training examples with reasoning traces and labels. Routing evidence explicitly could make social AI less likely to answer from the loudest channel while ignoring the cue that actually decides the question.
arxiv-2606-21170:
Tobias Biegert and three colleagues propose a fair comparison method in 2026 for AI and physics-based weather models on extreme events. Deterministic forecasts from both kinds of model are first post-processed into probabilistic forecasts. A regression method with optimality properties does that step. Weighted scores then focus the assessment on extreme outcomes rather than average weather.

Their weighted potential score extends an earlier measure. Fairness comes from the shared post-processing: each model gets the same chance to express uncertainty. The framework is applied to WeatherBench 2 forecasts. AI models GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, and FuXi face a high-resolution physics model as reference. Extreme events carry the greatest social cost in weather forecasting. A fair yardstick for extremes helps agencies decide where AI forecasts can be trusted for warnings.
arxiv-2606-21270:
Yi Wang and seven colleagues present a non-line-of-sight imaging method in 2026 that reconstructs objects hidden around corners from scattered light timing data. Most methods assume a large flat relay wall and dense sampling, but real scenes offer odd, partial surfaces, such as the backs of pedestrians. Their pipeline makes no geometric assumption about the relay surface and handles both confocal and non-confocal capture setups.

The hidden scene is represented by 3D Gaussian primitives, smooth blobs whose combined shape forms the image, rendered through a differentiable transient model. Fitting directly to measured light transients yields top reconstruction quality on a public dataset and a custom capture rig. The gains are largest on complex, arbitrary relay surfaces and under sparse sampling, where older methods break down.
arxiv-2606-21370:
Hanna-Friederike Poggemann, Tim Dirks, Timo Jacob, and Christoph Jung use computer simulations in 2026 to redesign an enzyme called Cvi UPO. Unspecific peroxygenases are prized catalysts that add oxygen to saturated hydrocarbons using only hydrogen peroxide, but peroxide also destroys the enzyme over time. The team asked how two changes near the active site would alter the energy barriers of the catalytic cycle.

Simulations with nudged elastic band paths compare the variants in fine detail. Swapping the helper glutamic acid for shorter aspartic acid raises the barrier, likely hurting activity. Replacing the heme-anchoring cysteine with histidine lowers barriers markedly, though it might convert the enzyme into a peroxidase. The study highlights active-site water and spin state, and argues simulations must pair with experiments.
arxiv-2606-21470:
Yitao Jiang returns with five colleagues in 2026 to show that a text-only language model can steer a robot when the scene is drawn for it in ASCII art. Vision-language-action controllers normally need image encoders and heavy multimodal training. Rendering the camera view as ASCII characters turns vision into text, so standard language model training stacks can condition on the scene, follow instructions, and emit constrained, executable actions.

The team fine-tuned several language and vision-language models with demonstrations from a planning teacher, plus DAgger rounds that correct the learner's own mistakes. In a two-dimensional manipulation benchmark, in simulation and on a physical arm, the ASCII controllers picked out task-relevant objects and planned workable action sequences. The interface is lightweight and human-readable, a useful complement to conventional pipelines.
arxiv-2606-22070:
Barry's 2026 note examines Pascal-like Sprugnoli arrays, triangular arrays of numbers related to Pascal's triangle and to the Riordan group of infinite matrices. Sprugnoli arrays generalize Riordan arrays by building each entry from a triple of power series rather than a pair. The note focuses on the palindromic members of this family, whose rows read the same forwards and backwards.

Barry shows these arrays split into two closely related families. For each family he gives closed-form expressions for the elements, turning recursive definitions into direct formulas. He also describes the form of the inverse arrays in each case, which matters because inverses govern how the associated transformations undo each other. Finally, the note reduces the arrays modulo two and studies the arithmetic sequences that result. Such mod-two patterns often reveal fractal structure in combinatorial triangles, linking this note to work on binomial coefficient parity.
arxiv-2606-22170:
Bisicchia and colleagues present StableShots in 2026, an online rule for deciding when a quantum circuit has been measured enough times. Each measurement, or shot, samples the circuit's output distribution, and developers usually fix the shot budget in advance. Too few shots under-sample the distribution, while too many waste measurements.

StableShots runs a fixed circuit in small batches. It watches the total-variation distance between cumulative output distributions and stops after repeated signs of local stability. The authors evaluate it on 180 QSimBench traces across six circuit families, sizes from four to fourteen qubits, and five noisy simulated IBM backends. The chosen configuration met the accuracy target on every held-out test, with a median of 7,650 shots. Fixed-shot baselines either failed more often or spent substantially more.
arxiv-2606-22270:
Alpay and Sarıoğlu study, in 2026, aligned eviction in tiered cache networks as a problem of graph separation with checkable evidence. Evicting one aligned storage block can cut off downstream demand that never named that block, so recency alone cannot price the action. Their selection rule computes, for every candidate block, the exact weighted downstream demand cut.

The rule rejects any action that would disconnect protected demand, then selects the minimum-impact allowed eviction. Reclamation is framed as vertex separation. Finding the minimum-location version reduces to node-capacitated flow. Minimum aligned block actions, by contrast, are NP-complete. In two-hop networks one streaming pass evaluates every candidate. A matching adversarial construction shows a history-only victim selector can suffer unbounded one-step damage. A 144-scenario evaluation over hundreds of trillions of simulated packets validates the design, and invalidation is shown to converge under fair delayed delivery.
arxiv-2606-22670:
Duc-Thien Nguyen, Ngoc Minh Do, Xiem HoangVan, and Thanh Nguyen Canh add semantic awareness to drone exploration in this 2026 paper. A UAV exploring an unknown indoor space must plan informative paths while building a map at the same time. Most existing methods use only geometry, so they treat a blank wall and a cluttered desk as equally worth visiting.

The framework builds on the Dynamic Exploration Planner, which grows a probabilistic roadmap as the drone flies. A semantic layer joins that roadmap, fed by an RGB-D sensor supplying depth and object labels. A semantic reward steers the drone toward regions with meaningful objects, and the roadmap updates continuously. Implemented in ROS Noetic and Gazebo, the system reached coverage between ninety and ninety-four percent across several simulated environments. It also cut exploration time and travel distance compared with geometry-only methods.
arxiv-2606-22770:
Eunho Koo, Tongseok Lim, and Jinwon Sohn tackle statistical matching in this 2026 paper. Matching merges two datasets that share some variables: one records the outcome of interest, the other records extra helpful variables, but nobody appears in both. Standard methods assume the extra variables add nothing once the shared ones are known.

That assumption, conditional independence, makes matching solvable but throws away real predictive links. The authors instead build a dependency-aware Schrödinger bridge, a transport method that tilts the standard baseline with a compatibility cost measuring how well the two sources fit together. The result recovers a joint distribution and gives probability rules for filling in missing values. They prove conditions where the bridge strictly beats the baseline, plus an exact recovery guarantee for Gaussian data. Tests on synthetic data and the CelebA and Adult datasets showed consistent gains in downstream prediction.
arxiv-2606-23470:
Schunck couples two computer model systems to judge pesticide risk to pollinators at landscape scale, in a 2026 paper on risk assessment. Pesticides are hazardous by design, yet rules must protect non target species such as pollinators. Standard assessment leans on lab toxic limits without population or landscape dynamics, which can be too coarse.

The coupling joins ALMaSS, a map based simulator of wildlife, habitats, and farming, with BufferGUTS, a model that estimates pesticide effects through several exposure paths. A case study follows the solitary bee Osmia bicornis exposed to a sulfoxaflor product. Lab survival data calibrate the toxic model with Bayesian inference, a way of updating beliefs with data. Even a dose far above the legal limit gave tiny population effects in the models. Early runs warn that larval deaths could change that picture.
arxiv-2606-23570:
Niroshana, Wimalasiri, and Hettiarachchi redesign contrastive learning so heart-rhythm models keep each patient's individual pattern, in a 2026 biomedical machine learning paper. The task is spotting paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, a heart rhythm disorder that comes and goes, from RR-interval sequences, the gaps between heartbeats. Standard contrastive learning groups all same-class examples together. That can erase the personal baseline rhythm each patient shows when healthy, which is exactly what a model needs for new patients.

Their patient-aware objective pairs only segments from the same patient and same class as positives. Healthy rhythm structure per patient stays far more consistent than with rival losses. On the IRIDIA-AF dataset, a simple probe on the learned features reaches an area under the curve near ninety-nine percent for unseen patients. Its results also vary much less across random seeds, showing that per-patient consistency, not global class separation, drives transfer.
arxiv-2606-23670:
Bayat, Behrouz, and Courville argue that language models should be built wider at the front and narrower at the back, in a 2026 paper on neural network design. Nearly all language models stack identical layers, spreading parameters evenly across depth, a default inherited from the original transformer. Evidence suggests later layers mostly refine an almost finished answer rather than transforming it. If layers contribute unevenly, capacity should too.

A controlled experiment confirms the hunch: under a fixed budget, giving earlier layers more capacity and later layers less improves perplexity, the standard score of prediction quality, while the reverse hurts. The authors define tapered language models, where a component shrinks steadily with depth. They taper the feed forward blocks, which hold most parameters, on a smooth cosine schedule. Across three scales and four architectures, tapering improves both perplexity and downstream benchmark scores, at no extra parameter or compute cost.
arxiv-2606-23770:
Nawaz, Saleem, Anwar, and Anjum build one framework meant to cover classical, quantum, and gravitational wave equations at once, in a 2026 paper on the foundations of physics. Entropic dynamics treats physical law as inference. Probability patterns evolve by raising entropy as high as stated constraints allow, with no quantum postulates added. In that view, the Schrödinger equation emerges as a smooth diffusion process that does not dissipate. The authors extend this into a unified version spanning heat and gravity too.

By raising entropy under constraints on diffusion, drift, and gauge behavior, they derive one universal field equation. It blends the Fokker Planck structure, which tracks probability flow, with the Hamilton Jacobi structure of classical motion. Applied to different variables, it gives back the harmonic oscillator, the Schrödinger, Maxwell, and Klein Gordon equations, and equations for gravitational waves.
arxiv-2606-23870:
Dantas, Cordeiro, and Junior present a unified tool for mathematically proving the safety of industrial controller programs, in a 2026 paper on formal verification. Programmable logic controllers run nuclear plants, water treatment, and railway signaling, where proof matters more than testing. CERN's PLCverif, the established platform, cannot read Ladder Diagram programs, the dominant industrial notation, and its main backend only proves bounded properties. ESBMC-PLC+ routes everything through the ESBMC checker, which supports unbounded proofs.

A frontend built on the MATIEC compiler accepts Structured Text programs. The graphical Ladder Diagram resolver now models timers, counters, and edge triggers as persistent state across scan cycles. On eight benchmarks the framework matches PLCverif's coverage with stronger guarantees, running hundreds of times faster on timer heavy programs.
arxiv-2606-24070:
Huang and Gao offer one explanation for the faint hum of gravitational waves that pulsar timing arrays recently detected at nanohertz frequencies. Domain walls are sheet-like defects in the early universe, and if they formed by quantum tunnelling during inflation, their ripples could seed the density variations that later generate gravitational waves. Earlier models formed the walls almost instantly, producing signals too weak to match the observations reported by NANOGrav and EPTA.

Allowing tunnelling to stretch over a finite time changes the spread of wall sizes, and Huang and Gao show that wider spread strengthens the resulting curvature perturbations. A two-field inflation model makes the wall tension fade smoothly as the inflaton field rolls, setting a cutoff scale that places the signal peak in the nanohertz band. For three example parameter choices the computed spectra match the reported background, and other choices predict signals other detectors could see.
arxiv-2606-24270:
Jatmiko and colleagues profile the open star cluster NGC 6134 using Gaia's third data release. Open clusters are families of stars born from one molecular cloud, so members share age, composition, and distance, making clusters precision tools for stellar astronomy and even for studying exoplanet hosts. The team's 2026 study combines photometry, the measurement of starlight, with kinematics, the measurement of motion, across the cluster's membership.

Bayesian analysis yields distances to individual member stars, while the ASteCA software package derives the cluster's fundamental parameters: metallicity, age, distance, and the dimming caused by intervening dust. Gaussian mixture modelling searches for substructures inside the cluster, groupings that might betray a complicated birth or mergers of smaller clumps. Evidence of mass segregation, heavier stars sinking toward the centre, is also examined. Jatmiko's comprehensive portrait connects the cluster's present structure to its formation and long dynamical evolution.
arxiv-2606-24470:
Li and Shi couple a slow, thoughtful model to a fast, reactive one, through a learned channel instead of text. A real time game agent must act within tens of milliseconds, while planning over seconds. Their testbed pairs a deliberative reasoning model, needing over a second per response, with a reactive model answering in milliseconds. Both are frozen; only the channel trains.

The standard coupling makes the slow model write text the fast model reads. Their Latent Bridge instead projects the slow model's internal residuals directly into the fast model's input embedding space. The text round trip is skipped entirely. On seven Atari games and a driving domain, the Latent Bridge matches or beats the text bridge everywhere. Large significant gains land in two games. Safe drop in behaviour covers the rest. Li and Shi's 2026 result suggests model teams should talk in vectors, not sentences.
arxiv-2606-24570:
Khlaut and colleagues teach a medical foundation model to align CT scans with reports organ by organ, not just globally. Vision language contrastive pretraining dominates three-dimensional medical imaging, but scans span dozens of organs and reports run long. CLIP style training compresses each side into one global token, and loses detail. Their method, ConQuer, adds localised alignments on top of the global one, one alignment per concept.

Reports split into concept specific sections, and learned cross attention queries pool the matching image features for each concept, with no segmentation masks or spatial supervision required. Contrastive learning then applies independently per concept. The liver's text aligns with liver features, rather than the whole scan. Concepts here are anatomical regions, one query per organ. The system, developed at Raidium in Paris and presented as Jolia in 2026, aims at foundation models that know which part of the scan a sentence describes.
arxiv-2606-24770:
Samin Khan asks whether the wording and pictures inside a question help predict how a student will score. Learning platforms usually forecast performance from past interactions alone. Yet questions themselves vary in language and visual complexity. Khan studies chapter review questions from CourseKata, an online textbook platform. Lightweight features are extracted from the question text. Image features come from the textbook visuals attached to the same chapters.

The dataset holds 4,742 student chapter observations drawn from 562 class student pairs. Adding content features improves quiz score prediction by about nine percent over the prior performance baseline. That test groups students into five folds. A stricter test holds out whole chapters instead. There, text features still reduce prediction error. Models using image features, however, do worse than the baseline. Khan concludes that question text carries useful signal about difficulty, while the visual features tried here do not.
arxiv-2606-24870:
Laura Colazzo and Giuseppe Anzillotti report a case study of agentic web browsers used as assistive technology. Agentic browsers are language model powered systems that navigate the web for a user. They turn browsing into a conversation: state a goal, and the agent acts. For visually impaired users this could remove many barriers that screen based interaction creates. The study follows one low vision technology expert. It examines how these browsers support his navigation in practice.

Despite current limitations, the experience proves notably fluid and flexible. The expert could steer tasks conversationally rather than fighting page layouts. Colazzo and Anzillotti read this as strong potential for accessibility gains. Barriers in web interaction shrink when an agent mediates the interface. The authors also draw implications beyond accessibility. Agentic user experience design, they suggest, can learn from how well the conversational pattern worked here.
arxiv-2606-24970:
Pietro Tropeano, Maria Maistro, Tuukka Ruotsalo, and Christina Lioma ask what pruning attention layers does to a language model's trustworthiness, beyond accuracy. Pruning cuts memory and inference costs, and attention layers are the most resource hungry parts of these models. Earlier work showed up to a third of attention layers can go with minimal accuracy loss. Nobody had checked the interpretability side: whether explanations stay faithful and confidence stays calibrated. The authors study exactly that, across five large language models and eight datasets.

Accuracy often survives pruning, as expected. Faithfulness and calibration often do not. Both can swing widely even while accuracy holds steady, exposing a mismatch between a model's confidence, its interpretability, and its correctness. A pruned model may answer as well as before while explaining itself worse and misjudging its own certainty. Tropeano and colleagues recommend that checks of pruned models include explanation and calibration metrics as standard.
arxiv-2606-25070:
Ky Huynh and eight colleagues study eight outbursts of comet 7P/Pons Winnecke in the summer of 2021, brief brightenings that open a window into the physics of the nucleus. The Las Cumbres Observatory network imaged the comet from June 3 to August 31. The eight events strengthened the comet by up to about one magnitude against its coma. Their ejecta differed widely in brightness and shape. The varied shapes suggest eruptions from different sources across the nucleus.

Mass estimates for the ejecta land between a hundred thousand and a million kilograms, in line with mini outbursts seen at comets. Normalised by surface area, the outburst rate resembles those of comets 41P, 9P, and 46P, and runs ten times higher than at comet 49P. One tension stands out: ground based rates disagree with what the Rosetta spacecraft measured at comet 67P. Huynh and colleagues examine the comet's nineteenth century outburst record.
arxiv-2606-25170:
Many decision problems mix a state the agent controls with a context it cannot, like the next piece falling in a Tetris style game. Corentin Pla, Hugo Richard, Marc Abeille, and Vianney Perchet analyse learning in such settings in 2026, asking how many samples provable learning truly needs. Contexts arrive independently from an unknown distribution and can shift both rewards and transitions. Sample use is counted separately before and during execution of the learned policy.

When only the context distribution is unknown, their variance reduced method works with a sample count that never grows with the number of contexts. They prove that rate is best possible up to small factors. Even with transitions also unknown, policy evaluation stays free of context count dependence. Matching lower bounds accompany the main algorithms.
arxiv-2606-25270:
Typing rhythm has long been used to flag Parkinson's disease, usually through summary statistics fed to a classifier. Navin Bondade tries a different lens in 2026: inverse reinforcement learning, which treats each keystroke as a choice and works backwards to the reward function that would explain a person's timing. Four candidate reward ingredients, covering speed, effort, smoothness, and hand switching cost, were fitted for each of eighty five subjects in a public dataset, forty two of whom had Parkinson's.

Two ingredients turned out to be measuring the same thing, so Bondade pruned the model to three identifiable parts. The recovered speed preference weight tracked clinical severity scores strongly and held up across subgroups and repeated checks. It also added predictive value beyond raw typing speed alone, while the other two weights failed the confound checks and stand as negative results.
arxiv-2606-25570:
Two senders each hold half of a puzzle: correlated binary sources, encoded separately, while the receiver wants only their sum modulo two. Yohsuke Tsujino and Shun Watanabe revisit in 2026 when structured coding beats plain random coding on that classic Körner Marton problem. Linear codes exploit the sum structure directly, and a hybrid scheme mixes structured and random ingredients through auxiliary variables. A multi letter extension of the hybrid, taking exclusive ors of neighbouring bits, had been shown numerically to beat the standard Slepian Wolf region for some sources.

Numerical sightings are not a characterisation, so the pair derives the exact analytic condition for the improvement. Their condition is tight: it is precisely the complement of the known condition under which Slepian Wolf coding is already optimal. The method of types reduces the multi letter comparison to single letter divergences, a trick they flag as independently useful.
arxiv-2606-25770:
Medical learning systems that judge a whole patient from many small samples starve when patients are few. Rare diseases are the hard case. Muhammed Furkan Dasdelen, Fatih Ozlugedik, and colleagues introduce RECIPE in 2026. It manufactures realistic synthetic patients inside the model's embedding space. A Gaussian mixture model clusters pooled sample embeddings from all patients. Each disease then gets a recipe: the pattern of how its samples spread across clusters. New patients are mixed by sampling embeddings to a recipe. An uncertainty filter keeps the most useful ones.

Three scarcity tests were run. One invented a missing healthy class from an outside cohort. One learned from very few patients. One used small non image cohorts, from single cell and flow cytometry data. Performance beat the baselines throughout. In the missing class test, generated patients matched full dataset training. That has clear value for rare disease work.
arxiv-2606-25870:
Designing a quantum code is a thicket of coupled choices. Kenny Heitritter, James Brown, and Tarini Hardikar let a language model search it in 2026. The loop is evolutionary program synthesis. The model edits a constructor program. A verifier scores it. Winners are kept and mutated again. Their target is the generalised superfast encoding, which maps fermions to qubits for molecular simulation. Hand built versions stopped at code distance three, the error catching reach of the code.

The search found readable constructors reaching exact distance five on tested molecular instances, and six on one twenty mode case. A second hunt found a circulant pattern hitting a five qubits per mode floor across several sizes. The encodings used far fewer data qubits than a standard route. The moral is about rewards. Paying for distance alone bred trivial dense graphs. Fixing distance and paying for compression bred structure.
arxiv-2606-25970:
Siqiao Li, Mahnam Saeednia, and Patrick Stokkink study delivery routes where packing and driving cannot be planned apart. In their pickup-and-delivery problem with two-dimensional packing limits, vehicles collect and drop items along the route, so free space inside rises and falls in a non-monotonic way. Checking whether each new load still fits is the expensive bottleneck inside routing algorithms.

Reuse of earlier checks is their remedy. Under a no-relocation rule, a new packing state can inherit feasibility from a verified one. An order-preserving map must tie the two together. The map respects both geometry and the pickup-delivery sequence of items on board. Three search rules steer the hunt for a matching verified state, with tailored storage and ranking of past states. Experiments cut feasibility-checking time by up to forty-two percent against a benchmark without the dominance shortcut.
arxiv-2606-26070:
Siqing Zhang works in algebraic geometry on curves over fields of positive characteristic. Pulling bundles back along the Frobenius map defines a rational map between moduli spaces. The map, called the generalized Verschiebung, links spaces of rank-two vector bundles with trivial determinant. Its generic degree varies with the field's characteristic. Kondo and Wakabayashi recently showed that variation follows a quasi-polynomial law.

Zhang proves the law is simpler than it looked. The quasi-polynomial is in fact a genuine polynomial, for every genus from two upward. The paper writes the polynomial out explicitly. Earlier cases fit the pattern: genus two gives a known cubic-style formula in the characteristic. Kondo and Wakabayashi had verified genus three by direct computation. The general proof replaces case-checking with one argument. Degree counts for Frobenius pullbacks across all genera now have a closed form.
arxiv-2606-26170:
Henrique Oliveira studies how a population measure reacts to small changes in birth and survival rates. The measure is evolutionary entropy, coined by Demetrius. It captures how spread out a life cycle is across time. Age-based models got the first formulas. Many real populations are grouped by stage, not age. Stage-based Lefkovitch matrices describe them, and Oliveira covers the well-behaved case in full.

Plain formulas are the payoff. The stable stage mix, the generation time, and the entropy itself all come out in closed form. So do the rates at which entropy moves when fertility, growth, or retention rates shift. The entropy splits into two parts, one from stage changes and one from staying put. That split shows two distinct ways spread arises. Open-group age models drop out as a special case. Worked examples compare species and life histories.
arxiv-2606-26270:
Benjamin Bobbia and Stilian Stoev study how best to predict extreme events, the largest values of some outcome. Data in that extreme range is scarce by definition, yet good forecasts matter most where examples are fewest. Floods, market crashes, and solar flares are examples. The authors work where outcomes and predictors share a heavy-tailed pattern under regular variation, the framework for extremes.

They seek the best predictor built as a scale-free function of the predictors, one growing in direct proportion to its inputs. Prediction quality then reduces to a tail-dependence coefficient, a number capturing how strongly extremes move together. Finding the best predictor becomes a variational problem, an optimisation over whole functions. Their solution uses a conditional quantile, a threshold value, from a tilted angular distribution. Their estimation method proved consistent over wide model classes and performed well in tests, including solar flare prediction.
arxiv-2606-27070:
Grašič and colleagues study how many agents can cross a network at once while keeping a safe gap between them. Graph capacity counts that largest crowd for a given minimum distance. Their focus is the Cartesian version, where exactly one agent moves at each step. Branching points and bridges, single links whose loss would split the network, shape the answer strongly. In the 2026 study, general lower and upper bounds come from basic structural features of the graph.

For trees, which are networks without loops, exact capacity values are derived. Those results show precisely how branching raises or limits the moving crowd. Bridges act as bottlenecks that cap simultaneous crossings. The bounds give quick estimates for networks too large for exact work. Collision-free group motion, from warehouse robots to spaced walkers, motivates the whole question. New structural insight links local shape to global capacity.
arxiv-2606-27370:
Leong and Roy ask what happens to massless Dirac fermions when the magnetic field acting on them is non-Hermitian. Hermitian physics guarantees real energies; non-Hermitian terms allow gain, loss, and complex spectra. Their construction applies a spatially modulated anti-Hermitian mass term that acts as a non-Hermitian gauge field. A finite flux of that field produces zero-energy modes pinned at flat bands. The modes come out handed, purely right-handed or purely left-handed depending on the setup, in a condensed matter paper published in 2026.

Numerical checks on a graphene honeycomb lattice anchor the analytic picture. The flat-band modes stay localised rather than spreading across the sample. Their existence ties to an index theorem, the deep link between zero modes and topology. Chiral zero modes emerge without any Hermitian field at all.
arxiv-2606-28170:
Étienne André, Sarah Dépernet, and Engel Lefaucheux work on timed automata, mathematical models of systems that react to events while tracking real time with clocks. Their question is opacity: can an attacker who watches a system's actions and timing work out whether it visited a secret state?

André and colleagues give the attacker a blurred view. The attacker sees actions in order but only the whole-number parts of their timestamps. The team then asks whether a controller can steer the system to keep the secret. They prove the general problem cannot be decided by any algorithm. Decidability returns under two realistic limits. In the first, the controller changes strategy only a fixed number of times per time unit. In the second, every controllable action is visible and distinct to the attacker.
arxiv-2606-28270:
Bo Shen, Lifeng Chang, Tianyuan Wei, and Yunpeng Li argue that autonomous artificial intelligence agents need defenses living inside the agent itself. Agents now carry lasting memory, use tools, and cooperate with other agents, and attacks can poison that memory or hijack tool chains even when the underlying model was carefully aligned during training.

Shen and colleagues propose the Agent-Native Immune System, modeled on biology. A six-layer tower includes a barrier layer isolating the agent physically and logically. Their taxonomy separates agent viruses from vaccines, and distinguishes surface fixes from deeper parametric ones. A self-monitoring backbone keeps vaccines learning as threats evolve. They frame alignment as a static constitution set at training time and immunity as runtime law enforcement, then list open problems.
arxiv-2606-28470:
Henry Groves, Lucia F. Jackson, Barbara-Anne Robertson, and Jonte R. Hance model how children remember emotional objects in sequence. In their study, correctly recognizing a toy depended on whether that toy was pleasant or unpleasant. It also depended on the emotional tone of the toys shown just before and after it. That is an order effect standard psychology models handle poorly.

Standard models confirmed the problem: their accuracy stayed low and they missed how one emotional item colors memory for its neighbors. A classical tensor network model wove valence into its structure. Borrowed from the mathematics of quantum systems but run as an ordinary computation, it reached about seventy-eight percent accuracy in reproducing the children's results. The introduced task protocol also gives researchers a real-world tool for studying emotional temporal memory in children.
arxiv-2606-28770:
Courtis and Hu ask whether the personality of a language model can be adjusted from inside, rather than by clever prompts or retraining. They work with the OCEAN traits, the five broad personality dimensions psychologists use, such as openness and extraversion. Their tool is a sparse autoencoder, a network that pulls apart a model's inner activity into separate features that are easier to read.

By comparing inner activity for texts showing a target trait against texts without it, they locate directions linked to that trait. Adding a small shift along those directions, applied while the model writes, strengthened the chosen trait. A simple search over how strongly to weight each feature balanced personality change against normal task scores. The result is a way to steer tone and style while benchmark performance stays largely intact.
arxiv-2606-29370:
Zhang and four colleagues analyse breathing-mode oscillations of quantum droplets in dipolar quantum gases. Such a droplet is a self-bound lump of ultracold atoms, held together when quantum fluctuations balance attraction. The breathing mode is a collective mode where the cloud periodically swells and shrinks. The team study dipolar Bose gases in anisotropic traps, traps that squeeze differently along different axes.

Combining a Gaussian variational ansatz with a sum-rule analysis, they derive explicit formulas for the axial and radial breathing frequencies. Computer solutions of the time-dependent Gross-Pitaevskii equation back them up, and predictions match experiments on erbium and dysprosium gases well. Their phase diagrams, spanning scattering length, atom number and trap shape, show sharp first-order transitions and smooth crossovers between the dilute condensate and dense droplet phases.
