Herbal compounds act on many targets at once, yet they dissolve poorly, break down quickly, and rarely reach the brain in useful amounts.

Engineered nanoparticles can ferry such compounds across the barrier by several routes and release them where needed. The review covers design principles including surface disguises that mimic body molecules, size and charge tuning, combined cargoes, and carriers that respond to local triggers. Together these principles form a practical framework for translation into therapies.
pmc-13229170:
Bridget S. Wade and co-authors synthesise a 2026 fossil puzzle: the shells of planktonic foraminifera, tiny ocean animals, have repeatedly flipped their coiling direction worldwide within a few thousand years. Such speed rules out gradual evolution of the trait itself. Reviewing cases from the Eocene to today, spanning fifty-six million years, the team asks what sudden reversals actually record.

Their answer is hidden species turnover. Rival populations with different coiling preferences, adapted to different water masses, can sweep past each other abruptly, and the flip is the only visible trace. That challenges the idea that reproductive isolation alone defines species in these plankton and supports ecological speciation through habitat partitioning in the open ocean. Coiling becomes a lucky marker of invisible evolutionary change.
pmc-13230270:
Jiri Fremuth and colleagues test in 2026 whether lung ultrasound plus a blood marker can spot a bacterial cause in sick children. One hundred sixty children admitted with lower airway infections received ultrasound within a day of arrival. Three senior doctors, blinded to the ultrasound, later judged the cause from the full clinical record.

Large solid areas in the lung, air patterns inside them, and fluid around the lung pointed toward a bacterial component. Small scattered patches on both sides pointed more toward viral illness. Ultrasound alone separated the groups well, and the blood marker C-reactive protein performed about as well on its own. Used together at the bedside, the two could help doctors decide sooner about antibiotics.
pmc-13230870:
Abdul Waheed Khan and colleagues propose in 2026 a steadier way to group moving vehicles into clusters for road networks. Cars that talk to each other can share safety and traffic messages, yet fast motion breaks groups apart often. Grouping cars under a chosen head car cuts message flooding and makes the network easier to manage.

Their method scores candidate head cars on relative speed, distance, connection count, and how long past heads lasted. A backup head is picked at the same time, ready to take over and hold the group together. Computer simulations beat older methods on head lifetime and member lifetime by clear margins. Groups also needed rebuilding less often, which signals steadier links on busy roads.
pmc-13232270:
Jason Z Kim and colleagues model in 2026 the mental map mice use to search memory for safe places to run. Imaging thousands of hippocampus cells while mice learned a memory-guided task fed a new geometry-aware model. A good map must keep nearby places distinct while still letting distant options be found fast.

The population code solved both needs with a small-world layout, much like efficient social networks. Slow rotation and drift of activity kept fresh maps separate from older ones without losing local detail. Certain cells fired across distant spots, forming shortcuts that link far-apart memories. During quiet rest, activity often leapt along those shortcuts, as if the brain rehearsed distant options offline.
pmc-13234370:
Jenifer Malumbres-Talavera and colleagues reported in 2026 on nursing students who took part in a Death Café as part of palliative care teaching. Death Cafés are informal gatherings where people can talk openly about dying without pressure or judgment. Talking about death remains difficult for many nurses and students, even though end-of-life conversations matter in practice. The activity was required in a third-year course at a public university in Catalonia.

All thirty-nine students later answered open-ended questions about their experience. Their answers grouped into themes about speaking about death without fear and managing emotions with group support. Many described relief, less taboo, and a stronger sense that they could support patients and families. The authors present the café as a comfortable teaching tool that invites reflection and varied views.
pmc-13234770:
J. E. Umaña and co-authors explored in 2026 which chemical features make ionic liquids carry electric current well. Ionic liquids are salts that stay liquid at room temperature and could serve as safer battery electrolytes. Their ions interact strongly, so ordinary chemical tools predict conductivity poorly. The team built a molecular description that highlights how electric charge spreads across a structure.

That description simplified the link between structure and conductivity and improved predictions when data were scarce. Spread-out charge and a flexible negative ion emerged as the strongest helpers of ion motion. Polar, alkyl, and fluorinated decorations slowed transport by adding interactions between molecules. Many positive ion centres performed similarly, shifting design focus toward the negative ion. All data and models were released as open-source code for other researchers.
pmc-13235470:
Birsen Yilmaz and colleagues followed in 2026 children in an urban Indian birth cohort to trace how undernutrition and overweight emerge together. About two hundred fifty children from Vellore were measured from birth through age nine. Body mass was calculated at several ages, and later patterns were modelled against early-life factors. The double burden means thinness and obesity rising within the same population, or even the same families.

Nearly half the children were stunted at age two in the cohort. Thinness still affected about a quarter of children at age seven, while overweight remained uncommon then. By age nine, underweight had eased somewhat and overweight or obesity had climbed to roughly fifteen percent. Mother's body mass predicted child thinness, especially at ages five and nine in the models. The authors urge age-specific action plus attention to maternal health.
pmc-13236770:
Barbora Loncová and colleagues tested the growth factor betacellulin on human granulosa cells, the cells that support eggs inside the ovary, in a 2026 laboratory study. They measured how the cells survived, multiplied, died, and made the hormone progesterone. Some dishes also received the reproductive hormones FSH or LH.

Betacellulin raised cell survival, growth markers, and progesterone output in a dose-dependent way, while lowering signs of cell death. Adding FSH or LH strengthened every one of these effects. The results point to betacellulin as a local signal that works alongside the main reproductive hormones. That role could matter for understanding fertility and for future work on ovarian cell culture.
pmc-13240370:
Hanadi Ghurmallah Alzahrani and team test ozone water as an add-on to deep gum cleaning in smokers in a 2026 split-mouth study. Smoking worsens periodontitis, a gum disease that eats the support of the teeth. Each of the twenty-six patients had one side cleaned in the standard way, while the other side also got ozone care, so each person served as their own control.

Six weeks on, both sides had improved. Careful models built for the paired design still found extra gains on the ozone side. Pocket depth, attachment loss, bleeding, and plaque scores all improved more there. The gains were small in size but steady across measures. The authors present ozonated water as a helpful short-term add-on for smokers.
pmc-13240470:
Takanori Izumi and co-authors report distorted taste and smell as the calling card of a hormone failure in a 2026 case paper. A 54-year-old man endured three months of persistent taste and smell disturbances alongside fatigue, lost appetite, weight loss, and widespread body pain with stiff thighs.

Stimulation testing showed markedly low cortisol and low levels of the pituitary hormone that drives the adrenal glands, confirming secondary adrenal insufficiency. This form lacks the darkened skin and salt disturbances of the primary disease, which helps it hide. Replacement steroid treatment gradually restored his taste and smell. The authors advise considering the diagnosis when sensory complaints arrive with such general symptoms.
pmc-13241670:
Watson's team at Northwestern compared cutting out torn knee meniscus against fixing it, using a national hospital database. Matching balanced over 36,000 knees, half per procedure. 90-day returns, redo operations, and later osteoarthritis care were tracked. Age subgroups under and over forty were looked at apart.

Returns stayed low and similar for both paths. Repair patients needed redo surgery far less often, roughly two percent against four. Cut-out patients sought arthritis treatment within two years sharply more often. Watson reads the pattern as support for keeping the meniscus across all ages.
pmc-13241770:
Crystal A. Olivas-Rasmussen and co-authors publish a 2026 study of an enzyme called nocturnin and how evolution changed its control. The enzyme breaks down NADP(H), a helper molecule involved in hundreds of chemical reactions and in balancing oxidative stress. It is produced in both the cell body and its energy factories.

Comparing frog and mammalian versions revealed a new off switch in mammals. Certain sulfur-containing building blocks link up under oxidizing conditions, clumping the enzyme into an inactive form. Reduction breaks those links and restores activity. The frog enzyme lacks these building blocks and stays always on. The pattern suggests mammalian nocturnin acts as a redox sensor in energy factories.
pmc-13241870:
Ming He and co-authors present a 2026 nanomedicine study aimed at acute respiratory distress syndrome, a severe lung failure condition. Harmful splitting of mitochondria inside lung vessel cells drives inflammation and oxidative damage in this syndrome. Singling out that process without harming the rest of the body is difficult.

The team built nanoparticles carrying a fission-blocking drug inside a metal-based scavenger network. A surface peptide steers the particles to a protein found on inflamed lung vessels, where it also discourages damaging white cell entry. In animal models, the particles reached lung mitochondria, calmed a major inflammatory alarm system, and mopped up harmful oxygen species. The authors propose the design as a translatable strategy for severe lung inflammation.
pmc-13242370:
Chong's team in Singapore review acute-phase proteins as signs of inflammation in turtle care. Albumin, haptoglobin, fibrinogen, and MRP-126 lead the list of hopefuls. Few studies exist, spread across gel runs, immune tests, and blood chemistry. Mass spectrometry proteomics is a newer, sharper tool.

Known ranges exist for only a handful of turtle species. Tested shop-bought assays are rarer still. Values swing widely between and within species, so each species needs its own range, or each animal its own. The team calls for new marker hunts and test building to serve endangered turtles.
pmc-13242470:
Kara Schick-Makaroff and co-authors gathered qualitative studies of response shift, the way patients change how they judge their own quality of life. Their meta-synthesis appeared in Quality of Life Research in 2026. Response shift can hide real change when people rate their health before and after illness or treatment. The team searched six databases and screened more than a thousand records to find studies that explored the idea through interviews and similar methods.

Fourteen studies qualified, and every one of them found signs of response shift. Patients recalibrated by comparing themselves with their past health or with sicker others. Some shifted their priorities to cope, and some redefined what quality of life meant after their condition changed. The review also catalogs rival explanations, like faulty recall, that researchers must rule out. It ends by urging dialogue across research traditions on how people remake meaning.
pmc-13242670:
Megha Bhardwaj and co-authors built a blood test model that estimates a person's future lung cancer risk from DNA methylation marks. Their paper appeared in BMC Medicine in 2026. Low-dose CT screening saves lives, but choosing exactly who benefits most remains difficult and costly. The model was trained on 2,459 participants in a German population cohort, using methylation sites already linked to lung cancer in earlier genome-wide studies.

In a separate Norwegian cohort, the model kept its accuracy for cases diagnosed up to eighteen years later and for near-term cases alike. Its discrimination scores in external testing matched the strong results from development. Because the model covers never-smokers as well as smokers, it could widen or sharpen screening eligibility beyond smoking history alone. The authors present it as a step toward a practical blood-based risk test.
pmc-13242770:
Jin-Peng Fu and co-authors present a 2026 prospective study of low-dose lidocaine during gynecological keyhole surgery. Lidocaine given in a vein may change how much muscle relaxant patients need. The trial randomly assigned women to a lidocaine drip or a placebo drip of equal volume.

Pain scores some hours after surgery were lower as well. No extra side effects appeared. The authors caution that the single-center sample was small, so confirmation in larger studies is required before routine adoption.
pmc-13243070:
Ya Li and co-authors present a 2026 study of a small regulatory RNA in acute myeloid leukemia. The RNA, miR-2110, is unusually abundant in leukemia samples, yet its job was unclear. The team combined public sequencing data with cell and animal experiments to test its role.

Raising the RNA slowed leukemia cell growth, trimmed cell-cycle proteins, and nudged cells toward death. The RNA also made both ordinary and drug-resistant leukemia cells more sensitive to a standard chemotherapy drug. Tumors grown in mice shrank when the RNA was raised. The authors call it a tumor suppressor despite its abundance.
pmc-13243370:
Fatimah Abdulhakim and co-authors probe a protein switch that tunes plant defense in 2026 experiments. The protein G3BP1 helps form stress granules, small stores of RNA that appear when cells face stress. A phosphate tag on one site of the protein had already been linked to weaker immunity in Arabidopsis.

The mimic form changed how plants fought bacterial infection, altering reactive oxygen output and defense hormone levels. The tag also held leaf pores open, easing entry for germs, and slowed breakdown of the protein itself. The work shows how one small tag can reset several layers of plant defense.
pmc-13243870:

Their Mendelian randomization study appeared in the International Journal of Genomics in 2026. Observational links between the gut and this cancer are plentiful but cannot prove direction. The authors offer the results as leads for biomarkers and for prevention aimed at the microbiome. Genetic evidence, they note, is a hint, not a clinical verdict.
pmc-13244870:
Lele Xiao, Zheng Ren, and Haoyang Li map the mental web behind organ donation choices in a 2026 survey of Chinese students. Willingness to donate depends on attitudes toward donation and toward death, which tangle together in complex ways. Standard models flatten that tangle, so the team used a network approach instead.

They surveyed 960 university students in late December 2024. Perceived barriers to donation sat at the very center of the network, linking donation attitudes with death attitudes. Willingness itself acted as a second bridge between the two clusters. Repeated checks confirmed the pattern was stable. The authors advise tackling barriers, teaching about death, and stressing donation's value together.
pmc-13245370:
Hassan, Elawady, Wanas, and co-authors engineered metal nanoparticles wrapped in a natural polymer to attack liver cancer, in this 2026 RSC Advances study. Their nanohybrids combine selenium and silver particles, made by green chemistry using onion extract and vitamin C, locked inside chitosan, a shellfish-derived polymer. Tumor tissue showed restored antioxidant defenses and switched on a mitochondrial self-destruct pathway through p53 and caspase-9, while normal tissue was spared. The authors credit the chitosan cage for metering metal release.
pmc-13245870:
Bilal Ahmad Rahimi and a large team survey knowledge of a skin disease in rural Kandahar, Afghanistan, in 2026. Cutaneous leishmaniasis, spread by sand fly bites, is very common in the province. What residents know and do about it had never been measured at scale.

The team questioned 2,118 adults in two districts from September 2024 to March 2025. Most participants were farmers from poor families, and most had no schooling. Only about a quarter showed good knowledge, and fewer than a fifth used good prevention habits. Being unable to read stood out as a strong tie to poor prevention. The authors call for teaching campaigns fitted to low-literacy villages.
pmc-13246470:
Balkiş and Uysal measured the carbon footprint of growing strawberries in Türkiye's Mediterranean Silifke district, in this 2026 Global Challenges study. Using life cycle assessment from field preparation to the farm gate, they traced emissions for each kilogram of fruit grown in open fields, drawing on standard inventory databases and current climate-impact methods.

The footprint landed at the low end of Mediterranean figures. Cultivation dominated the total, and synthetic fertilizer was the single biggest hotspot, far outweighing irrigation electricity. Cutting fertilizer use by a fifth trimmed the footprint noticeably, while solar-powered irrigation barely moved it. The authors say smarter fertilizer use and stable yields are the real levers for lower-carbon fruit.
pmc-13246970:
Shen, Xia, and Han review why braces sometimes damage tooth roots, in this 2026 Progress in Orthodontics article. Orthodontically induced root resorption, the loss of hard root tissue under sustained force, is frequent and often permanent. Its severity depends on force size, direction, and duration, combined with each patient's biological susceptibility.

The review traces the chain from mechanical pressure to chemistry: ligament and bone cells sense the load and signal osteoclasts, the cells that dissolve hard tissue, to attack the root surface. Hormones, metabolism, genes, and oxidative stress all modulate the process. The authors appraise early-detection methods and prevention ideas, including locally delivered osteoclast blockers and biomaterial carriers, while noting most evidence still comes from rodents and cell cultures.
pmc-13247070:
Sangeeta Sharma and co-authors show that laser light can grow a magnet's strength, not just shrink it, in 2026 theory work. A fast laser pulse was long known to drain magnetic moment within femtoseconds. The team asked whether the right light could do the reverse in two flat magnets.

Calculations on chromium iodide and chromium sulfur bromide found gains of up to a third of the starting moment. The trick lies in the spin texture of one band, which lets strong light flip spins between bands. Both a simple model and a high-grade simulation agreed on the effect. The mechanism opens a path to writing magnetic states with light alone.
pmc-13248970:
Cong and co-authors built forecasting models for small liver tumors, in a 2026 study. After curative surgery for hepatocellular carcinoma, some patients relapse within two years and fare poorly. The team balanced a hospital cohort using propensity matching, leaving one hundred sixty-five patients, then tested inflammation and nutrition markers from routine blood work.

Several combined indices, covering inflammation, liver function, and clotting, carried independent prognostic weight. Among a chart-based nomogram and three machine learning approaches, a regularized Cox model performed best for both early relapse and long-term survival. The authors recommend that model to guide how closely each patient is watched after surgery.
pmc-13249170:
Kallio and co-authors mined spinal fluid for early warnings in childhood meningitis, in a 2026 multicountry study. Bacterial meningitis still kills or disables many children, especially where intensive care is scarce. The team pooled one thousand five hundred ninety-eight confirmed cases from Latin America, Angola, and Finland, relating admission spinal fluid values to survival and brain outcome.

Death risk climbed steadily as spinal fluid sugar fell and as protein rose. Children with both the lowest sugar and highest protein fared worst of all. White cell counts added little by comparison. Because these tests are routine everywhere, the authors propose simple combined thresholds to flag children who need the fastest, closest care.
pmc-13250170:
Wang and colleagues trace a brain circuit that links the front of the brain to a stress center in male mice. Their 2026 Cell Discovery paper maps a direct path from the ventromedial prefrontal cortex to hormone cells in the hypothalamus. Those hypothalamic cells release a hormone that starts the body's stress response.

Using virus tracing, cell recordings, and live calcium imaging, the team showed that switching this pathway on spread activity through the local stress cell network. Strong signaling made mice avoid others after social stress and strengthened their fear memories. Blocking the pathway reduced that avoidance behavior. The authors identify the circuit as one driver of stress responses and susceptibility to conditioned fear.
pmc-13250470:
Toshihiko Goto and colleagues report a runaway heart device in this 2026 case report. An 86-year-old woman was receiving a tiny leadless pacemaker for the upper chamber of her heart, after years of device changes driven by infection, battery wear, and worsening heart failure.

During the procedure the new device came loose and drifted backward into a large vein in her left pelvis. The team retrieved it successfully, using a preventive approach they describe in detail. They also explain how the shape of her veins had made the implant difficult in the first place. The case offers guidance for a rare but serious mishap.
pmc-13250870:
Tang and co-authors test whether a simple metabolic score can warn which heart stents will narrow again. Their 2026 Annals of Medicine study reviews eight hundred eighteen patients who had repeat artery imaging for chest pain after stent placement between 2022 and 2025. The score, called METS-IR, estimates insulin resistance from routine body and blood measures.

Patients whose stents had renarrowed carried clearly higher scores, and renarrowing grew steadily more common across the score thirds. The score stayed an independent predictor after other factors were weighed, with the strongest effect on severe renarrowing. A cutoff value separated risk groups with moderate accuracy. The authors present the score as a cheap, practical way to flag patients needing closer follow-up after stenting.
pmc-13251470:
Raed Al-Taher and co-authors recount a 2026 case of giant hydatid cysts in both lungs of a ten-year-old boy from rural Jordan. Hydatid disease comes from a tapeworm larva and is common in farming regions around the Mediterranean and Middle East. Blood tests for the parasite often miss lung-only cases, as they did here.

Scans revealed three huge cysts spread across both lungs, found by chance during admission for an unrelated procedure. Despite the negative blood test, the imaging pattern strongly suggested hydatid disease. After anti-parasite drug treatment, surgeons removed the cysts in staged keyhole operations that preserved the lung tissue. Tissue examination confirmed the diagnosis. Three years later the boy remained well, with clear scans and no return of disease. The authors back keyhole, lung-sparing surgery for children with this condition.
pmc-13251670:
Jia Jun Chuah and colleagues profile the chemistry of Gastrodia elata, a plant long used in Eastern medicine for nervous system complaints, in 2026. They extracted the dried rhizome with ethanol and catalogued its contents using several laboratory methods. The extract held alkaloids, saponins, flavonoids, glycosides, terpenoids, and phenolic compounds, but no steroids. Chemical fingerprinting named the individual molecules present, and a standard test measured how well the extract neutralized harmful free radicals. Computer docking then tested how gastrodin fits proteins tied to oxidative stress and nerve degeneration, alongside predictions of how the body would absorb and tolerate it. The authors present the combined profile as a base for developing the plant into a therapy.
pmc-13251770:
Xiang, Li, and Zhu test expectation-based psychological nursing for women having their womb removed for fibroids. Their 2026 trial in the International Journal of Women's Health randomizes one hundred sixty patients to routine care alone, or routine care plus two structured sessions. The sessions build on the Rosenthal effect, where positive expectations lift outcomes. Self-perceived burden was the main measure.

By three months, the supported group felt less burden and showed better anxiety, self-esteem, confidence, and quality-of-life scores. Stress hormone and heart rhythm markers also improved more in that group of patients. Patients walked sooner, left hospital earlier, reported less pain, and rated nursing higher. The authors present the nurse-led model as a practical way to build expectation-focused support into routine surgical care.
pmc-13251870:
Aikaterini Lampada and colleagues find new brain cells born from bad experiences in this 2026 mouse study. Adult brains keep making neurons in a few spots, a process tied to memory and resilience against depression, and stem cells there answer to life events.

Fear training switched on stem cells in the dorsal septum, a midline brain area sitting near fibres that deliver serotonin, the mood chemical. The antidepressant fluoxetine, which raises serotonin, had the same effect, boosting stem cell division and neuron birth. The new cells were calming interneurons that wired into septal circuits. The authors read this as an adaptive answer to stress in mice.
pmc-13253870:
Wenjin Sun and co-authors set out a future plan for high-altitude medicine in a 2026 review. More people now travel, work, and live where air is thin, raising illness tied to low oxygen. The authors propose one frame, the HSMI spectrum, which treats low-oxygen harm as injury across many organs at once.

Gaps remain in who gets sick and why, in firm tests, and in turning lab finds into care. Their plan pairs large-scale gene and protein data with machine learning, seeks core pathways, and builds fast tests with markers and portable scans. They also urge precise, mechanism-based treatments for groups at special risk.
pmc-13254270:
Jason Hou and co-authors test three-dimensional ultrasound in augmented reality in a 2026 study. Ultrasound users must build a 3D mental picture from flat slices, which makes training slow. Their AR-VIU system streams live 3D ultrasound into a headset at true scale.

Eighteen people, nine novices and nine experts, tried four display setups and did object finding tasks. The augmented reality 3D system gave the highest accuracy and the lowest spread in results. It also nearly erased the gap between novices and experts. The authors offer the set-up as a training and education tool.
pmc-13254370:
Jianfu Zhu and a large team study a chemical tweak to heart scar tissue in a 2026 paper. After a heart attack, collagen in the scar can stiffen the heart. The team found histaminylation, a histamine-based modification made by an enzyme called TGM2, in mouse heart collagen seven days after infarction.

Mice unable to make histamine had more crosslinks and stiffer scars. In lab tests, histaminylated collagen formed fewer crosslinks, stayed softer, and slowed scar-forming cell change. A gel releasing histamine, placed at the injury, restored the modification and reduced heart dysfunction in those mice.
pmc-13254970:
Ayoub Boutahar and colleagues describe a 2026 case of a rare infant tumor found in an unusual place, the shoulder. Their patient was a 4-month-old boy whose parents noticed a growing swelling on his right arm at two months of age. The tumor type, melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy, usually appears in the jaw area of babies.

The authors advise considering this tumor for any fast-growing mass in an infant.
pmc-13255270:
Robert Chen and colleagues present a machine learning tool that ranks drug targets for rare diseases in a 2026 paper. Across 161 disease traits, RareGPS beat existing tools at predicting drug uses and trial progress. Top-ranked targets were 58 times more likely to reach late-stage trials than mid-ranked ones. The team validated the tool in records of two million patients and published predictions for over three million gene-disease pairs.
pmc-13255870:
Jianhua Si and a large team report a 2026 study of greenhouse gas release from urban wetlands in Xining, a high-altitude city on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. Constructed wetlands shaped by urban activity generally emitted more than the more natural riverine wetland. The authors say plateau cities cannot borrow lowland emission assumptions, because altitude and cold change the picture. Their results feed into wetland restoration choices and low-carbon planning for high-altitude urban areas.
pmc-13256370:

pmc-13256770:

The review urges family-centered care and sustained psychosocial support.
pmc-13257270:

pmc-13258570:

pmc-13258670:

pmc-13258770:

pmc-13259270:

Network analysis grouped those genes into modules tied to hormones and signaling. Twelve genes rose only in the tolerant line, and five passed a yeast drought test. Breeders gain candidate genes with early functional support for drought hardy rice.
pmc-13259470:

pmc-13259570:

pmc-13260570:

pmc-13261370:

pmc-13262170:

pmc-13263170:

Ventilation itself, the authors suggest, reshapes the lung's microbial and immune balance.
pmc-13263370:

pmc-13263570:

pmc-13264170:

pmc-13264270:

pmc-13264570:
Jessica Michala Jindra and Angela Duff Hogan wrote a 2026 review on bringing new asthma guidance into schools. Since 2019, global guidance has favored a rescue inhaler that pairs a steroid with formoterol, a long-acting opener drug, over the old quick-relief inhaler alone. Schools have been slow to switch.

The authors list the blocks: old-style asthma action plans, gaps in nurse and parent training, and dosing rules that differ from the old inhaler. Their fixes include updated, personal action plans for each child and full training for all parties on the new dosing. They argue schools must adapt plans and teaching so children get the better rescue treatment during the school day.
pmc-13264670:
Koki Takabatake and colleagues published a 2026 benchmarking study on how well large language models talk about multi-cancer early detection tests, blood tests that screen for many cancers at once. Clear talk about such tests matters, and models that sound sure while wrong could mislead. The team set expert-checked questions and graded five models.

The set held 94 multiple choice and 13 free response questions drawn from 19 papers. Each model answered three times and rated its own confidence. All scored high overall, with Gemini on top at 96.3 percent, though its test terms differed. Most errors were wrong recalls of exact numbers. Several models still made errors while claiming high confidence. The authors urge human checks before clinical use.
pmc-13264870:
Júlia Campos Clímaco and colleagues report an early evaluation of Indigenous engagement in research in Northern British Columbia in a 2026 paper. Indigenous peoples remain under-represented in Canadian research, and rural engagement guidance is thin. Deep work with rural and remote Indigenous communities surfaced their research aims, system barriers and the principles they require for partnership. Trust, reciprocity and respect count as working conditions, not slogans.

The result is a co-created, culturally grounded framework with hands-on steps for researchers and institutions. Community-led paths and decolonizing practice run through the advice given. Health equity is framed as bound up with who sets questions and owns decisions. The study offers lessons that travel for research far beyond one province.
pmc-13265670:
Kathryn Grace, Nathaniel M Schuster, and Clark C Smith present an emergency protocol for epidural hematoma after spine procedures, issued in 2026. Bleeding inside the spinal canal is rare yet can cause paralysis if missed. Risk rises with blood thinners, difficult needle placement, and clotting disorders. Warning signs include severe back pain and new weakness.

The protocol stresses urgent imaging and rapid spine surgical consultation. A sample case describes a woman who needed three needle attempts during an injection. Bowel or bladder changes also signal danger. Speed matters because compression can permanently injure the cord. The guidance aims to standardise recognition and response across pain practices.
pmc-13266170:
Adrienne K Kramer and the team examine pandemic blocks and fixes in EMS training (2026). Training paths must survive crises to keep the workforce stable. Focus groups gathered thirty-five plan directors across eight sessions. Discussions were transcribed and thematically analysed.

Blocks and fixes fell into six domains, from rules to students. Directors reported heavier workloads, stress, and doubt where online learning was absent. New tech proved key to keep going. Simulation and distance learning rapidly replaced lost medical placements. The authors urge plans to build disaster plans from these lessons before the next shutdown.
pmc-13266370:
Md Wahidul Islam and co-authors published a 2026 bioinformatics study of two collagen genes in thyroid cancer, the most common hormone-gland cancer. Collagens shape the tissue around tumors, and these two genes had prior links to the disease. The team mined large cancer databases for gene activity, gene changes, chemical tags, and survival ties.

One gene, COL13A1, was raised in tumors, while the other, COL23A1, was lowered, and both varied by tumor stage and type. Lower levels of the first and higher levels of the second each tied to poorer outlook. Tagging of the second gene's promoter also rose in tumors. Two partner genes stood out as the most co-expressed. Checks in outside data sets supported both genes as markers. The authors propose them for diagnosis and prognosis work in precision care.
pmc-13266870:
Shiksha Mohan and a large group of co-authors examine in 2026 a puzzling trial result about kidney protection during heart-lung bypass. Kidney injury strikes a sizable share of patients after heart surgery, and low oxygen delivery is a suspected cause. The trial they discuss raised pump flow by about a fifth in 36 patients and measured kidney function with precise catheter methods.

Higher flow improved filtration and reduced signs of tubule injury, yet total blood flow through the kidney did not rise. Oxygen supply and demand for the kidney as a whole also stayed similar. That split outcome pushes attention toward how blood is shared inside the kidney, rather than toward simple total flow numbers.
pmc-13266970:
Ana Castillo-Luna and Feliciano Priego-Capote measure in 2026 how healthy phenolic compounds in extra virgin olive oil break down during repeated deep frying. Phenols give the oil stability and some pass into the food. Using sensitive mass spectrometry, the pair tracked two oil varieties, Picual and Arbequina, across frying cycles with breaded and plain foods.

Phenol levels in the oil fell sharply in every case. Losses were steepest with plain foods such as chicken wings and anchovies, while breaded foods and potatoes spared more of the compounds. Certain oil compounds, named secoiridoids, carried most of the oxidation burden, and some forms protected better than others. Food choice, not just oil choice, shapes what survives frying.
pmc-13269070:
Nora van Gaal and co-authors survey in 2026 Dutch hay fever patients on whether live pollen data could help them manage symptoms. Seasonal allergic rhinitis affects up to a fifth of the Dutch population, and many patients still control symptoms poorly despite medicines and avoidance habits. The online questionnaire ran from April to June 2024 and drew 961 adults with self-reported or diagnosed disease.

Most respondents used medication, and over half used behavioral measures, with mixed satisfaction. One in four wanted more information on managing symptoms, especially younger people and those moderately affected. About a third believed real-time pollen data could help, by confirming symptoms, guiding time outdoors, and timing medicine. Men and university graduates were most likely to see that value.
pmc-13269970:
Haeyoon Ryu and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on patient experience in an Australian hospital recovery unit. Fifty-one patients in a row filled in a survey across seven areas of care, from shared choices to physical comfort. Their gains in daily function were also scored with two standard tools.

The median age was 68 years, and fifty-four point nine percent were women. Bone and joint problems led at twenty-nine point four percent, followed by stroke at twenty-three point five percent. Support for mood, shared choices, and teaching scored highest, while family input scored lowest. Patients improved a lot in function by discharge on all measures. The authors propose the survey as a quality check beside routine outcome tools.
pmc-13270070:
Fathola Mohamadian and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on aggression, acting without thinking, and thoughts of suicide among teens in a region of Iran. Two hundred secondary school students from four schools, chosen by staged random sampling, filled in standard surveys. Background details were also collected.

Boys reported much higher aggression than girls, while acting without thinking did not differ by sex. Aggression varied across school grades. Aggression moved strongly with thoughts of suicide, at zero point six one, while acting without thinking moved weakly, at zero point one eight. In combined analysis, aggression alone predicted thoughts of suicide. It made up 36 percent of their spread. School results linked to both traits, but parents' schooling and jobs did not. The authors urge early spotting of aggressive teens.
pmc-13270570:
Sanna Mansoob is lead author of a 2026 Perspective paper on RaraSwed, Sweden's national quality registry for rare diseases. A Perspective paper sets out the authors' view and plans rather than a trial result. The registry gathers uniform data on rare disease diagnosis across a very mixed group of illnesses.

The authors describe what helped and what hindered building the registry inside Sweden's public health system, using systems thinking and social innovation ideas. They say RaraSwed supports research and evidence-based care for people with rare diseases, who often face delays and unequal care. Planned additions will record patient- and doctor-reported care, treatment, and daily experience.
pmc-13270870:
Liang Ying is lead author of a 2026 retrospective study, one looking back at treated cases, of telitacicept for IgA nephropathy in children. In this kidney disease, protein leaks into urine, and all ten children in the study also received steroid therapy, with half getting extra immune-suppressing drugs.

After a median follow-up of 3.75 months, eight children reached remission of protein in the urine, four fully and four partly. Six children cut their steroid dose by between a third and almost all of it, and four stopped steroids entirely. Side effects were mild, including two injection-site reactions and single cases of infection, rash, and low white blood cells, with no severe events.
pmc-13270970:
Melinda A B Petrina and colleagues report in 2026 on vaginal health during two HIV prevention trials covering pregnancy and breastfeeding. Women in four African countries used either a monthly dapivirine vaginal ring or daily oral tenofovir tablets. The team tracked vaginal infections, bacterial communities, and immune signals called cytokines.

In the pregnancy trial 558 women took part, and 197 joined the breastfeeding trial. Infections, bacteria, and cytokine patterns looked similar between the ring and tablet groups at the start and over time. Bacterial vaginosis and Candida stayed common, while one helpful Lactobacillus type appeared less often after birth. Because neither product disturbed the vaginal environment more than the other, the findings support ring use during pregnancy and breastfeeding.
pmc-13271070:
Qing Wang is lead author of a 2026 journal article describing a double-helix patch for holding drainage tubes in place after head and neck surgery. Loose tubes cause pain, skin damage, and extra work, and the standard method uses a bridge of medical tape. The patch uses two spiral strips, an elastic strap, and wide wings to spread pressure.

In a non-randomized trial of 125 patients at one hospital in Shanxi, 61 used the patch and 64 used tape. The patch group had far fewer adverse events, faster fixing time, higher comfort and satisfaction scores, and 43.2 percent lower material costs. Pain from pulling and skin injury rates did not differ between groups.
pmc-13271970:
İskender Samet Daltaban and coauthors test in 2026 whether biological sex changes artery spasm severity after bleeding around the brain in rabbits. Spasm of brain arteries is a major cause of further injury after subarachnoid hemorrhage. Women suffer this bleeding more often, yet controlled lab evidence on sex and spasm was missing.

Twenty-four rabbits were split among control, sham, and bleeding groups, balanced by sex. Seven days after induced bleeding, males showed severe narrowing of the basilar artery while females showed only moderate spasm. Tissue scoring agreed with the measurements. No sex gap appeared without bleeding, which ties the difference to the injury response itself.
pmc-13272270:
Malfertheiner and Schulz commented in 2025 on how to keep stomach biopsy tests accurate for Helicobacter pylori when patients cannot stop acid-blocking drugs. Proton pump inhibitors cut the accuracy of nearly every test for this stomach infection, so guidelines ask patients to stop them two weeks before testing, which real practice often cannot manage. The commentary discusses a study of 164 dyspeptic patients that sought a fix while the drugs continued.

Gene-based PCR testing proved most accurate and lost nothing on the drugs, since it needs only traces of bacterial DNA, but cost and availability limit its use. The study's practical trick, pooling paired biopsies from two stomach regions into a single rapid urease test sample, raised the routine test's yield against the PCR standard. The commentators endorse PCR where feasible and the pooled-biopsy workaround elsewhere, so treatable infections are not missed.
pmc-13272670:
Simon Sanwald leads a 2026 matched case-control study of chemical marks on DNA in depression and response to treatment. The marks, called methylation, were measured on three genes linked to stress, serotonin, and oxytocin in blood. Such marks have been proposed as markers of who will improve.

The study followed 66 patients and 66 healthy controls at entry and after two weeks of inpatient care. One gene's marks looked lower in patients at first, but that gap vanished after accounting for blood cell mix. Symptoms improved, yet mark changes in none of the three genes tracked improvement. The authors urge care with confounders in such studies.
pmc-13273370:
Lisa Thoenen and co-authors described a customizable high throughput method for chemical phenotyping of root bacteria in a 2026 protocol paper. Phenotyping tests how bacteria grow under different chemicals, but classic plate methods are slow and use much material. Their system screens many strains at once in liquid culture.

Bacteria grow in 96 well plates, and a stacker feeds plates to a reader so large collections can be tested with many repeats. Users can vary strains, media, chemicals, doses, and exposure time freely. Target chemicals range from plant made compounds to antibiotics and pesticides. The setup uses gear many labs already own and keeps supply costs low. The authors offer it as a flexible bench tool for studying how root bacteria handle chemical stress.
pmc-13273470:
Wei Zhang and co-authors reported early findings on dual target deep brain stimulation for treatment-resistant depression in a 2026 study. Many patients do not respond to drugs or talk therapy, and stimulation offers another route. Their approach targeted two sites at once: the nucleus accumbens and a capsule pathway nearby.

In a small patient group, symptoms eased and thinking performance improved after stimulation. Brain recordings taken during treatment showed that improvement tracked with stronger gamma rhythms at the target site. Theta rhythm power also rose in frontal and limbic regions. The authors frame the work as preliminary, offering a first map of how the therapy may act and which signals might guide tuning for each patient.
pmc-13273770:
Yoshihiro Kawaguchi reported a severe gas forming urinary infection in a 2026 case report. In emphysematous infections, bacteria produce gas inside the urinary tract, a rare but dangerous event. Spread across the kidney pelvis, ureter, and bladder at once has seldom been described.

The patient was a 79 year old woman with type 1 diabetes who arrived with fever, septic shock, clotting failure, and kidney injury. CT scans showed gas in all three structures plus a swollen kidney. A ureteral stent was placed to drain the system, and antibiotics were started promptly. She improved steadily, and three dimensional imaging showed the gas clearing fully by day fifteen. The author stresses early drainage and well chosen antibiotics in such extensive infections.
pmc-13274170:
Ali Zare and co-authors report a 2026 case report of cells growing on an artificial lens inside the eye after a corneal transplant procedure. The patient was a sixty-one-year-old woman who had already had several eye operations, including cataract surgery. She came in with steadily worsening vision.

Examination found stubborn deposits across the front of her implanted lens, limited to the pupil zone. Laser treatment and surgical polishing both failed to clear them, so the lens was removed and studied under a microscope. It carried a sheet of epithelial skin-like cells, likely strayed from the lens capsule, with no calcium deposits. The authors urge doctors to consider this rare cause when lens clouding resists treatment.
pmc-13274370:
Qiqi Chen and co-authors profiled medication literacy in older adults with several chronic diseases in a 2026 study from China. Knowing how to use medicines safely matters more as prescriptions pile up, yet skill varies widely. The team also probed links with fear of technology and feeling like a burden.

They surveyed 611 hospitalized patients over sixty in Shizuishan City in early 2024. A profile analysis sorted patients into four groups, from high literacy down to low, with the largest group showing weak critical skills. Education, marital and work status, and drinking history were among the factors tied to group membership. The authors frame the profiles as a base for tailored teaching programs rather than one size education for all older patients.
pmc-13274870:
Xia Huang and colleagues present a 2026 journal article measuring stroke knowledge among non-neurology health workers in an underdeveloped county of southwestern China. Outside specialist units, general staff often give the first stroke care, where minutes matter. The team first adapted a standard stroke management questionnaire into Chinese and confirmed it was reliable, then surveyed local staff.

Of 252 completed questionnaires, 225 qualified for analysis, and 69.4 percent of staff reached a good overall score. Knowledge was weakest for the hyperacute phase, the first urgent hours, at 64.7 percent good performance. Nurses scored lower than doctors, and staff in smaller facilities or without a neurologist partner scored lower than peers in full hospitals. The authors target training at those gaps.
pmc-13275270:
Pai Zhou and co-authors reframed glaucoma through the lens of cellular recycling in a 2026 review. Glaucoma blinds by killing retinal ganglion cells, and many patients worsen even when eye pressure is controlled. Autophagy, the cell's cleanup system, and its mitochondria specific form may explain part of that gap.

The authors argue the effect depends on place and stage. In the eye's drainage tissue, cleanup supports pressure balance, but chronic stress can stall it and raise pressure further. In the retina, ganglion cells lean heavily on cleanup for protein and mitochondria quality, which may protect early yet fail or turn harmful in chronic injury. Specific gene and energy pathways recur in recent studies. The framework points to timing aware treatments rather than simply boosting cleanup.
pmc-13275770:
Louise Harra and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on what the Sun's outer atmosphere does just before a solar flare. Flares are huge bursts of energy from the Sun. Predicting where and when one will start could help protect satellites and power grids from space weather.

The team studied two large flares from the same active region on two days in March 2024. They used images from two space telescopes that watch the corona, the Sun's glowing outer layer. Spots with high stored magnetic energy also showed frequent tiny flickers in brightness. That flickering peaked at least two minutes before the flare's X-ray burst. The authors say this signal could help pinpoint where a flare is about to begin.
pmc-13276070:
Martin Johansson and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on vision in adults born with extremely low birth weight, meaning at or below one kilogram. Such adults face higher risks of trouble seeing motion. Motion of living things, like a walking person's pattern of movement, matters for social life.

Thirty-eight adults born tiny and twenty-nine full-term controls did eye-tracking tasks with moving dot figures. Some figures formed a walking person; others were scrambled versions of the same dots. Extra visual noise made some rounds harder. The low birth weight group spotted both kinds of motion more slowly overall. They also read the walking figures less accurately when noise was low. Early development scores in toddlerhood hinted at links to adult performance, though those links faded after stricter statistical checks.
pmc-13276270: Yang Gao and co-authors studied cinnamon essential oil packed into tiny capsules to protect a medicinal plant stem from fungi. Their 2026 correction notice addresses errors in one figure of that article. During figure assembly, two pairs of images were duplicated by oversight in separate panels showing fungal growth tests. The notice reprints the original figure and its caption so readers can see the context. The original article has been corrected.
pmc-13276570:
Jing Tao and colleagues map the global spread of Shigella bacteria through their genomes in a 2026 study. Shigella causes bacterial dysentery, a major killer of young children in poorer countries. Its many serotypes complicate tracking and vaccine planning.

Genomic data were used to chart where species and strains occur and how they travel between continents. Core-genome typing gave molecular evidence of cross-border transmission chains. The analysis also linked serotypes with sequence types in a systematic global picture for the first time. Predicted drug resistance genes were widespread across the collection. The authors offer the map as a base for surveillance and control planning.
pmc-13276770:
Rebecca Sebastian and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a tool that grabs disease-linked protein seeds right at the synapse. In Alzheimer's and related diseases, clumped proteins like tau spread between connected neurons in a prion-like way. Studying those proteins in their actual synaptic setting has lacked methods.

Their platform, called synCAR, fuses a small antibody fragment to a natural synaptic anchor protein. The antibody arms the synapse to capture chosen proteins in place. Armed with a tau antibody, synapses in mouse and human neuron models caught pathogenic tau species effectively. Expressing the trap actually increased tau clumping, likely by concentrating seeds at the synapse. The authors call it the first published method to isolate and manipulate synaptic proteins in context, useful for research and drug development.
pmc-13276870:
Ahmad Mourad leads a 2026 study of pneumonia testing in patients whose immune systems are weakened. Finding the germ fast matters, yet test success varies a lot between hospitals. The team reviewed 222 patients at ten sites and looked at timing of a lung scope test and a blood DNA test.

Usual testing found a cause in as few as eight percent and as many as fifty-eight percent of cases, by site. A scope test done within three days of an abnormal scan found more causes than one done later. Adding the blood DNA test raised the yield for both early and late groups. Prompt testing, the authors argue, should be the norm for these patients.
pmc-13277570:
Andy Bécue wrote a 2026 Interpol review of research on fingermarks, the residue left by fingertips, covering July 2022 to June 2025. The review was built for forensic work: what fingermarks are made of, and how to make them visible at crime scenes. A total of 761 papers were collected, nearly twice the count in the prior report.

Most collected papers were set aside for weak methods, missed forensic needs, or safety problems, leaving 219 for close discussion. Composition papers were sorted into fields such as aging, donor profiling, and contamination. The author adds personal notes where work departs from good practice. The review aims to give forensic readers a quality-filtered map of a fast-growing field.
pmc-13277770:
Emily C Scheffel leads a 2026 case report of a pregnant patient who needed a cesarean birth and repair of a torn aorta at the same time. The 23-year-old, at thirty-five weeks of pregnancy, had Marfan syndrome, a connective tissue disorder that weakens the aorta, plus sickle cell trait. She arrived with sudden back, belly, and chest pain.

Scans confirmed a tear running from the upper aorta down into the abdomen. Teams delivered the baby, replaced part of the aorta, and rebuilt a heart artery in one operation. Despite a complex course afterward, she had fewer blood-flow complications than earlier similar cases. The authors credit joint planning across specialties and careful heart-lung bypass technique.
pmc-13278370:
Seong Woo Shin and Sung Hwoan Cho present a 2026 feeding trial that swaps fish meal for duck by-product meal in diets for olive flounder, a farmed flatfish. Fish meal is costly, so cheaper protein matters for fish farming. Four hundred fifty young fish were spread across eighteen tanks and fed six diets for fifty days, with duck meal replacing zero to all of the fish meal.

Fish on the control diet and on diets replacing twenty or forty percent of fish meal grew best and earned the best economic returns. Higher replacement levels cut weight gain and feed intake. Feed use, blood chemistry, and body composition otherwise held steady. Duck by-product meal can replace up to forty percent of fish meal without harming growth or profit, the authors conclude.
pmc-13278870:
Martínez-García Rosa María and colleagues measure selenium status and thinking skills in Spanish university students, in a 2026 study. Selenium supports antioxidant enzymes and brain function, yet evidence in young adults is thin. One hundred thirty-two students aged eighteen to twenty-nine gave diet records and blood samples.

Over half of the women fell below the reference blood selenium level, against a smaller share of men. Students scoring below average on the intelligence test carried lower blood selenium than higher scorers. Blood selenium tracked overall scores and two subscales in simple analyses. Adjusted models told a mixed story, with selenium intake showing a small negative link instead. The authors urge monitoring and longer studies.
pmc-13279170:
Amir Lotfi writes a 2026 letter that critiques surveys of staffing in cardiac intensive care units. Such units care for the sickest heart patients. The surveys, run by a national cardiology group, map how units are staffed and how heart doctors roles shift. Lotfi finds the maps useful for peer comparison, yet urges care in reading them.

Just twenty percent replied, and most came from academic centres, so rates may not fit the whole country. The survey tool was new and not yet validated, meaning not yet proven sound. Terms like high intensity staffing lump unlike models in one group. Cross section data, taken at one time, cannot prove trends over time. Lotfi urges set terms, better sampling and long term follow up.
pmc-13280470:
Haoyan Sun and colleagues report a 2026 study of dung beetle kin diversity along a mountain gradient in a tropical island rainforest in China. Mountains serve as ideal natural laboratories for biodiversity patterns. Scarabaeoidea assemblages, the scarab beetle superfamily, were sampled from March to November 2024 across thirty two plots. Elevation ran from about three hundred seventy to one thousand four hundred seventy metres. Ground and canopy traps caught the beetles.

Species richness showed no significant link with elevation, but rose with litter biomass. Abundance peaked at mid elevation, driven primarily by temperature, reflecting thermal sensitivity of these ectotherms, cold blooded animals. Overall compositional dissimilarity was high and dominated by species turnover, meaning species replacement across sites, not nested loss. Predator assemblage patterns correlated with beetle beta diversity as well. Temperature and food web drivers shape the gradient.
pmc-13280570:
Eeman Ahmad and team report a 2026 study of trends and disparities in lung clot death rates in adults with atrial fibrillation in the United States. Pulmonary embolism, a lung artery clot, is a major cause of cardiovascular death, and fibrillation worsens its outcomes. Long term trends were poorly characterized. The CDC WONDER database from 1999 to 2020 gave deaths with embolism as the underlying cause and fibrillation as a contributing cause.

A total of five thousand four hundred ninety nine deaths were recorded. Overall mortality stayed stable from 1999 to 2009, then rose sharply from 2009 to 2020. The yearly change flipped from slightly negative to a clear positive climb. Males had higher age adjusted mortality than females, with faster rises over time. Non metropolitan areas showed greater mortality than metropolitan areas. Subgroup checks covered the pre, during and post COVID eras.
pmc-13281770:
Yixuan Li and colleagues used gene data to probe clotting and pregnancy blood pressure in a 2026 study. High blood pressure in pregnancy can kill mothers worldwide. Its worst form brings seizures and organ strain. Clotting switches on in that illness, but whether clotting drives it is unclear. The team used genes as natural levers, since genes are fixed before illness. They checked clotting traits and blood proteins against illness risk in large gene datasets.

First passes hinted at links. Higher levels of two clotting factors went with higher risk. Lower levels of a clotting brake went with higher risk too. Extra checks found no wide bias in the data. But when the team applied the strictest error bar, none of the links held firm. A sharing test also gave low odds that the same gene spot drives both traits. The authors call the proof suggestive at best.
pmc-13281870:
Siqi Han and colleagues built a membrane that sorts mirror-image molecules in a 2026 study. Many drugs come in left- and right-handed forms that act unlike in the body. Sorting them with membranes is cheap in energy but hard to make sharp. Weak grip differences wash out under fast flow. The team laced carbon sheets with DNA-wrapped carbon tubes. That built chiral paths, paths that favor one handedness, through the stack.

Each handed form of a test amino acid reshaped the paths in its own way. The reshaping split the energy cost of crossing for the two forms. One form then sped through far faster than the other. The membrane held its sorting for a full week of runs. Stacked passes enriched one form to near-perfect purity. The authors say coupling grip with structure can amplify faint sorting cues.
pmc-13282070:
Jasmine Lee and Alan Kubey describe a 2026 case where a sudden drop in blood sodium pointed to hidden trouble after gallbladder drainage. Sodium is a key salt in blood, and a fast fall can be dangerous. The patient had necrotizing pancreatitis, a severe form where pancreas tissue dies, which had also burst the gallbladder. A drain placed through the skin, called a percutaneous cholecystostomy, was used to empty the gallbladder.

The drain then lost large amounts of bile, the digestive fluid made by the liver. That loss drove the sodium down and, in doing so, revealed a blockage further down the bile path. Fluids given by vein, a stent to hold the duct open, and internal drainage fixed both the sodium level and the symptoms. The authors show how a lab abnormality after drainage can guide a team across specialties toward the real fault.
pmc-13282170:
Fangyi Chen and co-authors describe a 2026 software tool that reads doctors' notes to find when a disease trait first appeared. Knowing that onset time helps doctors diagnose and track illness, but record dates often mark when a note was written, not when symptoms began. Older text methods also struggled with vague time phrases. Their open-source tool, TimeX, uses a large language model called Llama to extract onset times.

TimeX filters out family history, spots traits, handles negated mentions, and then pulls time details. On one hundred two hand-checked notes from a New York medical centre, it reached about eighty-one percent accuracy. That beat five rival methods by a wide margin. In four rare disease groups, note-based onset times proved sharper than record dates. The authors say the tool could support faster, more precise diagnosis at scale.
pmc-13282870:
Community voices shaped mental health research in Pakistan, as Shumaila Hamid and partners recount in their 2026 account. The work sits inside the THE HOPE project on early help for psychosis in young people. It covers work with patients, families, and local communities.

A six-member advisory group with lived experience helped shape study design and topic guides. The team also held 34 community sessions using sermons, posters, leaflets, and direct outreach. Themes included medicine use, service delivery, and the role of healers and primary care. The authors support shared decisions and training that fit local culture and needs.
pmc-13283170:
Memory clinic visitors in Sweden were screened for a treatable brain inflammation mimic in work A Freitas-Huhtamaki's team published in 2026. Autoimmune encephalitis can mimic dementia but can be treated. Wide regional gaps in diagnosis in Sweden hint that cases are missed.

Blood samples from 1,021 clinic visitors were screened for five nerve antibodies. Positive results were checked with added cell and tissue tests for confirmation. Eleven patients were positive in two or more tests in the screen. Chart review suggested true immune or tumor-linked disease in three patients. Four cases lacked enough detail to judge, and three looked like false positives. Screening found few clear cases.
pmc-13283270:
Sixty years of European youth fitness data are stitched into trend lines by Daniel Domingo-del-Val and associates in 2026. Fitness in childhood signals current and future health for young people. Past reviews often used single tests or stopped before the pandemic years.

Data covered 417,362 children and teens aged 6 to 16 years in 20 countries. Studies with repeated measures and full test data were pooled for trends. Scores were standardized so varied tests could be compared fairly. Heart fitness, strength, and speed traits were tracked by sex and age. Some traits fell over time, with shifts that sped or slowed by period. Results can guide school and health policy.
pmc-13283870:
Bo Song and a large team reported in 2026 a Chinese family carrying a rare gene variant behind heart amyloidosis. In this disease, a blood protein called transthyretin misfolds and clogs the heart muscle. More than 150 variants are known, but the Ser43Asn change is rare and Asian data are thin. The first patient was a 51-year-old man with chest tightness and breathlessness on exertion.

Heart tracings and scans showed thickened heart walls, weaker pumping, and a strain pattern typical of amyloid. A nuclear scan lit up the heart strongly, while tests ruled out the other amyloid type. Gene testing found the variant, and he started the stabilising drug tafamidis. Family checks found more carriers and affected relatives, confirming the inherited pattern.
pmc-13284070:
Jingjing Lu and colleagues reviewed real-world use in 2026 of PARP inhibitor maintenance therapy in older ovarian cancer patients. These drugs block a DNA repair enzyme and are proven in ovarian cancer generally, yet older patients lacked dedicated study. Records came from Peking University People's Hospital for patients aged sixty-five and over treated between 2018 and 2023 with olaparib or niraparib after a good response to platinum chemotherapy.

Fifty-six patients qualified, most on niraparib. In first-line maintenance, median time without progression reached twenty-four months. Complete surgical clearance, BRCA mutation status, and a low tumour marker level each independently tied to longer benefit. Anaemia was the top severe side effect on olaparib, and low platelets on niraparib. Dose changes clustered in the first six months, and long use was generally tolerated.
pmc-13284170:
First opioid use and later dependence pull gene activity in opposite ways, argues Ngo Cheung in a 2026 gene study. Many past studies merged both stages into one trait, which may blur distinct biology. The work used gene-based tests on summary data from a large opioid study set.

Risk for first use tied to lower activity in immune and cell pruning genes. Gene sets for star cells and cell aging also trended down for first use. Risk for dependence instead raised activity in energy and fuel sensing paths. Signals for nerve contacts and DNA repair joined that second profile. Some driver genes flipped sign between stages.
pmc-13284470:
Marta Milà-Alomà and colleagues report a 2026 analysis of how fast Alzheimer disease moves from amyloid to tau buildup on PET scans. Data came from two cohorts, ADNI and the Harvard Aging Brain Study, with hundreds of participants who had positive amyloid or tau scans. The team modeled the age at each scan milestone and the gap between them.

The gap length differed a lot from person to person. It ran shorter for women, for people carrying the APOE-ε4 variant, and for those whose amyloid scans turned positive later in life. Carriers and women also reached both milestones younger. A shorter gap after amyloid positivity predicted earlier symptoms. The authors say the timing can help find people at risk of rapid change for early trials and treatment.
pmc-13284870:
Bobur Ataev, Balhen Bolathan, and Weimin Zhang describe a 2026 case of a large hydatid cyst pressing on the heart. Such cysts in the sac around the heart are very rare and can cause tamponade or severe allergy if they burst. A 36-year-old farmer arrived with chest tightness and short breath.

Imaging showed a large mixed cyst inside the pericardium, next to the right heart chambers, squeezing and warping them. Planned surgery removed the cyst under ultrasound guidance through the food pipe, which helped guide exact cutting and limit leftover disease. Recovery went well. The authors urge doctors to suspect hydatid disease when a pericardial mass appears in patients from endemic areas or with animal contact.
pmc-13285370:
What helps or blocks pharmacists when they try to cut unneeded drugs for older patients is the focus of a 2026 focus group study by Sanne Bakker and co-authors. Taking many drugs raises harm risk, and a new guideline with drug fact sheets aimed to aid reviews. Nineteen community pharmacists from a trial arm shared their hands-on experience in online groups.

Coders found twenty-six factors across seven domains. The guideline itself drew few complaints, with praise for its layered build and short summaries. Pharmacists flagged their own skill at spotting cut chances and tracking results. Patient knowledge gaps, mixed patient feelings, and how well family doctors knew the approach also shaped success.
pmc-13285970:
Velina Banda and Deng Gang weigh the place of urodynamic testing in men with urinary symptoms in a 2026 narrative review. Pressure-flow studies long stood as the gold test for telling a blocked outlet from a weak bladder muscle. Newer trial proof and guidelines now question whether every man needs the invasive test before treatment.

Simple tools such as flow rates, leftover urine checks, and ultrasound measures can sort many men well enough for first steps. The invasive test still earns its place when the picture stays cloudy: young men with stubborn symptoms, suspected weak muscle, nerve-based bladder trouble, or symptoms that persist after surgery. Test quality varies between operators, which limits trust in borderline calls. The authors favor a stepwise path that saves the full study for cases where its answer would change care.
pmc-13286370:
Elena Corujo-Simon and co-authors mimic the embryo's physical cradle to grow a missing cell type in a 2026 stem cell study. Lab-made embryo models need early endoderm cells, the layer that becomes yolk sac and gut lining, but older cell lines had already aged past that stage. The team copied the inner cell mass's softness and grip chemistry to coax fresh precursor cells out of mouse blastocysts.

Inner cells were settled on gels of differing stiffness dressed with chosen matrix proteins. The right mechanical setting let brand-new endoderm precursor lines expand through several rounds of growth. The system stayed short-lived, yet long enough to reveal which supports the young cells demand. Better starter cells should slot more smoothly into blastoids, sharpening a key tool for studying the first days of development.
pmc-13286570:
Bruno Miranda and co-authors listen to single neurons while monkeys choose by two learning styles in a 2026 neuroscience study. Goal-directed choice uses a mental map of how actions lead to rewards, while habit simply repeats what paid before. Electrodes sat in two frontal and two striatal regions as two macaques played a two-step choice game whose surprise transitions expose which style drives each pick.

All four regions tracked rewards and the odds of each transition. The anterior cingulate, though, carried the signature blend of reward, transition, and choice that goal-directed math requires, and its cells priced options the map-based way. Caudate cells even flipped their value estimates after a rare transition, exactly as structural knowledge demands. Striatal cells separately echoed the reward-prediction errors of habit learning, sketching a division of labor across the circuit.
pmc-13286870:
Zahra Hatami Asl and colleagues test group therapy for the mental aftershocks of preeclampsia in a 2026 quasi-experimental study. Women whose pregnancies were complicated by the dangerous blood-pressure disorder face higher risks of depression, anxiety, and stress after delivery, yet postpartum care usually stops at the body. Ninety-five such women at a Kermanshah hospital were split between eight group sessions of transdiagnostic training and routine care alone.

The therapy teaches shared skills for handling negative emotions across disorders rather than treating each symptom separately. Scores for depression, anxiety, and stress all fell clearly in the trained group at one week and again at two months. The routine-care group showed no such movement. The authors recommend folding this kind of group training into standard postpartum protocols after high-risk pregnancies.
pmc-13287270:
Carolina De Toma and co-authors describe in 2026 the setup and early results of ALIGNED, an Italian network for rare diseases of brain blood vessels. Forty-nine centres joined. The network standardises records, surveys local care capacity, and offers virtual specialist input to narrow regional gaps.

The first group held 308 people across five conditions, led by CADASIL with 162 cases and Moyamoya angiopathy with 80 cases. Site surveys showed wide unevenness in testing and care. Early gene and protein profiling in Moyamoya samples pointed to disturbed vessel growth signals. The authors argue that mapping expertise is a first step toward equal access to diagnosis.
pmc-13287370:
Candice Marie Sage wrote a 2026 news and perspectives piece arguing that a short writing-based treatment for posttraumatic stress deserves a far wider place in care. Sage reports as a journal correspondent and draws on her own long wait for publicly funded help in Canada.

In written exposure work, patients write about the traumatic event in a small number of guided sessions. Take-up and completion in everyday services are described as high. Sage notes that global access to trauma care is poor, with few patients receiving adequate therapy. Online delivery is presented as a route to fairer access, especially where trained therapists are scarce.
pmc-13287470:
Ulrik Röijezon and colleagues measured body sway in 2026 in 28 young adults and 25 older adults. Each person stood on a force plate. Each watched a virtual roller-coaster ride five times in a row. A time-frequency method split sway signals into bands to reveal how balance strategy changed.

The first ride raised sway energy at higher frequencies and lowered it at very low frequencies. Older adults leaned more on high-frequency corrections. With repeats, high-frequency energy fell in both groups, showing quick adaptation. Older adults still shifted their patterns more overall. The authors suggest virtual challenges can expose age differences in balance resilience and could serve in balance training.
pmc-13287670: A 2025 study comparing a modified method for preserving donor hearts before transplant with standard methods was retracted in 2026. Scientific Reports issued the notice for the work by Xiaoke Shang and colleagues. After publication, worries arose over mistakes in the statistical work and gaps in the data that could not be reconciled. The team also could not provide ethics approval papers when asked. One author agreed with the retraction wording. The other five authors did not reply to the editors. The notice adds no new clinical findings.
pmc-13287870:
Akhila Madulapalli Reddy and colleagues profile cyclin-amplified bile duct cancer in a 2026 study. Bile duct cancers are uncommon and often hard to treat. Some tumors carry extra copies of cyclin genes, which push cells to divide. The team sequenced tumors from 263 patients and split them into amplified and non-amplified groups. They compared survival, other gene changes, and immune features between the groups.

Seventy-one patients fell in the amplified group, and their median survival was about 21 months against about 28 months for others. Adding immunotherapy to chemotherapy helped only the non-amplified group. Amplified tumors often carried TP53 changes and showed signs of genomic instability. Gene activity patterns showed few immune cells inside these tumors, a picture the authors call an immune desert. Drug resistance genes were also turned up, which may explain the poor response to standard treatment.
pmc-13287970:
Tingting You and co-authors tracked tumour DNA floating in blood in 2026 in 127 patients starting first treatment for advanced pancreatic cancer. Blood was drawn at the start, at the first response check, and later, and read with deep gene sequencing to follow change over time.

Tumour DNA was found in 78.7% of patients at the start, falling to 55.7% at the first check. High starting levels, and a high share of the strongest mutation signal, meant shorter time before growth and shorter survival. Falling or cleared signals meant better control. In patients whose standard marker stays silent, the DNA signal still carried useful forecasts.
pmc-13288370:
Eda G Christensen and co-authors held two focus groups in May 2025, reported in 2026. Twenty Aymara women took part in Sajama, a remote high town in rural Bolivia. The aim was to learn how they see cancer risk and care. Cancer causes nearly a fifth of deaths in Bolivia, yet remote indigenous views are seldom recorded.

Women described cancer as feared, silent, and usually found too late to cure. Five themes covered risk views, barriers such as distance, cost, and mistrust, and the side-by-side use of traditional and clinic medicine. Daily habits and environmental worries also surfaced. The authors call for teaching and screening shaped with the community itself.
pmc-13288670:
Viviana Dovale-Farelo and Kamal Choudhary test how calculation choices affect predicted contact barriers in a 2026 study. A Schottky barrier is the energy step charges face where metal meets semiconductor. Getting its height right matters for diodes, transistors, and sensors. The team modeled silicon joined to aluminum, copper, silver, and gold. They varied both the math used for electron exchange and the reference setup for bulk materials.

The biggest accuracy factor was consistency between the interface model and its bulk references. Matching strain and electric alignment mattered more than the choice of functional alone. A mixed approach, pairing hybrid and semilocal math with strained references, gave barrier heights close to experiment. It did so at favorable computing cost across all four metals. The authors offer the protocol as a grounded recipe for interface predictions. Device designers can use it to screen contact metals before building prototypes.
pmc-13288770:
XinYi Jiang and co-authors test how motion capture features shape learning in animation courses, in a 2026 study. Motion capture turns a learner's body movements into character motion in real time. The study varied two features, immersion and action-linked interactivity, in a two-by-two experiment. One hundred seventeen students took a virtual lesson on character motion design. Surveys and knowledge tests measured presence, agency, and learning gains.

Interactivity that responded to the learner's own actions raised presence and agency the most. It also linked to larger gains in conceptual knowledge from before to after the lesson. Immersion reliably deepened presence and improved the training experience, yet its learning advantage was not consistent. Combining both features at high levels gave diminishing extra returns.
