First found in fluid from a breast cancer line, it can slow some tumor cells while urging healthy cells to grow, a two faced pattern that still draws study.

Proof from cell and animal work is weighed across heart, lung, gut, cancer, and infection settings. In many of them the factor guards tissue after harm yet also drives disease when its signal runs too long or too strong. Turning that balance into safe drugs will need exact control of dose, place, and timing, the review argues.
pmc-13320470:
Aili Wang and colleagues present a 2026 mouse and cell study on fine dust in the air and asthma. The team asked how a lung protein called CC16 guards airway cells against a type of cell death linked to iron and fat damage. Dust exposure is known to worsen asthma and harm the lining of the airways.

Tests with proteomics and cell assays pointed to E-cadherin, a protein that holds lining cells together, as a key partner for CC16. Dust lowered E-cadherin and raised cell damage, while added CC16 restored it and cut fat damage. Blocking the E-cadherin gene removed the benefit, which marks a fresh target for asthma care tied to polluted air.
pmc-13320570:
Takhellambam P Devi and colleagues compare, in 2026, three antibiotic pastes used inside teeth during regenerative root treatment for young patients. Such pastes disinfect the canal in immature teeth with dead pulp, but the classic triple paste can stain the tooth because of one ingredient. A modified paste swaps that ingredient for clindamycin, which does not stain.

Fifty-one teeth from patients aged twelve to twenty-five were assigned to double, triple or modified triple paste groups. Success rates at one year were high and closely matched across groups. At two years, rates had eased in all groups and still showed no significant differences. The authors conclude the modified paste is a reasonable alternative where tooth colour matters.
pmc-13321070:
Dimitri Breda and co-authors build a data driven method to forecast vector borne disease in a 2026 study. Illnesses spread by ticks and other vectors pose growing risks, yet records are sparse and transmission involves long delays. Past infection and exposure shape later cases, so memory effects matter for any honest forecast.

The framework learns hidden transmission dynamics with memory straight from time series, using only a few basis functions in a sparse discovery step. Tick borne risk to humans is the test case, where tick numbers, weather, and human contact are all uncertain. Checks are reported to back the method's reliability and steadiness under scarce data. Better forecasts could guide early public health action.
pmc-13321370:
Claudius Jelgersma and co-authors compare one stage and two stage spine correction in older patients in a 2026 study. Pedicle subtraction osteotomy is a demanding fix for stiff spinal deformity, with high risk in old age. Splitting surgery into two sittings has been proposed to ease the burden, but proof in older patients was thin.

Records for 51 patients treated from 2014 to 2023 were compared, with median ages near 70 in both groups. Total operating time was far shorter in one stage care, at 431 minutes against 653 minutes on average in the study. Blood loss, hospital stay, and complication rates within 90 days did not differ clearly. Overall surgical load, not staging, seemed decisive.
pmc-13322970:
Xinyu Liu, Wei Meng and Xun Huang comment on a newly found mitochondrial carrier in a 2026 article about fat storage. They discuss work by Yamamuro and others, published in Cell, that names SLC25A35 as the long-sought carrier moving phosphoenolpyruvate out of mitochondria.

That export supplies the glycerol backbone needed to build triglycerides and related fats in liver and fat tissue, a process called glyceroneogenesis. Fatty acid control has drawn far more attention than backbone supply, the authors note. Linking this carrier to triglyceride formation and fatty liver gives a fresh target for metabolic research, and the commentary sets out why the finding matters for energy balance.
pmc-13323270:
Laura Krause and colleagues report, in 2026, the first routine-data picture of how often adults in Germany attend dental check-ups. Regular examinations help cut the oral disease burden, yet national uptake figures from billing data were missing. The team analysed statutory insurance dental billing records covering 2015 to 2024.

Uptake held near sixty-four percent until 2019, dipped in the first pandemic year, then climbed back to its starting level by 2024. Men, younger and very old adults, and people in western Germany attended less often than average. The east-west gap narrowed over the decade. More than a third of insured adults had no check-up in 2024, which the authors read as a clear case for stronger prevention efforts targeting the low-uptake groups.
pmc-13323570:
Naoki Ishibashi and colleagues searched for genetic variants that predict a dangerous heart-rhythm side effect of bepridil, a drug used for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Their 2026 study enrolled 523 patients who started bepridil after catheter ablation at Hiroshima University between 2013 and 2023. Heart rhythm was measured one month after starting the drug, with QT prolongation defined by sex-specific cutoffs on the corrected QT interval.

A genome-wide scan in 445 patients, checked in a separate group of 78, pointed to a variant in the FSHR gene, rs12622919, which reached genome-wide significance when both groups were combined. Adding the variant improved prediction of QT prolongation, and a sex-split look hinted at a stronger signal in women, though no formal interaction was found. The authors offer the variant as a possible marker for individual risk, while stressing that independent validation is still required.
pmc-13325070:
Jéssica Alves Bonamichi and colleagues compare how packaged forms of the herbicide clomazone move through soil, corn residue, and soybean plants in a 2026 study. Clomazone suits no-till farming but can evaporate or wash away before it works.

Two microencapsulated and two standard concentrate products were tracked under controlled conditions. The encapsulated forms leaked slowly at first, then reached 42.3 and 36.9 percent leaching by day 30 of the trial. Standard forms leaked fast on day one, near 20 percent, yet lost less overall. Encapsulated products clung to corn residue and kept over 90 percent of the dose on leaf surfaces. No form harmed the soybean plants.
pmc-13325370:
Yunus Emre Toprak and co-authors make glowing carbon dots from pine cone waste to sense copper in water in a 2026 study. Trace copper threatens both ecosystems and health, and field tests need to be fast and cheap.

Dots cooked from pine cone lignin and doped with lysine changed brightness in step with copper levels. The working range spanned 2.81 × 10^-7 to 5.87 × 10^-5 mol per liter, with a detection limit of 2.8 × 10^-8 mol per liter. Trials on drinking water, seawater, and wastewater standards gave recoveries of 98.9 to 104.4 percent. Results matched the standard absorption method at 95 percent confidence. Real lake and tap samples also read cleanly.
pmc-13326870:
Daniel C. Payne and team wrote expert advice to strengthen chikungunya outbreak tracking and reports for visitor health. Their 2026 paper notes that the virus, a crippling bug-borne disease, has surged in the past two decades, with outbreaks growing rapidly and weighing on warm and subtropical regions and tourists. Health staff need timely, exact outbreak information, yet finding is often weakest where outbreaks are most likely, causing test and reports delays.

The panel checked tracking and reports tools and found no single tool sufficient: judging outbreak risk requires combining multiple local and international sources. Challenges included weak tracking infrastructure and test capacity, varying case definitions, limited understanding of local health contexts, low awareness in health care settings, and restricted or delayed access to real-time data. The advice aim to improve timely, sensitive, specific testing and rapid communication to clinicians and tourists, especially in resource-poor regions.
pmc-13327870:
Yanyan Zhang and colleagues gather diagnostic clues for liver amyloidosis in a 2026 review of ten confirmed cases. AL amyloidosis deposits abnormal protein in the liver and is rare enough to be missed. The team re-read clinical notes plus CT and MRI scans for shared patterns.

Every patient had an enlarged liver and low blood albumin, and all showed sharply raised alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase with near-normal other liver enzymes. Scans showed delayed contrast uptake, narrowed or poorly seen main liver veins, and fluid around portal veins in all cases, while bile ducts stayed open. Belly swelling affected 90 percent of patients, so the full pattern should prompt early biopsy thinking.
pmc-13328170:
Seon-Chil Kim and colleagues test personalized digital therapy for children with ADHD in a 2026 study. Forty children aged 5 to 12 were split evenly between a standard digital training program and one tuned to each child's first-week performance profile. Training volume was held equal, and attention tests plus a Korean ADHD rating scale bracketed the four weeks.

Profiling showed performance decline tied more to commission errors, the impulsive kind, than to missed targets. The personalized arm then adjusted content mix, difficulty, and feedback to each child's error pattern during weeks two to four, while controls followed the fixed plan. Data-driven tuning of digital practice may beat one-size programs, the design sets out to show.
pmc-13328270:
Hao Kang and Xiaofen Cao review stroboscopic visual training for basketball in a 2026 narrative review. Training under flickering eyewear is meant to sharpen how athletes take in a fast game, but basketball-specific studies are scarce. The pair gathered work from comparable open-skill sports published between 1997 and 2026.

Across sports, the training improved three markers tied to information processing: reaction time, decision accuracy, and motor control. They sort training settings into a three-phase frame matched to processing stages and to basketball-specific measures. Every suggested setting, though, rests on cross-sport trends, so the framework stands as a hypothesis until basketball trials test the numbers directly.
pmc-13328370:
Jianbo Song and co-authors review sound-based pain relief in a 2026 narrative review. Pain affects over 30 percent of the world's people, and drug or surgical routes carry misuse and complication risks. The authors gather evidence on acoustic stimulation, from music and natural sounds to vibroacoustic therapy and immersive sound systems.

Sound seems to work through several brain routes at once: retuning cortex-thalamus loops, switching on the body's own descending pain brakes, and shifting neurochemical messengers. Clinical reports back music, natural sound, and vibration-sound mixes as add-ons for both sudden and lasting pain. The review argues sound deserves a planned seat in multimodal pain care, with dosing standards still to settle.
pmc-13330670:
Jiwei Li and team found lecithin cholesterol acyltransferase to be a molecular switch for rooster sperm motility. Their 2026 study picked Yufen 1 roosters with big movement gaps among highly motile sperm samples stored in varied ways, using seminal plasma proteome and metabolome data. Sperm movement largely shapes semen quality, yet its control remains unclear, and the team found 181 proteins and 112 metabolites that differed between high and low motility groups.

LCAT was upregulated in the low motility group. Targeted activation much reduced sperm movement and plasma membrane integrity, causing membrane disruption, chromatin loss, and mitochondrial swelling. It also reduced both the longest fertile days and the number of fertilized eggs. LCAT controls movement in vitro by changing sperm membrane structure and function through shifts in glycerophospholipid metabolism. The findings offer new insight into stretching the artificial insemination window and better semen preservation strategies in poultry.
pmc-13332370:
Ruoyu Zhang and colleagues developed a 2026 method for spotting social media posts that quietly offer prescription drugs for private sale in Japan. Such one-to-one dealing bypasses pharmacies, risks unsafe use, and is hard for regulators to track by hand.

Working from the hashtag “#Okusuri mogumogu,” tied to trading psychiatric drugs, the team crawled 7,499 posts from 2022 and 6,461 from early 2023, then labeled which ones truly offered private transactions. Of 3,228 distinct words, 452 were significantly tied to dealing posts, with terms meaning request, transfer, and direct message among the strongest signals. A decision tree trained on 2022 data reached 82.31 percent accuracy on the 2023 set, with area under the curve values around 0.83 to 0.84. The authors suggest the approach can help monitors flag risky drug trading automatically.
pmc-13332970:
Begonya Nafria and colleagues audited children's trial protocols across Europe in a 2026 study of whether language rules quietly shut families out. Europe has 32 official languages, children with rare diseases may find their only treatment option abroad, and some patients report being turned away over language.

The team searched the eligibility text of 1,754 pediatric protocols run in Europe between 2007 and 2024 on ClinicalTrials.gov. Most, 95.2 percent, never mentioned language at all. Among the 85 protocols that did set language requirements, only 23, or 27.1 percent, offered a scientific justification such as testing that must be done in a shared language or questionnaires validated in few tongues. English at 20 percent and French at 16.5 percent were the most demanded languages. The authors urge ethics committees to demand reasons for language criteria and protocols to plan translation and travel support.
pmc-13333370:
Liming Yang and co-authors engineered a swallowable nanoparticle in 2026 to rescue celastrol, a plant compound with strong promise against fatty liver disease but poor absorption and a narrow safety margin. Their target was nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, the inflamed stage of fatty liver that can march toward cirrhosis.

Instead of loading the drug into a carrier, they let it self-assemble with natural polysaccharides, building 42 candidate assemblies and screening them for the best partner. Chondroitin sulfate won. The winning mix raised total body exposure 3.12-fold over free celastrol, and tracer studies suggested it crosses gut cells through several uptake routes with partial escape from digestive compartments. In a mouse model of the disease, the particles calmed liver inflammation and cut fat buildup while softening the free drug's toxicity. The authors present the design as a platform that widens celastrol's usable window for oral liver therapy.
pmc-13333470:
Shi-Ning Luo and colleagues test two inflammation markers against angiogram-proven coronary disease severity in a 2026 retrospective study. High-sensitivity C-reactive protein is a familiar inflammation gauge, while Lp-PLA2 comes from the vessel wall, and the authors asked how each lines up with how blocked a patient's arteries are.

The Henan cohort covered 438 patients scoped between April 2023 and April 2024, split into 329 with at least half-blocked coronary arteries and 109 controls below that bar. Both markers rose with lesion burden, though in different patterns. Lp-PLA2 climbed to its peak in three-vessel disease, while hs-CRP topped out in two-vessel disease. Both ran higher in heart attack patients than in angina patients. Lp-PLA2 separated coronary disease with an AUC of 0.900 and severe lesions at 0.952; adding hs-CRP barely moved the curve. The authors favour the pair, saying the signals carry complementary information for risk stratification.
pmc-13334270: Jiashun Li and co-authors issued this 2026 correction notice. It concerns their systematic review and meta-analysis of CD3 bispecific antibodies targeting BCMA or GPRC5D in relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. The notice itself carries no study results; it only replaces the article's funding statement, which had been published with errors. The corrected statement lists the supporting grants. They include Xinjiang regional health and medical research projects, a National Natural Science Foundation of China award, and Xinjiang Medical University programs.
pmc-13336970:
Sicong Ren and colleagues design a blood-derived gel that rebuilds gum lining in a 2026 study. Keratinized mucosa, the tough gum tissue around teeth and implants, is hard to regrow. The mouth is wet, moving, and hostile to grafts. Their double-network gel blends treated platelet-rich fibrin, sticky alginate, and microspheres carrying plant compounds.

Two interlocked networks give strong wet grip and fatigue resistance, so the gel stays put under chewing stress. Slow release of growth factors and plant compounds boosts blood vessel growth and steers neutrophils toward a germ-eating state. The gel's stiffness also instructs gum fibroblasts to rebuild matrix faster. Animal tests confirmed strong regeneration of the gum lining.
pmc-13337770:
Regina Idu Ejemot-Nwadiaro leads a 2026 survey of job stress among university teachers in Nigeria. Academic stress in sub-Saharan Africa has had little study that mixes questionnaires with body measures. The setting was the University of Calabar, with staff drawn from all 15 faculties.

A total of 401 permanent staff completed the ASSET stress tool alongside height, weight, and body measurements. Stress proved widespread, with 84.3 percent of respondents falling in stressed ranges in the reported summary. Sources of pressure and links to habits and health factors were tested with standard comparisons. Results underline a heavy strain burden that university policy has yet to address well.
pmc-13339770:
Qingyu Zhang, Yat-Long Cheng, and Ying-Yeung Yeung convert ethers into acetals without a catalyst in a 2026 study. Acetals serve as drug parts, materials, fragrances, and protecting groups. A bromoamide reagent called DBDMH mediated direct editing beside the ether oxygen.

Common ethers such as THF and diethyl ether plus varied alcohols gave acetals in high yields under mild conditions as reported. The method built two commercial fragrances, Cyanophyll and Efetaal, proving practical reach. Trace bromine and acid impurities in the reagent proved crucial to speed, an honest detail that helps others reproduce the reaction.
pmc-13340070:
Juanjuan Zhou and colleagues profiled a rare drug resistant germ in 2026 from a child with diarrhoea and fever. Drug resistant Salmonella is seldom seen in clinics, yet this Salmonella Stanley strain, SAL22057, carried blaNDM-13 resistance. The team tested drug response, read the full genome, and checked whether its resistance plasmid can move to other germs.

The strain fought off meropenem at 32 micrograms per millilitre and imipenem at 16, fell in sequence type 29, and carried many harm genes plus resistance to many drugs. Plasmid tests probed spread risk. The case warns hospitals to watch for last resort drug resistance even in rare Salmonella infections.
pmc-13340670:
Setareh Mahmoodi and colleagues reported a giant splenic artery aneurysm in 2026 found after blunt belly trauma in a cirrhotic patient. Giant visceral artery aneurysms are exceedingly rare yet carry a high rupture risk, above all with cirrhosis, portal hypertension, or connective tissue disease. Timely recognition and surgery are critical.

A 66 year old man with hepatitis B cirrhosis arrived after trauma, and imaging showed a large contrast filled lesion in the mid splenic artery plus a small liver lesion. Surgeons removed the aneurysm with the spleen and took a liver wedge biopsy. Pathology confirmed a true aneurysm with wall calcification. He recovered well with better platelets and stable liver function.
pmc-13341270:
Canhada and colleagues charted weight gain across adult life in 2026 using the ELSA-Brasil study, a long-running cohort of Brazilian adults followed from 2008 to 2024. The 11,611 participants, aged 35 to 74 at entry, had repeated measures of weight, waist, and body fat and muscle, with weight at age 20 recalled at the start. The team modeled how each measure changed with age.

Adults gained an average of 15 kilograms between ages 20 and 60, when weight peaked, and half of that gain arrived before age 35. Yearly gains were steepest up to the early forties, then slowed, held steady in the late fifties and sixties, and fell in older age. Waist size kept rising to about age 75 even as weight leveled. The authors argue that curbing gain in young adulthood could do the most to cut later obesity burden.
pmc-13341570:
Europe's heart and diabetes prevention needs a life-course reset, argues Sarah Cuschieri in a 2026 policy analysis. Cardiovascular disease and diabetes remain the top causes of early death in Europe despite decades of pledges and cheap, proven preventive tools.

Cuschieri points to early-life risk exposure, patchy surveillance, and care systems built around late treatment rather than prevention. Priority moves include weaving prevention across the lifespan, strengthening front-line and community services, funding equity-focused data, and scaling joint efforts such as JACARDI and JA PreventNCD. Accountability, she concludes, is the missing muscle behind existing ambition.
pmc-13341870:
Digital skills help diabetic foot patients manage their condition, mostly through confidence, in a 2026 survey by Jianxia Yao and colleagues. The cross-sectional study enrolled 328 patients with diabetes-related foot disease in a tertiary endocrinology department between February 2024 and December 2025.

Digital health literacy correlated moderately with self-management behavior (r = 0.42), while self-efficacy correlated strongly (r = 0.53). Mediation analysis showed self-efficacy carried 41.8% of the literacy effect, with an effect size of 0.23, even after adjusting for age, disease duration, and ulcer grade. Teaching patients to find information may fail unless programs also build belief they can act on it.
pmc-13342170:
Research on childhood adversity and personality disorders is mapped bibliometrically by Liuyin Jin's team in the 2026 analysis. Records from three sources through December 2025 were screened and deduplicated to 5,084 publications, analyzed with network and burst-detection tools.

Output grew year by year with a marked climb after 2000. The United States dominated publications, citations, and collaborations; Canada, Germany, the Netherlands, Australia, and the United Kingdom also carried weight. Harvard, the University of London, and Heidelberg led institutions, and authors such as Zanarini and Fonagy anchored the field. The maps expose core themes and emerging fronts for new readers to explore.
pmc-13342570:
Rody Ngurthankhumi and colleagues profiled wild edible fruits in 2026 from Mizoram in northeast India, part of the Indo Burma hotspot. These fruits back nutrition, folk medicine, and sustainability for native peoples, yet detailed data on nutrition, active compounds, and food traits were scant. Seven chosen fruits were tested, with Antidesma bunius, Carallia brachiata, Emblica officinalis, and Embelia species among them.

Nutrition profiles, active plant chemicals, mineral levels, and food traits were measured. Wild fruits offer untapped food and medicine resources for the region. The profiles back care, growth, and product work that respects folk knowledge and local livelihoods.
pmc-13344270:
David J Carr and colleagues asked in 2026 whether gentle electrical stimulation of leg and belly muscles could ease insulin resistance in pregnant rats made obese by a rich diet. Obesity in pregnancy raises risks for both mother and child, and pregnancy itself already makes the body less responsive to insulin.

Nineteen obese pregnant rats received 12 to 14 sessions of low-frequency stimulation under anaesthesia, while nineteen obese pregnant rats received anaesthesia alone and ten lean non-pregnant rats served as controls. Insulin sensitivity was then measured with a gold-standard clamp test near the end of pregnancy, alongside body composition and fasting glucose and insulin. The design tests a drug-free approach that might one day help protect mothers with obesity and their offspring.
pmc-13347670:
Tinyiko P. Hlungwani, Pheagane M.W. Nkoana, and Velibanti N. Sukati survey satisfaction with private eye care in South Africa, in a 2026 study. Questionnaires shared through social media drew 283 users across all nine provinces, with a mean age of 36.3 years. Visits most often aimed at renewing glasses or lenses, routine checks, or blurred vision.

Overall satisfaction averaged 4.38 out of 5 in the reported score, with cleanliness, facilities, and staff conduct rated highest by patients. Waiting time and cost scored lowest, and among patients who had switched provider, moves were led by relocation while 17.9 percent cited poor service. Shorter waits and clearer pricing are the clear fixes.
pmc-13347770:
Husin F. Khizar and colleagues pilot manual therapy against strength training for runner knee pain from the iliotibial band, in a study from 2026. Thirty-four runners were split evenly, with one group getting friction massage, stretching, and soft tissue work. The other following a set hip and knee strengthening plan over six weeks, scored for pain and leg function.

Both groups improved clearly on pain and function by the end of the program in the reported tests, with strong statistical signals in each arm. No loser emerged from this small pilot. So the authors offer both routes as workable starting care and call for larger head-to-head work that also tracks return of symptoms over time.
pmc-13348070:
Tripti Raghavendra and Sarita G. Bhat report the genome of a sea bacterium that eats naphthalene, in an announcement from 2026. Rhodococcus ruber PCTR3 came from harbour mud at Cochin Port, India, enriched on naphthalene alone. It cleared 1,000 mg per litre within 72 hours, matching its whole parent mix and beating four sister strains.

The genome spans 5,754,741 base pairs with 5,306 genes and a G plus C share of 70.34 percent in the reported assembly. Gene notes flag many pollutant-breaking enzymes plus routes to useful by-products, making the strain a candidate for cleaning tar-like pollution at ports.
pmc-13349770:
Siqi Wang and colleagues review ear-point therapy as an add-on for childhood attention disorder, in a scoping review published in 2026. Seven databases to July 2025 gave 21 controlled trials with 2,270 children, checked with standard bias tools, tabulated by design. Pooled where outcomes allowed, covering parent ratings, anxiety and mood scales, and life quality scores.

Add-on ear therapy improved parent ratings, anxiety and mood scores. Life quality in the pooled results, each clearing the set significance bar, while overall success rate only trended upward. No serious harms appeared, yet bias grades left evidence at low to moderate certainty, so the authors back longer, tighter trials before firm clinic advice.
pmc-13350370:
Jinxia Zhang and Cheng Liu discussed in 2026 the tangled link between clinical obesity and heart failure, moving beyond body mass index. Obesity is among the century's largest public health challenges, yet BMI alone fails to capture fat distribution, metabolic function, and obesity-driven abnormalities.

A Lancet commission now defines clinical obesity as a disease in its own right, emphasising metabolic consequences rather than weight alone. The authors trace how excess and dysfunctional fat contribute to heart failure through inflammation, volume load, and metabolic disturbance, while noting paradoxes where higher BMI sometimes appears protective. The discussion helps clinicians assess obesity as a systemic disease, not a single number, when managing heart failure risk.
pmc-13351570:
Lingzhao Min and colleagues report a 2026 case series on children who have both craniosynostosis and hydrocephalus. Care for the two conditions together is rare and the best order of surgery is debated. The series covers nine children treated at one hospital, seven boys and two girls aged 8 to 45 months.

Seven children had syndromic forms and eight had raised pressure inside the skull. All had cranioplasty, fluid leaked in two cases, and five later needed a ventriculoperitoneal shunt for lasting hydrocephalus. Over follow-up averaging 53.6 months, skull shape and symptoms improved in eight children. The authors favour cranioplasty first, with shunting held for cases that persist.
pmc-13353170:
Merve Acun Pınar leads a 2026 clinical study of coal workers' pneumoconiosis and related lung scarring. Long coal dust exposure scars the lungs and can also drive airway disease. All 100 patients were male, with mean age of 61.7 years. Large opacities appeared in 37 percent, while restrictive and obstructive lung patterns hit 35 percent and 38 percent. Bituminous miners fared worse than lignite miners on both opacity and lung function. Interstitial changes showed in 63 percent and frank interstitial disease in 42 percent, linked in models to longer exposure.
pmc-13353870:
Gunoh Lee led a 2026 study that embeds cell-free protein making inside porous parylene scaffolds for point-of-care biosensing. Cell-free systems can produce proteins without living cells, giving speed and programmability, but keeping them active inside a solid, portable stuff has been hard. Earlier work mostly placed them on flat paper faces, capping storage and multiplexing.

The team loaded the protein-making gear into a three-sized parylene scaffold that preserves its action, creating a solid-state platform. Such scaffolds could support long-term storage, portability, and parallel tests in one device. The work brings field-ready biosensors closer, where a stable, cell-free test could run far from a lab.
pmc-13355370:
Joice Carla Dorneles Zanin and co-authors ran a 2026 trial in Brazil on a coffee-flavored carbohydrate drink given before surgery. Long fasting before anesthesia was once standard, but it leaves patients hungry, thirsty, and anxious. Patients having planned surgery got either 200 milliliters of the drink up to two hours before anesthesia or the usual eight-hour fast.

Drinkers reported feeling fuller and less thirsty and anxious than fasters, and they liked the taste. Those who began very anxious felt the drink helped calm them. No harms were seen, though the trial was too small to catch rare events. The authors call for larger studies on wider outcomes and safety.
pmc-13357070:
Heyuan Jia and colleagues asked whether a traditional formula, Si Ni Powder, can rescue chemotherapy when breast cancer patients sleep poorly, in a 2026 mouse study. Sleep loss switched on swelling signals, matrix remodeling, and fat metabolism paths, all of which the powder countered. Chemical profiling found 168 powder components, with 20 reaching tumor tissue, pointing to a multi-target network around Stat3, Stat6, and related regulators.
pmc-13358370:
Fröhlich and colleagues probe how the calcium channel Orai1 opens in cell walls. The channel lets calcium into cells. A sensor protein, STIM1, tells it when to open. The team focused on where two parts of the channel meet. Three key building blocks sit at that join. Their size and their dislike of water both matter. Small changes there shifted how well the channel held shut. They also shifted how much calcium flowed in.

The right mix keeps the channel shut at rest. It also lets in enough calcium when the cell calls for it. Too loose a mix lets in too much. The work shows how fine tuning guards cell health.
pmc-13359370:
Yiqun Xu and co-authors simulate how porous materials form in a 2026 study. The materials start as emulsions loaded with soap-like molecules and tiny solid particles, then set into solids full of large pores. Pore size follows particle size, but the steps that shape the pore network were unclear. The team built a coarse computer model of the four-part mix.

Their simulations show particles change how the mix separates, slowing pore growth and yielding finer pores. As the mix evolves, the pore size pattern shifts from one hump to two. More of the soap-like ingredient and neutral particle surfaces refine the structure further. The model can guide recipes for filters and lightweight solids.
pmc-13359970:
Tzong-Yueh Chen and co-authors measure what a super typhoon did to ocean life in a 2026 study. Typhoons are often credited with boosting ocean productivity by stirring up nutrients. After Super Typhoon Maria crossed the East China Sea in 2018, the team sampled plankton and bacteria and compared them with satellite views.

Surface readings barely changed, likely because sampling came after the brief surface signal faded. Deeper totals told a fuller story: nutrients and plant plankton rose through the water column, though the bloom lasted only about a week, cut short by grazing and falling nutrient supply. Bacteria did not grow in mass, but their growth rates rose, showing a subtler microbial response.
pmc-13360170:
Hao Zhang and co-authors report a 2026 study from two hospitals on stage III lung cancer that surgery cannot remove. All 170 patients first had chemo with immune drugs, then radiation, and reached control of their disease. After that, 65 patients went on to extra immune drug treatment, while 105 did not. The team tracked both groups for a median of 33 months.

Patients who got the extra immune treatment lived longer without their cancer growing back. The gain held up after the team adjusted for differences between the groups. Extra checks suggested the benefit showed most in the early months, around 8 to 10 months in. The authors say the added treatment looks worth it, while noting the study looked back at past care.
pmc-13361070:
Shirong Dong and co-authors studied how salts shape protein threads from whey in a 2026 food science paper. When heated in acid, whey protein forms tiny fibrils that can thicken or stabilize foods. The team added eight salts in a grid design, mixing four positive ions with two negative ones at a fixed low dose. They tracked thread shape, yield, and growth speed.

Sodium, potassium, and zinc salts boosted fibril output, while iron salts cut it down. Iron's strong electric pull broke the protein apart too fast, though sulfate partly softened that block. Sulfate salts also gave shorter, clustered threads compared with chloride salts. The results give food makers a guide to which salts to pick when they want protein fibrils with set traits.
pmc-13361370:
Jasna Kalanj and co-authors assessed heart ultrasound measures in young patients with thickened heart muscle in a 2026 study. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy makes the heart wall grow too thick. Children with it can face serious heart events even when the heart's main pumping score looks normal. The team followed 31 children and teens at one center, all with preserved pumping strength.

They measured how the heart shortens along its length with several ultrasound tools, including strain imaging. These were set against MRI measures of heart mass, wall thickness, and scarring, and against major bad events over time. Length-wise measures can catch early weakness that the usual pump score misses. Finding which measures warn of trouble could sharpen watch and care for these young patients.
pmc-13362570:
Hong-Tao Li and colleagues present a 2026 computer study of a lead-free perovskite solar cell design. Perovskite cells soak up sunlight well, but the best ones use toxic lead, so this team modeled a germanium-based version flipped in structure. They tested choices for the layers that carry positive and negative charges out of the cell, plus layer thickness and defect levels.

Two layer materials, WS2 and SnO2, worked best in the model. With a tuned absorber about 900 nanometers thick and very low defect levels, the simulated cell reached about 23 percent efficiency. Nothing was built in a lab, yet the numbers give makers a clear recipe to try for safer, high-output solar cells.
pmc-13362770:
Camilo Andrés Cabarcas Castro and colleagues present a 2026 study on turning drinking water sludge into a usable soil material. Water plants produce sludge that usually goes to landfill. The team stiffened it with lime, comparing store-bought lime with lime made from waste eggshells, baked and slaked in the lab. They pressed 120 samples at four lime doses and tested strength after one and four weeks of curing.

Store lime reached the top strength at its highest dose and longest cure. Eggshell lime peaked earlier, at a mid dose and one week, and stayed competitive at mid and high doses, which marks it as a workable green swap. Adding strong alkali mostly weakened the eggshell mixes. Grain images helped explain the strength patterns.
pmc-13363170:
Xin Liu and colleagues report a 2026 study comparing diets and blood health in 356 adults in northeast China. The flip side was steep: nearly all vegans fell short on vitamin B12 and vitamin D intake, and blood levels of B12, vitamin D, iron stores, and selenium ran low. Meat eaters, in turn, overshot on salt and saturated fat. The authors urge planned supplements or fortified foods for plant-based eaters in the region.
pmc-13366770:
Mordenti and colleagues described in 2026 how patients and professionals together built transition care plans for young people with rare bone diseases in Italy. The process produced 11 practical solutions, each assigned to the body best placed to carry it out, covering short- and medium-term patient priorities. Patients and caregivers shaped every step, from design to final approval, rather than being consulted at the end. The authors present the model as a structured yet flexible way to build shared, realistic plans that both clinics and families will back.
pmc-13373270:

pmc-13373670:

pmc-13373870:

pmc-13374170:
Raquel Sánchez-Ruano and co-authors heard nurses on shared care words in Spain in a 2026 study. Shared word sets name health needs, care steps, and results in one tongue for all staff. The study sat with 33 nurses who work in care, teaching, leads, and research.

pmc-13374270:

pmc-13378170:

pmc-13378770:

pmc-13379970:

pmc-13381070:

pmc-13382070:

pmc-13382970:

pmc-13383470:

pmc-13385370:
Savitha Acharya and co-authors build a new student dataset for machine learning career guidance in 2026 work. pmc-13386670:
Walter D. Dawson and colleagues evaluate a global walking initiative against dementia stigma in a 2026 study. pmc-13386770:

pmc-13386870:
Ananya Chatterjee and Vidya Mangala Prasad review antibody sites that span flavivirus surface proteins in a 2026 article. pmc-13388370:

pmc-13389570:

pmc-13390470:

pmc-13391470:

The pair emerged from screening seven outlook-linked genes.
pmc-13392470:

pmc-13392570:

pmc-13393070:

pmc-13393770:

pmc-13393870:

pmc-13394070:

pmc-13395370:

pmc-13395470:

pmc-13395870:

pmc-13396670:

pmc-13396870:

pmc-13397270:

pmc-13397470:

pmc-13397770:

pmc-13398570:

pmc-13399270:

pmc-13399670:

pmc-13400470:

pmc-13400670:

pmc-13401470:

pmc-13401570:

pmc-13401870:

pmc-13402670:

pmc-13403370:

pmc-13403470:

pmc-13404870:

pmc-13405770:

Records span pain clinic visits from 2010 to 2026, gathered from electronic charts. The team charts pain types, medicines, procedures and how heavily patients used the clinic. Crohn's and colitis subgroups are compared with odds ratios. The aim is a clear picture of treatment burden in this selected group, which can guide service planning and future comparative studies.
pmc-13407470:
Mulavagili Vijayasimha and co-authors write, in 2026, in favour of a readiness passport before machine-learning prediction tools enter intensive care. Their letter responds to enthusiasm for prediction algorithms in intensive care. Such tools can forecast deaths better than standard severity scores. The authors argue that skill alone should never carry a tool to the bedside.

A model trained in one unit can stumble in another through different patient mixes, missing data, shifting protocols, or changed clinician habits. Alongside accuracy, the authors demand calibration checks, outside validation, subgroup performance, usefulness in real decisions, explainability, and monitoring after launch. The passport's first domain covers dataset legitimacy. It asks where patients came from and what kind of unit treated them. It also asks how outcomes were defined, how gaps were handled, and whether poorer countries appear at all.
pmc-13407670:
Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas, and Kamila Misiejuk introduce, in 2026, a software package for estimating networks in psychological and behavioural research. Networks built from survey, event, or diary data reveal how symptoms or behaviours connect. Each network type usually demands separate tools. Nestimate gathers them behind one standard workflow in the R language.

The package fits several network models from survey or event data. It then adds multi-cluster summaries. Dynamic networks track transitions and co-occurrence over time. Higher-order models look beyond the immediately previous state. Every network can pass through one validation pipeline covering bootstrap checks, permutation tests, split-half reliability, and stability analysis, which the authors present as a guard against over-reading fragile networks.
pmc-13408070:
Mohamed Mustaf Ahmed and co-authors warn, in 2026, that blockbuster weight-loss injections could split obesity care into two tiers. GLP-1 receptor agonists produce major weight loss. For semaglutide in patients with heart disease, they also bring fewer major cardiovascular events. Rolling them into primary care is hampered, though, by training gaps, clinical inertia, weight bias, high prices, and patchy insurance.

Minority groups, poorer communities, and publicly insured patients receive and fill these prescriptions least, despite carrying the heaviest obesity burden. The narrative review examines readiness in primary care, structural access barriers, prescribing disparities, real-world persistence, and policy options. Without aligned reform on coverage, pricing, workforce, and long-term support, the authors argue, access will keep tracking wealth rather than need.
pmc-13408170:
Mona El-Sabour, Hebat-Allah Tohamy, and Mohamed El-Sakhawy describe a 2026 route to longer-lasting paper made partly from rubbish. They recovered alumina from waste aluminium cans, doped it with sulfur and nitrogen, and coated paper sheets with the resulting nanoparticles. Paper normally weakens with heat, oxygen, and moisture, so a protective coating could serve archives and packaging alike.

The coating was mixed into a cellulose-based treatment and tested at several strengths and soaking times, before and after accelerated heat ageing. The best sheets, at a two percent coating soaked for fifteen minutes, gained tensile strength, stretch, and flame resistance, and held up better under ageing. Computer calculations supported the experimental picture. Readers in conservation and materials work get a waste-valorising recipe with measured performance.
pmc-13408570:
Mustafa Timurkaan and co-authors measure in 2026 a fat-derived, inflammation-resolving molecule in the blood of people with type 2 diabetes. Maresin-1 helps switch off inflammation, and the team wondered whether its level tracks eye damage or protein leaking into urine, two common diabetic complications. Ninety-three participants spanned healthy controls and three diabetes groups graded by retinal disease.

Blood maresin-1 was markedly lower in every diabetes group than in controls, at roughly a third of the healthy level. Within diabetes, however, levels did not differ between patients with no eye disease, mild disease, or advanced disease, and they did not follow urine protein once other factors were considered. The authors conclude the drop marks diabetes itself rather than any single complication, which tempers hopes of using it to stage retinal disease.
pmc-13409370:
Indira Putri Negari and colleagues test an acne vaccine idea in 2026 that targets not the bacterium itself but the digestive enzyme it secretes. The skin bacterium Cutibacterium acnes clearly drives the swelling inside spots, whatever its role in starting them. Lab analysis showed its lipase chops skin fats into free fatty acids. One product, palmitic acid, provoked oil-gland cells to send alarm signals directly.

Mice vaccinated with the lipase developed antibodies, conveniently checkable on a test strip, and were protected against bacterium-driven swelling in an ear model. Serum carrying those antibodies, moved into cell cultures, sharply cut how much of two key messengers the bacterium provoked. The authors argue disarming one secreted enzyme could calm acne inflammation without carpet-bombing the skin's resident microbes.
pmc-13410570:
Mathilde Jégo leads a large team reporting in 2026 on two-faced polymer nanorods that slow the clumping of a diabetes-linked protein. In type 2 diabetes, human amylin folds wrongly and piles into fibers that harm the insulin-making cells of the pancreas. Many past blockers lacked precision or worked weakly.

Lab assays showed the fitted rods kept amylin in its single form, delayed fiber start, and worked at doses below the amount of amylin present. Plain rods and free ligand did far less. The rods spared an unrelated clumping protein and cut amylin harm in cell models.
pmc-13410870:
Mamadou Boundoukhoura Bah leads a team mapping in 2026 three mosquito-borne viruses across Guinea: dengue, yellow fever, and West Nile virus. Guinea's climate and insects favor all three, yet current data on their spread were scarce. The work supports health goals tied to a national development program.

Lab tests found signs of past exposure to all three viruses in every surveyed region. Dengue antibodies ran highest in some zones, showing wide silent spread. Mosquito samples were checked for species mix and active infection. Wide circulation argues for stronger routine surveillance.
pmc-13411870:
Nayana Gunathilaka and co-authors gather in 2026 the world evidence on first aid and harmful traditional practices when snakes bite children. Children in poorer countries suffer most, since venom weighs heavier in small bodies. What happens before hospital often decides the outcome, yet folk responses fill that window.

Forty-four studies from 1973 to 2025 spanned six regions. Harmful practices ran highest in South Asia and Africa: tight tourniquets in up to about four fifths of cases in some settings, plus cutting and suction in large shares. Sound measures, like immobilizing the limb and rushing to care, competed with those traditions. Child-specific guidance and community teaching are the gaps the review names.
pmc-13412170:
Hanan Mohamed Ibrahim and co-authors ask in 2026 whether certain immune-system gene variants track with brain complications in children infected with SARS-CoV-2. Most childhood infections stay mild, yet some children develop neurological problems. The retrospective study typed HLA-B class I alleles, which shape immune responses, in children with confirmed infection and compared them with 120 healthy controls.

The allele HLA-B49 appeared most often among children with neurological disease, at 10.4 percent of that group. No allele, though, differed significantly between infected children with and without neurological involvement. One allele, HLA-B53, showed higher odds in unadjusted exploratory checks, and HLA-B52 appeared slightly less often. The authors treat every signal as tentative and call for larger multicentre validation.
pmc-13412770:
Deepak Parashar, Rishabh Sharma, and Sumant Puri show in 2026 that plentiful iron lets the yeast Candida albicans grow its invasive thread form without a master switch long thought essential. The switch, a small protein called Ras1, normally reads a sugar signal and starts hyphal growth through a well-known pathway. Working in cell cultures and in a worm gut colonization model, the team varied iron while feeding the yeast that sugar signal.

Cells lacking Ras1 formed true hyphae only when iron ran high; the parent strain filamented regardless of iron levels. The iron route skipped the usual signal molecule yet still needed two downstream factors, Efg1 and Tpk2. Gene readings showed iron repressed a brake protein, and restoring that brake blocked the effect entirely.
pmc-13413170:
Tingting Lu and colleagues infuse the amino acid L-citrulline directly into the small intestine of ewes in 2026 to watch what it does to metabolism and fertility hormones. Twelve non-pregnant Turpan black ewes were split into two groups of six; one received salt water through a gut fistula, the other a citrulline dose scaled to body weight, alongside identical feed.

Citrulline-fed ewes left less crude protein in dung and far less in urine a week later, suggesting better nitrogen use. Gut microbe communities shifted in composition without separating cleanly overall, and blood profiling showed purine and nucleotide pathways switched up. Five reproductive hormones, from GnRH to progesterone, rose sharply within two hours of infusion in treated animals. The authors read citrulline as a fertility-supporting supplement candidate.
pmc-13415570:
Yuying Huyan and colleagues tested deep-sensing geochemical methods in 2026 for hidden gold under grassland at Zhaishang in western China. Thick cover hides ore, so the team tried fine-soil sampling, mobile-metal leaching, and soil-gas surveys together over a concealed deposit in the Qinling gold belt.

No single method reliably found deep or thin ore, yet combined they improved detection, with soil gases hydrogen sulfide and sulfur dioxide proving most sensitive. Prospectors gain a field-tested recipe for hunting covered gold, plus cautions about sampling and biological noise in semi-humid grassland terrain.
pmc-13415870:
Jai Paris and colleagues grade how well large language models retrieve eye medicine literature, in a 2026 evaluation. Five completed systematic reviews supplied the correct article sets as ground truth, covering topics from orbital disease to a rare tumor type. Models tested included ChatGPT variants, Claude, Gemini, and Grok under default settings.

Each model answered a plain language request to retrieve all publications on a topic. Recall varied wildly by topic and model, from under ten percent to about three quarters of the true set. Precision was often perfect where models returned few items. One deep research mode led on several topics. Hallucinated references in older models motivated this domain specific check.
pmc-13415970:
Chukwuka Elendu and Mbanefo C. Uyanwune present an infant with many inflamed scalp nodules as a diagnostic puzzle, in 2026. A nine-month-old girl developed dome shaped, tender nodules and pustules across the back and sides of her scalp over five days. She had a mild fever and patchy hair thinning, without ulceration or draining tracts.

Swab cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus, while a fungal test came back empty. Blood counts showed raised white cells and inflammation markers. Bacterial folliculitis and furunculosis, deep hair follicle infection, was diagnosed. Ten days of oral flucloxacillin brought marked improvement within a week and near complete clearing by four weeks.
pmc-13416370:
Mantas Jurkonis and colleagues form a solid therapeutic foam from seaweed alginate and Rügen chalk, in 2026. Chalk from the German island has a long tradition in spa and rehabilitation packs for muscle and joint problems, yet powders and pastes are laborious. Their foam sets when an ingredient releases carbon dioxide and calcium crosslinks the alginate.

A response surface design varied alginate, chalk, and foaming components. Alginate content governed most traits, from foam expansion of about 31 to 57 percent to firmness. Springiness stayed high at seventy to seventy-eight percent. Microscopy showed mostly tiny closed pores. Heat loss behavior compared favorably with therapeutic peat.
pmc-13417970:
Xuefeng Li and co-authors link a blood ratio to chronic cough in United States adults, in a 2026 survey analysis. The ratio pairs HDL cholesterol, the protective lipid, with C reactive protein, an inflammation marker. Data came from a national survey between 2005 and 2010, covering 6,762 adults, of whom 672 reported chronic cough.

After full adjustment, each step up in the logged ratio meant about 13 percent lower odds of chronic cough, in a straight line pattern. The link was strongest in never smokers and weaker in other smoking groups. Smoking may blunt the protective balance the ratio captures, the authors suggest.
pmc-13419470:
Nabila Y Al-Tamimi and colleagues report custom scleral lenses restoring sight for a 24-year-old woman with keratoconus in both eyes. In this condition the cornea thins and bulges into a cone, blurring vision in ways glasses often cannot fix. Her right eye was worse than her left, with advanced steepening shown on corneal maps.

Large scleral lenses vault over the damaged cornea and rest on the white of the eye, giving a smooth front surface for light. Corneal shape scans guided the custom fit for each eye. Tear film checks and detailed curvature readings set the lens powers and landing zones. The case shows how a careful custom fit can return useful sight when standard lenses and glasses fall short.
pmc-13420870:
Chirayut Kathongthung and colleagues name two new yeast species in the genus Papiliotrema, found living on flowers in northern Thailand. Six yeast strains were gathered from five flower hosts in Chiang Mai Province during 2024, including allamanda, beggarticks, ylang-ylang, orchid, and frangipani. Flower nectar and petals feed such yeasts richly, and surveys keep finding kinds new to science among them.

Family tree analysis of gene sequences set the Thai strains apart from every known member of the genus. Full descriptions, drawings, and the tree itself accompany the naming, so later workers can test the claim. Flower yeasts matter beyond taxonomy, since they ride pollinators and can shape nectar chemistry. Each named species becomes a fixed point for ecology and for industry hunts for useful strains.
pmc-13421070:
Laura J Edwards and colleagues pool evidence on two oral antivirals for COVID-19 in the vaccine era, asking whether the early pandemic promise survived. Early trials in unvaccinated patients favored both drugs, yet the Omicron period brought immune populations and milder average illness. Their search covered trial databases for randomized studies and for observational work in vaccinated adults from January 2022 onward.

Trials have not shown a cut in hospitalization or death for either drug in vaccinated groups, the headline finding. Molnupiravir also missed on hospitalization across five studies, with pooled odds of 0.83 and a range crossing no effect in the reported figures, while its death results stayed mixed. Several registered trials never published in full, clouding the record. Prescribers get a sober base for weighing cost and interactions.
pmc-13421270:
Chavez and colleagues report a 2026 hearing study on how sound cues help people keep time with a beat. In speech, louder sounds tend to open a group and longer sounds close it, a pattern called the Iambic-Trochaic Law. The team asked whether the same cues help listeners tap along with musical rhythms. Thirty-six adults with little music training tapped to sequences in simple and complex meters, with cues aligned, neutral, or reversed.

For simple meter, cue patterns changed nothing. For the complex meter, reversed contours, which start with a long note, gave the most accurate tapping of all. Speech-like cues made tapping more cautious; reversed cues brought steadier tracking with fewer missed or extra taps. Duration cues help the brain lock onto hard rhythms; loudness cues add no such support.
pmc-13421570:
Alexandre Sita leads a twelve-author team reporting, in a 2026 study, a MERS-related coronavirus found in bats in southern Brazil. Coronaviruses from bats draw attention for their spillover potential, and relatives of the MERS virus had previously turned up in camels, humans and two bat families.

The team screened 65 velvety free-tailed bats with molecular tests and deep sequencing. One rectal swab, from a single bat, carried the virus, and five genome fragments placed it inside the Merbecovirus group, close to MERS viruses from bats and dromedary camels. The host species roosts commonly in towns and houses. The authors argue the find widens the known host range and strengthens the case for continued genomic surveillance of tropical bats.
pmc-13422270:
Shang-Chiao Yang, Yi-Chang Chou, Yu-Hsiang Chen and Yi-Jin Hu examine, in a 2026 registry study, how long resuscitation flows at low pressure before the brain's chances fade after an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Low-flow time — from CPR starting to hospital handover or the heart restarting — is a known outcome driver, yet useful thresholds for Asian city systems were undefined.

The pattern split by first rhythm: for shockable rhythms, passing twenty-seven minutes of low flow independently raised mortality, while non-shockable arrests followed a different curve. The authors frame rhythm-specific thresholds as quality targets for prehospital care.
pmc-13422670:
Lucas Evangelista Marques and co-authors present a laboratory protocol for extracting proteins from Mycobacterium species so the bacteria can be picked out by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry. This identification method reads a protein fingerprint, but it only works when proteins are extracted well. Their 2026 protocol targets species-level identification, which is hard in this diverse genus.

Troubleshooting and quality control steps are included, and the workflow is designed for Bruker MALDI Biotyper systems. Safety receives special emphasis: the steps meet biosafety level 2 and 3 requirements and limit aerosol generation when handling dangerous strains. The authors aim to standardise preparation across diagnostic and research laboratories.
pmc-13423070:
Mia Ritzau Ishøj Nielsen leads a Danish nationwide cohort study of inhaled corticosteroids and heart and vessel events in people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Earlier work on this question conflicted, so the team used national registers covering specialist-confirmed cases diagnosed between 2008 and 2022, grading each patient's prior-year inhaler dose from none to high.

Among 82,327 patients, 8,948 (10.9%) had a cardiovascular event during one year of follow-up. Low and moderate inhaler doses were linked with lower event rates than no steroid use, and the moderate-dose pattern held across several sensitivity checks, including competing-risk and negative-control analyses. The authors stop short of claiming protection, but the dose pattern argues against a simple harm story.
pmc-13424070:
Zhang and co-authors review design rules for covalent organic frameworks used as oxygen electrocatalysts, in this 2026 article. These materials speed the oxygen reactions at the heart of fuel cells and metal-air batteries. The frameworks are crystalline lattices built entirely from organic building blocks, so every atom of the catalyst's environment can in principle be picked one by one.

These include tuning pore geometry, planting metal centers, and adjusting the electronic environment around each site. Mechanistic sections explain why those changes work at the level of oxygen binding and electron transfer. The authors close with the field's open problems, including stability under operating conditions and scaling synthesis, framing the article as a rational-design manual rather than a catalog of record performances.
pmc-13424770:
Kirschfink and colleagues tested in 2026 a new heart CT method for finding clots in the left atrial appendage during acute stroke care. Their photon-counting scanner was added to the emergency stroke imaging routine, and results were judged against ultrasound passed down the gullet, the gold standard.

Kirschfink studied 101 patients, most with acute stroke, the two tests a median of two days apart. Overall accuracy was high, at about ninety-six in a hundred cases. The scan caught nine in ten true clots and, a negative scan was right ninety-nine times in a hundred. Patients with clots were older and far more often had atrial fibrillation. The authors call the scan a promising way to rule out this clot source fast, inside the workup patients already receive.
pmc-13424870:
Hailey A O'Neil, Misha Behi, and Paula C Fletcher interview five women studying at university while living with lupus, and five people who support them most closely, in Southern Ontario. Lupus brings unpredictable flares and fatigue into a setting already short on flexibility, and the study asks how that navigation feels from inside both roles.

In the second, lupus does not exist in a bubble: ignorance in healthcare, education, and wider society keeps generating friction for students and supporters alike. The authors call for better lupus education and stronger campus support services.
pmc-13425970:
Sarah K. Bublitz and coauthors examine ethical strain when treatment goals change for ventilated people with ALS in a 2026 case-based review. In advanced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, eye movement often remains the last channel for intentional communication, yet long-term survivors on tracheostomy ventilation show progressive eye control decline. Three home-care patients illustrate decisions that arise as eye-based communication grows unreliable.

Combining cases with literature, the authors trace how fading communication complicates consent, advance care planning, and shifts from life-prolonging toward comfort goals. Clinicians are urged to plan conversations early, before the final communication channel narrows. Time to talk through these hard calls is short once breath and speech fade, so the team urges care plans be set down in good time.
pmc-13426970:
Casely-Hayford and colleagues followed 745 professional staff at a Swedish higher education institution in 2026 through the shift from fully remote work to a hybrid pattern, over twelve months. The pandemic made home work normal, then employers blended it with office days. How that change felt, and for whom it strained, was the study's focus, with attention to gender and household type.

Most views of the work environment barely moved, but support from colleagues grew over the year. Stress and exhaustion rose during the transition even as job satisfaction held steady. Women reported worse work conditions and more stress than men, whose reports stayed flat. Staff living alone, and single parents, also fared worse than those living with partners. The authors urge equality and family-support plans so hybrid gains are shared fairly.
pmc-13427470:
Angus J. Grant and a large engineering team describe nanoparticle coating of tissue heart valves to slow their deterioration in a 2026 article. Structural deterioration still limits their lifespan once implanted.

Tissue valves spare the sick the blood drugs that steel valves force for life, and that gain is why work to stretch their span draws funds and care. Each new coat must be checked for wear, for clots, and for harm to blood cells as it flows past.
pmc-13427570:
Fabiana Corsi-Zuelli and colleagues ask, in a 2026 records study, whether a common arthritis drug might lower the chance of later psychosis. Over five years, new recorded psychosis was less common after methotrexate than after two common pain drugs, naproxen and diclofenac. No clear edge appeared against biologic drugs. Records can mislead, so the authors treat this as a lead for trials, not proof.
pmc-13428170: Physiological Reports issued a correction in 2026 to a rat study by Almutlaq and colleagues on a diabetes drug class and blood pressure in salt-sensitive hypertension. The notice is a correction only. It fixes the axis units in four figure panels, which wrongly read milligrams per milliliter and should read milligrams per 24 hours. The experiments were described correctly in the text, a corrected figure is supplied, and the authors state that the error leaves the study's conclusions unchanged.
pmc-13429370:
Ellis and colleagues weigh the hidden costs of stripping PFAS, the persistent 'forever chemicals,' out of treated wastewater and destroying them. The headline is stark: adding PFAS removal and destruction could double or triple a plant's greenhouse gas emissions, with other health and environment impacts rising too. Reactivating and reusing granular activated carbon, the filter medium, cut the burden, as did running the plant on renewable energy. The team converts results into impact curves that predict a plant's footprint from its size and technology, giving regulators and utilities a planning tool before they mandate upgrades.
pmc-13429570:

MYCN did not change helicase amounts, yet it bound gene tail regions, met DDX17, and bent termination toward fusion transcripts.
pmc-13430170:
Salma Alkhatib and Diego Marin present, in a 2026 case series, three patients whose chest scans revealed an azygos lobe, a harmless anatomical quirk. The catch is recognition: the fold can masquerade as a lung nodule, an air blister, or a collapsed lung on imaging. Radiology teaching files gain a tidy reminder that not every odd line is disease.
pmc-13431570:
Liyu Yang and co-authors tested in 2026 whether a plant compound called vitamin U can blunt sharp liver harm from a mold toxin in mice. The toxin taints animal feed widely and stirs cell stress and swelling that end in liver wounds. The compound comes from cabbage-family plants.

Toxin-dosed mice showed clogged liver blood paths, drops in two blood cell types, and a weaker guard enzyme. The compound partly undid these shifts: cell counts rose back, clogging eased, one guard enzyme grew stronger, and a calm-down gene spoke louder. Two harms stayed put, so the shield proved partial at best. Gene reads showed the compound moved immune and cell-cycle paths more than the classic stress shield path. The authors offer the work as a base for feed safety studies.
pmc-13431770:
Jung and colleagues tested in 2026 whether watching symptoms change over time improves tuberculosis screening in prisons, where the disease spreads fast and standard one-off symptom checks miss many cases. Their prospective study followed 2,282 incarcerated men in Brazil, checking symptoms every four months and confirming disease with molecular or culture tests.

The signal was strongest in those whose earlier chest images already showed abnormalities. Staying symptomatic throughout, by contrast, carried no clear extra risk, perhaps because chronic cough has many causes in prison. The authors say repeat symptom checks, above all paired with imaging, can sharpen screening in high-risk closed settings and catch cases earlier than entry-only checks.
pmc-13432670:
Jihyeon Kim and co-authors grew light-driven rods in 2026 from ring-shaped dye molecules bound to palladium or platinum, then used the rods to split hydrogen from water with light alone. The rods form in a plain water-alcohol mix with no soap help and no added helper catalyst. Five metal kin entered the first screen.

Tight stacking, long-lived excited states, and low drag on charge flow set the palladium rods apart on lab reads. The one-pot route skips soap scum and keeps output high and steady under visible light.
pmc-13433070:

Print error stayed under a hair's width, and break spots landed within a millimeter of plan. Ten surgeons and eight trainees graded the rig on feel, truth, and training worth. Top marks hit shape truth, break feel, and training worth across the board. Entry picks, wire runs, and scan-play each scored a notch lower. All graders backed the rig for training.
pmc-13433770:

Both scent paths meet in the front brain hub. Meets with beaten mates boost reward chemical flow from a deep hub into that front hub. In mice prone to catch the mood, the porter that sweeps the chemical away runs hot, which drains base levels and seeds the low state. Wild swings in the chemical alone could drive the catch. A drug aim at the porter beat a mood-drug class at care.
pmc-13434270:
Ladan Rezaee offers a clean maths model for radiation chemistry. It tracks hydroxyl radicals, the fragments that damage cells when radiation hits tissue. Their numbers shift with beam quality and with oxygen, not just with dose.

Monte Carlo track simulations show radiation-matter clashes in fine detail. Their bulk can hide what each factor does alone. The new model covers the indirect chemical stage. A source term makes radical output rise with LET, following known yield trends. A balance equation from a directional spread model, averaged over space, completes it. Oxygen and background scavengers enter the rates in plain view. Radiobiologists get a clear formula for radical yields.
pmc-13434370:
Sheng-Rong Gong and colleagues name two new stonecrop plants from central Yunnan, China, in 2026. Three wild groups were checked with both form and DNA evidence. The plants look close to four known relatives, so fine traits had to decide the split.

One new species has plain stem leaves, pale flowers with a red purple tint, and a small bump on each petal. The other has spotted leaves, pink purple flowers, and smooth petals. DNA trees place the pair as close sisters on their own branches. The find adds to the known plant wealth of Yunnan.
pmc-13435170:

His regimen was 240 milligrams during the day and 40 milligrams at night. The placed pump system delivered it nonstop. On this monotherapy he had no dyskinesia, painful dystonia, motor swings, or mental unrest. Those are problems oral levodopa often brings in late-stage disease. The result topped what the same therapy had done as an add-on in the earlier phase I/II trial. That trial gained 4.4 hours of perfect control and cut oral levodopa by 60 percent for patients. The authors note brain-delivered dopamine behaved unlike oral levodopa in this patient.
pmc-13435970:
Mawuli Kotope Gyakobo and coauthors interview teachers who built a palliative care course across Ghana and Canada in 2026. Ten faculty from a Ghanaian science university and a Toronto university shared the work from 2023 to 2025. Talks probe how joint building felt from both sides.

Joint design aims for fair, locally fit lessons that primary care can carry. End of life care gaps run widest in poorer countries. The partnership offers a template for shared curriculum work.
pmc-13437070:
Nele Kirsten Kanzelmeyer and colleagues report two children whose transplanted kidneys faced stubborn antibody attack, treated with daratumumab, a drug aimed at CD38 on immune cells. Published in 2026, their case report follows a ten-year-old girl and a nine-year-old boy after kidney transplant. Repeat tissue samples let the team watch the grafts heal or worsen.

In the girl, active rejection faded into mostly chronic change, with far less vessel inflammation and a turned-negative tissue stain. The boy first showed more chronic damage, then full clearing of active disease and a sharp drop in protein in his urine. pmc-13437370:

A stoma, an opening that lets waste leave into a bag, can change how people see themselves and how they fear others see them. Their 2026 survey covered 449 patients at large hospitals in the Sichuan-Chongqing region, using standard scales for stigma, stoma acceptance, and quality of life.

People without a spouse, those with low household income, and those fully dependent on others for stoma care were more likely to sit in the high group. pmc-13437770:

Fresh mouse skin work, at the center of their 2026 review, proves a return signal. When fibroblasts lost that factor, macrophages thinned out, and the fibroblasts then lost their quiet state and began dividing and misbehaving.

The authors name this two-way pact a homeostatic circuit, each side licensing the other to stay balanced. In human scleroderma, both the factor and macrophage counts run high while the circuit still fails, which they explain as exhausted licensing in worn-out macrophages. The frame is then carried into wound repair, tumor surroundings, and organ scarring. Their therapeutic pitch shifts the goal: instead of wiping out one cell type, restore the balance of the loop. That idea, they argue, could guide kinder and smarter treatments for fibrosis wherever it strikes.
pmc-13437870:
Ming Yin's team traced a lactylation chain in 2026 that rewires sugar metabolism in esophageal cancer. Histone lactylation primes cells toward malignancy, and DCBLD1 was already flagged as a cancer gene, but its role in esophageal tumors through lactate tagging was unclear. pmc-13437970:
Wei Deng, Bingyu Liu, and Songtao Xiang review a striking way cancers spreading to bone may resist treatment: they import fresh mitochondria, the cell's power units, from friendly marrow cells. Once inside, donated units rebuild the tumor cell's energy system. The cell shifts from a wasteful sugar-burning mode toward fuller fuel use, stockpiling energy that powers drug pumps, DNA repair, and survival tricks. The marrow setting, low in oxygen and rich in fat and cells, seems built to encourage the trade. Patterns differ by cancer type, and most evidence comes from dishes and animal models. pmc-13438770:
Mario Alles and colleagues examined the immune cells of Ugandan adolescents who acquired HIV around birth and now live on suppressive treatment, looking for early signs of heart risk. Their 2026 study compared blood cell profiles and artery thickness against adolescents without HIV.

The treated group's neck arteries measured thicker, a recognized warning marker. Their natural killer cells ran hotter: more activated, more memory-like, and readier to migrate, joined by a rise in inflammatory monocytes, patterns confirmed in gene activity. Several of these cell types tracked with the artery thickening itself. One twist stood out: oxidized LDL, the harmful cholesterol form, ran lower in the HIV group. The authors propose a chain from immune dysregulation to artery risk, urging heart surveillance from adolescence for this population.
pmc-13439170:
Changhyeon Han's team built a secure neuromorphic transistor in 2026 that joins ferroelectric switching, ion movement, and charge trapping in one device. Brain-like chips promise low-power parallel computing, yet stored weights are open to malicious readout. Their ferroelectric-ionic-trapping transistor runs in two modes. A plain mode gives fast, low-power switching and analog weight tuning, while a secure mode collapses the memory window under chosen read biases, hiding stored states.

The switch is reversible and voltage-controlled, multiscale tests showed reliable toggling between learning and concealment, and system simulations cut model inversion attacks with little accuracy loss. pmc-13439470:
Ilknur Yurtsever and colleagues trace how a pneumonia bacterium shields a host protein-destroying machine to weaken lung defences, reporting in 2026. Cells tag proteins with ubiquitin to mark them for disposal, and the ligase part FBXO24 helps choose targets. What guards FBXO24 itself was unknown. In macrophage cell tests, Haemophilus influenzae type B, a pneumonia cause, spared FBXO24 from disposal by cutting its ubiquitin tags.

In mouse pneumonia, silencing USP4 or deleting the Fbxo24 gene raised immune cell counts in air spaces while lowering bacterial loads. Lung swelling and injury eased in both cases. The authors show a pathogen exploiting the host's own tag-removal system to blunt innate defence.
pmc-13439570:
Kun Xing and co-authors boost the energy stored in plastic capacitor films by hiding two kinds of nanoparticles inside fibre cores, reporting in 2026. Polymer films charge and discharge fast, suiting pulse power gear, but they hold little energy per volume. Stirring in high-response fillers usually backfires because particles clump where plastic meets mineral. Their fibres carry a ferroelectric core doped with barium titanate and alumina particles that assemble themselves in the confined space.

A film with one percent of each particle discharged far more energy per volume than plain polymer, at high efficiency. Performance held steady across one hundred thousand cycles under a strong electric field. Confining the fillers inside the core kept interfaces clean and defects low. The authors present the confined co-doping route as a scalable path to compact, reliable capacitors.
pmc-13440570:
Cai and colleagues uncovered in 2026 how a chromosome scaffold protein in plants loads the enzyme that swaps DNA between paired chromosomes in meiosis, the division behind pollen and eggs. The protein ASY1 was known to be required for placing the recombinase DMC1, but the link was missing.
