Removing a known DMC1 brake rescued DMC1 spots in cyclin mutants but not in ASY1 mutants, placing ASY1 above both the accelerator and the brake. The authors cast ASY1 as coordinator of crossover formation, the exchanges that keep genome sorting accurate.
pmc-13441170:
Tsutsui and colleagues built a framework in 2026 that gives gene regulatory links a context, since a gene switch that matters in one disease or cell type may be idle in another. Databases and papers usually record gene regulations as bare facts, stripped of the setting where they were seen. Their method, powered by a large language model, mines the literature and assigns each regulation a quantitative weight for the context it belongs to.

Networks rebuilt with these weights matched gene activity data across many diseases far better than context-free versions, and drug-target predictions grew more accurate when context was added. As a showcase, the team automatically assembled a working differential-equation model, a set of rate equations, of a breast cancer signaling network from the contextualized network. The authors argue that context is not decoration but a requirement for biological prediction, and they release the code openly.
pmc-13441770:
Tongyuan Lin and colleagues profile blood metabolites in Crohn's disease patients on biologic drugs, hunting for markers that track treatment response, in a 2026 study. Diagnosis still leans on invasive scopes and tissue reading, and how biologics reshape metabolism was little studied. Eighty-one patients on infliximab or ustekinumab at week sixteen joined forty-five healthy controls. High-end chromatography and mass spectrometry catalogued their blood chemistry.

Both drug groups sat in clinical remission, yet their inflammation markers still ran above healthy levels. Each drug left a distinct metabolic fingerprint: infliximab touched amino acid pathways and core energy cycles, while ustekinumab touched glutathione and purine pathways. Arginine and kindred metabolites tracked with clinical indicators in correlation analysis. The authors argue that blood metabolite panels could complement scopes for judging whether a biologic is truly working.
pmc-13442570:
Jinbo Zhang's team tested stem cell sacs in 2026 for sepsis-linked acute kidney injury, where immune-cell swelling and sugar use drive organ failure. Sacs from fat-derived tissue stem cells were loaded with small RNA miR-574-5p. They were tested in mice with belly sepsis and in grown immune cells, tracking kidney function, swelling, glycolysis, and immune-cell shifting, with binding to glucose carrier GLUT1 confirmed.

Sacs raised miR-574-5p, curbed GLUT1, limited sugar burning, blocked M1 shifting, promoted healing M2 immune cells, and eased kidney dysfunction and swelling in septic mice. Kidney teams get a sac-delivered RNA mechanism for reprogramming immune cells in sepsis. Human safety and manufacturing must precede clinical trials.
pmc-13443070:
Hendriks and colleagues review burst deep brain stimulation, a new pulse pattern for the implanted electrodes that ease advanced Parkinson's disease. Standard stimulation runs as a steady train, while burst modes fire in clusters: theta bursts, burst cycling, or a coordinated reset pattern meant to resync faulty brain rhythms. Nineteen studies passed: nine in animals and ten in patients, split across the three burst modes. Acute benefit mostly matched standard stimulation, yet burst modes left after effects once the current stopped, a hint they may reshape circuits rather than just mask symptoms. No major adverse events appeared. Settings, though, scattered widely with no agreed optimum, and terms clash between groups. Randomized trials with shared protocols, the authors urge, are the only way to tell if bursts beat the standard.
pmc-13444370:
Jinrui Tian and colleagues test how human-like AI feels shape the need to belong in a 2026 survey. Students who had used AI tools or chat assistants numbered 473 in the pool. Each rated how human the AI seemed, how much they liked it, how much emotional support they felt, and how strong their belonging need ran.

Factor checks backed four clean traits in the data. Liking and felt support each carried part of the link from human feel to belonging need. A chain path ran the full route, from human feel through liking and support to belonging need, in that order. The authors read AI warmth as a layered social pull, not a single charm. Design that adds human cues may feed real social hunger in users.
pmc-13445670:
Xin Chen and coauthors define a 2026 cancer mechanism by which the nuclear pore protein ELYS drives liver cancer stemness and spread. Together these mapped a chain from ELYS through PI3K-AKT to a FOXO6-NUP205 module and Hedgehog signaling.

pmc-13445770:
Toli and colleagues assessed in 2026 how much Trop-2, a surface protein targeted by newer antibody-drug conjugates, appears in breast cancer and what its level means. They combined a meta-analysis of 41 studies with lab work on their own early breast cancer cohort of 564 patients, comparing human and digital readings of protein levels.

Across studies, about seventy-two percent of tumors were Trop-2 positive. Targeted drugs beat chemotherapy on progression-free survival at every expression level, with the largest benefit in high-expression tumors. In the local cohort, higher protein and gene expression both predicted earlier distant recurrence, especially in the Luminal B subtype. Human and digital scoring agreed closely. The authors suggest Trop-2 carries prognostic value and should be measured carefully when targeted therapy is planned.
pmc-13446070:
Chern and colleagues present a 2026 review linking uterine fibroids to allostatic load, the wear on the body from chronic stress. Fibroids are the most common gynecologic tumors; they are benign but can wreck quality of life, and Black women carry the highest burden, with lifetime risk near eighty percent. The review gathers emerging evidence that stress load helps explain both the tumors and the disparity.

Allostatic load is scored from strain across hormone, immune, and metabolic systems, and it runs high where low income, microaggressions, and discrimination concentrate. The authors present it as a hypothesis with growing epidemiological support, not settled proof. If stress biology feeds fibroids, stress reduction becomes a medical intervention.
pmc-13447070:
Gaochao Guo and colleagues trace a kinase chain that frees a growth driver in glioblastoma, the most lethal common brain tumor, in a 2026 study. pmc-13447270:
Gilvano Amorim Oliveira leads a multicentre study of physical complaints tied to series watching among university students in Brazil and Canada in 2026. Long streaming sessions can bring aches and strain, yet how those complaints cluster with mood and habits across cultures was little studied. Students reported watching intensity plus phone, food and mood measures.

Roughly fifteen hundred students, most from Brazil, fell into high, moderate and low complaint groups. The high group showed worse mood scores, stronger phone and food addiction signs, lower quality of life and heavier watching. Depression, stress and trouble managing emotions sat at the centre of the linked network, with watching complaints at the edge. Patterns looked broadly alike in both countries, slightly stronger in Brazil, with addictive eating more central in Canada.
pmc-13447570:
Shinsuke Mizuno and colleagues report brain infection after neurosurgery in an infant, caused by a drug-resistant Klebsiella strain in a 2026 case study. A previously healthy baby developed fever and seizures two days after a brain drain was placed and a tumour removed.

Cultures grew a strain resistant to many penicillin-type drugs, carrying several resistance genes plus features linked to aggressive behaviour. pmc-13448070:
Chuangye Song and colleagues grow single-crystal flakes of aluminium molybdate for studying light waves bound to crystal vibrations in 2026 work. A general route to related molybdate crystals for nanophotonics is claimed.
pmc-13448170:

pmc-13448470:
Chadha and colleagues present in 2026, as abstract DSAI-02, a machine learning study of MRI measurements in lung cancer patients whose disease has spread to the brain. It asks whether the measurements predict survival beyond what ordinary clinical information offers.

pmc-13448570:
Jianyu Yuan and co-authors prepare starch and vitamin E complexes using electron beam and ultra-high pressure treatments in 2026 food science work. pmc-13448670:

pmc-13449070:

pmc-13449470:

pmc-13449570:

pmc-13450570:

pmc-13451870:

pmc-13452770:

pmc-13453170:

pmc-13453570:

pmc-13454170:

pmc-13454470:

pmc-13454670:

pmc-13454770:

pmc-13455270:

pmc-13455370:

pmc-13455470:

pmc-13455970:

The purpose-built convolutional network classifies two-second windows as normal, slow waves, or spike and sharp waves.

On the expert-labelled NMT-Events set with splits by subject, raw-signal LEEDNet reached 81.2% accuracy and 77.5% macro-F1, beating four state-of-the-art baselines on three of four metrics. It needs only 0.25 million parameters and 37 megaflops per segment, inferring in under five milliseconds on a standard CPU. Fourier and wavelet features added no consistent gains, favouring raw waveforms for deployment.
pmc-13471170:
Hülya Tosun Söner and Fatma Acil compare in 2026 two simple blood based scores for predicting death after hip fracture surgery in older patients. Hip fractures carry heavy risks in old age, and the team wanted bedside markers that reflect nutrition and immune strength. Their retrospective study covered 257 patients aged sixty five and older who landed in intensive care after hip fracture surgery.

Forty patients died within a year, while 217 survived. Those who died entered surgery with clearly lower scores on both the HALP score, built from hemoglobin, albumin, lymphocytes, and platelets, and the prognostic nutritional index. After adjustment, only the nutritional index stood as an independent predictor, alongside male sex, cancer, and overall illness burden. The HALP score lost its predictive force once those factors were counted.
pmc-13471270:
Baykara Sayili and colleagues tested in 2026 whether variants of a drug-processing gene, CYP2C19, change how well the opioid meperidine relieves kidney stone pain in emergency patients. The prospective study enrolled 203 renal colic patients and gave each 100 milligrams of meperidine. Pain scores were recorded at baseline and at 15, 30, and 60 minutes. A further 102 people with other abdominal pain contributed genetic frequency data only. Gene types sort people into slow, normal, and rapid drug processors.

Genes mattered after the half hour. All groups eased similarly in the first 15 minutes. By 30 and 60 minutes, normal and rapid processors reported significantly lower pain and bigger percentage drops than moderate processors. One gene combination, written *1/*1, stood out for strong late relief. Age, sex, and stone position did not influence response. Eleven patients had side effects, mostly nausea and dizziness, none serious. The authors suggest genotype could one day tailor opioid choice in the emergency department.
pmc-13471370:
Yan and co-authors investigated why some children keep running a fever long after surgery for a head injury, and built a simple risk score to spot them early. Their 2026 retrospective study reviewed 238 children treated surgically for craniocerebral injury, meaning damage to the skull and brain, at one center.

Persistent fever, defined as temperature at or above 38.5 degrees lasting over 36 hours in the first three days, affected 28.99% of the children studied. Severe injury carried the strongest link, with odds more than six times higher, and children aged five or younger had odds roughly 3.5 times higher than older children. A bedside score built from six risk factors reached a sensitivity of 0.754 with specificity of 0.879 at its cutoff, though the authors warn it still needs outside testing.
pmc-13471470:
Rastegar and colleagues interviewed adult e-cigarette users in Bandar Abbas, southern Iran, where vaping has been banned since 2012 yet persists. Their 2026 qualitative study used thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with 45 current users, 37 men and 8 women whose average age was 25.8 years.

Six themes explained the habit, including flavor and design appeal, stress relief, and social normalization through peers, family tolerance, and influencer marketing. Many users believed vaping was far safer than smoking and could help them quit, beliefs the authors call industry-fed misconceptions. Participants themselves reported breathing problems, strong dependency, and regret, which the team says underlines the need for corrective public health messaging.
pmc-13471670:
Hedayati and co-authors studied whether healthcare services management graduates in Iran actually find work, pairing a graduate survey with in-depth interviews. Their 2026 mixed-methods study at Zabol University questioned 132 graduates from 2010 to 2022 and interviewed 37 of them about the job hunt.

The employment rate was 63.6% overall, and doctorate holders fared best at 85.7% employed after graduation. What predicted a job was practical, not academic: soft skills raised the odds of employment with an odds ratio of 1.06 per scale point, and hard skills reached 1.14 per point, while academic skills showed no significant effect. Interviewees leaned on social networks to find openings, and the authors recommend practical training and employer partnerships in the curriculum.
pmc-13473270:
Shinozaki and Tashiro present a 2026 editorial introducing a research collection on bioengineering for spinal cord injury. About nine hundred thirty thousand people suffer such injuries each year, and the cord, like the brain, barely regenerates, so rehabilitation remains the mainstay. The editors frame how engineering is opening new routes where medicine alone has stalled.

One route is waking up spared circuits: since nerve signaling is electrical, stimulation and engineered interfaces can modulate the pathways that survive injury. Other work in the collection pursues cell and material approaches that support repair. The editorial's role is to map the field's fronts and the gaps between lab promise and clinical routine. Framing matters because spinal cord injury research is scattered across engineering, surgery, and rehabilitation journals that rarely speak to each other.
pmc-13473370:
Gregory E. Paradis offers a two-stage method in 2026 for fitting tree trunk size patterns when records are cut off at set limits. Forest plots often skip thin trees or cap thick ones, which skews standard curve fits. The new workflow first fits a scale factor with the curve shape, then locks that factor for a clean second fit. Data came from fixed plots in Québec, Canada.

Across 32 mixes of tree type and cover, the two-stage fits closely matched true cut-off fits. The method also gave the best fit score in most of those mixes. Code shared with the report lets field staff run the steps in common software. Forest planners gain fair size curves without giving up tools they already know.
pmc-13474070:
Yang and colleagues review in 2026 how cryoablation, freezing a tumor to kill it, might strengthen immunotherapy for non-small cell lung cancer. Advanced disease still has poor long-term outcomes, and only a minority of patients gain lasting benefit from immune checkpoint drugs alone.

Freezing destroys tumor tissue in a way that releases tumor antigens and danger signals, a process called immunogenic cell death. The review argues this can act like a vaccine made inside the body, helping T cells recognize cancer elsewhere too. Early clinical studies suggest better tumor control and survival in selected settings, but the evidence is mixed and small. The authors flag open questions on treatment order, biomarkers, technique standards, and long-term safety.
pmc-13474670:
Shang and co-authors mapped two decades of research on predicting who fares worst after a STEMI, the deadliest form of heart attack, using bibliometric tools on the Web of Science. Their 2026 analysis covered 416 English-language publications from 2003 to 2025, charting output by year, country, author, journal, and keyword bursts.

Publication volume climbed steadily and surged after 2016, with China the leading contributor and 115 core authors producing 165 of the papers, 39.66% of the field's output. BMC Cardiovascular Disorders published the most, while Circulation carried the highest citation impact, and keyword analysis showed the frontier moving toward risk stratification and biomarker prediction. The authors note a concrete gap: no dedicated risk score exists yet for STEMI prognosis, and building one is the obvious next hotspot.
pmc-13474770:
Sharifzadeh and co-authors reviewed 161 children treated in intensive care for diabetic ketoacidosis, the dangerous acid buildup of uncontrolled diabetes, at a large center between December 2018 and December 2022. Their 2026 retrospective study, covering children with a mean age of 8.22 years, counted how often complications strike and which children they strike hardest.

Electrolyte chaos dominated: low phosphate appeared in 60.9% of children, low potassium in 50.9%, and low sodium in 46.6% of cases during treatment. Brain injury, the feared complication, occurred in 8.1% of patients and ran 9.1-fold more likely in severe than in moderate ketoacidosis, with high sodium independently tripling the risk at 3.53 times on the adjusted analysis. Kidney injury, by contrast, stayed rare at just 3.7% of all cases treated. The authors urge severity-aware monitoring, especially of sodium, during the first critical hours.
pmc-13474970:
Liang and colleagues built an interpretable machine learning model in 2026 to spot hidden prostate cancer in men first diagnosed with benign prostate enlargement. Blood PSA testing alone cannot cleanly separate the two conditions, so cancers get missed at the first visit. The team used records from 1,071 patients, defining hidden cancer as cancer found at least six months after the benign diagnosis, and trained six algorithms on routine blood measures.

Feature selection narrowed the signal to four blood markers: total PSA, lactate dehydrogenase, red blood cell count, and creatine kinase-MB, an enzyme usually tied to heart muscle. The neural network and logistic regression models scored best on held-out patients, reaching accuracy areas of 0.949 and 0.946 on the standard curve measure used. Explanation tools showed how each marker pushed a prediction up or down, and the authors stress the model is for research use, not clinic decisions.
pmc-13478170:
Yun Ji Ga and Jung-Yong Yeh developed in 2026 a simple method to clear Mycoplasma from HeLa cell lines, a stubborn problem that skews experiments. They inserted a neomycin defence gene into contaminated cells, then applied high-dose G418 drug plus single-cell cloning to kill off the germs.

Clearance was confirmed by PCR and by antibody staining, and the combination proved effective for long-term eradication. Cleaned cells also showed markedly higher gene delivery and reporter output than contaminated cells. The method offers labs a reliable route to trustworthy cell-based results.
pmc-13478470:
Alicia Richards and fourteen colleagues linked in 2026 blood immune profiles to colorectal cancer survival. Tumour-infiltrating immune cells shape prognosis, but blood profiles drawn before surgery had been little studied as a source of early risk clues.

From 134 untreated stage I-III patients, they estimated blood cell types from DNA methylation patterns and tracked recurrence and death over a median 7.4 years. Higher neutrophil and regulatory T-cell counts tied to worse disease-free and overall survival, as did higher memory B-cell counts for disease-free survival and higher basophil counts for overall survival. Blood cell mix thus flags patients at higher risk before treatment starts.
pmc-13479370:
Uludağ and colleagues crossed in 2026 two widow spider kinds to learn how the male's mate time self kill act is passed down. In one kind, the male flips his rear onto the female's fangs as they mate, and a waist pinch keeps him alive long enough to seal his claim. His sister kind does no such thing. The team bred the two kinds, crossed the young back, and scored grandson males for flip and pinch in live matings.

The two traits did not travel as one pack, against the team's guess. The flip split clean, half and half, the mark of one gene on the sex strand. The pinch spread in a blur, the mark of many genes at work. A grand act of self kill can rest on one plain gene, the team shows. Fast trait birth needs no deep new wiring.
pmc-13479570:
Ibrahim Karakaya published a 2026 cross-sectional content analysis, as sole author, of how well chatbots explain bipolar disorder. People increasingly ask large language models about this sensitive and complex condition, where fuzzy information can delay care or distort treatment choices. Twenty questions drawn from Google Trends were put to ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek, each in three fresh sessions, yielding 180 responses.

Two trained scales measured information quality and reading difficulty, including grade level and reading ease scores. Statistical models accounted for repeated answers to the same question when comparing the three systems. The study benchmarks which model explains bipolar disorder most completely and most readably, giving clinicians and developers evidence for guiding patients toward safer sources.
pmc-13479870:
Meik Neufurth and coauthors present a study of sodium polyphosphate as a candidate treatment for atopic dermatitis, the chronic itchy skin disease that today can only be managed symptom by symptom. Their theory centers on calcium: mast cells and platelets in inflamed skin raise calcium around nerve cells, and that calcium burst acts like a death signal for the nerves, fueling damage.

Polyphosphate is a natural energy-rich polymer that platelets themselves store and release. In laboratory work the sodium form bound calcium by forming coacervates, swapping sodium for calcium and thereby canceling the harmful burst. The authors also report clinical case experience with the approach. They argue that neutralizing a chemical trigger, rather than suppressing immunity broadly, could open a gentler treatment path.
pmc-13479970:
Tingting He, Guangzhi Ma, and Gang Yuan published a 2026 review of FOXK1, a gene-switching protein that rewires cell metabolism. The protein responds to signals and coordinates growth, specialization, and stress adaptation. Its own activity is controlled at many levels, from gene alterations and chemical DNA marks to small RNAs and protein modifications.

When that control breaks, FOXK1 stays switched on and drives disease. In cancer it mostly acts as an accelerator, promoting metabolic rewiring, stem-like traits, invasion, spread, and treatment resistance. The review also covers roles beyond cancer in other diseases where the same switch misfires. The authors organize a scattered literature into one map of how a single regulator can be targeted, and what might go wrong if it is.
pmc-13480070:
Qun Li and thirteen colleagues mapped in 2026 severe viral brain inflammation in Chinese children. Few recent studies had covered its causes, outcomes, and burden, leaving high-risk children hard to spot.

Across six hospitals from 2015 to 2021, they gathered 801 episodes in children up to age 14, of whom 29 cases counted as severe. Enterovirus drove over half the severe cases, and deaths reached about 1 percent with lasting sequelae in 4 percent. Abnormal brain scans and enterovirus infection flagged severe illness, offering clinicians a sharper way to pick out children headed for poor outcomes sooner.
pmc-13480170:
Xiaoqin Gan and co-authors offer a 2026 pooled review of blood thinner strategy around a catheter valve procedure. Many patients who need a new aortic valve also take oral anticoagulants, and teams must choose whether to pause the drugs or carry on through the procedure. The review searched six databases to February 2026 and kept five studies with 3,316 patients.

Carrying on with the drugs showed no clear rise in major bleeding or major vessel harm compared with pausing. Stroke rates leaned slightly lower with continued use, and transfusion needs also leaned lower, with device success leaning higher. Trial checks warned that the proof base stays thin and mostly drawn from past records rather than trials. The authors judge continued use as workable for now while calling for large trials before firm rules are set.
pmc-13480270:
Yalin Zhang and co-authors present a 2026 genetics study of wood quality in Japanese larch, a fast-growing timber tree. The team measured fifteen wood traits in 84 families from six source regions grown together for twenty-two years. They also fitted growth curves for height and trunk width to see how wood traits trade off against growth speed.

Wood anatomy traits varied most between families and showed the strongest inheritance, while growth curve traits passed down more weakly. Faster trunk thickening linked to higher cellulose and wider fibres, yet to lower wood density. Height growth showed few firm links to wood traits. Breeders can use the pattern to pick families that grow fast early while keeping wood fit for solid timber or pulp, rather than chasing growth alone.
pmc-13481470:
Kangyu Wang and co-authors present a 2026 multi-layer study hunting a master switch in acute kidney injury, a sudden loss of kidney function with no drug that reverses it. The team fused human single-cell and tissue-wide gene data with protein maps from mouse kidneys and from patient urine. A learning model ranked five candidate genes, and one called TRIM28 topped the list.

The switch ran high in injured kidney cells in both dish and mouse tests, and it showed up in human urine, which hints at a test that needs no biopsy. Dimming the switch calmed inflammatory signals through a known immune lane and cut cell death, while boosting it did the reverse. A screened compound bound the switch in cells, eased injury signs, and lifted survival of stressed cells. Human trials remain far off, yet the urine link makes the target unusually reachable.
pmc-13481670: Health Policy and Planning issued a 2026 correction tied to a paper on tracking child health and well-being within the climate change agenda. The notice is a correction only. It states that the file holding legends for its Figure 1 and Table 2 was left out of the online supplementary material by mistake. That file, named Supplementary_Legends.docx, has now been added for readers. Nothing in the paper's findings, tables, or wording is changed by the notice.
pmc-13482470:
Barakat, Massoud, and Alhalabi train deep learning models in 2026 to read hysteroscopy images for IVF patients, sorting views of the womb lining into normal tissue, polyps, and endometritis, an inflamed lining. Expert reading of these scope videos varies with experience, so the team built a decision support system from 1,500 annotated stills drawn from 200 clinical videos. Four established image networks were adapted and compared on the three-way task.

The models scored between 85 and 89 percent accuracy overall, and DenseNet-121 came out strongest across the detailed measures reported by the team. For polyps it reached 93 percent sensitivity, catching nearly all true cases, with a discrimination score of 98.8 percent on the standard curve in testing. It also hit 90 percent precision for endometritis, and heat-map overlays confirmed the networks stared at the tissue features clinicians use, though outside validation is still owed.
pmc-13484470:
Das and co-authors built a small wetland planted with castor to clean wastewater flowing from rice mills while growing a useful crop. Rice mill effluent carries heavy loads of nutrients and organic matter that pollute streams in India's paddy regions. Their 2026 study soaked castor seeds in the effluent, grew plants in wetland cells at several dilutions, and then checked field plots enriched with the water.

Seeds soaked in effluent germinated at 90 percent and showed a vigor index about twelve times the control value reported. Half-strength effluent worked best, giving plants 52 centimeters tall and removal of roughly two thirds of nitrogen pollutants. Removal of oxygen-demanding pollutants passed 70 percent at that dilution in the wetland trials. Field seed yield quadrupled, from 22 to 91 grams, on effluent-enriched soil. Das sees a route to treat waste and grow industrial castor together.
pmc-13487570:
Bartosz Woźniak treats benign wart-like growths on the head and neck with tight beams of high-frequency focused ultrasound. Published in 2026, the single-center retrospective study reviews 178 seborrheic keratoses from 38 patients treated at twenty megahertz. Mixed models hunt baseline skin-scope features that predict complete clearance, accounting for repeated lesions per patient and body site.

Complete clearance reached 74.7 percent of lesions, with another 14.0 percent nearly clear. Scalp lesions cleared far less often at 40 percent than face and neck lesions at 78 percent. Cosmetic results rated good or excellent in 86.0 percent of cases, while side effects stayed mostly mild, led by lightened pigment. A sharp lesion border roughly doubled clearance odds and a brain-like surface pattern roughly tripled them, helping clinicians choose which growths suit the beam.
pmc-13487970:
Vivek K. Pandey and colleagues gather evidence on spinal cord stimulation for body functions lost after spinal cord injury in a 2026 scoping review. Injury often disrupts automatic control of blood pressure, bladder, bowel, and sexual function. The team searched three databases through September 2025 for studies in people or animals that tested stimulation effects on those functions, and sixty-eight studies qualified.

Most evidence comes from case reports, small series, and cohort studies rather than controlled trials. Reports describe better bladder capacity and control, steadier blood pressure, easier bowel care, and gains in sexual function. Methods varied a lot between studies, which limits comparison. The authors set out priorities for rigorous trials and basic research on how stimulation works.
pmc-13488170:
Amanda Magalhaes Vilas Boas Cambiais and colleagues audit antibiotic prescribing at a Brazilian university hospital in a 2026 cross-sectional study. A stewardship framework called the Four Moments guides decisions at starting treatment, choosing a drug and taking cultures, reviewing progress after a few days, and setting total duration. Records covered 228 patients given systemic antibiotics during two months in late 2023, many of them in intensive care.

Three quarters of treatments followed all four moments fully. Early steps scored highest, while culture taking and duration choices left the most room to improve, since cultures were sometimes skipped when advised. Intensive care used far more antibiotic days than wards did. Most use fell in the World Health Organization Watch group, which needs monitoring.
pmc-13488570:
Sophie Sergerie-Richard, Guillaume Fontaine, and Marie-Helene Goulet compare theories for removing low-value care in a 2026 guidance paper. Low-value practices waste scarce resources and can harm patients, and de-implementation means deliberately reducing, restricting, replacing, or stopping them. The field often treats stopping as implementation run backward, which the authors challenge through a theory-based narrative review comparing models side by side.

Stopping has its own psychology, including habit, loss aversion, and threats to professional identity. Politics, incentives, and rules constrain change at several levels at once, and the right endpoint depends on the practice itself. Ten recommendations follow, covering clear classification of low-value care, logic linking barriers to strategies, patient experience, and harms from stopping.
pmc-13490270:
Marcos Fumero-Hernandez and colleagues describe manual plasma exchange for a dog with seizures after shunt surgery in a 2026 veterinary case report. The four-year-old Yorkshire Terrier had a congenital vessel defect that let blood bypass the liver, surgically closed without early trouble. Within two days she developed whole-body seizures that resisted standard drugs, a syndrome seen after such repairs whose cause and best treatment remain unclear. Liver failure was judged unlikely to explain the signs.

The team performed a modified manual exchange of the dog's plasma over eight hours, a simpler version of a machine procedure that swaps blood plasma to remove circulating triggers. Marked improvement followed, seizures and nerve signs resolved, and she went home without procedure complications. The authors note a single prior cat report.
pmc-13490570:
Qing Zhou and others build an explainable machine-learning tool to predict leg vein clots after womb lining cancer surgery. In 2026, the study uses around surgery data from 841 patients across multiple centers, testing twenty-six algorithms with data augmentation methods. Standard clot scores perform poorly in gynecologic oncology and cannot use changing after surgery lab values.

A support vector machine model won, refined to four variables: after surgery D-dimer, age, fibrinogen, and medical stage. It scored 0.828 internally and 0.819 in an external cohort, while SHAP explanations revealed non-linear effects such as a key D-dimer threshold. A web interface delivers real-time, interpretable risk estimates to guide preventive care.
pmc-13490870:
Ciliento and colleagues measured sleep signals in 2026 in people with focal epilepsy, a form of the disorder where seizures start in one brain area. Sleep normally resets brain excitability overnight, and broken resetting may help seizures persist. The team used a dense cap of 256 electrodes to record brain waves through the night.

Thirty-nine patients and 48 healthy matched volunteers took part. Patients showed stronger slow-wave activity during sleep and steeper slow waves than controls. By morning, their values looked like the fresh evening values of healthy sleepers, as if the reset had not finished. One marker, local peaks in a mid-speed wave band, sorted patients from controls well on its own. Night seizures on the left side tracked with weaker overnight decline in slow waves, hinting that seizures themselves wear down the reset.
pmc-13491870:
Catriona R Mayland leads a large collaborative team following in 2026 the pain experience of 150 people newly diagnosed with mesothelioma, an incurable cancer of the chest lining, across twenty British hospitals. Questionnaires every three months for a year captured pain, breathlessness, mood, and quality of life. The average participant was seventy-two, and three quarters were men.

Breathlessness troubled more participants than pain at the start. One in seven reported moderate or severe chest pain, which had typically lasted about fourteen weeks, yet none of them was taking strong opioid painkillers. By the final quarter, those with significant pain scored far worse on quality of life and daily functioning than others. Forty-four percent died within the year, and the authors urge earlier pain identification and specialist palliative input.
pmc-13493670:
Kim Rand leads a nine-author team writing in 2026 to challenge a published indirect comparison claiming two eczema biologics, tralokinumab and lebrikizumab, maintain their benefit equally over a year. The original analysis compared week fifty-two results only among patients who had already responded by week sixteen in separate trial programs. The letter argues that this design bakes in an unfair advantage.

Response rates at week sixteen differed hugely, about fifty-two percent for lebrikizumab against twenty-eight for tralokinumab, so the tralokinumab survivors were a far more select group of best responders. Statistical matching can balance measured traits but cannot erase that enrichment. The shared placebo anchor also fails, they argue, because each withdrawal group had spent sixteen weeks on a different active drug first. The exchange, later answered by the original authors, is a pointed lesson in indirect comparison pitfalls.
pmc-13493770:
Sojung Lee and others run a multi-site randomized trial of a digital healing game for planning skills in children with ADHD. In 2026, the single-blind, sham-controlled trial assigns 122 children aged six to twelve to an adaptive multitasking game called STAR RUCKUS or a look-matched driving-only sham. Children played five daily sessions for four weeks. Executive function deficits mark ADHD and drug treatments carry limits.

At week four, the game group improved more on clinician-rated ADHD scores, by 7.50 points versus 4.00, with gains in both inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity. Effects were small to modest, adherence and tolerability were favorable, and 114 children completed the trial. The game offers a hopeful non-drug option pending longer-term testing.
pmc-13494070:
Jimmy Chun Yu Louie offers a 2026 perspective on trials of ultraprocessed foods, arguing that claims drawn from them often run ahead of the data. He reviews four randomized trials that set ultraprocessed diets against diets built on foods with little processing. His concern is how other writers have summed up those trials in reviews and comment pieces.

In each trial the two diets differed in far more than processing, so no result can pin cause on processing alone. Louie notes that reports stressed results that fit a harm story while giving less weight to neutral or even favorable findings. He urges future trials to match diets on nutrient makeup and to report dropout and adherence as main outcomes. He also urges testing subgroups within the broad ultraprocessed class before policy leans on class-wide claims.
pmc-13494270:
Daehee Lee and eight colleagues published this 2026 modelling paper on hearing risk in pilots and other aircrew. The authors ask whether these harms cluster in one sound frequency band, and whether that band matches frequencies used in threshold sound conditioning, a protective low-level sound treatment.

The work is a computer framework, not a trial in people. The team built a Cumulative Cochlear Stress Index that merges the three stressors across frequencies. The overlap of the three harm curves peaked near 4.23 kilohertz, inside a 3 to 6 kilohertz band. That band matches the 3, 4 or 6 kilohertz options used in an earlier conditioning trial. Repeated random checks reproduced the 4 kilohertz peak in 99.2 percent of model runs, which the authors report as a robustness test.
pmc-13495170:
Rachelle Sherman, Andrew Tabner, and Graham Johnson investigate, in a 2026 study, how often English ability bars people from emergency research in England's East Midlands. The team reviewed trauma and emergency trials with a site that finished in the five years before late 2020.

Nearly one in five of the 129 trials screened out people who could not communicate in English. Screening logs, where kept, showed two to seven percent of patients turned away for language, a rate above the share expected from local population data. A survey of staff found awareness of the fairness and science costs, with money seen as the main driver of the rule. Because logs were scarce, the scale stays unknown, and the authors call for national study of fixes such as interpreters.
pmc-13495270:
Lu Chen and colleagues test, in a 2026 mouse study, how prenatal dexamethasone, a steroid given in pregnancy to mature a preterm baby's lungs, affects the unborn ovary. Pregnant mice got the drug at two late stages, at three doses, in one or two courses.

Fetal ovaries taken near term showed early breakdown of egg cell nests, less cell growth, and more cell death. The drug pushed hormone-making genes up while pressing egg and follicle genes down. Harm peaked with mid-to-late timing, high dose, and a single course. A gene web analysis named a signaling chain linking the steroid's receptor to inflammation as a likely driver. The authors offer the results as evidence for weighing fetal ovary risk in pregnancy prescribing.
pmc-13495470:
Rongbin Liang and Bei Zhang present a 2026 case report, with a review of past reports, of a rare eye infection in a 9-year-old girl who wore overnight shaping lenses. She had three weeks of red eyes and a gritty feeling in both eyes. Her family had also just taken in a pet parrot. Microsporidia, tiny fungus-like parasites, were the suspected culprits.

Exam found a swollen, bumpy lining and widespread tiny damage across the clear front of both eyes. Scrapings and gene sequencing named the species Encephalitozoon hellem. Such infections usually strike people with weak immunity, so a healthy child is unusual; lens wear and animal contact may have opened the door. The authors urge doctors to think of this parasite when eye surface infection drags on despite standard drops, since the right test is a scraping, not a guess.
pmc-13499970:
Sydney Lash leads a 2026 pilot trial of immersive education for patients starting external beam radiation therapy, who often feel anxious and unsure what treatment involves. The programme used first-person 360-degree videos showing the treatment experience, watched either through a virtual reality headset or as a flattened video, chosen by patient preference and tolerance. Immersive education produced larger drops in treatment-related, cancer-related, and care-plan anxiety, with the care-plan gain reaching statistical significance in the reported tests, and patient understanding improved clearly against standard care. Satisfaction rose in both groups, more so in that group. Workflow measures trended favourably too, with shorter treatment times and fewer imaging repeats and position corrections, supporting a larger trial of the approach.
pmc-13500470:
Daniela M Hernández and colleagues catalogue in 2026 a family of protein-cutting enzymes in holm oak, an evergreen Mediterranean tree threatened by a root-rotting water mould. The enzymes, subtilisin-like proteases, take part in growth and stress defence yet were barely mapped in forest trees. Gene structures showed strong evolutionary conservation, and one subfamily was packed with genes lacking the usual spacer segments. When seedlings were infected with the mould, family members responded unevenly, and three genes switched on strongly, rising several-fold up to roughly thirtyfold in the reported values. The catalogue gives breeders and pathologists candidate defence genes for building resistance in a keystone oak.
pmc-13503270:
Shiho Uchida and others check single-letter DNA-variant-based outside-body before birth testing against newborn gene checks. In 2026, the single-center study looks at 4,466 high-risk pregnant women tested between 2013 and 2022, backing high-flag results by womb fluid test and low-flag results by after-birth cheek glow test. Most prior rightness guesses relied on pre-birth results alone.

pmc-13503670:
Boqin Song leads a large team reporting a strange charge density wave in a layered crystal, in a 2026 paper. A charge density wave is a ripple in how electrons spread through a solid, and it often sits near superconductivity. The crystal here, Au6Te12Se8, is built from clusters of atoms rather than single atoms.

Most such waves shift atoms by a tiny amount and fade as a crystal thins. In this crystal, atoms shift about ten times more, driven by sideways sound waves in the lattice. The team used cold electron microscopy, fast light probes, and flow tests to track the wave. Its change point rose from under 2 kelvin in bulk to 110 kelvin near the thin limit. The clash with superconductivity may reveal new electron-lattice links.
pmc-13503770:
Chuan Li and four colleagues judge what phone-based contact tracing achieved in Peru during the COVID-19 pandemic, in a 2026 study. The national app was meant to warn people after risky contact. Few people used it, which limited person-to-person tracing.

The data still covered 1.66 million users, with about 80,000 confirmed cases. The team read travel habits across policy phases and mapped contact webs over time. People with richer contact webs and those at smaller gatherings faced higher infection risk. Poorer users moved farther and caught the virus more often than richer users. The authors argue that such data can guide fair policy and resource plans even when app uptake is low.
pmc-13503870:
Wenting Ruan and others compare three test meshes of outside-cell matrix for soft tissue remodeling. In 2026, the study builds a same-form cross-species plan testing human acellular dermis, porcine acellular dermis, and porcine small intestinal submucosa. Testing runs through lab characterization and rabbit under the skin plus rat belly defect models. Mesh performance varies sharply by tissue source, yet no common review standard existed.

Human dermis proved most stable, retaining 82.3 percent mass after seven days of collagenase digestion, while intestinal submucosa degraded fastest and provoked severe foreign body reactions. Human dermis uniquely sustained healing-type M2 eater cell dominance, reducing swelling and improving collagen remodeling. Implantation also reprogrammed host amino acid fuel use, notably methionine pathways.
pmc-13504370:
Li and colleagues followed a community cohort over time to map how a low score on an imaging index relates to spreading tissue damage, in a 2026 study. The index, called ALPS, estimates glymphatic function, the flow that washes solutes from the brain, from diffusion scans. The team analyzed scans voxel by voxel and also modeled brain network connections.

Li found a lower baseline index predicted progression of white matter microstructural damage over follow-up, concentrated in deep regions carrying association fibers, the long wiring between cortical areas. Network analysis tied the low index to a disconnected sub-network across the midline and right frontal lobe. Cross-sectional links to cortical thinning appeared in projection areas of both fiber types, though those faded in the longitudinal analysis. The authors read the index as a combined marker of perivascular dynamics and white matter integrity in populations.
pmc-13504970:
Santos and a large Brazilian team report what happened when a heart surgery service adopted patient blood management. That is a bundle of practices that treats donated blood as a scarce resource to be spent reluctantly. Their 2026 study compared 2,150 bypass patients from 2010, before the protocol, with 1,414 from 2012 after it, all undergoing planned coronary artery bypass grafting. The programme combined anaemia treatment before surgery, meticulous blood conservation during it, and transfusion decisions based on patient tolerance rather than fixed numbers.

Red cell transfusion fell from well over three fifths of patients to under half after the change. Plasma and platelet use roughly halved on the reported rates. Infections and deaths also dropped significantly in the protocol era, and receiving donor blood itself emerged as a strong predictor of dying in the adjusted analysis.
pmc-13505070:
Naoki Inoshima leads a team identifying pneumonia risk factors in older Japanese adults after child pneumococcal vaccination changed germ patterns, in a 2026 study. Community pneumonia stays a top killer of older people. Risks may differ between the young-old and the oldest, yet few studies split them.

The analysis used a national case-control study with 142 cases and 596 matched controls aged sixty-five and over. Living with a child aged six or under raised odds about sixfold, the strongest factor at both age splits. Low body weight and trouble with daily tasks also raised risk, while high body weight lowered it. Past seventy-five, lung diseases joined the list. The authors advise age-tailored prevention, with grandchild contact in mind.
pmc-13505170:
Carol Heckman studied why image-based cell assays often fail to repeat, testing whether data cleaning steps change how samples get classified. In five trials, matched samples received either the same chemical mixture or a plain solvent, and one low-dimensional measure summed up much of the image data. Batch effects from materials, staff, and culture conditions could not be fully controlled.

Scaling the data within each trial let the treated and control groups separate clearly on that measure. Standardising against large reference databases left the classification pattern unchanged, whichever suitable database was used. Removing outliers hurt instead, wiping out more than three percent of many samples and creating both false positives and false negatives. Heckman argues that some non-repeatability is built into cell assays, and that correct class assignment is a fairer quality check than matching repeat means exactly.
pmc-13507070:
Sıddıka Yusra Özkılıç, Esra Nida Öztürk, Semanur Buse Altınpulluk, and Derya Arslan test, in 2026 work, how paste acidity during olive oil mixing shapes oil yield and quality. They used Gemlik olives and set paste pH from 2.7 to 6.7 during malaxation, the slow mixing step before oil separation. Measures covered yield, acidity, oxidation, healthy compounds, and color.

Yield peaked at the highest pH, while total healthy phenol compounds peaked at the lowest pH and fell as pH rose. A mid-acid level gave the highest amounts of two prized bitter compounds, oleacein and oleocanthal. Acidic batches looked brighter and less yellow. Tuning paste pH could let mills trade yield against flavor and health value.
pmc-13507270:
Hoi Yee Chu leads a 2026 team that rebuilds, piece by piece in the lab, the first assembly steps of a bacterial secretion machine. Helicobacter pylori uses that machine to inject toxins into stomach cells. The machine's core cylinder starts from three proteins, CagX, CagY, and CagM, but their joining order was unknown. Test-tube reconstitution with imaging and binding measures traced the sequence.

CagX first links with itself into rings, then CagY joins to form a stable ring complex. CagM couples next through paired units stacking together, with CagY strengthening the grip. Knowing the build order exposes early chokepoints where assembly could be blocked. Anti-virulence drugs might someday jam the machine before it forms.
pmc-13507570:
Tang and colleagues present in 2026 a neuron-on-chip platform that injures living human neurons in a dish so researchers can watch the earliest responses to traumatic brain injury. What neurons themselves do after impact, apart from surrounding tissue, was poorly defined.

The device grows mature human prefrontal cortex neurons inside three-dimensional gels and strikes them with a weight-drop impactor. Calcium imaging across thirteen activity measures revealed two phases. Within the first day came overexcited, hyper-synchronized firing followed by network collapse, and by day eight, sustained abnormal activation with structural remodeling. Released tau protein, a marker tied to degeneration, rose steadily over five days, and cell-death enzymes switched on in an ordered sequence ending in tangle-like tau clumps. The authors offer the platform as a scalable model for drug discovery.
pmc-13508370:
Shaoxiao Li and five co-authors train computer models on CT scan patterns to tell fungal sinus disease apart from ordinary chronic sinusitis, in 2026 work. The two conditions share symptoms, which makes them easy to confuse. Records covered 106 fungal cases and 146 chronic cases, all confirmed by surgery at a Wenzhou hospital between 2022 and 2025. Software pulled hundreds of texture measures from the scans. Filtering steps kept the nineteen most useful measures. Three model types then competed on accuracy.

A random forest model won, sorting cases with accuracy above nine in ten on unseen test data. Its probability estimates also matched real outcomes closely in checks. The authors argue this image-based approach could cut misdiagnosis and sharpen treatment choices. They flag one key limit plainly: the model has not yet been tested on patients from other hospitals.
pmc-13508770:
Fadil and colleagues released FastRet, a 2026 software tool that predicts how long molecules take to pass through a liquid chromatography column. That timing is a fingerprint that helps identify unknown compounds in metabolomics, the study of small molecules in biology. Knowing expected timing helps rank candidate identities, but collecting measurements for every compound is slow. FastRet trains in seconds on a processor and works from an R console or a web page.

Fadil validated the tool on three in-house data sets across different separation styles plus an external set, using two learning methods on molecular descriptors. Tree-based models trained from scratch predicted held-out timings for reversed-phase data and moderately for harder mixed-mode data. FastRet can adapt a model to changed conditions from 25 remeasured compounds, gaining over training fresh. It picks which compounds are most worth remeasuring, a feature that beat random selection in tests.
pmc-13510070:
Yuecheng Wang, Michael Nguyen-Truong, Raghavan Chinnadurai, Peiman Hematti, William R. Wagner, and Zhijie Wang study how stiffness and fiber direction in heart-like scaffolds affect vessel-forming cells, in 2026 work. The right side of the heart stiffens and loses small vessels as pressure overload advances. Scaffolds built to mimic that tissue let the team vary stiffness and alignment for two kinds of lining cells that form blood vessels.

Aligned fibers raised cell numbers yet lowered metabolic activity in both cell types. Vessel forming split by cell origin: one type formed fewer new vessels on stiffer or aligned surfaces, while heart-derived cells formed more on stiffer surfaces yet fewer on aligned ones. The proteins each type released also shifted with the surface. The authors say scaffold design for heart repair must be tuned to the exact cell type used.
pmc-13512370:
Francesco Branda and ten co-authors compare three deep learning designs for naming malaria parasite species in microscope images, in 2026 work. Microscopy remains the standard test, yet it leans on scarce expert readers, above all where malaria hits hardest. All three models were trained from scratch on real thick blood smear images plus public sets, with no borrowed pre-trained weights.

A classic layered network took the top scores, with accuracy near ninety-seven percent and near-perfect separation scores. A transformer model that reads images as patch sequences scored a few points lower, and a hybrid joining both designs fell between in the checks reported. Cross-validation held steady for all three. The authors say automated species reading is close to dependable, while telling similar Plasmodium species apart remains the hardest part for field use.
pmc-13512670:
Maja Ribar, Josip Razum, and Goran Milas examine how perceived stress is structured and how steady it stays across adolescence, in 2026 work. A probability sample of 1679 Croatian high school students was followed over three waves about six months apart. Stress was rated in six domains: school, the future, parents, friends, romantic partners, and the self.

Models favored a layered picture, with six domain factors feeding one general stress factor. The measure worked the same across time and across boys and girls. General stress proved strikingly stable from wave to wave despite being a here-and-now judgment. It also tied moderately to strongly with depression, anxiety, inward and outward symptoms, life satisfaction, and happiness, with no sex gap in those links. The authors treat teen stress as both layered and trait-like in its core.
pmc-13513570:
Rachadaporn Jantasuwan, Suda Jaihow, Sumoltip Sontimuang, Kanyapak Pluemjai, Hasni Embong, and Salwismawati Badrin identify what predicts a small head circumference at birth, in 2026 work. The babies were born to women anemic in late pregnancy. A small head can signal slowed fetal brain growth and later developmental trouble. Anemia in the third trimester is common and itself harms fetal growth, so the team hunted for added maternal factors inside that high-risk group.

Three changeable factors stood out: how many pregnancies a woman had carried, her body mass before pregnancy, and how much weight she gained during pregnancy. First-time mothers and women whose starting weight or gain sat off target faced higher risk. The authors advise close watch of weight gain in anemic pregnancies, stronger nutrition programs, and wider anemia prevention and screening. Better antenatal tracking, they argue, can protect fetal brain growth before birth.
pmc-13514870:
Wang and colleagues report a 2026 study of a plant compound mixture from Prunella vulgaris, a traditional herb, tested on insomnia in mice. Sleeplessness was induced with a chemical that drains the brain's sleep signal serotonin. The team profiled the mixture's contents, recorded sleep with brain and muscle sensors, and examined the hippocampus, a memory region that insomnia injures.

Chemical profiling tentatively identified 198 constituents in the mixture. Treated mice slept better on both drug-induced sleep tests and overnight recordings, with sleep structure closer to normal. Their hippocampi showed less tissue damage, healthier transmitter balance, and lower activity of the NLRP3 inflammasome pathway, which drives a fiery form of cell death called pyroptosis. A traditional sleep remedy with a mapped chemistry and a named pathway gives modern insomnia research a testable lead beyond sedation.
pmc-13515070:
Abdusattorov and co-authors propose in 2026 a combined ultrasound strategy for grading fatty liver, called hepatic steatosis, more accurately. Radiologists grade liver fat by eye from ultrasound images, but judgment varies with experience, while quantitative tools such as attenuation imaging measure fat differently. The team tested whether blending the two approaches against biopsy results would beat either one alone.

They studied patients who had ultrasound, attenuation imaging, a hepatorenal index measurement, and a liver biopsy on the same day in 2023 and 2024, with three radiologists grading images independently. Reading images alone reached about eighty-seven percent accuracy for detecting any steatosis. The best combined strategy kept the visual grade when it differed by one grade from the measurement-based grade. It used the middle grade only for two-grade gaps, and it reached up to ninety-three percent accuracy. The improvement held across experience levels.
pmc-13516170:
Hyeran Jung and Minsun Jung chart two decades of reportable infectious disease in South Korea in a 2026 analysis of national surveillance data from 2001 to 2024. Because the legal classification changed in 2020, their trend and forecasting work rests on the consistent 2001 to 2019 period, with later years described separately. Statistical models estimated yearly change, hunted for break points, and tested whether disease classes truly moved together.

Total reports rose steeply across the period once the 2009 flu pandemic outlier was handled. Respiratory and vaccine-preventable diseases drove the climb, growing fastest with a clear break around 2004. Several apparent links between classes dissolved once shared time trends were stripped out; only one pair stayed linked. Adults in their thirties and forties showed the sharpest rise in the most serious class. Ensemble forecasts project continued growth to 2028, with wide uncertainty bands the authors stress.
pmc-13516370:
Tomomi Suda and colleagues evaluate in 2026 a virtual exchange program linking nursing students across four countries: Belgium, Indonesia, Japan, and Thailand. They met online to discuss the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. The aim was to grow international skills without anyone traveling.

Twenty-nine participating students were compared with thirty-four matched non-participants, using a self-rating tool before and after. The exchange group improved significantly more on three fronts: working across cultures, personal growth, and digital skills. Language skills, global engagement, and subject learning did not differ reliably between groups. Because ratings were self-reported, the authors treat the gains as promising rather than proven. They present the program as a workable template for low-cost international learning in health education.
pmc-13518670:
Francisca N Amoah and colleagues reviewed five embryo mix-ups at five separate fertility clinics. In each case, patients were matched to the wrong eggs, sperm, or embryos. Published in 2026, the work treats these errors as among the gravest mistakes in assisted reproduction, partly because shame and fear can block honest reporting of what went wrong.

The authors show that human slips played a part in every case, yet each mix-up grew from a chain of weak checks rather than one lone lapse. They call for clinics to probe the full chain of causes after any near miss and to write clear rules for checking identity before transfer. Watching each critical step would let faults surface early. Readers gain a plain account of how such harm happens and what safer routines might prevent it.
pmc-13520170:
Emily E. Munn, Jake W. Griffin, Mary R. Ciccarelli, and Melissa M. Pangelinan question caregivers in 2026 about Indiana's Complex Care Coordination Collaborative, which embeds nurse coordinators in primary care practices for medically complex children. Thirteen caregivers gave hour-long talks covering unmet needs, care quality, shared care plans, workload, and quality of life.

Five themes emerged, led by the coordinator's central role and proactive, personalized support. Caregivers called coordinators trusted advocates who eased their way through the health system and spread the shared plan to other staff and kin. Support came in hands-on, factual, emotional, and social forms. Some caregivers still felt lonely and struggled to connect with families unlike theirs, a gap the program has yet to close.
pmc-13520270:
Wolazihan Madeniyati leads an eight-author biomarker study in 2026 on TIM-1, an immune-regulating protein, in pulmonary tuberculosis. Blood plasma from 60 active tuberculosis patients, 50 people with latent infection, and 50 healthy controls at a Xinjiang hospital was tested for TIM-1 and two signaling molecules, IFN-gamma and IL-17.

Active patients carried significantly more TIM-1 and IL-17, with less IFN-gamma, and TIM-1 levels tracked IL-17 levels closely. Alone, TIM-1 separated patients only moderately well. A combined predictive model reached a discrimination score near 0.79. The authors frame TIM-1 as a candidate aid for early diagnosis and a possible treatment target, while stressing that larger multicenter validation must come first.
pmc-13522070:
Takashi Yamanaka and colleagues report in 2026 quality of life results from the Asian PATHWAY trial, where adding palbociclib to tamoxifen lengthened time without progression in hormone-sensitive advanced breast cancer. Longer control matters little if daily life worsens, so patient questionnaires were tracked across treatment.

Women were randomised evenly between drug and dummy combinations, answering standard cancer quality questionnaires at set cycles and treatment end. Average changes in global quality scores differed little between arms at each check. Subscale detail, including pain deterioration timing, fills the full analysis. Comparable daily-life scores strengthen the case that progression gains came without a broad quality penalty.
pmc-13522470:
Amin Hosseini Nami and co-authors describe improved prenatal diagnosis of cystic fibrosis in three families in a 2026 genetics report. Cystic fibrosis is an inherited condition passed on when both parents carry a changed gene copy. The team layered three checks: clinical review, family pattern analysis using linked DNA markers, and direct sequencing of the CFTR gene.

The layered approach caught cases that routine screening had misclassified, reducing the risk of errors from problems such as maternal cell contamination or specimen mix-ups. Earlier and more accurate results allow better planning for pregnancy and newborn care. The authors argue that the same layered testing strategy could improve prenatal diagnosis for other recessive disorders where a single test can mislead.
pmc-13523370:
Juanjuan Sun and co-authors follow how sensitive mothering shapes young children's emotional problems in a 2026 longitudinal study from Shanghai. Two hundred twelve mother-child pairs were observed when children were about four years old. Mothers reported emotional problems then and a year later. Teachers rated social skills at the second point. Internalizing problems cover anxiety and withdrawal rather than acting out.

Sensitive mothering at the first point predicted fewer internalizing problems a year later. Children's social skills partly carried that effect, explaining part of the protection. Gender also mattered: the link from sensitive mothering to stronger social skills was stronger in girls. The authors highlight social skill building, with attention to gender, as a route for parenting interventions in early childhood.
pmc-13524670:
Seda Babroudi and colleagues examine, in a 2026 national cross-sectional study, whether social risk factors track with lower use of peritoneal dialysis among maintenance dialysis patients in the United States. Peritoneal dialysis, done at home through the abdomen, is used less in the United States than elsewhere. Patient-level social risks had not been well measured.

The study covered 7,237 patients at 244 facilities of a national provider between 2023 and 2025, with dialysis started within two years. About 18 percent used peritoneal dialysis. One social risk was present in 9 percent of patients and more than one in 3 percent, with food insecurity and housing instability most common. Each step up in risk burden raised the adjusted odds of not receiving peritoneal dialysis, and housing and transport insecurity mattered independently.
pmc-13525970:
Cláudia Santos Constantino and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, a deep-learning system that stages breast cancer automatically from FDG PET and CT scans. Staging sorts tumors by primary size, node spread, and distant spread, guiding treatment. The system first outlines sugar-avid lesions, then converts those outlines into a metabolic stage.

The retrospective set held 403 patients with confirmed breast cancer, split into 303 for training and 100 for testing. Lesions were grouped into primary tumor, armpit nodes, other regional nodes, and distant metastases. Automated staging agreed with physician staging on tumor, node, and spread categories in roughly three quarters to seven eighths of cases. Sensitivity for advanced nodal and metastatic disease was high. The authors present the tool as support, not replacement, for expert reading.
pmc-13527070:
Bae and colleagues introduce LLPSense in 2026, a machine learning framework that predicts when proteins will separate into droplet-like clusters inside cells. This process, called phase separation, builds membrane-free cell compartments, but it shifts with protein amount, temperature, and the surrounding fluid, which older sequence-only models ignore.

LLPSense combines protein language model summaries with these environmental inputs, and lab tests confirmed its predictions. It revealed complex temperature-linked behavior in the protein SGTA, which was not known to phase separate before. It also correctly predicted which changes to alpha-synuclein, a protein linked to Parkinson's disease, would raise or lower separation. Guided by the model, the team could tune phase behavior on purpose through chosen mutations.
pmc-13528070:
Mona M. Alshahrani leads a large team reviewing bloodstream infections in dialysis patients in southern Saudi Arabia in a 2026 study. Records at Aseer Central Hospital ran from 2013 to mid-2024. The cohort held 201 patients with 297 infection episodes. Nearly 390 germs were isolated. Death within thirty days in hospital was about eleven percent.

Gram-positive germs caused about sixty-nine percent of episodes. Skin staphylococci other than the famous aureus type led the list. A quarter of isolates resisted multiple drug classes. Among named threats, resistant Acinetobacter was most common. Linezolid and vancomycin stayed active against nearly all germs. One resistant gut germ group showed higher death rates, but numbers were tiny. The authors call the signal a hypothesis only. They urge local tracking to guide drug choice.
pmc-13528170:
Ali Nikparast and six colleagues link a gut-friendly diet score with fatty liver risk in Iranian adults in a 2026 study. The cohort held 5,058 adults free of the liver disease at the start. Diet was captured with a long food questionnaire. The score rates how well a diet feeds good gut microbes. Five years of follow-up followed.

In that span 562 people developed metabolic fatty liver disease. The top quarter of diet scores had about forty-two percent lower odds than the bottom quarter. Each standard step up the score cut odds by about twenty-eight percent. The link ran stronger in women and in people over forty-five. Insulin resistance and a liver stiffness measure explained part of the path. The authors back gut-aware eating as a prevention lever.
pmc-13530170:
Emiliano Di Cicco leads a 2026 first report of the bacterial disease tenacibaculosis in wild Pacific salmon. The illness was well known in farmed salmon yet never confirmed in wild fish of this group. Chinook salmon caught in Barkley Sound, Canada, in 2022 developed skin lesions during holding experiments.

Lesions appeared in 16 of 99 fish, and deaths ran high. Gene screening, DNA sequencing, and microscope work traced the worst cases to one bacterial species. The finding matters for conservation and fisheries because a farm-associated disease now has documented reach into wild salmon.
pmc-13530270:
Magdalena Rutkowska leads a 2026 chemical and biological profile of leaves from the Japanese rowan tree Sorbus commixta. Extracts and enriched fractions underwent detailed compound identification plus tests against oxidation, inflammation, and diabetes-linked processes. Human blood components and immune cells supplied living test systems.

Seventy-eight compounds were identified, making up a large share of the dry extract weight. The full extract and one fraction best shielded blood parts from chemical attack and calmed inflammatory signal release. The same fraction blocked a sugar-processing enzyme far more strongly than a standard drug. Activity tracked with several polyphenol groups.
pmc-13530470:
Mansour and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 130, a comparison of psychological readiness to return to sport after two hip operations. One is arthroscopy alone for impingement; the other adds a pelvic operation for hip dysplasia.

From one surgeon's registry, 34 arthroscopy-only and 35 combined-surgery patients, all active, completed two scales at three, six, and twelve months. The scales measured readiness to return and sport function. Readiness scores never differed between the groups at any time point, and both groups improved steadily across the year. Sport function did differ early: the arthroscopy-only group scored higher at three and six months. By twelve months the gap had closed. The authors read this as dysplasia patients catching up psychologically from the start and physically by year's end.
pmc-13530670:
Paliobeis and colleagues present in 2026, as conference paper 08, a test of the reflection index as a predictor of needing revision hip arthroscopy. The index is a new X-ray measure of how completely a hip impingement bump has been shaved. The standard measure, the alpha angle, misses some bad resections.

The single-surgeon study compared 37 patients revised between 2016 and 2021 with 61 matched patients whose primary surgery never needed revision. A higher alpha angle raised revision risk, as did certain coverage angles, while a lower offset ratio also predicted revision. A reflection index farther from one, its ideal value, likewise predicted revision. The new index earned its keep where the alpha angle looked normal, still separating future revision patients from the rest. The standard measure could not.
pmc-13531070:
Yasunori Inoguchi and co-authors report in 2026 a laser rescue for a heart stent that clogged early because a calcified lump pushed back through its struts. The 81-year-old man, on dialysis, had received the stent during a heart attack three months earlier. Imaging inside the vessel showed a protruding calcified flap.

An excimer laser catheter broke apart the protruding calcium and cracked the stubborn ring behind it. Some contrast staining appeared briefly during treatment. Six months later imaging showed the vessel still open with stable healed tissue. The case reframes early clogging as a structural problem, not just tissue overgrowth.
pmc-13532970:
Stenmark, Msghina, and Nordenskjöld use Swedish national registers to ask whether electroconvulsive therapy keeps people with schizophrenia out of hospital for longer. Evidence from Western populations was scarce despite ECT's known power to boost antipsychotics. Their 2026 design is elegant: 351 patients who had received both ECT and non-ECT inpatient care over a decade each serve as their own control. They contribute one admission of each kind, which cancels out fixed personal differences.

Admissions involving ECT were followed by significantly more time before readmission or suicide at every checkpoint, from thirty days to a full year after discharge. The risk was reduced by roughly a quarter to a third across those windows in the hazard analyses. Fifteen patients went on to continuation ECT, and their advantage looked even larger at ninety and one hundred eighty days, though such small numbers demand caution.
pmc-13533570:
Syed, Walter, and Meyer built in 2026 a software pack, plinkQC, that cleans gene data for population studies in one pass. Gene hunts fail when stray kin, mixed roots, or poor samples sneak in. Labs once juggled split tools for each check. Their pack, written for the R stats tongue, folds three jobs into three plain calls: root calls, kin cuts, and quality checks, with a full report for each run.

The root caller, a trained forest of decision trees, hit near exact scores with just a small slice of shared gene marks. The kin cut uses a graph trick that weighs both blood ties and sample worth. On the famed 1000 Genomes set, it kept scores more clean samples than the shared cut lists did. The authors aim the pack at small labs that need firm, shared ground rules.
pmc-13539270:
S Casquero and colleagues report a bird study and literature review, published in 2026, testing whether mother birds load different compounds into egg yolks depending on the embryo's sex. In wild spotless starlings they measured hormones and antioxidants in freshly laid eggs and determined each embryo's sex from DNA.

Embryo sex had no effect on any yolk compound measured, including testosterone and vitamin E. Their review of the wider bird literature agreed: nearly three quarters of studies found no significant effect, and positive reports were often context-dependent or possibly distorted by sampling eggs late. They conclude there is no robust evidence for sex-based yolk allocation in birds.
pmc-13540070:
Mustafa Burgaç and Gözde Çelik Niftaliyev report a 2026 case from Türkiye. Doctors drained fluid from around a fragile heart. They did so without putting the patient on a ventilator. The 73-year-old man had bypass surgery ten days earlier. A large late fluid collection now squeezed his heart.

Pressure breathing could have cut blood return in such a patient. The team chose keyhole chest surgery instead. He breathed on his own during the operation. Nerve blocks numbed two layers of a chest wall muscle. Light sedation kept him nearly awake for forty minutes. The team drained about 950 millilitres of fluid in all.
pmc-13541570:
Chutimon Junkrasien and colleagues describe hospital practice in a 2026 article. Their topic is electrical storm at Kyorin University. A storm means three or more dangerous rhythm episodes in one day. The heart races out of control again and again in such a storm. Modern care reaches well beyond rhythm drugs and ablation. The team treats the first hours as a race to calm the heart and keep the patient safe.

Two contrasting patients illustrate the framework. One had a weak heart muscle and stubborn rhythm trouble. The other had a storm after a heart attack. Care starts with early sedation and tuned medicines. Nerve-calming techniques and tailored ablation come next. Rehab work and structured follow-up close the path. The authors say steady care over time shapes outcomes.
pmc-13542170:
R Mukesh leads a space weather study in 2026. The team forecast how solar flares disturb the upper atmosphere. Flares change its electron content over low latitudes. That disturbance degrades radio links and satellite navigation. Four powerful X-class flares supplied the test cases. All four came from the current solar cycle.

A newer network design did the forecasting. It is called a Kolmogorov-Arnold network. Training used solar and geomagnetic indices. Checks ran against GPS-derived measurements at two stations. One station was Hyderabad in India. The other was Chumphon in Thailand. A deep belief network served as a rival model. So did the standard international reference model.
pmc-13542270:
In a 2026 study, Samia Parvez and colleagues ranked waste materials able to replace part of the cement in green concrete. Ten candidates were tested, ranging from silica fume and rice husk ash to granite dust, marble powder, coconut shell powder, and plastic waste. Each mix was measured for compressive, tensile, and flexural strength, plus ultrasonic pulse velocity, a check on internal quality and durability.

Rather than judge by one test, the team combined correlation analysis, a structured weighting method, and clustering to score the materials fairly. Compressive strength carried the greatest weight, and silica fume came out as the most balanced performer across all measures. Clustering split the candidates into stronger and weaker groups with a statistically clear separation. The framework gives builders a repeatable way to pick lower-impact ingredients without guessing.
pmc-13543370:
Xin Sun and colleagues published a 2026 education study evaluating a structured teaching module on follow-up care after kidney cancer surgery for urology residents. Follow-up teaching is hard to fit into short rotations. The module was therefore built around a simple four-item risk model, shortened to IMDB, covering vein invasion, tumour size, systemic symptoms, and invasion of the renal sinus fat. Forty residents completed eight to ten hours mixing lectures, simulation, clinic practice, and debriefing, organised as a health management passport.

Knowledge scores climbed from about 66 to about 91 points on the study's questionnaire. Graders rated residents' follow-up plans highly, with a pass rate above ninety percent, and satisfaction reached 96 percent, with every resident willing to recommend the module.
