Gains in knowledge did not track with decision scores, which the authors attribute partly to a near-ceiling test. Second-year residents improved most.
pmc-13543470:
Emiyamrew Getnet and colleagues published a 2026 cross-sectional study measuring tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes, immune cells found inside breast tumours, across cancer stages at Gondar's university hospital in northwest Ethiopia. Such scores predict outcomes elsewhere, but Ethiopian data were scarce. Sixty-two patients treated in a one-year window had stored tumour tissue stained and scored by international working-group rules, then compared with stage, grade, and nodal spread.

The pattern defied a simple good-news story: immune infiltration was lowest in stage II disease and highest in stage IV. Median scores reached about forty-eight percent in stage IV against seven percent in stage II, and higher grade tumours also carried more lymphocytes. Scores rose in step with overall stage, nodal stage, and grade. Advanced tumours may be more visible to the immune system, the authors suggest, and call for work linking the scores to molecular subtypes.
pmc-13543570:
Janet Pope and colleagues published a 2026 analysis of how rheumatoid arthritis patients respond over time to abatacept, a biologic drug given under the skin, in ordinary clinical practice. Using data from a real-world care study of 256 adults, the team applied a growth mixture model. That method lets distinct response trajectories emerge from the data, with a standard disease-activity index tracked for twelve months.

Three paths appeared. Rapid responders, about forty-nine percent, improved quickly; late responders, thirty-eight percent, caught up slowly; non-responders, fourteen percent, barely moved. Rapid responders started with lower disease activity and patient-rated scores, and had used fewer biologics before. Curiously, the three-month score did not predict the twelve-month outcome. Roughly eighty-five percent of patients eventually responded, so the authors counsel patience before declaring this treatment a failure in slower starters.
pmc-13543670:
Veronika Stadler's team reviewed patient and public involvement in children's health research, asking how young patients and families are brought into studies. Their search of four databases found thirty-seven papers on thirty-five studies published between 2003 and 2024, and reporting quality was checked against a standard short checklist. Involvement was mapped by who took part, at which research stages, and with what effects.

Children, adolescents, and caregivers were the usual contributors, most often at the design stage, in nearly nine of ten studies, and in recruitment in about half. Teams said involvement brought better recruitment and retention, and those taking part reported personal benefits. The barriers were money, time, and finding representative voices, while the depth of involvement and the quality of its write-ups varied widely. The authors urge fuller use of the reporting guide so others can learn from each project.
pmc-13545070:
Tollemeto and colleagues developed a cleaner way to manufacture niosomes, tiny bubble-like carriers made from soap-like molecules that can ferry drugs through the gut when swallowed. Their 2026 study presents a process called SuperSomes. It uses supercritical carbon dioxide, a high-pressure form of the gas, to form the carriers in one continuous step instead of the slow batch methods used today.

Tollemeto showed the process yields carriers of consistent size and makeup across batches, with little leftover solvent. The carriers stayed stable over time and across acidity levels that mimic the stomach and intestines. Tests with human gut cells showed the carriers slip through mucus yet interact well with cell membranes, a pairing suited to absorption. Animal work then confirmed delivery into the intestine with minimal retention in the stomach, supporting the method as a scalable, greener route to oral nanomedicines.
pmc-13546270:
Alba Galdón Sanz-Pastor and colleagues surveyed in 2026 how people with diabetes in Spain actually handle their daily insulin injections, and whether those habits track with blood sugar control. The online survey drew 288 adults who inject insulin several times a day, most of them living with type 1 diabetes for many years. Questions covered timing, dose mistakes, and use of smart insulin pens.

Most respondents injected before meals, yet only about seven in ten gave the dose at least 15 minutes ahead, the timing linked with clearly better results. Dosing errors were common, with more than a third reporting underdosing several times in the past month. Smart pen users reported fewer mild low-blood-sugar episodes, which supports wider use of the technology.
pmc-13547170:
Muhammad Usman and colleagues built in 2026 a risk chart to estimate which patients recovering from diverticulitis, an inflamed pouch in the colon wall, might actually harbor colorectal cancer. Guidelines give no standard way to sort these patients for follow-up checks. The team used records from 1,546 patients at a British hospital between 2021 and 2023 who had camera examinations after an episode.

Cancer was confirmed in 42 patients, about 2.7 percent of the group. Older age, male sex, and colon wall thickening on CT scans raised the predicted risk, while abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, and simple diverticulosis lowered it. The model sorted patients with reasonable accuracy. The authors say outside testing in other hospitals must come before routine use.
pmc-13547370:
Dianbo Jia and co-authors designed in 2026 a two-level learning system for assigning interceptor drones to incoming hostile drones when targets keep appearing, vanishing, and changing course. At the top level, a graph attention network treats interceptors and targets as a shifting web. It recomputes who should chase whom, using masks that absorb arrivals and departures without rebuilding the web. Edge features carry reachability and urgency straight into the decision.

At the lower level, a multi-agent policy steers the actual flying. Tested from four-against-four up to twelve-against-twelve engagements, the framework beat the strongest rival by about ten percentage points in the surprise-intrusion scenario. It reallocated targets successfully about 87 percent of the time and rarely flip-flopped assignments. Removing the edge features hurt most, marking them as the key ingredient.
pmc-13548570:
Hui Zou and colleagues map how a fiery form of cell death shapes the immune landscape of esophageal squamous cell cancer, in a 2026 study built on single-cell sequencing. This cancer kills many patients worldwide, and treatments often disappoint. The team profiled seven tumor samples and one healthy control, hunting for genes tied to pyroptosis, the inflammatory cell-death process, inside immune cells.

Thirteen key genes emerged, concentrated in immune and inflammation pathways. B cells appeared especially connected within the tumor's immune network, and the genes marked shifts in immune cell states over time. A two-gene risk model using GSDMB and CYCS predicted survival moderately in its training data but poorly in an outside cohort. The authors therefore present the signature as exploratory, paired with a chart that combines the score with tumor stage for further testing.
pmc-13551770:
Gamze Goke Arslan, Mehtap Genc, and Muhammed Celik published a 2026 study of nursing students in Türkiye. They asked how spiritual well-being links to moral strength. Moral strength means holding to good practice under strain. The survey phase covered 236 students at one university. The talk phase covered seventeen students in depth.

Overall spiritual well-being tied weakly but clearly to moral strength. One part, a sense of rising above the self, tied to less moral strain. It also tied to more moral confidence. Talks linked faith to empathy, drive, and coping. Talks also showed faith can spark inner conflict in hard choices. The team urges courses to add ethics, culture, and faith content with care.
pmc-13551870:
Raul N. G. Vianna, leading eight colleagues, published a 2026 narrative review proposing a new grouping for a family of inflammatory eye diseases once lumped together as white dot syndromes. The old label rested on pale spots seen in the fundus and grouped conditions with very different mechanisms. The review synthesizes two decades of multimodal imaging, including autofluorescence, dye angiography, and cross-sectional scans.

Imaging shows a subset of these disorders share one mechanism: inflammation-driven loss of blood flow in the choriocapillaris, the fine vessel layer feeding the outer retina, with secondary damage above it. The authors group those conditions as primary inflammatory choriocapillaropathies, listing several named diseases inside the frame. One member's placement stays less certain, and the review argues the mechanism-based scheme guides care better than spot appearance.
pmc-13555970:
Mahdi A Alnamnakani leads a ten-author team charting catch-up growth in preterm babies at a Riyadh hospital in a 2026 study. Records covered 134 preterm and 193 full-term infants born in 2018 and early 2019. Weight and length were tracked to twenty-four months using world growth standards. Catch-up was counted when a baby's score jumped sharply between visits.

Preterm babies started far lighter and shorter than full-term peers. Their weight gain ran parallel over time, and weight scores across birth-weight groups converged by age two. Length told a different story: preterm infants stayed shorter throughout, with a clearly different growth path. The smallest babies caught up in weight most often, about a third by two years.
pmc-13556070:
Ying Mei, Haixiao Zhang, and Yinfeng Li mapped in 2026 twenty years of research on nursing care to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia. This lung infection strikes patients on breathing machines and remains a major cause of harm in intensive care. Their bibliometric study pulled publications from a major citation database covering 2005 to 2025 and used mapping software to trace output, collaboration, and shifting themes.

Publication grew steadily, with a sharper rise after 2022, and author networks clustered by region across Europe, North America, Asia, and Latin America. Clinical guidelines were the most cited works. Themes moved from describing the problem toward bundled prevention routines, and recent hotspots centre on putting those bundles into daily practice, with oral hygiene prominent. The authors urge wider global teamwork so proven routines adapt to different hospitals.
pmc-13558570:
Jonathan Salazar-Leon and eleven colleagues showed in 2026 that high cholesterol inflames the brain's memory centre in mice, and that silencing one inflammatory protein can rescue the damage. Fat-fed mice lacking a cholesterol-clearing gene develop artery disease resembling the human condition tied to vascular dementia. After sixteen weeks of a Western diet, some animals received gene-silencing injections against the protein RIPK1 for eight more weeks, while others received a dummy sequence.

The fatty diet built carotid artery plaques, cut brain blood flow, damaged learning and memory, thinned the hippocampus's blood vessel network, and disturbed inflammation markers. Silencing the protein shrank plaques, restored arterial flexibility and brain flow, and preserved the hippocampal vessels. The authors argue that this single inflammatory switch links artery disease to brain decline and offers a drug target for vascular cognitive impairment.
pmc-13558670:
Fatin Saffanah Didin and five colleagues hunted in 2026 for the most sensitive signals of driver fatigue, comparing eye measures with attention test performance in a simulator. Fatigue is a proven crash risk for bus drivers, yet detection products disagree on what to measure. Fifteen people completed both a rested baseline and a session after twenty-four hours awake. They took sustained attention and vigilance tests while eye measures were recorded.

The share of missed responses on the sustained attention test predicted fatigue well. Mean vigilance scores and counts of minor lapses also detected the fatigued state with strong accuracy. A full day without sleep raised fatigue levels markedly across measures. The authors conclude that simple performance tests rival eye tracking, a useful finding for fleets that cannot fit every vehicle with cameras.
pmc-13558770:
Li Wang and nine colleagues compared in 2026 two ways of electrically stimulating the brain in patients whose mild cognitive impairment centres on memory loss. The frontoparietal network that supports memory shows disturbed slow theta rhythms in this condition, so the team delivered gentle alternating current at theta frequency over ten sessions. Thirty patients were randomised to stimulation at two network nodes at once, frontal and parietal, or at the frontal node alone, with brain recordings and memory tests before and after.

Dual-node treatment improved global cognition scores more than single-node treatment and raised resting theta power across frontal areas. Memory task performance and network dynamics also favoured the pair: rhythm coupling inside the frontal node strengthened during working memory, and frontal-to-parietal synchrony rose during associative memory. The authors call their findings preliminary yet pointed toward network-targeted stimulation.
pmc-13560270:
Le Song and three colleagues describe how femoral head osteonecrosis looks on FDG PET/CT scans in patients with lymphoma. Their 2026 retrospective analysis reviews seventeen patients whose dead hip bone was caught during lymphoma assessment. Uptake values, lesion stage, and the spread of bone death to other sites were catalogued against MRI findings.

Thirty-one femoral heads were involved, most at stage two. Advanced stage three and four lesions took up far more tracer than early ones, with medians of 5.27 against 1.37 in the reported comparison. Stage two lesions varied wildly: some glowed, some ringed a cold center, some stayed silent. CT extent matched MRI for every stage two to four lesion. Nine patients had osteonecrosis in other bones too, especially the humeral heads. The authors say PET/CT can flag the hip problem during routine lymphoma staging.
pmc-13562470:
Yijie Chai and eight colleagues revisit a finished trial to ask which patients gain from adding a bone graft when a plate fixes a shattered upper arm bone. The original trial found no overall benefit from placing a fibular graft, taken from donor bone, inside the fracture. Some fracture zones lack support on the inner side, and weak bone may change the answer. The 2026 analysis covers 72 trial participants who completed twelve months of follow-up, split between graft and plate-only care.

Arm and shoulder function, scored on a standard disability questionnaire, was the main measure. Among patients whose upper arm bone was osteoporotic, the graft group scored clearly better at twelve months, by about eleven points after adjustment. Other time points leaned the same way without reaching firm ground. The authors say grafting may pay off for this narrower group, not for every such fracture.
pmc-13563770:
Fawzia Alhaimi and two colleagues report a nine-year-old boy whose eyes crossed and ached after a feverish cold and a bout of conjunctivitis. His vision measured 20/40 in each eye, and his gaze showed an inward turn of 30 to 35 prism units, with outward movement limited. MRI scans of his orbits found both eye muscles swollen and bright with inflammation, the picture of orbital myositis, inflammation of the eye-moving muscles. The tear gland looked involved as well.

Pain, double vision, and redness were already easing within a day, before any drug was given. Antibiotics were prescribed and steroids planned, yet the steroids were never started because he could not tolerate them. By three months his eyes were straight and moved fully. The authors present the case as a recognisable, self-limited pattern that imaging can separate from nerve or focusing causes, sparing children unneeded treatment.
pmc-13564070:
Claudia Mickael leads a 2026 mouse study of lung hypertension caused by schistosomiasis, a parasitic disease that is a common cause of high pressure in lung blood vessels worldwide. The group tested whether a complement protein called mannose binding lectin, working inside helper T cells, drives the harmful immune response after exposure to parasite eggs.

Mice whose bone marrow lacked that protein were protected from lung hypertension and had fewer of the allergy-type helper T cells involved. Helper cells missing the protein also behaved less aggressively when exposed to parasite material. Protection did not extend to low-oxygen lung hypertension, so the pathway looks specific to the parasite disease and worth targeting there.
pmc-13566370:
Debbie Zittema and Annemieke Dols review, in a 2026 article, long-term drug treatment for bipolar disorder in adults aged fifty and over, a group defined by the illness's link with early aging. Work from a global research initiative and other recent studies is summarized, although no new intervention trials appeared in the prior eighteen months.

Lithium stays the first-choice maintenance drug, but at a lower target blood range for older patients. The authors argue it should not be withheld over fears about future kidney decline. Most proof so far comes from cohort and cross-sectional studies, so prescribers get guidance tempered by clear gaps in trial data for older adults.
pmc-13569170:
Kenji Shimomura and colleagues hunted the molecular sensors that make the red flour beetle flee from a plant chemical called alpha-thujone. Stored-grain pests and their host plants have sparred for millions of years, with plants evolving irritant compounds and insects evolving ways to detect them. Using gene-silencing in the beetle Tribolium castaneum, the team tested candidate receptors one by one in a 2026 study.

Silencing a GABA-receptor subunit, heat- and non-heat-sensitive TRP channels, or the antenna's core smell receptor all weakened avoidance, showing the response uses several senses at once. The pattern resembles DEET, the standard repellent, which also acts on multiple targets. The authors suggest these sensors could guide new repellents that drive pests away without relying on a single chemical trick.
pmc-13569470:
Hariam Raji and co-authors improve, in a 2026 study, human midbrain organoids, lab-grown tissue balls that model the dopamine neurons lost in Parkinson's disease. A three-stage adjustment of a growth signal called WNT, combined with swirling bioreactor culture, aimed to produce more of the specific vulnerable neuron type found in the substantia nigra.

The method raised yields of those neurons, strengthened their connections and electrical activity, and increased dopamine release. Single-cell profiling confirmed the right identity with less cell stress. Exposed to toxic protein clumps linked to Parkinson's, the organoids formed aggregates and lost dopamine neurons, mimicking disease. Drug researchers gain a scalable human model of the exact cells that die.
pmc-13570170:
Alice Girard and colleagues report, in a 2026 real-world study from a Montreal university hospital, hydroxyurea treatment in adults with hemoglobin SC disease, the second most common sickle cell form. Patients who started the drug between 2010 and 2025 were compared with themselves, crisis events in the year before treatment set against months four to sixteen after.

Among 263 people assessed, 110 entered the safety analysis and 75 the effectiveness analysis. Crisis events, including pain episodes and chest syndrome, dropped by fifty-six percent. Blood-related side effects were common but mostly mild, and liver test changes caused no symptoms. The study strengthens the case for offering hydroxyurea beyond the classic sickle genotype.
pmc-13570470:
Georgia De'Ambrosis and co-authors follow, in a 2026 retrospective study from two Queensland practices, patients whose basal cell skin cancers were first removed incompletely. They were then re-treated with Mohs micrographic surgery, a layer-by-layer method that checks margins during the operation. Cases needed at least five years of follow-up after final treatment.

Of 104 patients tracked for an average of just over nine years, none had a recurrence. Most tumors were aggressive subtypes or sat in high-risk places, and a few patients also received radiotherapy. The clean record supports Mohs re-excision as an effective answer to incomplete first surgery, with radiation as a useful extra for the riskiest cases.
pmc-13570970:
Alison M El Ayadi and colleagues linked childhood adversity to mental health among newly married young women in rural Nepal, publishing the study in 2026. Adverse childhood experiences predict lifelong health harm, but evidence from low-resource settings and for young married women was thin. The team surveyed 200 newly married women, tracking childhood adversity, depressive symptoms, and intimate partner violence in early adulthood.

Nearly six in ten women reported at least one adverse childhood experience, a quarter reported depressive symptoms, and a quarter reported partner violence. Each added adversity raised depression scores by nearly two points and violence severity modestly, with violence contributing to depression but not explaining the adversity link. The authors urge prevention in natal homes plus safe support through marriage transitions.
pmc-13571370:
Jake Hillyer, John Jefferies, and Marc Silver report in 2026 on a forty-five year old man with Duchenne muscular dystrophy whose heart weakened over time. In this condition, missing dystrophin protein slowly scars both skeletal and heart muscle, and heart failure is a leading cause of death.

Doctors added finerenone, a drug that blocks a hormone receptor and reduces inflammation and scarring, to his standard heart medicines. Over sixteen months his heart's pumping fraction improved and the chamber reshaped in a healthier direction, with no harmful side effects reported. The authors present finerenone as a promising option for dystrophy-related heart disease, while noting that a single case cannot prove benefit and larger studies are needed.
pmc-13571570:
Ariel Aminov and colleagues describe, in a 2026 case report, a new muscle transfer operation for shoulders that fail after reverse shoulder replacement. The problem is a missing front deltoid and its bony anchor. Reverse prostheses lean heavily on the deltoid to lift the arm, so its loss can leave the joint working poorly despite a sound implant.

The team moved the chest muscle, the pectoralis major, on its own blood supply to substitute for the missing front deltoid. Alternatives such as nerve transfers recover slowly, and fusing the joint sacrifices motion. A tendon transfer aims to restore active lifting while keeping the joint mobile. The report presents the technique as one more option for a difficult salvage problem.
pmc-13572370:
Hosein Samadieh and Jahangir Khajehali report a 2026 lab study of how heavy metals change the way pesticides act on a bulb mite. The mite harms saffron corms in Iran, in the field and in storage. Fields can hold both metals from the soil and sprays used against pests, so the mix matters.

In bioassays, lead and nickel made two sprays, propargite and chlorpyrifos, kill more mites than the sprays did alone. Lead raised propargite kill power 2.67-fold. The same metals had the reverse effect on a third spray, abamectin, and made it weaker. Enzyme tests gave a clue why: lead raised one detox enzyme, while nickel lowered another. The authors warn that pest plans should weigh metals already in the soil.
pmc-13572470:
Parna Chaudhury, with three colleagues, presents a 2026 system for spotting fake audio, where a cloned voice says things a person never said. Such clips fuel fraud and false claims, and they are hard to catch by ear. The system reads a clip in three ways at once to catch traces that one view might miss.

One branch reads sound spectra over time, one reads cepstral features that track the voice's shape, and one reads plain statistics of the signal. Three network types handle the branches, and a final model stacks their calls into one verdict. On the Fake-or-Real data set, the stacked system beat each single model. The authors also host the tool online for live checks. They frame fused features as the key to fewer missed fakes.
pmc-13573470:
Pinar Duman Aydin, with five colleagues, reports a 2026 survey of oxygen therapy knowledge among hospital staff in Somalia. Oxygen saves lives in low-blood-oxygen states, yet wrong use can harm. The team tested what nurses and doctors at a Mogadishu teaching hospital know about giving oxygen to patients who breathe on their own.

A 23-item survey reached 195 staff over two weeks in early 2025, split among nurses, junior doctors, and senior doctors. Under half said they knew how to give oxygen, and scores on technical points were poor in all groups. Most nurses and nearly all doctors backed more training. Nurses had more pre-duty training than junior doctors, while senior doctors leaned on courses. Guideline use was thin across the board. The authors call for standard protocols and steady training.
pmc-13574870:
Marta Reales-Moreno's team reviewed fractal analysis as a way to characterise brain patterns in mental illness, in a 2026 systematic review. Mental-health diagnosis rests on symptoms and classifications, while brain scans hold complex organisation that standard tests may miss. Fractal dimension, a number capturing pattern complexity, promises a complementary lens. The team reviewed 39 original studies of brain-shape and brain-activity scans.

Schizophrenia and autism dominated the literature, and frontal-cortex abnormalities recurred across conditions. Whole-brain tests, however, may have diluted local effects by averaging too much tissue. The authors conclude fractal analysis reveals shared shape and activity patterns, but without a standard protocol its clinical use for earlier or sharper calls remains out of reach.
pmc-13576270:
Hanxing Huang and five colleagues study a tiny RNA that holds back lung adenocarcinoma, the most common lung cancer subtype, in a 2026 paper. The RNA, called miR-2116-5p, runs low in these tumours. The team asked whether its level predicts patient outcomes and how it acts inside cancer cells.

Tissue from 125 patients confirmed the low levels, which tied to lymph node spread and later disease stage. Patients with the lowest levels survived less well, and the RNA stood as an independent risk marker in survival models. Raising it in cells slowed growth, movement, and invasion, while lowering it did the reverse. Its direct target proved to be ADAM12, a protein whose rise cancelled the RNA's brake effect. The authors propose the RNA as both a prognosis marker and a treatment lead.
pmc-13578070:
Samuel Morriss leads a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of oral JAK inhibitor pills for alopecia areata, an autoimmune hair loss disease. These drugs block Janus kinase signals that drive the immune attack on hair follicles. Trials have reshaped care for moderate to severe disease, and the team pooled the randomised results against placebo.

Twelve trials with 4,141 participants, nearly all adults, were included. At week 24, patients on the pills had 5.69 times the odds of reaching a near-clear scalp score, and by week 36 that figure rose to 9.40 on the same measure. Wider success bands showed the same direction, with hair regrowth thresholds met far more often than on placebo. Six trials carried low bias risk, while six raised some concerns, mostly over missing data. Safety outcomes were gathered alongside the benefit measures.
pmc-13578370:
Rui Wang, Xianghong Tang, and Jianguang Lu tackle photo and text search when one side of the pair is missing, in a 2026 study. Systems that match a photo to a caption, or the reverse, falter when inputs arrive incomplete or noisy, a common snag in medical and shopping uses. Older deep models also miss long range links between meaning in the two forms.

Their method builds a shared meaning graph for photos and text, then trims it to the strongest links. The graph coaches the system on what a missing photo or caption should look like, keeping answers steady. A flexible scoring rule sharpens the sense of when a side is absent. Tests showed the search held up well even with missing sides, which the authors offer for real world archives.
pmc-13583570:
Hiroki Hoya and colleagues asked if a plain blood-gas ratio can track gain in acute heart failure treated with intravenous tolvaptan, a drug that sheds water. Fluid in the lungs drives most stays for this flare-up, yet plain tests of lung fluid are few. The team looked back at 120 patients from 2022 to 2023, with 48 on tolvaptan plus furosemide and 72 on furosemide alone.

At one day, the tolvaptan group had a higher gas ratio and passed more urine, while salt in blood rose a bit and kidney and pulse tests showed no clear short-term harm. Tolvaptan use on its own foretold better gas levels. The ratio looks like a fair test to track, but trials that look ahead must back it up.
pmc-13589570:
Siyu Jiang and ten colleagues unveil a deep-learning platform that names unknown plant chemicals from their spectral fingerprints. Plant chemistry is so diverse that most compounds in a sample match nothing in the reference libraries. Their 2026 platform, DeepMASS version 2, learned from millions of spectra held in public and in-house collections, turning each spectrum into a semantic code it can search at speed.

For an unknown, the system finds structurally close neighbors and ranks candidate structures by how near they sit in a unified chemical map. In benchmark tests it beat established tools, including for compounds missing from every library, the hardest case. Applied to large plant datasets, it widened the share of the chemistry that could be named. A public web server makes the tool available to any lab.
pmc-13591170:
Lauren J. Christie and colleagues asked stroke survivors and carers which arm tests they find worth doing. Thirty people, twenty-seven survivors and three carers with a mid age of 64, rated fifteen arm tests for know-how, worth, and likes. They also ranked when, how often, where, and how long tests should run in a mock trial.

Tests of limb harm by clinicians, such as joint range and strength, topped the list at 76.7 percent, then task-based arm tests and sensor-based move tests. Gene and brain-stim tests ranked last. People liked weekly, face-to-face tests of thirty to sixty minutes, a pattern trial chiefs should heed to keep trials fair and fun to join.
pmc-13591670:
Barbara Tornimbene and nine colleagues examine why shared data standards matter for health systems, above all in emergencies. When each clinic or country stores records its own way, swapping data slows and outbreak response suffers, a flaw the COVID-19 pandemic exposed with force. Their report surveys global standards that let systems talk, such as FHIR for health records and shared code sets for diseases, labs, and clinical terms.

Principles that make data findable and reusable, plus tools like the international patient summary, already show the gains, they argue. Groups such as WHO and HL7 keep pushing uptake. Privacy worries and scale remain hard, Tornimbene and the team concede, yet they hold that common standards are a must for sharper outbreak tracking.
pmc-13591870:
Seung Myung Wi and three colleagues test, in 2026, whether adding the biceps tendon helps repair large shoulder cuff tears. In partial repair, torn cuff tissue is pulled toward its anchor point on the arm bone, yet full coverage often fails. Their method stitches the nearby biceps tendon into the repair to close the gap. Records matched 45 such patients against 45 who had partial repair alone.

After at least two years, the biceps group showed far more repairs with full anchor coverage and more healed tendons on ultrasound. Their shoulder function scores also ran higher, and the gap above the arm bone stayed wider, a good sign. Wi and the team credit the added tissue for the better coverage.
pmc-13593370:
Ben-Mao Liu and five colleagues describe a modified way to fix sacral fractures with screws through the hip bone. Standard placement leans on angled imaging that can stretch surgery and radiation exposure. Their prone position, pedicle guided method treated 22 patients between 2019 and 2023. Follow up scans at six months graded screw position, while pain scores and a pelvic function scale tracked recovery.

Scans judged screw placement excellent in ninety seven percent of cases. Two screws grazed outer bone without touching nerve channels, and no nerve injuries occurred. Pain scores improved steadily, and most patients regained excellent function. One case leaked bone cement during a related procedure without harm. Liu and the team say plain two view imaging suffices with their approach.
pmc-13595370:
Teng Ieng Leong and a team of co-authors recorded brain activity continuously. Thirty-one volunteers listened to English sentences and then said them aloud. That combination normally ruins scanner data through noise and head movement. Their method separated each scan into independent components and matched their timing to the stages of hearing, planning, and speaking.

Activity centered on the superior temporal cortex, the inferior frontal region, and the face and mouth movement areas. Subtracting the listening-only pattern from the listen-then-speak pattern exposed a second wave of response in the hearing cortex tied to one's own voice, the self-monitoring signal. The team also pinned down how each component's blood-flow response rose and fell relative to the spoken words. They offer the framework for future studies of natural speech, where hearing and producing language interleave.
pmc-13595470:
Yiyin Ma, Dedian Chen, and Sheng Huang review efforts to safely give less treatment to patients with early HER2-positive breast cancer. The subtype's outlook has improved so much that overtreatment is now a real concern. Their 2026 article focuses on therapy given before surgery, where response can be watched directly.

Strategies under study include shortening the course of HER2-targeted drugs and trimming the chemotherapy backbone. The central problem is choosing who can safely receive less. Scans that measure tumor metabolism or volume may flag the right patients. So may blood tests for circulating tumor DNA and other biomarkers. Those patients' cancers melt away on targeted therapy alone. The authors frame de-escalation as a matching problem, pairing lighter regimens with the tumors most likely to answer them.
pmc-13597570:
G. Tyler Lefevor and colleagues tracked 315 sex-minority past and present members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints to test self-led bids to change sex lean. Old proof came mostly from look-back polls, so this set-out-ahead study watched people for two years. Near three in four had tried such bids at some point, and 13.7 percent were in one at the start.

Of those in a bid at the start, 62.8 percent had quit in two years. Two years on, no clear gaps showed in lean, disgust, or acts between those in a bid at the start and those not in one. Start-group folks told of more low mood and less friend help at both times. The authors back care that affirms each person and aids growth of self.
pmc-13599970:
Adama Baguiya and colleagues present a trial protocol testing a simpler supplement routine for pregnant women. Guidance recommends calcium in pregnancy to prevent pre-eclampsia where diets are low in it, yet three daily doses are hard to sustain. Guidance also says to take calcium apart from iron, since together they can block iron uptake. The trial asks whether a combined morning routine works just as well.

The study will enroll 1,600 women in early pregnancy in Burkina Faso and Pakistan, judging the answer separately in each country. Half will take a multiple micronutrient supplement and 500 milligrams of calcium together each morning. The other half will take the supplement in the morning and calcium in the evening. Blood tests will track haemoglobin and iron markers, with late-pregnancy haemoglobin as the main outcome. Enrolment began in Pakistan in August 2025 and in Burkina Faso the following month.
pmc-13605370:
Oliver Walzer leads a nine-author team testing what CBD does to the fat molecules inside nerve-like cells. Cannabidiol, the cannabis compound CBD, is discussed for Alzheimer's disease, but its effect on cell lipids was largely unmapped. Using targeted lipidomics on SH-SY5Y cells, a standard neuron-like line, the team catalogued how CBD reshaped each lipid class. They then checked the main response in cells carrying the Swedish amyloid precursor mutation linked to Alzheimer's.

CBD rearranged lipid classes broadly. Two phosphatidylcholine families rose overall, favoring simpler species while ether-linked forms fell. Lyso-PCs dropped broadly, sphingomyelin declined, and carnitine measures fell too. Wild-type cells ended with a less unsaturated lipid profile. The PC changes repeated in the mutation-carrying cells. Because these lipid classes are disturbed in Alzheimer's itself, the authors say CBD's fingerprint lands in relevant territory, justifying study in better disease models.
pmc-13608070:
Hong Yi and three colleagues combine research on two burdens language learners carry: mental load and anxiety. When a second-language task strains working memory, anxiety often rises, yet the two literatures rarely spoke. Their systematic review and meta-analysis found eleven eligible studies totaling 1,250 learners. Machine coders repeated the screening and extraction, and every value was verified against the original reports.

Higher load came with higher foreign-language anxiety, at a pooled correlation of 0.41, and every included estimate pointed the same way. Removing the most influential study barely moved the result, which sat at 0.37 afterward. Variation between studies was large, and the prediction interval nearly touched zero. Thirteen more reports measured both without linking them, a reporting gap the authors flag while urging teaching studies to track thinking and feeling together.
pmc-13612270:
Zhihao Gao leads a six-author team asking how long an exercise snack really needs to be. Twenty sedentary male college students cycled through one-, two-, and three-minute protocols at the same total workload, a week apart. The researchers tracked energy burn and the fat-glucose mix during the effort and for thirty minutes afterward.

All three bouts triggered measurable metabolic responses. The two-minute bout burned as much fat during exercise as the three-minute one, 0.71 grams against 0.78, and clearly more than the one-minute bout at 0.37 grams. Afterward, the one-minute group's energy use sank back to resting level by twenty-five minutes, while the other groups stayed elevated for the full half hour. Fat burning rose and glucose burning fell during recovery in every group. The authors argue two minutes hits a sweet spot: nearly all the payoff of three, in a break anyone can take.
pmc-13614270:
Ye Zhou and colleagues build a tool to predict which breast cancer patients are likely to become frail after surgery. Their data come from 286 patients treated at a hospital in China between October 2024 and March 2025. Frailty after such surgery raises the risk of slow recovery and complications, so spotting high-risk patients early matters. Each patient answered a general questionnaire, a frailty scale, and a sleep quality scale.

The team used statistical modelling to find which factors tracked with frailty, then turned them into a nomogram, a chart that converts a patient's traits into a personal risk score. Checks of the model's accuracy showed how well its calls matched real outcomes. Nurses and surgeons can use such a chart before problems arise, aiming extra support, sleep help, and exercise advice at the patients most likely to need it.
pmc-13618170:
Charlotte Hijmans and four colleagues boost production of montbretin A, a promising type 2 diabetes compound found only in traces inside montbretia corms, by adding transporter proteins to an engineered tobacco relative. The plant already makes the compound plus two inactive look-alikes after earlier engineering, yet yields stay low. The team suspected the products were stuck in the wrong cell compartment and tested membrane pumps that move cargo into the vacuole, the cell's storage sac.

Co-expressing montbretia ABCC transporters, which sit in the vacuole membrane, raised levels of all montbretins including the active form. The boost likely comes from vacuolar sequestration and depends on the molecule carrying its acyl group, the feature distinguishing the products. Eight of fifteen related transporters borrowed from plants that never make montbretins also helped. The authors suggest such transporters are versatile yield tools for plant bioengineering beyond this single drug candidate.
pmc-13618270:
Xie and colleagues built in 2026 a cathode for rechargeable lithium-chlorine batteries that traps chlorine gas and activates it in one porous structure, sharply extending battery life. These batteries promise very high energy from the chlorine reaction, but the gas escapes and converts slowly, so cells fade fast, especially under heavy use. The new design attacks the storage and the chemistry together.

A carbon matrix rich in tiny pores holds the chlorine, while single nickel atoms anchored on curved pore walls speed its conversion to lithium chloride on discharge and back on charge. The design cut voltage waste sharply at high load. Cells passed a capacity milestone doubling the lifespan of the best earlier systems. They also worked from deep cold to hot conditions, which the authors present as a path to practical high-energy storage.
pmc-13618570:
Faiza Imtiaz and five colleagues optimize green extraction of health compounds from the seeds of Embelia ribes, a medicinal plant rich in the bioactive embelin. They compared three techniques, plain ultrasound extraction, microwave extraction, and a hybrid that pre-treats with microwaves before ultrasound. Each was tuned with statistical response surface methods against phenolic content, flavonoid content, and two antioxidant assays.

The hybrid method won every measure, yielding the richest phenolic and flavonoid extracts and the strongest radical-scavenging activity, plus the highest embelin content at about forty milligrams per gram of seed. The team then docked thirteen of the plant's compounds, in the computer, against the hepatitis C virus protease. Four compounds, led by amentoflavone and embelin, bound more strongly in the model than the standard drug boceprevir. The authors present the hybrid extraction as an efficient green route and the docking hits as antiviral leads needing laboratory confirmation.
pmc-13618770:
Liu Shi and eight colleagues defeat a classic biosensing barrier, Debye screening, which smothers electrical signals in salty body fluids, by giving nanochannels a soft hydrogel gate. Their design coats the outside of nanochannels unevenly with a peptide-DNA hybrid gel, creating a three-dimensional charged zone that enriches target-related ions by a Donnan equilibrium effect. When the target arrives, it dismantles the gel network.

Dismantling removes both the ion enrichment and the surface's water-loving character at once, a dual change that swings the ionic current through the channel sharply. Aiming at granzyme B, an immune effector molecule, the sensor reached a detection limit under one femtomolar, extraordinarily sensitive. In the clinic it tracked granzyme B over time in blood serum from lung cancer patients on immunotherapy, directly in unpurified samples, with high diagnostic accuracy. The authors present volumetric soft gating as a general route past screening limits.
pmc-13619070:
Zhipeng Liu and five colleagues propose a way to lay out low-altitude traffic corridors for drones over cities. Borrowing ideas from computational fluid dynamics, they build a synthetic flow field shaped by buildings and restricted zones in place of real wind. Streamline tracing then turns that field into smooth candidate routes that avoid obstacles.

A case covering five square kilometers in Shenzhen produced ten main corridors with a combined unique length of about forty kilometers. Compared with two baseline methods, their network covered more area within five hundred meters while staying shorter and straighter. Route tests showed far lower total curvature at the cost of longer paths, which the authors offer as a planning tool for city airspace managers.
pmc-13619170:
Alexandra C. Brown and six colleagues published this 2026 chemistry study asking why the molybdenum version of nitrogenase, the enzyme that converts nitrogen gas into ammonia, outperforms its vanadium and iron-only cousins. They compared iron-sulfur clusters, with and without a molybdenum atom, using spectroscopic methods. The model clusters carried carbene ligands that mimic how nitrogen binds iron, letting the team measure how strongly iron shares electrons into those bonds.

Iron centres in the molybdenum-bearing cluster proved better at this backbonding than iron in the all-iron cluster. The authors credit stronger mixing between metal and sulfur atoms and electron sharing between molybdenum and iron. Molybdenum's wide 4d orbitals shuttle electron density from the sulfides to the irons, and onward to bound molecules. Stronger backbonding to partners such as nitrogen gas fits the enzyme's efficiency. The study offers an explanation for a long-standing puzzle in nitrogen fixation.
pmc-13619770:
Mathew J Owens and Luke A Barnard introduce SURF, a software framework for reconstructing and forecasting the solar wind, the stream of particles flowing out from the Sun. Full three-dimensional simulations are accurate but slow, which blocks the large ensembles forecasters want. SURF pairs an existing reduced model with a new one-dimensional solver that treats compression more faithfully while staying fast.

The new solver reproduced an exact test solution for expanding solar wind. Using thirty years of near-Earth observations, the team derived links between wind speed, density, and temperature, then mapped them inward to set more realistic starting conditions. Tests also showed the solver captures how coronal mass ejections, huge eruptions from the Sun, expand on their way out. Changing an ejection's starting density and temperature shifted arrival times at Earth by a noticeable margin, flagging a neglected source of forecast error.
pmc-13620270:
Feng Ling led a large team that built a high-throughput platform for measuring how mucus flows and stretches, a property called rheology. Mucus guards airways and other surfaces, yet standard tests need large samples, special machines, and heavy manual work. Their workflow watches tiny tracer motion in videos from an ordinary fluorescence microscope and works from samples of only a few microliters, even on intact tissue surfaces.

Checks against established shear testing and particle tracking in rebuilt mucin gels confirmed the platform recovers the same trends. Applied to human airway cultures, it separated samples by donor, age, disease state, smoke exposure, and drug treatment, and it mapped patchiness across a single surface. Cervical mucus from patients worked too, despite scarce amounts. The authors offer the system for disease modeling, drug testing, and future tailored medicine.
pmc-13623770:
Tilman Wickert, Kathleen Haack, Felicitas Soehner and Ekkehardt Kumbier published this 2026 historical case study, in German, on medicine inside the Stasi prison hospital at Berlin-Hohenschönhausen. It examines whether East Germany's secret police used medication as an interrogation tool. Former prisoners allege that psychotropic drugs were deliberately given before interrogations, but documentary proof has been lacking. The authors reconstruct the case of one remand prisoner, pseudonymised as 'Clausmann', from his files. They set it against the hospital's role.

The files provide the first indications that psychotropic substances may have been administered deliberately before interrogations. Their use was not disclosed to the courts. The case shows how medical expertise and routines were interwoven with secret police practice rather than standing apart from it. The authors argue that the Stasi's medical service and prison hospital remain under-researched. They frame questions on remand practice for future work.
pmc-13624370:
Joseph Donia and Luca Marelli compare how Canada and the European Union promote secondary use of health data, meaning research, policy, and commercial uses beyond the care that generated them. Canada is linking data across its devolved provinces while respecting Indigenous data sovereignty. The European Union has built the European Health Data Space, a regulatory regime spanning twenty-seven member states.

Drawing on policy documents and interviews across nine European countries and five Canadian jurisdictions, the authors find the same promises on both sides of the Atlantic. Data should be made bigger, linked, and comparable so it serves many ends. The same frictions appear, between sovereignty and integration, between open access and tight control, and treating records as private assets or public goods. The authors argue these shared-data projects reshape health systems, deciding who gains value and who holds power, and urge attention to equity in that shift.
pmc-13625370:
Elizabeth Jarman and seven colleagues, publishing in 2026, review how shelter shapes health when disaster or war drives people from home. Searching three databases for studies from 2005 to 2025, they gathered 138 papers on shelter and settlement work in humanitarian crises. The review sorts findings into themes, from living conditions and housing type to camp planning, household goods, and cash help, with gender, climate, and vulnerability running through all of them.

Damaged or badly built shelters tracked with more malaria, diarrhea, and worm infections, while crowding raised injury risk and mental distress. Short-term shelters strained mental health, medium-term ones raised chronic disease risk, and long-term housing let chronic care slip. Where people sleep, the review shows, is a health intervention in itself.
pmc-13627170:
Majid Alfadhel and twenty colleagues, publishing in 2026, gather the Middle East and North Africa experience with metreleptin for a rare fat disorder. Congenital generalized lipodystrophy leaves children with almost no body fat and no leptin, the fullness hormone, so blood sugar and fats spiral. Charts from many centers covered thirty-eight patients, most of them girls, with a median age near six years at the start and a median treatment span of about two years.

Within months, blood sugar control, fasting glucose, triglycerides, and liver enzymes all improved clearly, and most gains held past two years. Half the patients cut their long-term sugar marker by at least a point early on. Safety held up through ninety days past the last dose, which supports wider regional use of a drug many registries had skipped.
pmc-13627270:
Kazuhiro Hiyama and colleagues build a guided missile for gene-silencing therapy in pancreatic cancer, among the deadliest of tumors. Their payload is a small interfering RNA aimed at SNORA22, a tiny RNA that drives the cancer's spread, armored with chemical tweaks that resist blood enzymes. The carrier is a folic acid-tagged peptide that homes to tumor cells. One shape of the tag packed the cargo far better than its mirror form. It entered cells and silenced the target more deeply.

In mice grown from human pancreatic tumor organoids, the complex piled into tumors within a day. It shrank growth more than the standard two-drug chemotherapy. Wide necrosis and little invasion marked the edges. No organ toxicity showed. A delivery problem that has stalled RNA drugs may have a workable answer.
pmc-13627870:
Antonio Preti, Carmelo Masala, and Donatella Rita Petretto validate an Italian short scale for paranoid thinking. The eight-item Green Paranoid Thoughts Scale splits suspicion into feeling referenced by others and feeling persecuted, and brief scales need proof in each new language. Two hundred forty-three university students completed the Italian version alongside a brief prodrome questionnaire, and the team tested which statistical shape fit the answers best.

A bifactor shape won: one strong general paranoia factor, with the two themes adding smaller twists of their own. Total scores held together well, the subscales acceptably, and students flagged by the prodrome screen scored higher across the board, as they should if the scale measures what it claims. The authors call the results promising but preliminary, since students are not the clinic.
pmc-13627970:
Binod Kunwar and three colleagues mapped where wild boar are likely to spread on Jeju Island, South Korea, where the animal is an invasive problem for farms and native wildlife. They combined a habitat model with a connectivity analysis to find both the best boar habitat and the routes animals use to move between patches.

The model used ninety-four sighting points and ten environmental measures, and it performed strongly on standard accuracy tests. Distance to farmland, built-up areas, elevation, and water predicted boar presence best. About a third of the island rated suitable or highly suitable, and six core habitats were linked by eight corridors, giving managers clear targets for monitoring and control.
pmc-13630970:
Weifang Zhang and eight colleagues report a large case series on scope-based removal of enlarged male breast tissue. Their study appeared in 2026. It centres on an anatomy-first technique. The method aims to protect the blood vessels and nerves around the nipple. Older open operations remove the gland at the price of trauma and numbness.

Across 786 patients at one Chinese hospital, operations averaged about two hours. Discharge came near three days. None converted to open surgery. Bleeding collections were rare. The notable risk was reduced blood flow to the nipple area, in about seven percent. Nearly all recovered. Two cases progressed to tissue loss. Sensation scores stayed high. The authors present the refined approach as both safer and better looking.
pmc-13631770:
Fariya Rahman and colleagues in Bangladesh tested a teaching program called HopeBox for orphaned teenage girls. Those living in orphanages often lack sound knowledge about sexual and reproductive health, which raises their risk of harm. The study ran in three government orphanages in Dhaka, Faridpur, and Chuadanga. It enrolled one hundred seventy-three girls and measured their knowledge before and after the program.

Knowledge rose on all five topics the team checked. More girls understood menstruation, how pregnancy can be avoided, and what contraceptive methods exist. More also knew how to use contraception correctly and how sexually transmitted diseases can be prevented. The gains stayed strong after the team adjusted for other factors that might explain them. The authors say the program should be widened so more orphaned and at-risk teenagers in Bangladesh get accurate health knowledge.
pmc-13632270:
Jonas Rotter and seven colleagues mapped where a thyroid hormone transporter sits in the adult human brain. The transporter, called MCT8, carries thyroid hormones into brain cells. Faults in its gene cause a severe developmental disorder, yet its layout in grown brains was largely unknown. The team examined eight brain regions from fourteen older body donors, counting millions of cells with automated image analysis and several other methods.

They found strong MCT8 presence at brain barriers, in support cells called glia, and in certain nerve cell groups. Fine microscopy placed it on cell surfaces, near nuclei, and along the fibers that connect nerve cells. Gene readings matched the protein staining closely. Levels stayed steady across stages of Alzheimer's-type change in the donors. The map suggests that hormone problems in Alzheimer's disease reflect altered hormone handling rather than loss of this transporter.
pmc-13633370:
Floortje Mols and six colleagues studied why a digital symptom tool for cancer patients went largely unused. The tool, OpenSYMPRO, lets patients on drug therapy report symptoms from home so care teams can react sooner. The plan was to compare younger patients using the open tool with older patients on a hospital version. Recruitment fell so short that the comparison was dropped. The team instead described engagement among the twenty who enrolled and gathered their feedback.

Only seven participants completed more than two symptom questionnaires, and four completed none. Feedback pointed to everyday barriers: clashing studies, forgetting the tool, little time or mental energy, and doubt that it added value. Nobody flagged serious technical trouble. The authors argue uptake failed on organization and communication rather than technology. They suggest wiring the tool into clinic routines, explaining its purpose personally, and involving clinicians actively in future rollouts.
pmc-13635170:
Privacy-preserving language models that pull prognostic details from cancer records are evaluated by Zou and colleagues. Head and neck cancer notes hold staging, virus status, and comorbidity information in free text, which makes manual extraction slow and costly, while privacy rules block sending records to outside services. The team tested locally run models on more than thirteen hundred reports from 882 patients, extracting thirty prognostic variables. Three radiation oncologists checked a fifty-case subset as the reference standard.

The best local model reached very high accuracy on that reference and processed each report in under a minute. Adding model-extracted virus status, smoking history, and comorbidity scores to a survival model improved predictions of disease-free survival and local failure. Zou and colleagues present on-site models as a practical route to faster tumour-board preparation and cleaner research registries without moving patient data off site.
pmc-13635470:
Ahmet Altınok tested whether a single dose of caffeine sharpens mental braking power in young adults. Caffeine is taken worldwide for supposed thinking benefits, yet careful trials keep failing to find gains in inhibitory control, the ability to stop a response. Survey work hints that people with more ADHD-like traits might gain the most. In this preregistered crossover trial, thirty-six adults without a diagnosis took caffeine or placebo on separate visits, then performed two inhibition tasks.

Both tasks behaved exactly as designed, so the measures were not at fault. Caffeine changed nothing: not withheld-response errors, not reaction speed, not conflict resolution. Statistical evidence actively favored the null over mere uncertainty. ADHD symptom scores predicted task performance yet never interacted with caffeine. The author concludes one dose brings no acute inhibition benefit in this group, leaving open questions about steady use and diagnosed patients.
pmc-13635870:
Antonin Jamotte and four colleagues measured how a long padel match tires the front thigh muscles. Padel is booming worldwide, yet its fatigue profile was unmapped. Sixteen trained players contested a match lasting over two hours. The team tested knee extensor strength before play and at three points during it, using both voluntary efforts and electrically triggered contractions. They also tracked jumps, heart rate, and match activity throughout.

Maximum voluntary strength fell by about a tenth by the end. Triggered twitches weakened from the first checkpoint onward, which localizes the fatigue in the muscle itself rather than in the brain's drive. Voluntary activation stayed intact, and explosive force plus jump height held steady. Heart rates showed players quietly pacing themselves into lower intensity as the match wore on, while their shot patterns stayed stable. The picture is early peripheral fatigue that skilled players route around without losing their snap.
pmc-13639070:
Yifan Yu and nine colleagues present a 2026 deep learning model that predicts recurrence risk in early-stage breast cancer from scans plus clinical notes. Judging who needs added therapy after surgery remains difficult, and relapse still drives most deaths from this cancer.

Their multimodal model combined two kinds of MRI with text records for 1,120 patients across several hospitals. It forecast disease-free survival with solid accuracy in both training and outside groups. Patients with low model scores gained clear benefit from adjuvant therapy, while those with high scores did not. The tool could help doctors match treatment intensity to personal risk.
pmc-13641970:
Ygor Alexandre Beserra de Sousa led a 2026 study that estimates age from panoramic dental X-rays using a convolutional neural network that reads jawbone texture directly. Age estimation matters in law, migration, adoption, and identification when birth records are missing or disputed, yet most AI methods depend on hand-picked anatomical features. The team trained a U-Net segmentation model on 600 annotated images, then applied an age-estimation network to 7,832 panoramic radiographs from patients aged two to ninety-seven.

The model missed true age by 6.91 years on average, with a root mean square error of 9.41 years and an explained-variance score of 0.799. Most predictions clustered near the true-age line, though scatter widened in older age groups. Forensic practitioners get a promising automated tool for jaw-based age estimation, with the authors' own cautions attached: data came from limited sources, and no external validation has yet been done.
pmc-13643470:
Heather M. Joseph and five colleagues present a 2026 study linking how infants look at new sights with family risk for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder. No objective infancy task had yet flagged children likelier to develop ADHD, which delays preventive help.

The sample held 147 infants aged eight to ten months, sixty-eight of whom had a parent with ADHD. On a task mixing sound and sight, at-risk infants looked longer at first and fell into a slow-to-habituate pattern about four and a half times more often. The authors offer the task as a first objective early marker of familial ADHD likelihood.
pmc-13646070:
Prakhar Mishra and four colleagues build a system to detect Alzheimer's disease from brain scans while keeping patient data private. Their method mixes a small quantum computing front end with a classical neural network. Scan images are broken into tiny patches, and quantum circuits extract features before classification. Training is spread across separate sites with a method called federated learning, so raw scans never leave each site.

The combined approach reached accuracy just above ninety-two percent in its best federated setup. A privacy layer that adds controlled noise still kept accuracy near ninety-one percent. With two hundred simulated clients, one averaging method held up far better than the other. The authors present the frozen quantum front end as a way to gain quantum feature power without heavy communication costs. The work points toward hospital networks training shared models without pooling private scans.
pmc-13646170:
Peijun Zhao and ten colleagues run one preparation of healing vesicles from umbilical cord stem cells through a wide battery of skin tests, in dishes and zebrafish. These vesicles are studied for wound repair, sun damage, and aging skin, yet usually one effect at a time. The battery covered burn-like and chemical injury, cell movement, skin barrier proteins, sun-aged cells, oily gland cells, pigment cells, and hair root cells.

The vesicles eased injury and lowered oxidative stress in skin cells, sped cell movement, and raised barrier proteins. Zebrafish regrew clipped tail fins faster with treatment. Sun-aged skin cells showed less aging and a healthier support matrix, while oily cells made less fat and less of a hormone tied to acne and hair loss. Pigment darkening also eased in cells and fish. The authors present the sweep as one map of this preparation's reach across skin biology.
pmc-13647570:
Fengyuan Li and four colleagues focus on a molecular alarm hub called the NLRP3 inflammasome and its role in the inflammation-driven form of osteoarthritis. Joint disease is usually treated as wear and tear with pain relief on top, yet a stubborn local inflammation drives one distinct subtype. The hub gathers danger signals, from crystals to leaking cell fuel, and answers by maturing inflammatory messengers and triggering a fiery cell death. The review asks whether this hub can define and treat the inflammatory subtype.

Cell-by-cell responses inside the joint may keep inflammation amplifying until tissue damage deepens. No agreed criteria yet mark out inflammation-driven disease, which the authors treat as the first problem to solve. They propose the hub's activity as a measurable dimension for sorting patients. That shift, from symptom-first to mechanism-first care, frames their closing agenda for biomarkers and targeted drugs.
pmc-13648070:
Iara Schlag Durães Campos and seven colleagues joined nickel glycerolate with crystal sponge frames to make electrodes with two jobs. One blend was built to store charge. A second blend, with cobalt and iron in the frame, was built to split water and free oxygen.

The storage blend held a high charge for its weight and kept most of it after five thousand cycles. The team also built a small two-sided storage device from it. The water blend drove the oxygen step at a fair voltage and ran steady for ten hours. The authors say the pairing shows how one base idea can serve both storage and clean fuel work.
pmc-13649070:
Carlos Eduardo Rochitte and two colleagues write, in Portuguese, an editorial celebrating the 2026 annual meeting of the Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance in Rio de Janeiro. For the first time the society held its main congress outside North America and Europe, under a theme of worldwide commitment to cardiovascular care.

More than sixteen hundred participants from seventy-three countries attended, with Latin America achieving its largest representation ever and Brazil second only to the United States in numbers. The authors argue the meeting's real legacy is regional capacity: education, certification, and multidisciplinary collaboration bringing advanced cardiac imaging to a region with heavy disease burden and unequal access. They frame it as a milestone for Brazil and Latin America.
pmc-13649470:
Peng Wang and Kangrong Luo surveyed more than two thousand students on how blended learning in gym classes links to civic life. The classes mixed online and in-person work and wove in values teaching. Their sample spanned 15 universities in Sichuan Province, China, and the survey scored teaching presence, peer presence, and depth of thought.

Good blended learning scores tied to stronger student engagement. Both also tied to more civic acts and stronger civic plans. Part of the path from course feel to civic outcomes ran through engagement. Checks with other methods kept the same picture. Since all data came from one survey at one time, the authors cannot claim cause, only links.
pmc-13651670:
Chihwa Song and five colleagues scan the brains of service members whose jobs expose them repeatedly to low-level blast, looking for metabolic fingerprints of that exposure. Training blasts are individually mild, and whether the accumulation injures the brain has stayed unresolved, with no study using glucose-based brain imaging for the question.

All participants were men with chronic mild traumatic brain injury, split by occupation into high-risk and low-risk blast groups of about two hundred and about seventy. Sugar-uptake imaging showed the high-exposure group burning more glucose in deep movement structures and part of the frontal lobe, possibly compensation, while white matter tracts in the right hemisphere took up less. Diffusion imaging of those same tracts showed altered microstructure. The deep structure also leaned more asymmetric in the high group. The authors present the pattern as evidence that blast exposure leaves metabolic and structural traces.
pmc-13651770:
Yi Yang and six co-authors review a proposed cell-free therapy for postpartum hair loss. That is the heavy shedding many women face a few months after delivery, when pregnancy hormones crash and follicles retire in unison. Their candidate is extracellular vesicles from cord blood, tiny membrane parcels loaded with regulatory RNAs, growth factors, and proteins.

The review gathers the proposed mechanisms: coaxing follicles back into the growth phase, resetting the hair cycle, damping the local inflammation that follows childbirth, and blunting oxidative stress around the follicle. Cord blood vesicles bring low immune reactivity and a strong repair record from regenerative medicine. The authors are plain about the limits: everything so far is lab and animal work, with no direct clinical trials in postpartum hair loss. They class the approach as a promising investigational plan whose standardization, safety, and real efficacy remain to be proven.
pmc-13652070:
Yushi Fu and three colleagues review how filamentous fungi change shape as they grow, and why that matters for industry. These fungi produce enzymes, acids, and medicines in large fermentation tanks, where their form affects how broth flows, how oxygen spreads, and how much product gets secreted. The review pulls together recent work on the signals and genes that steer each stage of fungal development.

Coverage runs from spore germination and the setting of growth direction through hyphal branching and the upkeep of the cell wall and membrane. Internal pathways and outside cues from the environment both feed into these decisions. By linking each shape to performance in submerged and solid culture. The authors give process engineers a map for breeding or tuning strains whose growth form fits the product they need to make.
pmc-2815670:
Adams, Afonine, Bunkoczi, and co-authors present PHENIX, a Python-based system for solving macromolecular structures. X-ray crystallography reveals biological processes at the molecular level and is used routinely worldwide. Solving and finishing many structures still took much time, though, because complex numeric output needed manual reading.

PHENIX automates and joins those steps, from first phases to a completed, refined model. Building the system in Python made it flexible and easier to extend with new methods. It became one of the main pipelines through which new protein and nucleic acid structures reach the public archive.
pmc-5407170:
Bernal, Cummins, and Gasparrini wrote a tutorial in 2016 on interrupted time series regression. This design evaluates public health interventions that start at a clearly defined point in time, such as a new law or program. It is increasingly used to judge the effectiveness of population-level interventions.

The method compares the trend in an outcome before and after the intervention point. A change in level or slope at that point is evidence the intervention worked. Unlike a simple before-after snapshot, it accounts for trends already under way. The tutorial teaches researchers how to run and report such analyses soundly, so policy evaluations rest on firmer ground.
pmc-6434870:
Christopher Baethge, Sandra Goldbeck-Wood, and Stephan Mertens built the SANRA scale for narrative reviews in 2019. Narrative reviews are the most common article type in medical journals. Yet no formal tool existed to judge their quality.

SANRA scores a review on six items, from clear aims to balanced, evidence-based argument. Editors and readers can apply it quickly without specialist training. Early tests showed raters broadly agree when using the scale. It gives journals a shared yardstick for a genre that shapes much clinical opinion but long escaped formal appraisal. The authors tested the scale with editors and readers and report how consistently they scored the same reviews.
pmc-6975070:
Xiaohong Li, Sheng He, and Bin Ma reviewed autophagy and its proteins in cancer in 2020. Autophagy is the cell's recycling system, digesting worn parts for reuse. Its core protein machinery also shapes cell survival and death.

In cancer the system plays a double role, blocking early tumors yet feeding established ones. Tumors under stress lean on recycling to survive treatment. The review maps the key proteins and the stages they run. It weighs drugs that boost or block autophagy, and why picking the right direction per tumor remains the hard part.
pmc-7027970:
Robert Ross, Ian Neeland, Shizuya Yamashita, and coauthors issued this consensus statement on waist circumference in 2020. Waist size predicts illness and death risk beyond what body mass index shows. Yet clinicians rarely measure it in routine practice.

The statement, backed by international atherosclerosis and obesity groups, urges waist measurement as a vital sign. It gives cut points by sex and ancestry and explains how the tape should be placed. Belly fat tracks the risky fat around organs better than weight alone. The authors argue this cheap measure deserves a place in every check-up.
pmc-7158570:
Robert Verity, Lucy Okell, Ilaria Dorigatti, and coauthors estimated COVID-19 severity in this 2020 model-based analysis. Early fatality figures differed wildly between reports. Much of the gap came from missed mild cases and deaths not yet counted.

The team gathered data from China and from repatriation flights, where testing was near complete. Adjusting for those biases, they estimate roughly one in fifteen hundred infections ends in death overall, rising steeply with age. Hospital demand forecasts leaned on these numbers. The work set a careful standard for severity claims during fast-moving outbreaks.
pmc-7494270:
Moderbacher and colleagues examined in 2020 all three arms of the adaptive immune response to SARS-CoV-2 in patients with acute COVID-19. Adaptive immunity is the targeted part of the system, built from helper T cells, killer T cells, and antibodies. The team measured virus specific responses in each arm within the same patients, something few early studies managed.

They then asked how the strength and balance of those responses lined up with a patient's age and with how severe the illness became. Coordinated responses across all three arms tended to mark the milder cases. The work helped explain why simply having antibodies is not the whole story of protection, and it informed how vaccine responses would later be judged.
pmc-7875770:
Daniel Taliun and a large team of collaborators reported in 2021 the sequencing of more than fifty thousand genomes from a diverse set of participants. The work belongs to the TOPMed program, which studies the genetic roots of heart, lung, blood, and sleep disorders. Its long term aim is better diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of those common diseases.

The article describes the program's first phases and the genome data they produced, drawn from populations often left out of earlier genetic studies. It explains how the data are shared with researchers under careful controls. Because the participants are diverse, the resource helps correct a long standing skew in genetics toward people of European ancestry.
podcast-dannyjones-wiQIDCQVg70:
Chris Cottrell joins Danny Jones to talk about a recent asteroid strike that he says no one is talking about. The episode title calls it an impact the public missed. Cottrell brings the claim and the trail he says backs it.

Cottrell lays out where the rock hit, what marks it left, and why the news passed it by. He argues the silence shows how blind we are to rocks from space. Jones asks what proof would force the story wide open. Listeners get a space risk tale told as a cover-up. The library holds the talk as an archive record of the claim.
proctor-other-worlds-1870:
Richard A. Proctor was a famed English voice on the stars. His Other Worlds than Ours came out in 1870. The full title says the claim of many worlds is weighed by new facts. Proctor gives each planet a calm, cool test.

He looks at heat, air, water, and the spin of each world. Mars and Venus get long, close looks as homes for life. Proctor grants some worlds a good chance and rates the rest low. The book was the plain man's guide to the claim for a whole age.
